20206-the-agony-of-the-church-1917:
The Agony of the Church, from 1917, weighs the state of the church in wartime. Its writer grants that churches have kept Christ as the world's treasury. Even rote prayer, he argues, lifts them above the secular world. They at least know who the Lord is, while the world does not.

That defense sits beside sharp grief over the church's weakness and pain. War in 1917 forced hard questions on faith, peace, and national pride. The book speaks to believers who felt their church failing its hour. Readers get a tense, searching tract from a year of crisis.
20752-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Volume two of The Journal of Negro History, from 1917, lists a rich table of work. Articles treat Haiti and Liberia, three Negro poets, and Catholics and the Negro. Documents print letters of George Washington that bear on Black life.

Carter G. Woodson founded this journal to prove Black history had real depth. Scholars here use records, wills, and petitions, not mere opinion. Book reviews and notes close the volume, with news of the field's first big meeting. Readers see a new field of study being built in public, one solid document at a time.
22103-with-a-highland-regiment-in-mesopo:
With a Highland Regiment in Mesopotamia 1916–1917 records a Scottish battalion's part in a hard campaign. One of its officers wrote the book, and a senior commander supplied warm praise. The regiment served in the land now called Iraq. British and Indian forces there fought the Ottoman Turks for rivers, oil, and the road to Baghdad.

Heat, disease, and flood plagued the troops as much as enemy fire. The writer follows the battalion's marches, trenches, and attacks month by month. His foreword insists that all ranks did well and suffered much. Such plain unit histories kept the memory of forgotten fronts alive when public attention stayed on France.
adler-neurotic-constitution-1917:
Alfred Adler published The Neurotic Constitution in German in 1912. The English text here is the 1917 translation by Bernard Glueck and John E. Lind. Adler, a former colleague of Freud, founds here his individual psychology. The feeling of inferiority, he argues, drives people to strive and compensate.

Neurotics, in his account, set fictional goals of superiority they cannot reach. Their symptoms serve those goals as excuses and safeguards. Adler stresses social feeling and conscious purpose over Freud's drives. Organ inferiority and childhood experience shape the striving style. The book is the founding text of Adlerian therapy. Its ideas on inferiority entered common speech.
arxiv-2510-00017:
En-naoui introduces a new unified notation for exponential congruences. A generalized k-th power symbol that records whether a raised to the k equals plus or minus one modulo n. Extending the spirit of the classical Legendre and Jacobi symbols. The paper systematically develops the symbol's full algebraic properties, organized by which of its three parameters, the base, the modulus, or the exponent, is being varied in this work.

For the base he proves multiplicativity, inversion symmetry, and power compatibility, for the modulus factorization rules, orthogonality relations. And Kummer splitting criteria, and for the exponent reciprocity laws and specialization back to classical symbols. New results add character-based additive behavior, Möbius filtering, exact counting formulas for prime moduli, and further connections with Dirichlet L-series. With the all-prime case generalizing classical reciprocity, Frobenius automorphisms, and Sato-Tate distributions in the theory.
arxiv-2510-00217:
Sung Hee Park and four colleagues published this 2025 statistics paper on sex differences in jaw joint mechanics. The temporomandibular joint links skull shape to the muscles used in chewing. Disorders of this joint strike women far more often than men. The team studied how skull form and muscle attachment sites relate, and how that relation differs by sex.

Their data came from ten male and eleven female cadaver heads measured in the lab. They propose a conditional cross-covariance reduction model for this two-block, two-sex problem. A sparse decomposition algorithm picks out the most telling skull and muscle variables. A sequential permutation scheme decides how many variables to keep. The method spotlights the strongest sex-specific links between bone and muscle. Such maps could guide better diagnosis and device design for jaw disorders.
arxiv-2510-00717:
Li, Shakouri, and Camlibel analyse how fragile data-driven feedback gains can be, in this 2025 arXiv paper on control theory. Data-driven control designs a stabilizing feedback law straight from input-state measurements, skipping system identification. Rounding, finite word length, and hardware faults then perturb that gain in practice. The collected data say nothing about such feedback perturbations, so a nominally stabilizing gain might collapse under tiny changes.

The authors parametrize all quadratically stabilizing gains obtainable from noisy data. They fully characterize extreme fragility, where arbitrarily small perturbations can destabilize the true system. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for complete immunity to perturbations. Between those poles, a data-computable measure quantifies fragility for any candidate gain. The least fragile gain can then be designed by solving a semidefinite program built from the same data. Results come in closed form or as linear matrix inequalities.
arxiv-2510-00817:
Leisegang, Casini, and Meyer compare two frameworks for reasoning with inconsistent knowledge in this 2025 arXiv paper on logic and artificial intelligence. Weighted knowledge bases assign costs to interpretations based on how many rules they break. The older c-representations instead rank interpretations by penalties for violated rules of thumb, such as birds usually fly. Both aim to answer queries sensibly when facts conflict.

The authors show that, under stated conditions, the two frameworks can produce the very same ordering over interpretations. They also translate entailment notions between the systems, so results proved on one side can inform the other. The paper frames itself as an initial bridge between the query-answering and defeasible reasoning communities. That bridge could let both fields inherit methods and broaden where each approach applies.
arxiv-2510-01017:
Bao, dos Reis, and Wilde establish Malliavin differentiability for McKean-Vlasov equations with common noise in this 2025 arXiv paper on stochastic analysis. McKean-Vlasov equations describe a particle whose dynamics depend on the distribution of the population, a mean-field effect. Common noise adds a shared environment that every particle experiences together, making the law conditional on that environment. Whether solutions respond differentiably to perturbations of the noise, in the Malliavin sense, was open for this class.

Under Lipschitz assumptions in the state and the measure argument, the authors prove that solutions are Malliavin differentiable. Their result also gives meaning to the Malliavin derivative of the conditional law with respect to the common noise. As an application they derive an integration by parts formula on Wiener space for these equations. Such formulas underpin sensitivity analysis and density estimates for mean-field systems in finance and physics.
arxiv-2510-01117:
Sur, Guo, and Mondaini propose a way to freeze highly entangled quantum states in place in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum physics. Entanglement normally keeps evolving after a state is prepared, so storing it without decay is a core challenge for quantum memory. Many-body localization can hold local information, yet global properties of the state still drift away. The authors instead quench the system to an emergent Hamiltonian that has the target state as an eigenstate.

In general that Hamiltonian is non-local and lacks a closed form, but they find cases where it is exact and fully local. Those examples allow, in principle, storage limited only by experimental imperfections. The protocol keeps both local and global properties of the stored state. Demonstrations cover products of Bell pairs and fragile GHZ states that real devices struggle to prepare.
arxiv-2510-01217:
Paterson and co-authors twist the walls of a microwave cavity and watch its light turn helical. Ordinary resonators keep electric and magnetic patterns separate, so no handedness emerges. A controlled geometric twist breaks mirror symmetry and couples the two field families.

The coupling produces measurable helicity inside a single resonant mode in empty space. Twisting further shifts the resonant frequencies, so one knob steers both properties in real time. Internal helical grooves add a surface-level chirality that skews tuning asymmetrically. Macroscopic control of light's handedness could serve sensors and quantum devices alike. Nearly degenerate modes mix most strongly, which the design exploits. Frequency shifts track the twist angle, giving a clean readout. Chiral light interacts unevenly with chiral matter, a sensing goldmine. Vacuum operation keeps the effect purely geometric. One device tunes pitch and handedness together at once.
arxiv-2510-01617:
Leong and co-authors let a multi-agent system redesign its own communication wiring for each incoming task. Fixed team charts, hand-drawn by engineers, fit some jobs badly and waste effort on others. Their framework, AMAS, includes a graph designer that picks a task-specific structure before work begins.

The designer learns through light adaptation of the language model itself, guided by a custom loss. Queries then travel along pathways shaped for their own demands. Benchmarks in question answering, mathematics, and code generation confirmed the advantage over static charts. Structure becomes a decision the system makes, not a cage it inherits. Sample sensitivity across tasks motivated the whole design. Industrial workloads vary wildly, which is exactly where templates crack. Lightweight adaptation keeps the designer cheap beside the agents it arranges. Topology becomes a per-query choice. Teams shaped per task outperform permanent org charts.
arxiv-2510-01717:
Shaon and Nguyen study federated learning carried by drones in this 2025 engineering paper. In their setup, unmanned aerial vehicles gather data with several kinds of sensors at once. The drones train a shared model together with a ground base station, without sending raw data away. The authors aim to cut the total system delay while keeping the learning sound.

They jointly tune sensing schedules, transmit power, flight paths, and computing resources. That joint problem is non-convex and hard, so they solve it with an iterative method mixing block coordinate descent and successive convex approximation. They also prove convergence results for the learning process under a non-convex loss. Numerical experiments beat existing approaches on both system latency and training performance. The work matters for drone fleets that must learn quickly in the field.
arxiv-2510-01817:
Filipek proposes a leaner attention mechanism for transformer models in this 2025 paper. Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, which blocks very long contexts. Popular fixes share key and value heads to save memory bandwidth during generation. They do not, however, cut the core arithmetic of the attention scores themselves.

Sparse Query Attention attacks that arithmetic directly by using fewer query heads. Cutting query heads shrinks the operation count in direct proportion. Filipek lays out the theory, the math, and a family of design variants. Benchmarks on sequences from thirty-two thousand to two hundred thousand tokens showed major throughput gains. The savings matter most for training and for processing whole long documents at once. Because the idea complements key-value sharing, the two tricks can be combined in future architectures.
arxiv-2510-02017:
Tayebi, Khodabandeh Yalabadi, Yazdani-Jahromi, and Garibay teach tabular models fairer representations through contrastive learning in this 2025 paper. Tabular data drives many high-stakes decisions, yet its features lack the tidy structure of images or text. Models trained naively inherit societal biases against sensitive groups. Fair representation learning tries to keep predictive signal while scrubbing that bias.

Their framework, FairContrast, selects positive pairs strategically and mixes supervised with self-supervised contrastive objectives. Customized augmentation methods adapt the contrastive recipe to tabular quirks. The learned representations cut bias substantially compared with state-of-the-art contrastive models for tables. Accuracy paid only a minimal price for those fairness gains. The same representations transferred across several downstream tasks. Results suggest contrastive methods, long proven in vision and speech, can debias tabular pipelines too. The authors frame fairness here as a moral duty, not just a metric.
arxiv-2510-02317:
Jaikissoon argues that rules for hybrid cryptography lag behind the technology itself. Her 2025 policy paper looks at the shift toward quantum safe security. Quantum machines threaten today's standard encryption. A full switch will take about ten years, she notes. Hybrid systems bridge the gap by mixing old and new methods. Artificial intelligence raises parallel misuse worries in her account. Both fields now grow faster than their rulebooks. She maps the gaps in current standards and oversight. She then offers fixes meant to guide organizations through the change.

Her plan starts with formal federal standards for hybrid methods. Published FIPS and special publications would show users what changes. She points to testbeds like Open Quantum Safe and Qiskit. Teams can practice the new tools safely there first. Planning early beats a rushed switch later.
arxiv-2510-02417:
Thakur and co-authors use deep learning to store digital data inside DNA strands. Their 2025 paper presents a pipeline called NeuroDNAAI. DNA packs huge density and lasts for centuries. Writing and reading it, though, introduces errors. Cost, sequencing mistakes, and chemistry limits block wider use. Balanced letter mixes and avoiding long repeats are hard constraints. The pipeline encodes binary data into symbolic DNA sequences. A simulated noisy channel then damages the strands. Substitutions, insertions, and deletions all strike the data. A neural decoder rebuilds the original stream afterward.

Benchmark tests covered both text and image payloads. The neural approach kept bit error rates low. Rule based and prompt based schemes failed under realistic noise. Quantum parallelism ideas inspired extra encoding diversity. The whole flow runs on modest, common GPU hardware. Sustainable archives need exactly this kind of resilience. DNA storage moves closer to practical deployment.
arxiv-2510-02617:
Lu, Chen, Xiao, and Zhu generate talking head videos from speech in real time. Their 2025 computer graphics paper tackles slow diffusion video models. Co-speech video helps video creation and virtual agents. Standard diffusion needs many denoising steps per clip. Its attention steps also cost heavily. The team distills a many-step teacher into a few-step student. Plain distillation hurt quality and still missed real time. Their fix uses the speaker's body pose as a guide. Pose keypoints tell attention where to look. Faces, hands, and the upper body get the focus.

A sparse attention module skips the unimportant regions. A matching loss weighs critical areas more heavily. The student reached real time inference speeds. Motion realism and lip sync even beat the teacher. Fine finger motion still blurs in some cases. Live avatars need exactly this speed and fidelity. Pose guidance turns wasted compute into quality.
arxiv-2510-02817:
Coulson and co-authors report a chemical detection on a rare visitor. The visitor is comet 3I/ATLAS. It came from outside our solar system. Only two such interstellar objects were seen before it. The team pointed the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at the comet in 2025. The comet was then about twice as far from the Sun as Earth is.

They detected hydrogen cyanide gas streaming from the comet. The signal passed five sigma on September 14, 2025. Modeling put the gas output near forty septillion molecules each second. Its share next to water looked high but normal. The share matched the top range seen in home-grown comets. A second ratio hinted that sunlight breaking up this gas explains the cyanide seen. The result shows that a comet from another star system is built much like our own.
arxiv-2510-02917:
Tahimic and Cheng peer inside a language model to find its sense of code correctness. Yet models still ship bugs at a worrying rate. The authors used sparse autoencoders to split the model's signals apart. That split revealed directions tied to whether code is right or wrong. They picked predictor directions with statistics. They picked steering directions by how cleanly they separate cases.

The correctness directions flagged bad code with reliable accuracy. Steering could fix errors, but it carried a trade-off. Always-on steering harmed some code that was already right. A closer look showed what good generation attends to. Models did best when they focused on test cases, not problem text. Directions found in the base model still worked after instruction tuning. That suggests fine-tuning reuses circuits built in pre-training. Selective steering, fired only when errors loom, is another.
arxiv-2510-03117:
Guan and co-authors generate videos with matching sound from a single text prompt. Most joint systems feed one caption to both towers. The caption that suits the picture may ill suit the sound. Their captioning frame, HVGC, splits the prompt in two. A video caption and an audio caption are built apart. Each is grounded in the visual side of the request.

A dual-tower diffusion transformer, BridgeDiT, does the generation. Dual cross-attention bridges the two towers both ways. Sound and picture thus shape each other as they form. Timing sync and meaning sync both come from that bridge. Three benchmark sets hosted the comparisons. Human judges joined the automatic metrics in scoring. The method took the top spot on most measures. Ablation tests confirmed each piece earns its place. The authors flag misuse risks for such media tools.
arxiv-2510-03217:
Cambronero and co-authors add two gatekeeper models that cut noise from automated bug fixing. Agent systems now patch real repository bugs at Google. Humans still review every patch before it lands. Bad patches waste reviewer time and erode trust fast. Their first policy abstains on bugs the agent cannot fix. Their second policy validates patches before showing them. Both gatekeepers are language models judging likelihood of success.

Three bug collections from Google's codebase tested the setup. One held one hundred seventy-four human-reported bugs. Abstention alone lifted success rates by double digits. Validation alone added a similar gain on top. Combined, the pair raised success by up to thirty-nine points. Reviewers went from one good patch in ten to one in two. Machine-reported crash bugs also benefited from validation. The design offers a practical path to industrial scale.
arxiv-2510-03417:
Asl and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on jailbreak attacks that unfold slowly across many turns of chat. Safety training often blocks a harmful request made all at once. Attackers instead spread intent across innocent looking exchanges until the guard slips. Their framework, NEXUS, builds such attacks in three stages. A first module grows a web of topics and question chains around a harmful goal. A simulator then sharpens those chains using feedback from attacker, victim, and judge models.

A final module walks the refined web in real time, picking the most promising next question. Across open and closed models, NEXUS beat leading attack methods by margins ranging from about two to about nineteen percent in success rate in the reported tests. The authors publish their code for defense research. Stealthy multi turn paths like these show why safety checks must judge whole conversations, not single messages in isolation.
arxiv-2510-03517:
Sarma and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper testing shortcuts for measuring cosmic distances near dense local structures. Surveys hint that the nearby expansion rate varies with direction, which strains the standard smooth universe picture. The team places an off center observer inside a lumpy exact solution of Einstein's equations. They compute true light distances there and grade two approximation schemes against them. One scheme expands distances in a covariant cosmographic series; the other uses linear perturbation theory.

Near the structure, the cosmographic method stayed accurate for stronger lumps than the linear method could handle. Farther out, the ranking flipped, with linear theory holding up better at large radii. Both schemes merge with the exact answer at great distances. The comparison also yields a dictionary between the two frameworks in the weak field limit. Astronomers can now choose the right tool by distance when reading local expansion maps.
arxiv-2510-03817:
Becker and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a better way to fine-tune language models with reinforcement learning. The standard method, based on PPO, limits each update by clipping, a rough guardrail meant to keep training stable. Clipping is a crude stand-in for a true trust region, and it can cause unstable updates. The authors replace it with a projection that enforces limits directly.

Their method, called TROLL, projects the model's token scores onto a trust region defined by a divergence bound. To save cost, the projection acts only on the most important token scores. Across datasets and model families, TROLL beat PPO-style clipping in speed and stability. It also reached higher final success rates in their experiments. Because TROLL changes only training, the finished model behaves as usual when deployed. The work offers a cleaner foundation for reward-based fine-tuning of language models.
arxiv-2510-03917:
Raman, Xie, and Zhou present this 2025 arXiv paper in learning theory, on prediction problems where the future is partly known. In online regression, a learner predicts values round by round while an adversary reveals the truth after each guess. Real streams often follow patterns, so hints about coming examples could help. The authors study two settings: full advance knowledge of the example sequence, and noisy predictions about it.

For the full-knowledge setting, called transductive, they pin down the best possible expected regret exactly. The answer depends on a complexity measure called the fat-shattering dimension. This separates transductive learning from ordinary online learning, where a stricter measure governs. They then build a learner for the noisy-prediction setting whose regret improves smoothly as prediction quality rises. With precise predictions it nearly matches the transductive learner's performance. The framework makes some previously unlearnable classes learnable when the future is known.
arxiv-2510-04317:
Dai and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on FairAgent, a language-model-powered system that automates fairness-aware machine learning for non-specialists. Building an unbiased model demands expertise in fairness metrics, sensitive attributes, preprocessing, and mitigation algorithms, plus delicate accuracy trade-offs. That expertise barrier keeps many practitioners from shipping fair models in high-stakes domains. FairAgent wraps the whole workflow in an automated agent.

The system analyzes a dataset for potential biases on its own. It handles preprocessing and feature engineering, then selects and applies mitigation strategies matching the user's stated requirements. Experiments across multiple datasets and backbone models showed the agent hitting user-defined fairness constraints efficiently. Development time and expertise requirements dropped significantly compared with manual workflows. Automating the mechanics leaves human judgment where it belongs: choosing which fairness objectives a deployment should satisfy.
arxiv-2510-04417:
Wenyuan Zhao and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on measuring how information sources combine. When a model reads text, images, and sound together, each source may add unique facts. Sources may also repeat each other, or create new meaning only when combined. Partial information decomposition, or PID, is the framework that splits these three shares. Older PID methods grow costly and shaky for continuous data.

The team found that the problem turns tractable when the data pairs follow Gaussian distributions. They built a gradient based algorithm for that Gaussian case. They also settled an open question by showing that Gaussian solutions are optimal there. For data that is not Gaussian, learned encoders reshape it into Gaussian form while keeping its information. Tests on synthetic data beat older methods on both accuracy and speed. Tests on large multimodal benchmarks showed the tool can rank models and explain data mixes.
arxiv-2510-04517:
Ashutosh Tomar and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on the dusty rings around feeding black holes. Each active galactic nucleus hides its center behind a torus of dust. The size of that torus should grow with the brightness of the nucleus. The team measured torus sizes for 51 nuclei using sixteen years of optical survey data. Infrared data from the WISE space telescope covered fourteen of those years.

Dust glows in the infrared after the center flares, so the lag between optical and infrared changes gives the torus size. Two methods, cross correlation and light curve modeling, put the lags between about one thousand and three thousand days. Fitted slopes for size against brightness came out near four tenths, shallower than the half that simple dust physics predicts. Torus size also shrank as the feeding rate rose, a pattern the authors tie to self shadowing by slim disks.
arxiv-2510-04617:
Zhejian Lai and nine coauthors at Nanjing University wrote this 2025 paper on a flaw in math models. Language models often reach the right answer through surface cues rather than logic. Such spurious reasoning breaks when numbers shift or the setting leaves the training zone. The team blames weak robustness and generalization on that habit. Their framework, AdaR, trains models to reason in an adaptive way instead.

AdaR builds twin problems that keep the logic but change the variable values. The true answer for each twin comes from running code, and a sanity check filters bad items. Training with rewards then punishes surface logic and rewards logic that survives the change. Data synthesis and reward training worked as a pair in their analysis. Results showed gains in math reasoning with data efficiency. The paper draws lessons on which factors matter most. It tests whether the lessons carry to instruction tuned models.
arxiv-2510-04817:
Madahar wrote this 2025 paper on steering language model reasoning with words attached to each step. Reasoning controllers like tree search mix two jobs: deciding what to try and setting how to run it. The mix leaves only coarse knobs, so behavior turns brittle and hard to audit. The overlay, Natural Language Edge Labelling, splits the jobs. A labeller writes a directive in language on each search branch.

A tuner then translates the directive into a control vector. That vector sets decoding choices, branch quotas, retrieval mixes, and passes. Rails validate the vector and keep it near safe defaults. The scheme contains chain of thought and tree search as special cases. It keeps a monotonicity property for selection over time. A bound ties selection loss to how much the control vector distorts. The author preregistered tests on math and question benchmarks with scoring. Forecasts expect accuracy gains at token budgets.
arxiv-2510-05117:
Nosratollah Jafari and Abdelmalek Boumali ask how quantum gravity might bend a textbook quantum system in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Dirac oscillator is a relativistic cousin of the harmonic oscillator with an exact solution. Doubly special relativity adds a universal Planck-scale length to Einstein's rules. Two rival versions of that theory exist, due to Magueijo and Smolin and to Amelino-Camelia.

The authors derive the oscillator's energy spectrum inside both versions. A deformation parameter tied to the Planck energy shifts the levels in model-specific ways. In the Magueijo-Smolin model, small values shift both energy branches unevenly, then flatten back as the parameter grows. The Amelino-Camelia model deviates more strongly and recovers more slowly. Comparing the two shows which Planck-scale predictions are robust for future precision tests.
arxiv-2510-05317:
Zhenyu Liu and Varun Ojha harden image classifiers against adversarial attacks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Adversarial training is the strongest known defense, and its loss function decides how well it works. The usual mean-squared-error regularizer forces two output distributions to match too uniformly. That rigidity limits the robustness the training can reach.

Their method, RegMix, borrows mutual learning from knowledge distillation. A decomposed divergence loss weights the main and auxiliary objectives unequally, giving finer control. A second regularizer adds a clean target distribution to improve generalization. Experiments on three datasets under varied attack strengths beat existing regularization approaches clearly. Training with full probability distributions even helped against stronger attacks than those seen in training.
arxiv-2510-05417:
Xinying Hou and four co-authors watch programming novices choose how to talk to AI in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most classroom studies cover text-only generative AI tools. Newer platforms accept voice, images, and live screen-sharing as well. The authors ask which modalities students pick for programming problems, and why.

Sixteen think-aloud sessions paired observation with follow-up interviews. Preferences varied widely across students and tasks. Some wanted seamless, human-like tutoring through voice and screen-sharing. Others stuck with text, valuing the pause it gives for phrasing questions carefully. Task demands, physical environment, and personal standards for good answers all shaped the choices. The authors urge designs that let learners switch modalities fluidly.
arxiv-2510-05717:
Zisling and colleagues disentangle sequences with diffusion models instead of autoencoders. Sequential disentanglement splits data into static and dynamic factors without labels. A speaker's identity is static, while speech content changes over time. Their 2025 DiffSDA framework brings latent diffusion to this task across modalities.

Earlier methods lean on variational autoencoders and adversarial networks with many loss terms. DiffSDA uses a new probabilistic model with efficient samplers instead. It works on time series, video, and audio without modality-specific redesign. The authors also introduce a tougher evaluation protocol for real-world data. Experiments show DiffSDA beating recent state-of-the-art disentanglement methods. Standardizing evaluation matters because real-world benchmarks were missing entirely. Future work targets computational efficiency and sensor data modalities. High-resolution video already works within the current design. Cleaner factors promise better interpretability and generalization downstream.
arxiv-2510-06017:
Agarwal and Paliya hunt for blazars that shine at very high energies in a 2025 astronomy paper. Blazars are active galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth. The team focused on BL Lac objects with high synchrotron peaks, the class most likely to emit gamma rays above 100 gigaelectronvolts.

They searched about sixteen years of data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope for a sample of just over a thousand candidate sources. The search found 92 blazars emitting at very high energy for the first time, each at strong statistical confidence. It also confirmed signals from 52 blazars already known as very-high-energy sources. These emitters sit at fairly low redshifts and glow brightly, and their photons arrived during both quiet and flaring periods. The list gives ground-based Cherenkov telescopes a ready set of targets.
arxiv-2510-06317:
Argillander and six co-authors demonstrate a quantum random number generator that needs no trust in its own detectors in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Certifying randomness is hard, yet cryptography depends on it. Measurement-device-independent designs remove the detectors from the trust assumptions.

The team extended the standard qubit beam-splitter generator to three outputs using high-dimensional photonic path states. Tunable fiber-optic interferometers act as adjustable beam splitters, and superconducting detectors record the outcomes. The device generated more than one bit per round and nearly two megabits per second of certifiably secure private randomness. Crucially, those rates hold without trusting the measurement apparatus at all, and the setup closes the detection loophole. High-dimensional states pack more certified randomness into each detection than qubits allow. The result points toward practical, scalable quantum random number generators built from relatively simple photonic hardware for real cryptographic systems.
arxiv-2510-06517:
Sánchez-Díaz and Mengshoel walk through ways to visualize multimodality in combinatorial search landscapes in a 2025 computer graphics paper. Search landscapes map candidate solutions to quality scores. Multimodality, many separate peaks, decides whether optimization is easy or treacherous. Seeing that structure helps researchers choose and debug algorithms.

The paper surveys landscape analysis visualization techniques. Each technique reveals some features while hiding others. Combining several yields a more comprehensive view than any single plot. Examples show how practitioners have deployed these methods. Choices are organized through the Grammar of Graphics, weighing geometric and aesthetic elements. Such visualization belongs to fitness landscape analysis, the standard diagnostic toolkit for metaheuristics. The central conclusion borrows a famous slogan: no free lunch in visualization. Every view trades something away, so analysts must choose deliberately. Recommendations close the paper, charting paths for future visualization work.
arxiv-2510-06917:
Cheng-Han Chiang leads a team teaching spoken language models to think while they listen. Their 2025 paper presents Shanks, a framework for speech models that react during a user's turn. Today's models wait until the speaker finishes, then think, then answer. That delay makes speech-to-speech conversation feel sluggish and blocks timely interruptions.

Humans reason while listening, and Shanks copies that habit. Incoming speech is chopped into fixed-length chunks as it arrives. After each chunk, the model silently reasons over everything heard so far. Those silent thoughts let it act mid-turn when needed. In one test, the model listened to a student solving a math problem aloud. It interrupted exactly when the student made a mistake. In a second test, it called software tools during a task dialogue without waiting for the end. The framework upgrades any spoken model, since it changes inference rather than training.
arxiv-2510-07017:
Hong Liu, a single author, lectures on how the algebra of quantum observables explains the birth of spacetime. The 2025 review covers von Neumann algebras and entanglement in quantum gravity. In gravity, the usual splitting of a system into separate parts often fails. Operator algebras give a language for subsystems that survives that failure.

The first part teaches the algebra framework from the ground up. It covers classification, modular flows, and the crossed-product construction. Modular flow turns out to generate a kind of emergent time. The second part applies the machinery to quantum gravity. An algebraic form of the AdS/CFT correspondence appears in the large-system limit. Bulk spacetime structure emerges through a duality between regions and subalgebras. Gravitational entropy gets an operator-algebraic reading as well. Simple toy models let readers see the ideas work concretely. The lectures chart how entanglement, organized algebraically, may underlie spacetime itself.
arxiv-2510-07517:
Choi, Zhu, and Li show that language model debaters play favorites based on whose answer they think they are reading. Their 2025 paper studies multi-agent debate, where models exchange and revise answers to reason better. Two identity biases corrupt the exchange. Sycophancy makes an agent adopt a peer's view uncritically, while self-bias makes it cling to its own prior output. The authors formalize debate as an identity-weighted Bayesian update, giving the phenomenon equations rather than anecdotes. Their fix is disarmingly simple: anonymize responses so agents cannot tell self from peer, forcing identity weights to equalize.

A new metric, the Identity Bias Coefficient, counts how often an agent follows peer versus self. Across models, datasets, and debate rounds, identity bias proved widespread. Sycophancy was far more common than self-bias. Anonymization measurably reduced the distortion in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-07617:
Bergman wrote this 2025 algebra paper on free monoids, which are sets of words built from a generating set. He asks what happens when universal one-sided inverses are added for chosen elements. Such inverses let some products cancel from one side only. The bicyclic monoid is the classic example of this one-sided behavior. The paper studies the structure of the larger monoid that results.

Bergman gives an elementary method that produces a standard form for every element. He shows the result is either a free group, a free product of simpler pieces, or a monoid with strictly one-sided invertible elements. He then extends the standard form to infinite families of adjoined inverses, though no method can compute it there. The work clarifies when added inverses stay tame and when genuinely one-sided behavior must appear. Free monoids are basic objects in algebra and computer science.
arxiv-2510-07917:
Switzer wrote this 2025 set theory paper on variants of Baumgartner's axiom. The classical axiom says that any two very dense sets of reals are isomorphic. Topological versions replace the line with other spaces. Switzer studies versions on Baire space and Cantor space where isomorphisms must be Lipschitz, controlling how much distances stretch. He adapts Baumgartner's argument to show these variants are consistent.

Unlike the classical case, these variants come with strong applications whose linear-order versions remain open. He proves implications running from the Baire space versions to the Cantor space versions. Some variants force every cardinal in the Cichoń diagram to be large. He also shows that none of the Lipschitz variants follow from a large fragment of Martin's Axiom. The paper maps a new family of axioms that behave quite unlike their famous ancestor.
arxiv-2510-08117:
Zheng, Jedra, and Proutière wrote this 2025 statistics paper on estimating a large matrix from linear measurements while letting the data choose how many singular components matter. Rank-adaptive methods estimate singular values and vectors up to an effective rank. The authors derive instance-specific lower bounds on the samples any such algorithm needs. The bounds expose how the optimal rank depends on the matrix, sample size, and noise level.

Their estimator pairs least squares with a universal singular value thresholding step. Finite-sample error bounds show its performance nearly matches the fundamental limits. The analysis also sharpens known results on matrix denoising. Applications to multivariate regression and system identification validate the theory. A small gap to the limits remains open. The work answers a question usually settled by guesswork: how much rank is enough.
arxiv-2510-08217:
Justus Viga and co-authors released FuelCast in a 2025 arXiv paper, a new test set for predicting how much fuel a ship burns. Fuel use drives both costs and air pollution in shipping, so good forecasts help crews plan better trips. Past studies used mixed methods and small private data sets, which made fair comparisons hard. FuelCast aims to give all models the same open test.

The team built the data set from real records of three ships, adding weather and sea conditions. They set two test styles, one based on tables and one based on data over time. Models that used weather and sea data beat simple ones based only on ship speed. TabPFN, a ready-made model that learns from examples in its input, scored best overall. Adding past time steps also raised accuracy in their tests.
arxiv-2510-08517:
Grace Liu and co-authors teach language model agents to stop gathering information at the right moment in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many tasks require several rounds of questions or searches before acting. Models often overshoot, wasting effort and drifting off course, or undershoot and act too soon. Knowing when enough is known is itself a learnable skill, they argue.

Their approach, CaRT, fine-tunes models on counterfactual pairs of interaction trajectories. One trajectory stops at the right point; its minimally edited twin stops wrongly. Training asks the model to explain its termination decision in words for both cases. This verbal reasoning is then baked into the base model through fine-tuning. They test CaRT on medical diagnosis tasks done interactively, and on math problem solving. In both domains, CaRT improved the efficiency of information gathering, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-08617:
Saumya B presents a fully reproducible study of brain tumor segmentation settings in a 2025 arXiv paper. Segmenting tumors in MRI scans guides diagnosis and treatment planning, but class imbalance and weak generalization stall progress. The work evaluates U-Net performance with focal loss and basic augmentation on a public MRI data set. All code and results are released publicly for verification.

Focal loss, which emphasizes hard examples, was tuned across its parameters for the segmentation task. Three augmentation strategies were assessed: horizontal flips, rotations, and scaling of training images. The U-Net with focal loss reached a precision of ninety percent, comparable to state-of-the-art results, the author reports. Saumya frames the study as a transparent baseline for future work. It is meant to guide future work on augmentation and loss design in this area.
arxiv-2510-08717:
Stamatis Dostoglou and Petros Valettas prove that random power series almost surely cannot be extended past their convergence circle in a 2025 arXiv paper. A power series defines a function inside a disk, but some series hit a natural boundary: every boundary point blocks analytic continuation. Strong versions of this barrier matter in complex analysis and mathematical physics. The authors take a probabilistic route to the phenomenon.

Their series have independent random coefficients that are asymptotically anti-concentrated, meaning they avoid clustering near single values. For such series, the convergence circle forms a natural boundary in a strong sense, one that holds even under Nevanlinna's growth measure. Nevanlinna theory measures function growth, so this strengthens classical non-extendability statements. The results complement and extend earlier work by Ryll-Nardzewski from 1953 and by Breuer and Simon from 2011. Randomness, in short, generically creates maximal barriers to continuation.
arxiv-2510-08817:
Dellmann and a very large collaboration report the first measurements of proton reactions on a stored beam of rare radioactive ions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The reactions matter for the gamma process, the forge inside exploding stars that makes a family of rare isotopes called p-nuclei. Most nuclei in that forge are radioactive and nearly impossible to study with normal targets. Their reaction rates are therefore guessed, which blurs models of how the elements form.

The team stored tellurium-118 ions in a ring at the GSI laboratory in Germany and fired protons at them. They measured two reaction channels at three energies that match stellar conditions. The values, plus a careful extension of the trend to lower energies, give modelers real anchors instead of guesses. The authors stress the milestone itself: the method opens many similar measurements on unstable nuclei.
arxiv-2510-08917:
Lit, Crowder, Vogel, and Khan test whether people follow a security chatbot that has secretly been turned against them, in this 2025 arXiv study. Companies increasingly deploy chatbots to explain internal security policy to staff. An attacker who poisons such a bot can feed employees advice that sounds sensible yet quietly weakens defenses. The user then becomes the last line of defense, if they notice anything is wrong.

In a controlled study with fifteen participants, the team's chatbot gave correct help on some tasks and manipulated, incorrect advice on others, without the users knowing. Whether people pushed back depended on two things. Familiarity with the task mattered: users spotted bad advice in areas they already understood. Confidence in their own judgment mattered too. The paper's title quotes a participant who sensed the advice was wrong yet followed it anyway, which captures the trust problem the authors document.
arxiv-2510-09017:
Bu and co-authors fix a wasteful habit inside transformer models, the architecture behind modern AI, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Transformers often park large amounts of attention on a few meaningless tokens, a glitch called an attention sink. It pairs with drained value states, the content those tokens carry, in a self-reinforcing loop: the model learns to do nothing, loudly. The glitches hurt accuracy, compression, and readability of the model's decisions.

Their mechanism, Value-State Gated Attention, adds a learned gate computed from each token's own value vector. The gate scales that token's contribution up or down. A gradient analysis shows gating on the value itself breaks the loop better than earlier gates keyed to the input. Experiments confirmed that sinks largely failed to form and value sizes stayed stable. Performance improved, compressed versions kept their fidelity, and the model's attention became easier to interpret.
arxiv-2510-09317:
Felix Brandt, Andreas Heuermann, Philip Hannebohm, and Bernhard Bachmann tackle algebraic loops in engineering models in a 2025 arXiv paper. An algebraic loop is a circle of equations that must be solved together, and it slows down simulations in Modelica, a language for modelling complex systems. Their idea is to replace each loop with a small neural network that mimics it.

The network learns from the loop's own residual, meaning the leftover error of the equations, so no ready-made training dataset is needed. Training on the error also avoids a trap where several valid answers blur into one average. On the large IEEE fourteen-bus power system, the method cut simulation time by sixty percent. Accuracy stayed at the same level, guarded by built-in error controls during each run.
arxiv-2510-09417:
Thomas Koopman, Jordy Aaldering, Bernard van Gastel, and Sven-Bodo Scholz present a faster convex hull algorithm in a 2025 arXiv paper. The convex hull of a point set is its tightest wrapping shape, a basic need in graphics and geometry. Quickhull is a classic fast method for finding it, and the authors reimplement it as VQhull, tuned for modern hardware.

VQhull exploits vector instructions, which process several numbers at once, and coordinates processor cores to keep data movement low. Against the best existing code on a standard benchmark suite, it ran between one point six and sixteen times faster in serial tests. Parallel tests gained up to about elevenfold, reaching most of the machine's peak memory bandwidth. The study also measures energy use, and finds that running in parallel can sometimes use less energy than running serially.
arxiv-2510-09617:
Dmitrii Gerasimov, the sole author, presents ChipmunkRing in a 2025 arXiv paper, a ring signature scheme built to survive quantum attacks. A ring signature lets one member of a group sign a message so that outsiders can verify some member signed, without learning which one. Blockchains use such signatures for privacy, and lattice-based designs are a leading post-quantum option.

ChipmunkRing builds on the author's Chipmunk lattice framework and adds Acorn Verification, its streamlined zero-knowledge protocol, which replaces the classical Fiat-Shamir method. Signatures range from tens to a few hundred kilobytes for groups of two to sixty-four members, and signing and verification finish within milliseconds. Proofs run to ninety-six bytes per participant, keeping verification cost linear in group size. Benchmarks show a nearly eighteenfold speed advantage for thirty-two-member rings over conventional techniques, with security argued at the one hundred twelve bit level.
arxiv-2510-09817:
Samanta Rodriguez, Yiming Dou, Miquel Oller, Andrew Owens, and Nima Fazeli teach touch sensors to translate for each other in a 2025 arXiv paper. Vision-based tactile sensors come in all shapes and sizes, and most models are tied to one specific design. A model trained on one sensor's images generally cannot read another's, which blocks general-purpose touch representations.

The authors propose two routes to cross-sensor generation. Touch2Touch learns the translation end to end from paired data, where one contact was recorded by two sensors. T2D2 passes through an intermediate depth representation and needs no paired data. Both let sensor-specific models run across sensors. On tasks such as held-object pose estimation and behaviour cloning, models trained on one sensor transferred to another.
arxiv-2510-09917:
de Alba and Cecilia Martínez-Reyes extend a coding theory result in this 2025 arXiv paper on linear codes. The generalized Hamming weights of a code measure how much support a subcode of each size needs. The second of these weights is a basic error-protection parameter.

For binary codes, Gröbner bases, a tool from algebra, can produce codewords of minimal support that reveal the second weight. The authors set out when the same property holds for a nonbinary code. Nonbinary codes use alphabets larger than zero and one, as in many real storage and communication systems. Extending the algebraic method to them widens where exact weight computation is practical.
arxiv-2510-11617:
François Schwarzentruber of ENS de Lyon wrote these lecture notes on checking whether graph neural networks behave correctly. The notes come from a master-level course taught in the autumn of 2025 and posted on arXiv that year. Graph neural networks sort nodes in a network, but proving what such a network can and cannot compute is hard. The notes link the networks to logic and to the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, a standard method for telling graphs apart.

The core of the course is a modal logic whose counting statements sit inside linear inequalities. Schwarzentruber gives a decision procedure for that logic. It extends the tableau method from basic modal logic. It adds tools from Boolean algebra and Presburger arithmetic, which handles whole-number addition. Along the way the notes pin down problem difficulty. Basic modal logic satisfiability is PSPACE-complete, and one network logic is far harder still.
arxiv-2510-11917:
Jun-En Ding and four co-authors improve the diagnosis of dementia from brain-wave recordings. Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia produce overlapping signatures in EEG, the electrical traces from the scalp. Methods that smear every band together struggle to separate the subtypes or grade severity. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes VMoGE, a mixture of graph neural experts.

The model first reads the EEG with a multi-scale transformer that extracts patterns at several time scales across four frequency bands. A graph encoder then treats the brain as a network, guided by structured priors. Adaptive gating assigns expert networks to bands with real meaning for the body. On two datasets, covering both subtype sorting and severity staging, VMoGE lifted the area under the curve by four to ten percent over leading methods. Its expert weights also track clinical signs, and its spatial patterns match known pathology, aiding the hunt for markers.
arxiv-2510-12117:
Lipeng He, Vasisht Duddu, and N. Asokan lock premium abilities inside a language model the way apps lock premium tiers. Providers currently sell whole models by subscription tier. Selling individual features, math here, coding there, would pay better but needs a lock that refuses locked features, preserves unlocked ones, resists evasion, and scales. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents LOCKET, built for exactly that.

LOCKET merges adapters into the model that enforce refusal of unauthorized features. Evaluation hits the design targets: complete refusal on locked features, at most seven percent utility loss on unlocked ones, and attack success rates at or below five percent. Password-locked models, the prior approach, were neither robust nor scalable; merging beats prompting because the lock lives in the weights. The system scales to multiple features and clients, enabling a pay-to-unlock marketplace of model abilities.
arxiv-2510-12217:
Mekky and colleagues propose HALF, a fairness evaluation for large language models that weighs bias by the harm it could cause, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models are now used in medicine, law, hiring, and education, where unfair outputs can do real damage. Existing fairness tests, the authors argue, ignore how severe the harm in each setting would be.

HALF sorts nine application domains into three tiers of harm, severe, moderate, and mild, and evaluates models through a five stage pipeline grounded in realistic deployment scenarios. The team tested eight large language models. They found that no model was consistently fair across domains, and that larger size or stronger general performance did not guarantee fairness. Reasoning models did better in medical decision support yet worse in education, showing that fairness must be checked domain by domain before deployment.
arxiv-2510-12317:
Tsujimoto and a large international team add missing iron lines to the atomic data used to read X-ray spectra, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The Resolve instrument aboard the XRISM telescope opened a new era of high resolution X-ray spectroscopy. Its spectra from neutron star and black hole binaries revealed inner shell lines of mildly ionized iron, including K beta lines that standard databases lacked.

The authors computed the iron K alpha and K beta lines with the FAC code and checked them against laboratory experiments and other calculations. They then implemented the new K beta lines in the cloudy radiative transfer code, which models how radiation passes through hot astrophysical gas. Synthesized spectra were compared with XRISM observations of X-ray binaries plus active galactic nuclei. That agreement was good, which the authors take as evidence that atomic databases must grow to interpret the new spectra.
arxiv-2510-12417:
Musso, Rybski, Helbing, and Neffke trace the life cycle of city growth and project how concentrated world population will become, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The share of people living in cities above one million rose from about eleven percent in 1975 to about twenty four percent in 2025, by their estimates. Whether big cities keep outgrowing smaller ones is an open question.

They built two data sets with consistent city definitions: a global one from satellite imagery covering fifty years, and a United States one from census microdata reaching back to 1850. They find a characteristic pattern. Early in urbanization, large cities grow more quickly than smaller ones, but as urban systems mature, growth rates level out across sizes. Projecting this life cycle, they estimate thirty eight percent of world population will live in million plus cities by 2100. That sits above the share implied by proportional growth theory but below a trend extrapolation.
arxiv-2510-12617:
Greco and Rawlik show that a genomics benchmark can make the same model look better or worse depending on the computer it runs on, in a 2025 arXiv paper. DNA language models are increasingly used to decode biological sequences, and standardized benchmarks are meant to rank them fairly. The authors dissect one such benchmark and trace a subtle validity problem to how data are shuffled.

Hardware dependent settings, the number of data loading workers plus buffer sizes, created spurious performance variations of up to a few percent for identical models. Inadequate shuffling interacts with the structure of genomic data to produce these artifacts. Experiments with three DNA language models showed the effects distort both absolute scores and relative rankings. The proposed fix is simple: shuffle the data once before storage, which removes the hardware dependence while keeping efficiency. The authors generalize the lesson to benchmark design in other specialized domains.
arxiv-2510-12717:
Jeon and colleagues let a reinforcement learning policy make small torque level fixes to a physics based locomotion controller, getting the strengths of both, in a 2025 arXiv robotics paper. Model predictive control is interpretable and tunable but brittle when its model mismatches reality and expensive to replan. Reinforcement learning produces robust behavior yet can fail unpredictably off distribution.

Their residual design runs a kinodynamic whole body predictive controller for thousands of simulated agents in parallel on a graphics processor. It evaluates fast enough for learning. The learned policy outputs targeted fixes blended with the controller torques. The model based prior starts and guides learning, so a simple reward set suffices. Against predictive control alone or end to end learning, the blend learned from fewer samples and won greater final rewards. It also adapted with no further training to unseen gaits and uneven terrain.
arxiv-2511-00517:
Shuochuan Li and five co-authors automate a tedious expert task: writing code review comments. One model asked to spot every kind of issue tends to produce vague comments, especially on complex changes such as bug fixes. Their framework, RevAgent, instead organizes the work around issue types, with specialist agents for each category of problem.

Five commentator agents draft candidate comments from distinct issue perspectives. A critic agent then picks the best issue-and-comment pairing. Finally, all agents are fine-tuned on curated, category-specific data to sharpen their specialties. RevAgent beat leading language-model baselines on standard text metrics by clear margins and identified issue categories more accurately in hard scenarios. Human judges also rated its comments accurate, readable, and context-aware, with a favorable balance of quality and cost.
arxiv-2511-00617:
Eric Bigelow and six co-authors unify two popular ways to steer a language model's behavior: prompting it with examples, and steering its internal activations directly. Accounts of each method have lived apart, yet both aim at the same target: controlling what the model does. The authors propose both are really belief updates about latent concepts inside the model.

In their Bayesian picture, steering changes the model's prior belief about a concept, while examples in context accumulate evidence for it. The result is a closed-form model that predicts model behavior across both interventions in several domains drawn from many-shot learning studies. It explains familiar sigmoidal learning curves and predicts new effects, such as additivity in log-belief space and sudden behavioral flips from tiny control changes. Control becomes something to compute, not just to try.
arxiv-2511-20217:
Kumano measures how an exotic hadron candidate is built from quarks and gluons. His 2025 paper determines fragmentation functions for the f0(980) particle. Fragmentation functions say how often a quark becomes that hadron. Ordinary hadrons hold two or three quarks. Exotic ones may hide stranger arrangements inside.

Belle experiment data on electron-positron collisions anchor the fit. The analysis extracts separate functions for each parton type. Up and down quark moments came out equal. Both sit far below the strange quark moment. The gluon moment rivals the strange one closely. Strange quarks also carry momentum at larger fractions. Together these facts point to a strange-antistrange core. At high energies the particle looks mainly like that pair. Low-energy studies instead favored a four-quark picture. A kaon molecule view also circulates there. The internal picture may genuinely change with energy. Exotic hadron physics gains a fresh diagnostic.
arxiv-2511-20317:
Perminov hunts faster matrix multiplication using only minus one, zero, and one. His 2025 paper searches ternary-coefficient schemes via flip graphs. Matrix multiplication underpins simulation, graphics, and machine learning. Fewer multiplications mean faster everything downstream. Hardware loves coefficients that are trivial to apply.

A GPU-accelerated meta flip graph drives the search. Schemes are nodes; small flips move between them. Ternary-safe arithmetic keeps coefficients inside the allowed set. Sign symmetry breaking prunes duplicate searches. Three new best ranks were found for rectangular formats. Thirty-two schemes matched known optimal ranks with ternary entries. Eight of those were known only with fractions before. Thirty rank improvements landed over the binary field too. Of 164 known schemes, ninety-two admit ternary versions. Seventy-two resisted, marking the method's current boundary. All code and schemes are open-source. The search runs on ordinary consumer laptops. Coefficient-simple algorithms can rival fancy ones.
arxiv-2511-20417:
Arduini and a CERN working group compare the colliders that could follow the LHC. Their 2025 report sizes up future facilities for European strategy planning. The High-Luminosity LHC program ends around 2041. A new major facility should start in the mid-2040s. Europe's stated priority is an electron-positron Higgs factory first. A highest-energy hadron collider would follow later.

The group was set up in June 2023 by CERN's directorate. It compares proposals under shared rules and standard criteria. The Future Circular Collider faces rivals like the linear CLIC design. Raw performance headlines the comparison. Effects on the environment are weighed alongside. Technical maturity, build costs, and running costs all enter the ledger. Staffing needs and realistic timelines complete the picture. Overseas rivals get an overview too, notably China's CEPC. Japan's planned linear collider is covered as well. Key decisions must land between 2028 and 2030 to stay on schedule.
arxiv-2511-20717:
Mikołaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki defend in 2025 a leading test for whether gravity is quantum. The test, proposed by Bose and by Marletto and Vedral, watches two masses interacting only through gravity. If they become entangled, linked in a way classical physics forbids, gravity itself must be nonclassical. A 2025 Nature paper by Aziz and Howl claimed classical gravity could still entangle masses, which would break that logic.

The Sienickis side with a critical note by Marletto, Oppenheim, Vedral, and Wilson showing the claim fails in the limit that analysis actually used. There the interaction becomes ultra-local, acting at each mass separately. The evolution factorises, and no entanglement can grow from an unentangled start. The comment restates the point in the language of quantum channels, making it model-independent. It also separates activating entanglement inside matter from a classical field mediating it. The original test's inference survives intact.
arxiv-2511-20817:
Luisa F. Zamudio-Ruvalcaba and colleagues reweigh in 2025 disk dust and find the usual scale reads low. They model 178 T Tauri stars, 18 in Serpens and 160 in the L1641 and L1647 regions, fitting spectral energy distributions with multiwavelength data including 1.3-millimetre ALMA fluxes. Their dust masses come out up to twice those previously reported.

The culprit is a hidden assumption: most estimates treat disks as optically thin at 1.3 millimetres, transparent to their own glow, but many disks are partly opaque there, hiding mass. Computing optical depths at 1.3 and 7 millimetres for a subset, they show the vast majority of disks turn transparent at the longer wavelength. The practical message for planet-formation budgets, where disk mass caps how many planets can form, is that 7-millimetre observations with ALMA's Band 1 are vital for honest accounting. The work bears on the missing-mass problem of young regions like Taurus.
arxiv-2511-20917:
Sourav Maji, with a co-author, studies in 2025 what happens to strings when their tension is dialled to zero inside a Kalb-Ramond background field. Tensionless, or null, strings obey Carrollian physics, where light cones collapse. The authors show this limit glues the worldsheet oscillators together in a universal way, now generalised to include the constant background field. Closed strings then morph continuously into open strings.

They derive the mixed boundary conditions, build the gluing matrix, and obtain the new vacuum as a squeezed boundary state, reached from the closed-string vacuum by a Bogoliubov transformation. On toroidal compactifications, the worldsheet Bose-Einstein condensation mechanism survives unchanged. In the second half, a symplectic argument shows the boundary geometry alone fixes the open string's noncommutativity. In the tensionless limit only the background-field term survives, yielding a parameter like the Seiberg-Witten one, but born from Carrollian dynamics.
arxiv-2511-21117:
Sheng-nan Han and colleagues calculate in 2025 whether the QCD phase transition leaves a fingerprint in how many deuterons heavy-ion collisions produce. Near the critical end point, where the transition line terminates, fluctuations of baryon density should surge, and coalescing protons and neutrons might form deuterons. The team combined the functional renormalisation group, a low-energy theory of quarks and mesons, and the nucleon coalescence model to test the idea.

The two-point baryon density correlation does grow, but only inside a wedge radiating from the critical point along the phase boundary. There, the correlation-driven deuteron yield stays small next to the leading-order contribution. At the low collision energies where baryon density is high, freeze-out curves bend away from the critical region. So the critical enhancement of deuteron production ends up mild, a caution for experiments hoping to spot the point through light-nucleus yields.
arxiv-2511-21217:
Computer scientists Chetan Gupta, Vimal Raj Sharma, and Raghunath Tewari tackle the perfect matching problem in a 2025 theory paper. A perfect matching pairs up every point in a network using its links, with no point left over. Matching is easy to solve with randomness, but doing so with very little memory, called logspace computation, is much harder. Their graphs are bipartite, meaning the points split into two camps, and are drawn on surfaces with few handles.

Gupta and his coauthors build an edge weighting, computed in logarithmic space, that makes the lightest perfect matching the only one of its weight whenever a matching exists. That isolation trick, extending a 1999 result by Reinhardt, Allender, and Zhou, places the decision problem for these graphs in the counting class SPL. The method works for surfaces whose handle count grows at most like the logarithm of the network size.
arxiv-2511-21417:
Mia Müßig and Jan Johannsen squeeze more speed from a logic solver with a small rule change, in a 2025 short paper. Their arena is pseudo-Boolean solving, optimization over yes-no variables with weighted constraints, inside the RoundingSAT solver. Its fastest known strategy mixes two propagation methods, watched literals and plain counting, switching between them by a hybrid heuristic that guesses which suits each constraint.

Müßig and Johannsen introduce new heuristics for that switching decision, and the change drastically outperforms the current method in their tests. The improvement needs only minimal edits to the solver's code. Since telling small instances from large ones costs negligible time, they propose an automatic policy: keep the existing heuristic for small instances and deploy the new ones for the rest. The result is a practical upgrade for a core routine that solver competitions and verification tools depend on.
arxiv-2511-21517:
Lina Conti and five coauthors at Fondazione Bruno Kessler and partner institutes open up a speech translator to see how it genders its speaker, in 2025. Translating English into Spanish, French, or Italian forces a choice. Words referring to the speaker need grammatical gender that English leaves open. A voice carries cues like pitch, so models might legitimately listen. Or they might lazily default to masculine forms, misgendering speakers.

Conti and her coauthors trace the decision through training data patterns, the model's internal language bias, and the acoustics themselves. The models do not memorize each word's usual gender; they learn a broad masculine prevalence, and the internal language model leans strongly masculine, though audio evidence can override it. The most accurate model uses a previously unknown trick. It routes gender through first-person pronouns, spreading the evidence across formant frequencies, the voice's resonant bands, rather than relying on pitch alone.
arxiv-2511-21617:
Peter van der Kamp, Anthony Overmars, Marcel Jackson, and Andrew Hone speed up an old number-theoretic computation, in 2025. Quadratic irrationals, square roots and their kin, have continued fraction expansions that eventually repeat, by Lagrange's theorem, and their convergents are the best rational approximations to them. Computing them one step at a time is slow when the period is long.

The team provides algorithms that leap along the sequence instead. For square roots, provided Galois' refinement of Lagrange's theorem holds, certain thinnings of the convergent sequence, taking every k-th term, turn out to be signed Chebyshev sequences with fast recurrences. The same subsequences can also be generated by a Householder method, giving two independent fast routes. The result connects continued fractions, Chebyshev polynomials, and root-finding methods, turning a linear crawl through convergents into a shortcut grounded in the period's own symmetry.
arxiv-2511-21817:
Frommer and colleagues show that a supposed planet found by the TESS space telescope, HIP-44302, is not a planet at all. TESS had recorded a dip in light repeating about every 10 days, the classic sign of a planet crossing its star. The team modelled all the stars in the system using transit data, images, and brightness measurements across many colours.

Their modelling shows the dips come from two stars eclipsing each other every 9.599214 days, with the pair orbiting a third, single star on a roughly 1,886 year orbit at about 297 times the Earth-Sun distance. The two larger stars are massive A stars, and the smaller companion is a G star like the Sun. The authors argue this kind of full-system modelling is a new paradigm for weeding out false positives, catching impostors that would otherwise pollute planet catalogues.
arxiv-2511-22117:
Chen, Ke, Li, and Li, researchers in China, make formal concept analysis safe to outsource to third-party cloud services. Formal concept analysis extracts concept hierarchies from data tables and is widely used in knowledge discovery and data mining. Its heavy computation pushes users toward external computing services, where uploading raw data risks leaking sensitive information. Their PFCA framework performs the concept construction under homomorphic encryption, which lets an untrusted server compute on encrypted data without ever seeing the underlying values themselves.

Binary representation plus encryption lets concepts be built securely, and experiments with security analysis confirm privacy holds at acceptable cost. They note honestly that computation time grows sharply for very large attribute sets. Point to faster algorithms for large attribute sets and mining knowledge directly from the privacy-preserving concepts as the next steps.
arxiv-2511-22317:
Cristiano, D'Antonio, Giglio, Mazzeo, and Romano, distributed systems researchers, move blockchain rollup sequencing inside trusted hardware. Rollups process transactions off the main chain through a sequencer. A dishonest sequencer can reorder or censor transactions; running it inside a Trusted Execution Environment such as Intel SGX promises integrity, but someone must verify the enclave is genuine. Their design pairs TEE-secured sequencers with decentralized attestation, so independent validators check the hardware proofs instead of trusting a single operator's claim.

The evaluation prices the security honestly. Wrapping the sequencer in SGX raises batch latency from roughly 2.5 to 3.5 seconds to over 25 seconds in their setup, and throughput falls from about 25 transactions per second to 7 or 8 with attestation costs included. Rollup designers get measured numbers for the trade between verifiable sequencing and speed.
arxiv-2511-22417:
Medvedev, Proskurnikov, and Zhusubaliyev design a feedback controller delivering a drug in repeated equal doses at regular intervals. Many treatments, from process control to medicine, need a steady effect level maintained by actions rather than a continuous feed. Their controller adjusts both dose size and spacing using measurements. It serves a smooth positive nonlinear plant of Wiener structure. In that structure, a linear dynamic part feeds a static nonlinearity.

The design builds a discrete map of the plant's state just before each dose and stabilises its fixed point, the desired steady dosing cycle. Stability guarantees a basin of attraction around the cycle, and the modulation functions' slopes set how fast disturbances die out. Applied to the muscle relaxant atracurium in closed-loop anaesthesia, using patient-specific models fitted to clinical data, the controller reduced underdosing events compared with the standard regimen.
arxiv-2511-22617:
Galindez-Acosta and Giraldo-Huertas dissect why people trust AI for facts but humans socially. 102 Colombian university students judged 30 hypothetical scenarios, half epistemic, half social, choosing whether to trust an AI or a human informant. They fitted a Bayesian hierarchical sequential sampling model, splitting each decision into a drift rate, how fast evidence accumulates, a starting bias, and caution.

Context-dependent trust was driven almost entirely by drift rate. In epistemic scenarios mean drift was strongly negative, at minus 1.26 in the model's units, evidence accumulating rapidly toward the AI, while social scenarios gave a positive mean of 0.70 favouring humans. Starting points stayed near neutral at 0.52 on the reported scale, so bias explained little. Drift rate also tracked stated confidence closely, average correlation 0.736 across people. They warn that fast, low-vigilance trust in AI for facts may be brittle, collapsing after visible errors.
arxiv-2511-22717:
Fatemiabhari, Nastase, Nunez, and Roychowdhury test a holographic complexity formula in a confining theory. Krylov complexity measures how fast an operator spreads through a system's state space, and a proposal equates its growth rate with a falling bulk particle's radial momentum. They apply it to the Anabalón-Ross soliton, a top-down string theory solution dual to a confining, gapped three-dimensional gauge theory from a twisted compactification of maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills.

They solve the probe particle's radial trajectory exactly, in elliptic functions, extending earlier asymptotic expansions. Unlike the conformal case, where momentum grows monotonically, here momentum and complexity oscillate, the particle reflecting off the geometry's infrared end-of-space. The oscillation is read as a holographic signature of the Hilbert space truncation that confinement, with the ultraviolet cutoff, imposes. The calculation is a test showing how spread-momentum duality changes when the dual theory confines.
arxiv-2511-23317:
D'Achille and colleagues study Voronoi percolation on spaces built as products. Where random points carve the space into cells and each cell is colored black with some probability, asking when the black region merges into a unique unbounded cluster. The key quantity is the uniqueness threshold, the smallest coloring probability guaranteeing one cluster. And the team develops a method to show this threshold stays small even at tiny point intensities.

Their argument exploits the unbounded borders phenomenon of the ideal tessellation underneath the model. And they apply it to products of regular trees taken two or more at a time and to products of hyperbolic spaces, in both discrete and continuum versions. As a by-product they exhibit new non-amenable Cayley graphs whose factor-of-iid processes support a sparse unique infinite cluster, settling a recent question of Pete and Rokob in the affirmative.
arxiv-2512-00917:
Qian Wan, Yehui Hou, and Minyong Guo ask whether black hole photos can test new gravity ideas in a 2025 paper. Horizon-scale images of black holes may reveal more than the hole itself. They can probe black hole hair, extra fields a hole carries beyond mass, spin, and charge.

The team builds an analytic model of a thick, magnetized disk around a rotating black hole with scalar hair, in Horndeski theory. They then analyze what the disk would look like in a 230 gigahertz image. Comparing such images with telescope data could show whether scalar hair leaves a visible mark.
arxiv-2512-01017:
Xinhang Li, Jingbo Zhou, Pengfei Luo, Yixiong Xiao, and Tong Xu present ChartAnchor in a 2025 paper on chart understanding. Multimodal models are getting better at reading charts, but judging that skill takes hard benchmarks. Chart grounding links a chart's visual appearance with its structured meaning, in both directions.

A grounded model must output a symbolic specification that faithfully captures the chart's intent. It must also recover the underlying data table, with precise values and relationships. ChartAnchor tests that structural-semantic fidelity and data recovery together. Strong grounding would let AI tools rebuild editable, trustworthy charts from mere images.
arxiv-2512-01217:
A 2025 physics paper reports an experimental witness of high-order exceptional points tied to quantum jumps. An exceptional point is a special setting where a system's states and energies merge. It produces strange effects linked to one-way behavior, sharp measurement, and topological dynamics.

The Liouvillian version describes open quantum systems, where energy loss and decoherence from quantum jumps shape the dynamics. It can capture the full evolution of such a system, not just averages.
