The experiment witnesses points of this kind at high order, induced by quantum jumps. Confirming them in the lab opens new ground for non-Hermitian quantum devices.
arxiv-2512-01717:
Ornig and Carlsson predict white-light flare emission from a grid of models. Much of a solar flare's energy may leave as continuum light. White light can be seen from the ground, which makes it prized. Its prevalence in flares is still not settled.

The F-CHROMA grid models flares driven by electron beams alone. The pair ask which runs emit white light and why. Traits that switch emission on or off are mapped. Ground observers can then use white-light rates to infer beam traits in real flares. Ground-based white-light patrols run nightly, so model rates translate at once into how many flares those patrols should log each season.
arxiv-2512-01817:
Zihao Yuan works on a basic question in statistics: how sure can we be about an average computed from data that are not independent? His 2025 working paper builds bounds, called concentration inequalities, for averages formed from a sequence where each new value depends on the ones before it.

The bounds are self-normalized, meaning they scale the average by a spread computed from the sample itself, so no outside knowledge of the true variance is needed. Yuan covers sequences with a martingale-difference structure and also weaker mixing conditions that include many processes older tools excluded. Such bounds help researchers judge when an estimate from dependent data can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-02317:
The rarest events in physics, a dark matter particle bumping a nucleus, or a decay that may never happen, need detectors of extreme sensitivity. S. Das and seven co-authors review in 2025 how cryogenic detectors, cooled near absolute zero, serve direct searches for these rare events.

Cold detectors reach energy thresholds down at the electron-volt scale and resolve tiny deposits of energy with fine precision. The review covers dark matter direct detection, coherent neutrino scattering, neutrinoless double-beta decay, and searches for fractionally charged particles. One technology serving four frontiers makes cryogenics a shared foundation of the hunt for new physics.
arxiv-2512-02417:
World models let self-driving systems imagine the road ahead inside a learned simulator, then plan within it. Huiqian Li and four co-authors improve in 2025 on the usual approach by embedding real vehicle dynamics into the world model, instead of learning motion purely from data.

Existing methods map high-dimensional observations into compact latent spaces and learn policies inside them, which can produce physically implausible imagined futures. Grounding the latent dynamics in actual vehicle physics should make predictions more faithful and decisions safer. Better world models are a route to autonomous driving that can rehearse rare situations without risking real ones.
arxiv-2512-02617:
Rutger Campbell and Noleen Köhler study laminar set systems, families of sets that never partly overlap. In such a family, any two sets are either separate or one contains the other, like a tree of folders. These systems sit at the core of modular, split, and bi-join decompositions of graphs.

The pair examines what counting quantifiers, logic tools that count how many elements fit a rule, can express about laminar systems. The results clarify which properties of these tidy structures logic can capture. That helps both logicians and algorithm designers who lean on such decompositions. Tree like sets are rare in raw data, so tools that spot them earn their keep in code bases.
arxiv-2512-02717:
Abdullah Shahin and three co-authors build modeling tools for hydrogen energy systems. Hydrogen plays a growing role in the shift toward climate neutral energy. Models built for natural gas miss what makes hydrogen systems distinct, the authors argue.

Hydrogen pipes couple tightly with electrolyzers, fuel cells, and electrically driven compressors. A gas only model cannot capture those electric links. Their port-Hamiltonian approach treats energy flow across the whole system in one structured framework. Better models help engineers design hydrogen networks that are efficient, stable, and safe to operate. Pipes, wires, and tanks act as one in a hydrogen plant, and the frame treats them as one from the start.
arxiv-2512-02817:
Sai Koneru and three co-authors build a lecture companion that translates teaching in every form at once. Global online learning makes localizing lectures a pressing challenge. Lecture materials mix spoken audio with visual slides, so a text only translation drops much of the lesson.

Their system preserves all modalities: readable text, slides for visual understanding, and speech for listening. Students get the full class in their own language, not a stripped summary. Tools of this kind widen access to strong teaching for students far from the lecturer's country and tongue. Full class packs in one's own tongue can close the gap for kids far from big schools with deep staff rolls.
arxiv-2512-03017:
Nikolai Erokhovets links graph cycles on exotic polyhedra to knots and links in three dimensional space. The polyhedra are ideal right angled hyperbolic polytopes of finite volume. On their graphs, he studies Eulerian cycles that never cross themselves transversally.

Any such cycle in the graph of one of these polytopes yields a hyperbolic link, he proves. The link's complement is built from four copies of the polytope, glued by its checkerboard coloring. Results of this kind connect combinatorics, geometry, and knot theory in one concrete construction. Glue rules that turn graphs to links give knot work new stock. Old claims gain new tests from that stock, a trade both fields gain from.
arxiv-2512-03217:
Yang-Mills theory describes the strong force, but it is hard to solve. Tolga Domurcukgül, Hao Geng, Mendel Nguyen, and Mithat Ünsal build a broader version in this 2025 work. Their version has two settings that can be tuned.

By tuning them, the theory slides between a simpler self-dual form and the full physical theory. One setting controls local fluctuations, the other controls instanton weight. Both fade at high energy, a trait called asymptotic freedom. A bridge between the two forms may make hard problems easier to attack. A tunable bridge between theories lets scholars study hard cases through easier limits.
arxiv-2512-04117:
A digital twin is only useful while it still matches the physical system it mirrors, and physical systems drift: parts wear, maintenance changes them, users err. Joost Mertens and Joachim Denil tackle that drift in a 2025 software engineering preprint. Their idea is to reuse the validation machinery of model-based design, continuously, rather than validating a simulation once and trusting it forever.

The approach computes validation metrics comparing twin and system. Anomalies in those metrics act as alarms that the physical side has changed. Detection is only half the job. The twin is then repaired by estimating new parameters from historical data. A port-style gantry crane serves as the case study. The authors offer the method as a generic pattern for cyber-physical systems whose twins are simulation models, where staying valid is a process, not an event.
arxiv-2512-04317:
Nikhil Deveshwar, Abhejit Rajagopal, and Peder Larson present a new version of the fast Fourier transform. The transform is a core math tool in signal work. Their version mixes high and low precision number formats. The goal is to save computing effort with little loss. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the method on MRI scan data. In MRI, this transform helps turn raw signals into clear pictures.

The design groups numbers into small blocks. Each block shares one scale factor. One broad scale applies to the whole set. Key wave values are stored in few bits ahead of time. The team ran tests on two public scan sets. They ran the transform forward and in reverse. They checked how quality shifts with format, image size, and block size. Depth of the number format proved to be the main limit. Block size set a clear trade, with larger blocks keeping more detail.
arxiv-2512-04717:
Aiqin Yang, Dian Jin, Mingkang Liu, and co-authors screened a giant materials library to find crystals that turn light into current with unusual strength, especially in infrared light. Such nonlinear optical materials power sensors and solar devices, yet strong candidates are rare and usually found one at a time. Their 2025 arXiv paper applies a multi-step filter to the Materials Project database, which holds well over a hundred thousand entries.

The filter passed a few thousand candidates to detailed quantum calculations. From those, a few dozen materials showed a shift current response above the team's strength bar. Layered crystals with threefold symmetry and heavy elements such as tellurium and antimony stood out. A handful peaked right in the infrared band, prized for night vision and heat sensing. The screening recipe shows how brute-force computing can shorten the hunt for optoelectronic materials.
arxiv-2512-04817:
I. Pillitteri, S. Bellotti, S. Benatti, and co-authors report new X-ray monitoring of L 98-59, a nearby red dwarf star hosting six Earth-like planets, two of them in the habitable zone. High-energy light from a star can strip or cook a planet's atmosphere, so the star's long-term mood matters for habitability. Earlier observations caught the star flaring above a steady glow. Their 2025 arXiv paper adds two short XMM-Newton visits from a survey tracking activity cycles.

In late 2024, the star's quiet X-ray brightness sat far below the level seen a few years earlier. The change hints at a long activity cycle, like the Sun's eleven-year rhythm, written in X-rays. If the cycle is real, the planets' radiation dose rises and falls over years. Knowing that rhythm helps modelers judge whether air and water can survive on those worlds, and when to observe them.
arxiv-2512-04917:
Matteo Masoni, Vincenzo Palermo, and Marco Gabiccini test whether race trajectories planned with disturbances in mind actually help professional drivers. Planning usually chases the perfect lap on a perfect track. Real driving adds gusts, grip changes, and small errors. Their 2025 arXiv paper compares three reference lines in a dynamic driving simulator. One line is nominal and time-optimal. One keeps wider margins to the track edges. One keeps wider margins to tire saturation.

Two professional drivers ran all three lines plus free driving with no reference. The car was a high-performance model on a virtual track. Lap time and steering effort scored the trade-offs. All lines shared the same speed goal with a small smoothness term. The only difference was the safety margin baked in. The study shows how robustness planned on paper survives contact with human hands, guiding racing and road-car trajectory design.
arxiv-2512-05017:
Andreas Brandhuber, Graham Brown, Paolo Pichini, Gabriele Travaglini, and Pablo Vives Matasan develop a new way to compute scattering in relativistic quantum field theory through the Magnus expansion. Scattering is usually calculated from the S-matrix directly; the team works with an operator whose exponential gives the S-matrix, and computes its entries, Magnus amplitudes, without passing through amplitudes. The payoff is a formalism free of inflated classical terms that plague standard calculations.

At the simplest level, Magnus amplitudes are built from forward- and backward-running propagators weighted by specific numerical factors. At loop level, one-loop results follow entirely from higher-point tree calculations. The authors conjecture the pattern persists for diagrams that matter in the classical limit, and they check it in an example. Because Magnus amplitudes connect to the radial action, the work lays groundwork for extracting classical physics, such as gravitational-wave signals, efficiently.
arxiv-2512-05117:
Prakhar Kaushik, Shravan Chaudhari, Ankit Vaidya, Rama Chellappa, and Alan Yuille report a regularity in deep neural networks. Whatever they are trained for, their weights settle into much the same low-dimensional patterns. The team analyzed the weight matrices of over a thousand models. These included language models adapted with add-on modules, vision transformers, and more. Each matrix was broken into its main directions of variation.

Across starting points, tasks, and domains, the same few spectral directions capture most of the variation, and networks exploit a sparse shared subspace. The finding suggests trained models are far less individual than their size implies. If the universal subspace can be found without training fleets of models, the payoff could be large. It would mean easier model merging, better multi-task learning, and cheaper training and inference. It would also mean a smaller carbon footprint for large-scale artificial intelligence.
arxiv-2512-05617:
Salvador Cardona-Serra sets out a roadmap for designing organic memristors, materials whose resistance depends on their past and can act like artificial synapses. Man made oxides lead the field today. But molecular and polymer based versions could bring easy tuning by chemistry, flexibility, cheap processing, and friendliness to living tissue. What is missing is theory that predicts how a molecule's structure shapes its switching behavior.

The 2025 paper argues for a multiscale computing approach. Quantum chemistry and molecular dynamics, among other tools, should be joined into one method for design. Three switching routes are examined in depth: ions drifting through the material, redox reactions that change charge states, and conduction effects in chiral molecules. For each, the paper weighs the promise and the hurdles. The aim is a guided path from promising molecule to working synaptic material, found on the computer before costly lab work begins.
arxiv-2512-05717:
Sofiia Chorna and five co-authors compare what the universal machine learning potentials for atoms have learned. These models aim to predict the energy landscape of any chemical structure, and each compresses chemical knowledge into internal features. Their 2025 study asks whether their inner pictures of chemistry agree, by measuring how well one model's features can be rebuilt from another's.

The answer is that the pictures differ a lot: cross model rebuilding errors are large, so each model encodes chemical space in its own way. Among close variants of one design, the pattern depends on the training set, target, and protocol. Fine tuning a model does not erase its start: a strong bias from pre-training survives in the features. The team also shows how per atom features stack into whole structure features, each layer adding fresh information. Choosing a potential thus means choosing a distinct view of chemistry.
arxiv-2512-05817:
Zhengquan Luo and Zhiqiang Xu give dataset distillation a unified theory. The practice squeezes a huge training set into a tiny synthetic one that teaches nearly as well. Methods match gradients, distributions, or training paths. Each rests on different assumptions, so why they all work was unclear. Their framework recasts all three families under one lens: generalization error.

Two laws follow. A scaling law bounds the error for a single training configuration and shows how it falls as the distilled set grows, explaining the saturation users see in practice. A coverage law says the needed distilled size grows in direct proportion to the diversity of configurations it must serve, and the bound is tight from both sides. The analysis also shows the rival matching methods are interchangeable surrogates shrinking the same error. Experiments across methods and settings confirm both laws.
arxiv-2512-06017:
Laurence Liang asks a disarmingly simple question: can a frontier vision language model, asked nicely, tell you the joint angles of a robot arm from a photograph? Joint readings would aid safety, and a visual check could verify robot policies. Liang evaluates leading vision language models on synthetic and real data.

One result is negative. Neither test time scaling, letting the model think longer, nor parameter scaling, using a bigger model, reliably improved the joint angle predictions. The errors did not melt away with more compute, the way they do on many language benchmarks. The bottleneck is the visual skill itself, not reasoning effort. Baselines like this are how a field calibrates its expectations: the off the shelf robot pose reader is not here yet. Knowing that early steers effort toward the representations that might.
arxiv-2512-06217:
Felipe Costa and six co authors work on chips that read out signals for high energy physics tests, where noise and radiation both cause trouble. Their chip must pick out the middle value among a set of noisy signals, a step that helps cancel noise shared across channels. They built two circuits for that task and made each in a form that can stand up to radiation faults.

The team then layered three guard schemes over the circuits: two forms of triple backup, and one that spreads backup copies over time. They compared chip area, power use, and delay for each pairing. One circuit stayed lean under the simple backup scheme but drew far more power under the stronger one. The time spread scheme gave solid fault cover at a fair cost. The findings guide the design of read out chips that must work for years near harsh beams.
arxiv-2512-06517:
Shifa Sulaiman, Akash Bachhar, Ming Shen, and Simon Bogh give a prosthetic hand eyes and a plan. A camera watches the scene in front of the hand. A vision method based on nested boxes picks out the target object and frames it, while a point cloud records its surface shape in space. The hand must then decide where each fingertip should land so the grip holds.

Candidate paths for the fingers are grown by a random tree search that favors short, smooth routes. The team picks the end poses closest to the object's surface, with each finger planned on its own, so the grip adapts to odd shapes rather than forcing one preset grasp. A damped solver turns those poses into joint angles, which are sent to the finger motors. The pipeline runs in real time and adjusts as the scene changes, aiming at natural grasping in messy daily settings.
arxiv-2512-06717:
David Sherwell argues that the laws of gases can be read straight off the randomness of their raw data, before any probability is assumed. Take a list of the energies of many helium atoms at one instant. Suppose that list is random in the strict algorithmic sense, Martin Lof randomness. Count its Kolmogorov complexity, and Sherwell shows the gas's Helmholtz free energy follows. With it comes all of thermostatics.

In this framing, disorder and entropy get objective definitions tied to the data itself, not to an observer's ignorance. A condition for equal prior probability falls out rather than being assumed, and the quantum statistics of fermions follows from the randomness requirement. The introductory study treats a cool, thin gas of helium in both quantum and classical regimes. It also draws fresh light on irreversible change and an objective second law.
arxiv-2512-06817:
Chengzi Jiang leads a team confirming two small planets that cross in front of cool red dwarf stars, first spotted by the TESS space telescope. Both worlds are larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, and both sit where liquid water could in principle exist. Rather than rely on heavier follow-up methods, the team checks the planets by watching their transits in several colors of light. A true planet dims its star in a pattern fake signals rarely copy.

Data came from TESS plus ground telescopes, including a fast multi-color camera on a large telescope in the Canary Islands. Careful joint fitting confirmed both planets and pinned down their sizes and orbits, one circling in about nineteen days, the other in about thirteen. Their estimated makeup suggests worlds rich in lighter materials, perhaps water or gas. Both are strong targets for future study of their air.
arxiv-2512-07517:
Loïse Attal, Cyril Falvo, and Pascal Parneix wrote this 2025 chemistry paper on how complex molecules move and absorb light. A molecule with many atoms has too many motions to track in full. Heat makes the bookkeeping even harder.

The authors extend a method called the effective bath state approach. It watches a few key motions directly and treats the rest as a bath. The bath is compressed into a small set of effective energy states. That compression makes calculations at real temperatures far more feasible. The new version also allows polynomial couplings in the bath coordinates. They first test it on a model system with ten vibrational modes. It reproduces infrared spectra resolved by temperature and tracks energy moving between modes. They then apply it to phenylacetylene, a realistic molecule. The work points toward practical spectra for molecules once out of reach.
arxiv-2512-07817:
Miguel Teixeira, Mohamed Foudad, and Paul Williams wrote this 2025 fluid dynamics paper. Stratified flow, layered by density, can break into instability under shear. They study parallel flow whose shear plane tilts at any angle to the vertical.

The analysis follows the classic analytical approach of Miles and Howard. Two-dimensional wobbles, thought to be the most dangerous, are the focus. For vertical shear, their general setup returns the famous Miles-Howard stability rule. For tilted shear, no clean stability condition emerges from the formulation. That silence confirms what earlier studies had expected to find. The work is not only negative, though, in its conclusions. Howard's semicircle theorem extends to the tilted case in their hands. A new upper bound on how fast instability can grow also appears. That bound extends Howard's classic estimate for vertical flow. Published numerical results agree with the new bound, they report.
arxiv-2512-08517:
Xiaoyong Chu, Josef Pradler, and Daris Samart, particle theorists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They work in SIMP scenarios, where dark matter consists of stable dark pions that set their own abundance through three to two reactions in the early universe. Recent calculations showed shallow bound states of two dark pions could strongly affect that story, but nobody had proven such states form.

The authors settle the question inside a chiral unitary framework, solving a scattering equation and tracking the two pion amplitude in the complex energy plane. A pole below the two pion threshold appears across a definite range of the pion mass to decay constant ratio, proving a scalar bound state exists. They extract its strength and the wave function at the origin, which controls bound state assisted annihilation and decay. Simple variational estimates agree within modest factors, supporting the assumptions earlier phenomenology had to make.
arxiv-2512-08617:
Lifeng Han, Paul Rayson, Andrew Moore, Goran Nenadic, and Suzan Verberne, language technology researchers, posted a tutorial overview on arXiv in December 2025. It maps language processing for healthcare: what has been achieved, and what comes next. Earlier reviews skip key tasks, from synthetic data for privacy to explainable clinical systems.

The tutorial organizes the field in three layers. One layer covers data and resources, from annotation rules to synthetic data. A second covers core tasks like entity recognition and coding, toward explainable health AI. A third covers patients: public involvement, health literacy, and decision support. A hands on session lets attendees try the tools. No prior knowledge is assumed. As hospitals drown in text, the tutorial argues, this specialty is becoming essential.
arxiv-2512-08917:
Gabriele Benomio and Rita Teixeira da Costa study the Maxwell equations for electric fields around rotating Kerr black holes. The equations are written for field parts in a special frame tied to the Kerr geometry. Extreme parts decouple into Teukolsky equations, while middle parts form a coupled system of transport and elliptic equations.

Assuming control of the extreme parts, the authors prove uniform boundedness, with no loss of detail, and decay estimates for the middle parts. That result covers the full range from sub extremal to extremal black holes. Their method builds a decoupled system for modified middle parts and splits solutions into dynamic and steady parts. The steady part is set by electric and magnetic charges read from data at the horizon. In the sub extremal case, prior work supplies the needed control, giving full results. The extremal case remains part on a stated conjecture.
arxiv-2512-09017:
Mila Winter Granic and Eliot Quataert present a time dependent model of accretion disks around black holes. The model covers a wide range of black hole masses and is applied to late time emission in tidal disruption events and in luminous fast blue optical transients. It generalizes past work.

Outflows during rapid accretion, loss of mass and angular momentum during debris circularization, and heating of the outer disk by the inner flow are all included. A range of viscous stress models is also allowed. Many late time plateaus in disruption events can be explained by disks born with a wide spread in angular momentum. Standard thin disk collapse predicts plateaus that are far too faint, favoring magnetically dominated disk models instead. The same models can explain late optical and ultraviolet emission in a well known fast transient,.
arxiv-2512-09117: Luciano Floridi, Yiyang Jia, and Fernando Tohme present a formal categorical framework for analyzing how humans and large language models turn content into truth evaluated propositions about a space of possible worlds. Using that framework, they argue that large language models do not solve the classic symbol grounding problem. Instead, they circumvent it, achieving their results by a route that avoids the grounding step the problem demands.
arxiv-2512-09417:
Yanan Wang leads a team presenting DirectSwap, a method for swapping a person's whole head in video while keeping pose, expression, body motion, and scene intact. Progress has been blocked by missing training data: footage cannot show two different people performing the same motion, so there are no paired examples or frame-aligned ground truth. Earlier methods learned from masked reconstructions of the same person, which limits what they can change.

The authors build a synthesis pipeline that decouples identity from expression, keeping the expression-bearing face regions under small consistent distortions while regenerating the rest of the head with a new identity. That yields paired cross-identity videos with footage as targets, forming HeadSwapBench, a dataset for both training and benchmarking. Their mask-free DirectSwap model, trained on those pairs, beat masked same-identity training under matched settings, especially where the head's outline changes in both directions.
arxiv-2512-09617:
Hubert Kompanowski and colleagues present FROMAT, a lightweight method for changing the appearance of objects in multiview diffusion models. Such models generate views of a scene from angles without explicit geometry, but they offer little control over material, texture, or style compared with meshes or radiance fields.

The method learns to combine an object's identity, taken from an input image, with appearance cues from a reference image. It produces multi-view output with the material while the geometry and view consistency are preserved. It works by running three diffusion runs, for the original object, the reference, and the target. Reverse sampling gathers a subset of layer-wise self-attention features from the first two to steer the third. Only a few training examples are needed to teach a pretrained multiview model this appearance awareness. The authors present it as a simple step toward multiview output with appearances.
arxiv-2512-10017:
Delaram Moradi, Narad Rampersad, and Jeffrey Shallith measure the complexity of building automata from automatic sequences. A k-automatic sequence is generated by a finite automaton reading the base k digits of each index. The authors construct automata for basic relations on such sequences and count their states. They also study basic moves on automatic sequences and the state complexity those moves cost. A central thread links subword complexity of an interior sequence to state complexity of its linear subsequences.

The team settles a recent question by Zantema and Bosma about linear subsequences when digits are fed most significant first. They also measure runtime for building these automata via Büchi arithmetic. The work is basic to the thriving practice of automatic theorem proving in combinatorics on words, where software decides properties of sequences by building exactly these automata.
arxiv-2512-10317:
Ziyu Wang leads a team translating human written mathematics into machine checked proofs, using an intermediate chain of states. Formalizing a proof in Lean is hard for language models because informal proofs leap between logical steps, while Lean demands every proof state and tactic spelled out. The authors' key move is to not generate tactics directly. First the system extracts a chain of states: a sequence of formal proof states aligned with the informal argument's logical skeleton. Then tactics are generated to cross each gap between neighboring states, a far smaller and better specified problem.

The team built dedicated datasets and benchmarks for both stages, plus an interactive framework supporting tactic generation from a given state. Empirically the method substantially outperforms existing baselines in proof success rate.
arxiv-2512-10517:
Maurice Rohr and co-authors release Pulse3DFace, the first dataset of three-dimensional blood pulsation maps of the face. Such maps show how the pulse moves through facial skin. And they can be used to make synthetic videos that improve and test camera-based pulse reading, a contact-free method that infers heart signals from subtle colour changes.

The dataset covers fifteen subjects filmed at thirty frames per second from twenty-three viewpoints with an ordinary colour camera, alongside true pulse reference measurements. Facial scans built from the video feed processed maps that fit the FLAME head model, carrying signal quality, local pulse strength, and phase data. The authors check the lighting conditions, the consistency of the maps. And whether the maps capture real physiology in the face and neck, including multi-view ways to fight lighting effects.
arxiv-2512-10717:
Xenia Miscouridou, Francesca Panero, and Antreas Laos model communities in networks that never sit still. Groups in social and other temporal networks are born, persist, merge, and dissolve, and members often belong to several groups at once. The authors propose a Bayesian nonparametric model for sparse, time-evolving networks that lets all of that happen naturally.

The model is built from vectors of completely random measures, coupled through a latent Markov process that steers how each node's affiliations drift over time. It captures the heavy-tailed degree patterns of real networks, where a few hubs hold most connections, and generalises earlier overlapping block models into the sparse, scale-free regime. The authors prove asymptotic results about sparsity and degree spread, build an approximate inference method to recover community histories. And show on synthetic and real networks that the recovered group trajectories are accurate and readable.
arxiv-2512-11517:
Franco Fagnola and Federico Girotti give a systematic account of irreducibility for quantum Markov semigroups, the math models of quantum systems that evolve while leaking into an environment. Irreducibility, roughly the inability to confine the motion to a smaller corner of the state space, shapes whether a system settles to a unique steady state. Its links to other dynamical traits were scattered across the literature.

The authors characterise irreducibility in several equivalent ways and relate it to primitivity, positivity improvement, and relaxation toward equilibrium. When the semigroup has an invariant density, irreducibility, primitivity, and relaxation toward a faithful steady state turn out to be equivalent. For the common uniformly continuous case, they supply useful checks phrased through the operators in the generator. The exposition gathers known results with elementary proofs, adds new ones, and covers both finite and endless in extent systems.
arxiv-2512-11617:
Sasha Glendinning, Susana N Gomes, and Marie-Therese Wolfram ask a sly math question: how should a liar steer a crowd? In their model, one agent shows fake views to others, hoping to push the group to agree on the liar goal view. Each person updates toward what they see.

The team frames the best lie as a control problem and tries several rules that keep lies near the liar true view or otherwise socially plausible. They show what snap controls do in each case. They then scale up to a Boltzmann style model for crowds, with Fokker-Planck limits, and test the math with simulations. The results map when one voice can quietly move a whole group.
arxiv-2512-11717:
Simonas Draukšas offers a cleaner way to handle mixing angles in particle physics calculations. Mixing matrices, like the quark mixing matrix, normally need their own correction terms, called counterterms, in loop calculations. Those terms add bulk and room for error.

The trick is a change of basis. In the right basis there are no mixing matrices at all, so no counterterms are needed. The recipe is stated with self energy terms only, and it works for any model or process. As a test, Draukšas computes the one loop rates for W boson decay to hadrons under several known schemes and the new one. The same basis rule is applied to the Weinberg angle for full consistency.
arxiv-2512-12717:
Mattia Catellani, Marta Gabbi, and Lorenzo Sabattini present HMPCC, a human aware control method for robot teams covering an unknown area, in a 2025 paper. Coverage control spreads robots to survey a space, but classic methods assume known or convex spaces and static targets, and they stumble when people move through the scene. Safety around non-cooperative humans is a core concern.

Their framework uses model predictive control, which plans over a short horizon, and feeds in predictions of human motion. Robots then coordinate proactively and adapt as conditions change. Areas of interest are modeled as a Gaussian mixture. Team members work in a fully decentralized way with no explicit communication, vital where links are hostile or limited. Tests showed more efficient coverage.
arxiv-2512-13017:
Vaibhav Rajoriya, Prateek Priyaranjan Pradhan, and Ketan Rajawat develop training methods for convex optimization problems that carry functional constraints, limits stated as functions that must stay below set levels. Such problems arise in machine learning and control, where plain gradient steps can break the constraints.

Their hinge-proximal stochastic gradient methods handle noisy gradient data while respecting those limits. The name reflects the tools involved: a hinge-like penalty for constraint breaches and proximal steps that keep updates well behaved. The work adds practical algorithms for a class of constrained problems where both the goal and the limits are convex, and data arrive in random batches.
arxiv-2512-13117:
Kenji Bekki, Kenji Furuya, and Takashi Shimonishi present new galaxy simulations that track where molecules sit in gas and ice phases. Recent telescopes have found that molecule abundances vary a lot between galaxies of different types. Explaining those patterns needs chemistry inside the simulation itself.

Their code follows dust formation, growth, and destruction along with interstellar chemistry for 400 molecule species. Given local gas and dust conditions, it predicts abundances cloud by cloud. Early results map water, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and methanol ices in a Milky Way like disk. Dust temperature and elemental mix prove key controls on the patterns.
arxiv-2512-13517:
Raymond Khazoum and co-authors build a deep learning model of mental rotation, the skill of comparing objects seen from unlike views. Their design draws on past lab studies plus new tests in virtual reality. In those tests, people could at times handle the objects while they compared them.

The model has three stacked parts that build 3D maps, turn them into symbol-like object forms, and choose rotation steps. It matches human scores, response times, and behavior in the authors' tests and in past work. Tests that remove one part at a time show each part is needed. The work links neural, spatial, and symbolic views of how minds reason about space.
arxiv-2512-13717:
Ekaterina Sysoykova and co-authors build a privacy-preserving method to detect epileptic seizures from EEG data. Deep learning tools for this task usually need large, centralized, labeled data sets. In real clinics, EEG data are scarce, patient-specific, split across sites, and barred from pooling by privacy rules.

Their two-stage federated few-shot framework first fine-tunes a pretrained biosignal transformer across simulated hospital sites without moving EEG records. Next, it personalizes the classifier for each patient with only five labeled EEG segments. Personalized models reached a mean balanced accuracy of 0.77 and a weighted F1 of 0.73 across four sites. The results suggest patient-adaptive detection can work under real privacy limits.
arxiv-2512-14517:
C. Pezzotti and eight co-authors revisit how a star's spin, age, and magnetic activity fit together, using the sharpest stellar data available. Space telescopes now measure star vibrations, a method called asteroseismology, giving precise ages and masses. The team matched sixty-six well-measured Sun-like stars from the Kepler LEGACY sample against an X-ray sky survey and found thirteen detections.

Those thirteen stars anchored updated activity-age and activity-rotation formulas. Feeding the new relations into a star-planet interaction code matched observations better for seven stars. The changes slightly altered estimates of how planets in the so-called radius valley lose mass, but the overall picture stayed similar.
arxiv-2512-14917:
Changshu Liu and three coauthors test whether large language models can truly reason about code as it appears in the wild. Most code reasoning tests use tidy snippets. Real code has calls between functions, deep nesting, and complex data types, all of which could break a model's reasoning.

The team built a dataset of 1200 reasoning problems from older benchmarks and from popular Python projects on GitHub. Their pipeline uses static and dynamic analysis to handle compound and custom data types that earlier tests skipped. Each problem is sorted into lower or higher complexity by a vote over nine measures of code difficulty. That sorting shows most older test problems fall in the lower group. The dataset thus gives a more honest yardstick for how models reason about real software.
arxiv-2512-15717:
Dipankar Das studies bid shading in real time advertising auctions through minority game theory in a 2025 paper, dated December 2. In first price auctions run at impression level, advertisers often bid below their true value to improve payoff, a practice called bid shading. Classic theory, built for ascending auctions, does not capture this setting well.

Using large scale auction data from the Yahoo Webscope data set, Das combines minority game ideas with clustering and variance scaling diagnostics. Bidders appear to split hourly ad slots into submarkets and bid where they expect to be in the numerical minority. That endogenous shading cuts spending while raising win probability, shaping prices in high frequency markets.
arxiv-2512-16017:
Yumeng Xue and five co-authors address a chart design problem in this visualization paper, released on arXiv in 2025. Density plots summarize huge sets of lines, such as paths or time series, but they blur the paths themselves. Rare odd lines vanish, and smooth trends become hard to follow.

The team adds a bin-based lighting model that separates structure from density. A new score ranks each line by how unusual it is, and lighting in the brightness channel then highlights either main trends or rare outliers, as the analyst chooses. Tests on real data showed details that simpler plots missed, with less color distortion than standard shading. The method stays interactive for up to 10,000 lines.
arxiv-2512-16317:
Arther Tian and five co-authors redesign rewards for shared AI computing in an arXiv paper posted in 2025. Decentralized language model inference lets a network of machines answer queries without a central provider. Proof of Quality replaces heavy cryptographic checking with consensus on answer quality, but the original scheme ignored that nodes have very different costs.

The cost-aware version scores answers with token-level F1, learned evaluators, and GPT judgments, then pays nodes through a linear reward balancing quality against cost. Simulations over 5,000 rounds showed the scheme rewarding high-quality, low-cost models and efficient evaluators while penalizing slow, weak nodes. One finding surprised: a similarity-based evaluator tracked ground truth far better than cross-encoders, and the biggest models tested were also the most efficient per unit of latency.
arxiv-2512-16517:
Leonor N L Simoes and four co-authors study ghostly particles shaping the universe in an arXiv paper posted in 2025. Neutrinos have tiny masses, but across cosmic distances they should smooth out structure. Using the FLAMINGO simulations, the team classified the cosmic web into voids, sheets, filaments, and clusters to see exactly where neutrinos bite.

Heavier neutrinos shrink the volume held by both clusters and voids, shifting the density distribution toward higher, narrower values, a sign of delayed structure formation. The team also built minimum spanning trees from simulated subhalos at DESI-like densities. About 70 percent of tree edges lie in filaments at every neutrino mass, and edge lengths at different scales trace different environments. Baryonic physics leaves a distinct fingerprint from neutrinos, so the tree could classify large-scale structure in real surveys.
arxiv-2512-17217:
Hiroki Shibata and Dominik Köppl work on LZ78, a classic method for compressing data that sits behind formats such as compress and GIF. Most past work splits a whole file into pieces from the start. The pair instead study a setup where an index is built once, and later a user asks for the split of just one chosen substring.

Their algorithm answers such queries while staying inside compressed space, so the data never has to be fully expanded. The cost is a slowdown that grows only with the logarithm of the size, close to the best possible time. The same approach covers close variants of LZ78 as well. Work like this helps tools search and reuse parts of very large compressed files.
arxiv-2512-17517:
Siemen Brussee and five co-authors release PathBench-MIL, a workbench for a style of AI that learns from whole tissue slides. In multiple instance learning, a pathologist labels a giant slide as sick or healthy without marking each patch, and the model must learn from that bag-level label. Dozens of such models exist, yet labs build and test them in incompatible ways.

PathBench-MIL automates the full pipeline, from slide preparation and feature extraction to the final aggregation step. One shared setting file drives every run, and built-in viewers show what each model attends to. Dozens of models and feature extractors can be benchmarked the same way across data sets. The open code aims to make pathology AI results easier to repeat and compare.
arxiv-2512-18317:
Vincent Bezold leads a five author team putting a learning controller in charge of factory air compressors, with proof it can be trusted. Compressed air eats a large share of plant power, and set rules often keep pressure higher than needed. Their reinforcement learning policy runs the system under real limits while saving energy.

A three layer checking kit probes the policy with tweaked inputs, slope tests, and feature credit scores, so staff can see why it acts. Across several compressor setups the policy stayed within safe bounds, looked ahead to coming demand, and cut energy by about 4 percent against the plant's own controller. Pressure and forecast data drove most calls, an honest pattern engineers can accept.
arxiv-2512-18617:
Hollis Williams of the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology tests semiclassical gravity. In that theory, a spacetime is sourced by the stress energy of quantum matter. In the slow motion limit it becomes the Schrödinger-Newton equation, long assumed consistent in weak fields. Williams reexamines that assumption for a massive particle in a spatial superposition, with states properly normalized.

At leading order, no change to the Newtonian potential appears. One order higher, the picture breaks. The semiclassical coupling adds state dependent terms built from the superposition's mass density and mass current. Those terms scale differently from true relativistic corrections, with no Planck mass suppression. The mismatch is structural, not a small error. Sourcing the metric from expectation values alone, he concludes, cannot yield a consistent weak field expansion. Any viable version needs extra ingredients. The result sharpens a basic question: how can gravity and quantum matter coexist?
arxiv-2512-18817: Francesco Polizzi and Pietro Sabatino classify small quotients of surface braid groups, the groups that track how points move and swap places on a curved surface. For a compact Riemann surface of genus at least two, they take the pure braid group on two strands. A quotient counts as admissible when it does not factor through the simpler surface group. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, lists every admissible quotient whose target group has order at most 127, a complete census in that range.
arxiv-2512-18917:
Arjun R, Pratyush Prakash Patra, and A. V. Anil Kumar study a magnet where the two species push each other unevenly. In nonreciprocal systems, interactions break action-reaction symmetry, producing phases that cycle forever instead of settling. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Physical Review E, maps a two-species Blume-Capel model with a chemical-potential imbalance, mixing mean-field analysis with large Monte Carlo simulations.

Mean-field theory predicts disorder, a swapping limit-cycle phase, and static order, split by five kinds of bifurcation. In two dimensions, spiral defects wreck the global swapping, but an antisymmetric single-ion anisotropy tips the balance. It fills one species with vacancies, damps the nonreciprocal dynamics, and restores robust static order in the 2D Ising class. In three dimensions the swap phase yields to order through disorder. Vacancy control emerges as a practical knob for taming nonreciprocal matter.
arxiv-2512-19017:
Peng Yu and nine co-authors report a stronger superconducting diode effect in hybrid Josephson junctions. A diode of this kind lets supercurrent flow more easily one way than the other. Their devices sit on indium arsenide layers with aluminum grown on top, and the leads carry a regular pattern of holes.

Turning a top gate so it empties the electron gas near the holes made the one-way effect much larger, while the total supercurrent stayed intact. Theory ties the gain to a wider gap in how open the junction is for different electron bands. The result offers a practical knob for building nonreciprocal superconducting parts.
arxiv-2512-19317:
A. A. Gde Yogi Pramana and four co-authors harden medical vision-language models against adversarial attacks. Such models answer questions about scans, yet tiny crafted changes to an image can wreck their answers. Plain adversarial training often saves accuracy at the cost of warped clinical reasoning.

SafeMed-R1 defends in two stages. Training mixes adversarial examples with a group-relative policy method that toughens the reasoning itself. At run time, randomized smoothing adds a certified bound on how much an attack can move the answer. On a benchmark of more than eighty-eight thousand cases across eight imaging kinds, normal models collapsed under attack while SafeMed-R1 held up far better.
arxiv-2512-19417:
Johann Coraux, Nicolas Rougemaille, Cedric Robert, and Clément Faugeras write a critical colloquium on two-dimensional magnets. Single-layer magnetic crystals arrived about a decade ago and set off a worldwide rush. At first glance they look like cleaner versions of old two-dimensional spin models than thin films ever were.

The authors ask what is genuinely new. Some promises are only partly kept, and fresh light on old statistical-physics predictions is still an open question. Electric-field control, strain sensitivity, and moiré effects do set these crystals apart. The piece surveys van der Waals magnets and their stacks, separating real novelty from repackaging.
arxiv-2512-19517:
Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev study a jittery one-dimensional process that keeps resetting to zero. The motion is a piecewise deterministic Markov process on the unit interval. A small parameter controls its restlessness. As that parameter vanishes, the resetting pattern should simplify into something universal.

The authors prove the reset times converge to a decorated jump process. It has a Markov jump skeleton dressed with spikes, scattered as a Poisson process in time and space. The intensity blows up near zero like an inverse square. The theorem makes rigorous a picture sketched in earlier work, and partly confirms a conjecture posed there.
arxiv-2512-19817:
SaiKiran Tedla leads a seven-author team asking how much a single blurry photograph remembers. Motion blur smears a scene, but the smear encodes how scene and camera moved during the exposure. Earlier methods used that encoding to sharpen an image or guess frames near the moment of capture, leaning on handcrafted assumptions that break down in complex scenes.

Their technique repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model, trained at internet scale, to regenerate plausible video extending before, during, and after the photographed instant. It outperforms previous methods, copes with challenging real-world images, and supports downstream recovery of camera trajectories, object motion, and dynamic three-dimensional scene structure. Code and data accompany the release, inviting others to interrogate what blur preserves.
arxiv-2512-20117:
Jingqi Tian leads an eight-author team teaching machines to find what is making a sound in a video. Audio-visual segmentation must localize sound-producing objects at pixel level, but multiple overlapping sources get entangled, and audio-visual misalignment lets the loudest or largest object dominate while subtler sources vanish. Their framework, DDAVS, attacks both failure modes explicitly.

Learnable queries extract audio semantics and anchor them in a structured space built from an audio prototype memory bank, with contrastive learning sharpening discrimination between sources. Dual cross-attention with deliberately delayed modality interaction then steadies the alignment between what is heard and what is seen. Across the AVS-Objects and VPO benchmarks, spanning single-source, multi-source, and multi-class settings, the method reached state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv-2512-20317:
Ashish Ranjan Kumar and Sekhar Bhattacharyya survey India's position on rare earth elements, the metals behind strong magnets, batteries, and solar cells. India depends on imports for most of these elements, while home innovation and recycling remain young. The authors frame secure supply as central to energy independence and the national goal of a developed India by 2047.

Attention falls on overlooked home sources: copper tailings, fly ash, and electronic waste. Circular economy routes could turn those streams into supply while cutting environmental harm. Hindustan Copper Limited, India's only vertically integrated copper producer, is cast as the natural leader for co-recovery, research partnerships, and supply-chain building. Sustainability and community trust are treated as strategic requirements, not afterthoughts.
arxiv-2512-21017:
Xiaofeng Shi, Qian Kou, Yuduo Li, and Hua Zhou notice a quiet imbalance in how reasoning models are fine-tuned. A training example's chain of thought can run to hundreds of tokens while the final answer, the only part that is actually scored, takes a handful. Standard supervised fine-tuning spends its effort proportionally, so the answer tokens get comparatively little optimization. Their scheme, SFTKey, splits training in two: ordinary fine-tuning first to lock in format, then a second stage that trains only on the key answer portion.

Across benchmarks and model families, the two-stage recipe adds an average accuracy gain above five percent over conventional fine-tuning while output formats stay correct. The lesson for practitioners is cheap to apply: after teaching a model how to talk, spend focused effort on the few tokens that decide success.
arxiv-2512-21117:
Di Wu, Yifan Hu, and Kohei Kamada ask whether inflation itself could have made the universe's lepton imbalance. In pseudoscalar inflation, a Chern-Simons coupling links the inflaton to a gauge field. One circular polarization of that field then grows explosively. That seeds helical magnetic fields and, through the chiral anomaly, a handedness imbalance. If the gauge field respects a lepton flavor symmetry, the imbalance lands in the lepton sector. In simple setups, though, backreaction from the produced fields and fermions keeps it too small to observe.

Suppressing fermion production during inflation removes the brake. The magnetic helicity then decays later into a much larger lepton asymmetry. For the muon-minus-tau flavor symmetry, the asymmetry grows large enough to suppress primordial helium. That matches a hint in recent cosmic microwave background data from the ACT telescope. Early-universe magnetogenesis thereby gains a testable fingerprint in light-element amounts.
arxiv-2512-21317:
Yiqi Huang and Tristan Ozuch study what happens when a sequence of five-dimensional Einstein manifolds converges to a limit space. Einstein manifolds are shapes whose curvature is evenly spread, and they arise in geometry and in theories of gravity. The question is how smooth, or regular, the limiting space must be.

The authors prove that, away from a countable set of bad points, the tangent cones of the limit have a unique, simple form. The singular set sits inside a countable union of Lipschitz curves and points, and most of those curves are smooth geodesics. The proofs rest on a new result of independent interest: all spherical and hyperbolic four-dimensional orbifolds are isolated among Einstein four-orbifolds. That isolation yields gap theorems in four dimensions. The work sharpens the picture of how Einstein spaces can degenerate.
arxiv-2512-21517:
Thomas Schürmann sharpens a known lower bound for the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the Laplacian on a curved space. The eigenvalue sets the fundamental vibration frequency of a domain whose boundary is held fixed, like the lowest tone of a drum. Such bounds matter because they depend only on coarse data such as curvature and size.

The starting point is Ling's 2006 gradient-comparison method, which uses a positive Ricci curvature bound and the in-diameter, twice the greatest distance from an interior point to the boundary. Schürmann locates the single step where Ling's argument throws information away: an averaging step replacing a varying comparison function by its mean. Using the strong convexity of a power function, he refines that average with a variance term, keeping some discarded variation. The result is an explicit closed-form bound, strictly stronger than Ling's for every positive curvature bound.
arxiv-2512-21717:
Abd Ullah Khan, Adnan Shahid, Haejoon Jung, and Hyundong Shin survey multiconnectivity for space-air-ground-integrated networks. Such networks tie satellites, aerial platforms, and ground systems into one fabric. Multiconnectivity lets a user hold several links at once across those layers and across different radio technologies, improving reliability and capacity.

The catch is heterogeneity: link types range from air-to-air to space-to-ground, each with different delays and capacities, so allocating resources optimally is hard. The authors review current developments and catalog the main implementation challenges. They highlight artificial intelligence, especially reinforcement learning and agentic AI, as a promising way to make these allocation decisions in dynamic conditions. A case study applies agentic reinforcement learning to resource allocation across radio technologies. Learning-based control handled the complexity well, improving latency and capacity at a moderate power cost. The survey closes with open problems for the field.
arxiv-2512-21817:
Hong Su proposes DeMe, short for Method Decoration, a framework that helps Internet of Things systems invent new methods on the fly. Devices ask a language model to generate the steps for a task. When a situation is new, existing approaches fall back on fixed, device-specific logic that cannot adapt.

DeMe decorates the model's method-generation path with guidance drawn from three sources: hidden goals, methods the system has already learned, and feedback from the environment. These decorations are not hardcoded rules; they come from general principles and differences in conditions. The agent can then restructure its plan before, after, or between steps, or insert new steps. The aim is methods that are context-aware, safety-aligned, and adaptive. Experiments indicate decorated generation produces better methods when devices face unknown or faulty conditions.
arxiv-2512-22217:
Abdellah Zakaria Sellam and four co-authors present VLM-PAR, a system that reads pedestrian images and predicts fine-grained attributes such as clothing color, gender, and carried accessories. The task is hampered by lopsided data, attributes that depend on each other in tangled ways, and shifts between camera domains. Their system builds on frozen SigLIP 2 multilingual vision-language encoders rather than training from scratch.

A compact cross-attention module first refines the visual features by aligning them with prompt embeddings. On the highly imbalanced PA100K benchmark, the system set a new state-of-the-art accuracy. It also delivered clear gains in mean accuracy on the PETA and Market-1501 benchmarks. The authors credit large-scale vision-language pretraining plus targeted cross-modal refinement for beating the imbalance and generalization problems.
arxiv-2512-22317:
Xudong Ling and four co-authors present LangPrecip, a precipitation nowcasting system that lets written weather text steer radar-based forecasts. Short-term rain prediction is uncertain and under-constrained, mainly for fast-growing extreme events, and purely visual generative methods leave future motion ambiguous. LangPrecip treats meteorological text as a semantic constraint on how precipitation should evolve.

Nowcasting becomes a semantically constrained trajectory generation problem under the Rectified Flow paradigm, letting text and radar fuse efficiently in latent space. The team also built LangPrecip-160k, a dataset of 160,000 paired radar sequences and motion descriptions. On Swedish and MRMS radar data, the system always beat leading methods, with mainly large gains in heavy-rainfall detection skill at an eighty-minute lead time.
arxiv-2512-22417:
Vasileios Koutavas, Yu-Yang Lin, and Nikos Tzevelekos bring math guarantees to checking Ethereum smart contracts in an open world, where a contract's partners are unknown and possibly hostile. Their system models contract and environment as two players in a game. They prove soundness, meaning every flagged assertion violation is real, and completeness, meaning every open-world execution is captured, up to gas model shortcuts.

The tool, YulTracer, works on Yul, the Solidity compiler's intermediate language, exploring game traces within user-set bounds, step by step. On reentrancy benchmarks it achieved perfect recall and precision, the only tool examined to do so. It also caught the known flaws behind the DAO and PredyPool exploits while reporting no false positives on the fixed versions.
arxiv-2512-22617:
P. Marziani and seven co-authors present spectroscopic evidence that the winds blowing off quasar accretion disks come in layers. Active galactic nuclei shine partly through emission lines, and the lines' shapes carry the wind's structure. High-ionization lines such as ionized carbon show strong blueshifts and lopsided profiles, the signature of fast inner winds. Low-ionization lines like hydrogen beta and magnesium look more symmetric, coming mainly from slower, denser gas farther out.

Intermediate lines fall between the two in shift size, though in some super-Eddington candidates their outflow speeds rival the high-ionization lines. The pattern matches radiatively driven wind models with radial stratification. Preliminary photoionization modeling, with coronal and hot-disk radiation partly absorbed by a gas layer, adds support. The findings constrain the geometry and physical conditions of these outflows.
arxiv-2512-22917:
Between late 2007 and early 2008, Chile's three retail pharmacy chains raised prices together on more than two hundred medicines. The increases came weeks after advertising restrictions ended a price war in which comparative ads had pushed prices below cost. An economic study by Hao Yu reconstructs that switch from war to coordination using a structural model grounded in estimated demand.

Two forces did the work. Comparative ads once told shoppers exactly who was cheapest, so undercutting won traffic and sustained the war. The ban dulled price sensitivity, making undercutting unprofitable for most drugs, and the ban itself was a public event that aligned each chain's belief that rivals would match a rise. A dynamic model fitted by simulated method of moments reproduces the war, the failed coordination attempts, and the post-ban wave. The harm fell mainly as a transfer to the chains, since inelastic demand limited the deadweight loss.
arxiv-2512-23017:
Fuli Qiao and Mehrdad Mahdavi tackle continual learning for large language models, where a model must pick up new tasks without forgetting old ones and without the memory bill growing forever. Popular low-rank adapters, called LoRA, are usually frozen and stockpiled per task in current methods, so storage grows with every task and old adapters can interfere with new learning.

Their alternative keeps exactly one LoRA module. Each new task starts from an orthogonal basis extracted from what was learned before, which limits interference, and its update is then merged into the single shared adapter. A time-aware scaling balances old and new knowledge during merging, exploiting an asymmetry in how LoRA components behave. Memory stays constant as tasks accumulate. Theory backs the design, and experiments across continual learning benchmarks with several Llama models show strong performance with better efficiency than stockpiling approaches.
arxiv-2512-23117:
Daniel Levine and a large collaboration release OPoly26, a dataset meant to teach machine learning models the chemistry of polymers. Polymers underpin living things and drive advances in medicine, consumer products, and energy. Yet earlier training datasets for atomistic machine learning largely skipped them. High-quality quantum calculations on polymer structures are simply too expensive. OPoly26 fills the hole with more than six and a half million density functional theory calculations.

The calculations cover clusters of up to three hundred sixty atoms drawn from polymer systems, totaling over a billion atoms, and span changes in monomer makeup, chain length, architecture, and solvent. Adding OPoly26 to training improved models on polymer prediction tasks, the authors report. The dataset is released to speed development of polymer-aware models and, more broadly, of universal atomistic models that handle small molecules, materials, and macromolecules in one framework.
arxiv-2512-23317:
Kansei Ushiyama, Shun Sato, and Takayasu Matsuo ask what a convergence rate even means for an optimization method described by a differential equation. Analysts often model gradient methods as continuous-time flows because the equations feel simple. But rescaling time in the model speeds up or slows down its convergence at will, so chasing differential equations with fast rates is meaningless without a fix.

Their fix is the essential convergence rate, a notion designed to be immune to time rescaling. The backing is a theorem: under suitable rules for how the equation is discretized back into an algorithm, no discretization can converge faster than the model's essential rate. That makes the essential rate the honest ceiling a continuous model can promise. The paper reframes a popular design method, giving researchers a target that cannot be gamed by stretching the clock.
arxiv-2512-23417:
Navdeep Singh Dhindsa and co-authors pin down the masses of the triply charmed baryons, particles built from three charm quarks that no experiment has yet produced. Lattice QCD, which simulates the strong force on a space-time grid, is the tool. The calculation is presented as the most precise to date for the lowest spin three-half states of both parities. Six simulation ensembles with 2+1+1 quark flavors, generated by the MILC collaboration, feed the analysis.

Two treatments of the valence charm quark, the HISQ action and the overlap action, cross-check each other, and results are extrapolated to the continuum while systematic uncertainties are accounted. The predicted mass for the positive-parity ground state is about four thousand seven hundred ninety-three million electron volts. The negative-parity partner sits near five thousand ninety-four million electron volts. Such predictions tell collider experiments exactly where to look.
arxiv-2512-23517:
L. Saba and C. D. Fosco offer a teaching-oriented path through van der Waals forces, the weak attraction between neutral atoms. Textbooks usually treat the short-distance London limit with stationary perturbation theory, while the long-distance Casimir-Polder limit, where the finite speed of light matters, is derived with separate semiclassical methods. Students therefore meet the two regimes as disconnected topics.

The authors show that rewriting the stationary calculation in terms of time-ordered correlation functions simplifies the mathematics considerably. The same language then handles the higher-order terms needed at long distance, where retardation effects enter. One unified framework thus connects both limits. The article is pitched as a bridge between advanced quantum mechanics courses and field-theoretic treatments of dispersion forces, for graduate students and specialists.
arxiv-2512-23717:
Shenzhe Zhu confronts a gap in language-model safety training: filters are built mostly against openly harmful requests, but users can rephrase a harmful query so it sounds harmless while keeping its intent. Safety data rarely contains such disguised examples, so aligned models may not recognize them. HarmTransform is a framework for manufacturing them systematically.

Multiple agents debate over each transformation, critiquing and refining one another's rephrasings to keep the harmful objective intact while lowering its visibility. The resulting examples can then train safer models. Experiments show the method beats standard baselines at producing effective covert transformations. The analysis also warns that debate is double-edged: it sharpens stealth, yet can drift the topic or add needless complexity, lessons for anyone generating safety training data this way.
arxiv-2512-23817:
Seyed Mohamad Ali Tousi and three co-authors teach a neural network to clean up after quantum computers solving a fluid equation. The viscous Burgers equation is a standard test problem for shock formation. Through the Cole-Hopf transformation it becomes a diffusion equation, which they discretize and run on noisy quantum hardware and simulators using Trotterized circuits in Qiskit, comparing against high-accuracy classical solutions.

Standard zero-noise extrapolation helps, but the team goes further: they built a large data set sweeping viscosity, time step, grid size. Boundary conditions, pairing noisy, corrected, hardware, and classical results with circuit metadata. An attention-based graph network, fed the circuit's structure and outputs, learned to predict the error-mitigated solution. Across the parameter range it consistently reduced the gap to the classical answer beyond what extrapolation alone achieved.
arxiv-2512-24217:
Runtian Zhu and Lingfei Jin decode two families of error-correcting codes. Maximum distance separable codes sit at the center of practice. Most known examples are generalized Reed-Solomon codes. Codes outside that family are less understood. Their weaker structure can even be a virtue in cryptography. Twisted Reed-Solomon codes and Roth-Lempel codes represent the non-standard side.

Constructions of these codes are well studied. Their decoding was not. The authors build list and unique decoders on the Guruswami-Sudan algorithm. Under suitable conditions, running time is near-linear in code length. That improves the best known quadratic time. The twisted-code decoder handles many twists at fixed rate. Prior work managed only a single twist. For Roth-Lempel codes, this appears to be the first efficient decoder. List decoding also beats the classical unique-decoding radius for wide parameter ranges.
arxiv-2512-24517:
Fabian Retkowski and Alexander Waibel make paragraph segmentation a standard task for speech transcripts. Automatic transcripts arrive as unstructured word streams. Readability and reuse suffer for it. Paragraph breaks are the missing structuring step. Text segmentation research has lacked naturalistic benchmarks for it. The speech domain has mostly ignored the task.

Two benchmarks answer the gap. TEDPara holds human-annotated TED talks. YTSegPara holds YouTube videos with synthetic labels. A constrained-decoding method lets language models insert breaks without altering the transcript. Faithful, sentence-aligned evaluation follows. A compact model, MiniSeg, reaches state-of-the-art accuracy. A hierarchical extension predicts chapters and paragraphs together. Its extra cost is minimal. The package of data and methods aims to standardize paragraph segmentation in speech processing.
arxiv-2512-24817:
Ivan Novak studies how to count rational points with a given j-invariant on modular curves over a number field. The j-invariant labels elliptic curves up to isomorphism, and modular curves parametrize curves with extra structure. His method counts points above a chosen invariant on an arbitrary modular curve.

Applications list, for each positive integer, how many cyclic isogenies an elliptic curve over some number field can admit. Counts are also worked out above an invariant on split and non-split Cartan curves for odd prime powers. Number theory readers get concrete enumerations tied to Galois representation images for CM curves.
arxiv-2512-25017:
Chenguang Liu, Antonis Papapantoleon, and Jasper Rou — with co-authors — put deep gradient flow methods for partial differential equations on firm mathematical ground. Their analysis splits generalization error into approximation error and training error. Solutions of equations under reasonable, checkable assumptions are shown to be approximable by neural networks, so approximation error vanishes as networks widen.

The training process in the wide network limit follows an explicit gradient flow, which they derive and analyze. Applied mathematics readers get convergence understanding for a popular neural PDE solver family. High-dimensional equations are the target, where grid methods collapse and neural methods promise relief.
arxiv-2601-06617:
Giovani Braglia and co-authors design a robotic tele-operation system for microsurgery in 2026. Their target is the upper aerodigestive tract, inside the throat. Such treatments often employ transoral laser microsurgery for delicate procedures.

In that surgery, a laser beam cuts target tissue precisely. Forceps grasp, manipulate, and stabilize tissue within the tract meanwhile. Procedures include removal of tumors or polyps from those passages. Tele-operation would let a surgeon control instruments remotely and steadily. The paper covers system design and validation of their setup. Medical robotics readers get a full pipeline, from design to tests. It aims at steadier, safer work in a tight surgical space.
arxiv-2601-07017:
Andreas Langer and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with Ill-Posed foundations of Physics-Informed neural networks and their Finite-Difference variants. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Physics-informed neural networks based on automatic differentiation (AD-PINNs) and their finite-difference counterparts (FD-PINNs) are widely used for solving partial differential equations (PDEs).

Yet their analytical properties remain poorly understood. This work provides a unified mathematical foundation for both formulations. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07117:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Kexin Bao and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers few-shot Class-Incremental learning via generative Co-Memory regularization. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL) aims to incrementally learn models from a small amount of new data. Which requires strong representation and adaptation ability of models learned under few-example supervision to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

On old classes and overfitting to new classes. This work proposes a generative co-memory regularization approach to facilitate FSCIL. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07517: Marius Durea and Elena-Cristina Stamate, mathematicians based in Iaşi, Romania, study a boundedness notion for sets defined through cones in a 2026 preprint. Their title names the topic: dually cone-boundedness of a set, with applications. Cone conditions appear across optimization and functional analysis, where they shape how sets and mappings behave. The work develops the new boundedness concept and turns to what it can be used for. The record here is thin, so this note stays with the stated topic and scope.
arxiv-2601-07617:
A large BESIII collaboration reports a detailed study of a rare particle decay, using a huge sample of J/psi events. The detector at Beijing collected about ten billion J/psi particles. From that sample, the team performs a partial-wave analysis of one decay channel into a Lambda, an anti-Sigma-zero, and an eta, plus its mirror process. Their 2026 preprint states the analysis is the first of its kind.

Partial-wave analysis separates a decay into components with different spins and motions. Those components reveal which intermediate particles form during the decay. Branching fraction measurements state how often the decay happens at all. Together they test models of how quarks bind into hadrons. Particle physicists use such measurements to refine the map of known and predicted states.
arxiv-2601-07817:
D. R. Heath-Brown counts special solutions to the simple equation x plus y equals z. The solutions he counts use square-full integers, numbers whose prime factors all appear with exponent at least two. He bounds how many such triples exist with all entries up to a given size B. His 2026 preprint gives that bound with a small saving over the natural exponent. The result holds for any fixed positive epsilon in the exponent.

Square-full numbers are rare, so triples of them summing correctly are rarer still. Counting them tests tools from analytic number theory. Even simple equations become hard when variables are restricted to thin sets. Bounds like this feed work on Diophantine equations and additive problems. The paper serves specialists in analytic number theory. It is a counting result, stated for experts who track exponents closely.
arxiv-2601-07917:
Antti Rantala and colleagues simulate how mid-sized black holes form by runaway collisions in dense star clusters. Intermediate-mass black holes may seed the supermassive ones in galaxy centers. The team explores their formation across a wide range of cluster densities. Surface densities span more than three orders of magnitude in their study. Metallicity, the chemical makeup of the stars, is the variable in this third FROST-CLUSTERS paper. Their 2026 preprint reports the simulations.

Runaway collisions happen when massive stars sink to the center and merge repeatedly. The product can grow into a black hole far heavier than any single star leaves. Metal content changes stellar winds, which change how much mass stars keep before colliding. That link decides which clusters succeed as incubators. The paper serves astrophysicists modeling black hole origins. It maps formation chances across realistic cluster conditions.
arxiv-2601-08017:
Evžen Wybitul and colleagues show that image and text representations inside vision-language models align surprisingly early. For many concepts in adapter-based models, image representations and text descriptions align meaningfully from the very first layer. That contradicts the established view that such alignment appears only in late layers. Their 2026 preprint presents the evidence across a variety of concepts. The models studied connect vision encoders to language models through adapters.

Early alignment changes how scholars picture these models working. If matching begins at layer one, later layers refine rather than create the link. That view affects probing, editing, and safety analysis of multimodal models. It also simplifies some theories of how adapters bridge the two modalities. The paper serves machine learning scholars who study representation geometry. It revises a basic assumption with direct measurement.
arxiv-2601-08217:
Ali Mamaghani and four co-authors present Tiny-Twin, a digital twin for next-generation cellular networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that modern wireless apps need test settings that capture full network complexity. Digital twins promise realistic emulation for such tests.

Existing tools often trade away physical-layer fidelity or scalability, or they demand special hardware. Tiny-Twin runs a full-stack emulation on commodity CPUs instead. Realistic and repeatable 5G experiments become possible without a lab full of radios. For network researchers, a CPU-native twin lowers the cost of testing ideas before field trials. It also makes results easier for other teams to reproduce.
arxiv-2601-08317:
Ibuki Terada and three co-authors study Hall effects boosted by nodal lines in the magnet NbMnP. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers anomalous and nonlinear Hall effects in this parity-mixed antiferromagnet.
