The anomalous Hall effect is known to reflect the geometric nature of Bloch bands and impurity scattering.

A large anomalous Hall effect was recently reported in NbMnP, a noncollinear antiferromagnetic metal. Its magnetic order mixes even-parity and odd-parity components. The authors link the strong response to nodal-line features in the band structure. Quantum geometric effects like these may guide future spintronic materials that use antiferromagnets instead of ferromagnets.
arxiv-2601-08517: Tolgay Atinc Uzun, Dmitry Ignatov, and Radu Timofte use language models to discover channel configurations in vision models. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats channel search as a hard combinatorial problem. Layer widths must respect tensor shape compatibility and computational budgets at once. The authors argue language models can reason about architectural code structure in ways heuristics cannot. A closed-loop search lets the model propose, test, and revise non-standard channel priors. Smarter architecture search could yield leaner vision networks for phones and cameras.
arxiv-2601-08617: Leo Fillioux and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how sure a vision-language model should be of its own replies. Such models now serve in health care and self-driving cars, where a wrong reply can harm. Test-time prompt tuning, or TPT, adapts a model at the time of use by tuning its prompt. Past TPT work has chased sharp picks, not trust in them. The authors set out Semantic Orthogonal Calibration, or SoC. It aims at the trust side that past work left aside.
arxiv-2601-08817:
N. Brace tests cheap shake sensors at the cold heart of a lab fridge. Such fridges cool tools to near the coldest heat that can be reached. Shake there can harm weak quantum or space tests. Staff need to know the shake level, but lab grade sensors cost much and may not work in such cold.

Brace checks store bought sensors at heats as low as eight thousandths of a degree above pure cold. He also checks if the sensors give off rays that could harm a test. The aim is a cheap, safe way to watch shake in cold labs. A reader who runs such a lab gets hard facts on what these low cost sensors can and can not do.
arxiv-2601-08917:
Arhum Ansari, Sachin Jain, and Deep Mazumdar link rules from flat space physics to rules for the fast growth era of space. In flat space, a rule set says how a process can split into parts. Those split rules are called cutting rules. In curved, fast growth space, the same splits are more hard to track by hand.

The team gives a dress up step that lifts flat cuts to curved space. In that view, each flat cut maps to a jump in a key energy count. They show the map on tree form and one loop cases for a plain field type. A reader in theory work gets a clear path. It makes curved space cut rules less of a black art.
arxiv-2601-09117:
Shalmoli Ghosh, Matthew DeVerna, and Filippo Menczer study a paid market for AI made adult and fake content on a fan site. The site is Civitai, a hub for AI art tools and models. Its Bounties tool lets a user post a paid ask for a set work. A maker who fills the ask earns the pay. That market can fund deep fakes of real folk.

The team maps how the market works: what asks are made, what pay is set, and what gets made. Such a map is a first step to rules that can curb harm with out a ban on all AI art. A reader in net safety gets facts on a new trade that law has yet to catch.
arxiv-2601-09817:
L. L. Salcedo gives a precise meaning to a quantum state living inside a chosen subspace. His 2026 arXiv paper defines the localization probability of a state within part of its Hilbert space. The localized component of the state is identified explicitly, not just bounded.

The author establishes several mathematical properties of the definition. Applications and interpretations in quantum information are discussed. A clean definition settles arguments about how much of a state sits in a code space or a sector. Such bookkeeping underlies error correction and the theory of quantum resources.
arxiv-2601-10017:
Shu-Cheng Chang, Yingbo Han, Chien Lin, and Chin-Tung Wu study a class of curved shapes named Sasakian. These shapes have a rich extra frame. A past claim by Yau dealt with how such shapes must look when they spread with no end. The claim was for a like class of shapes.

The team works on the Sasaki form of that claim. Their shapes have cross curve that is not below zero. The shapes are whole and not closed. The paper probes what form such a shape must take. Work of this kind sorts curved shapes by the signs of their curves.
arxiv-2601-11217:
Matthieu Meunier, Huyen Pham, and Christoph Reisinger learn control rules with no model. Their 2026 preprint deals with mean-field control in discrete time. Mean-field control steers a vast crowd as one system. Each agent's best move depends on the whole crowd's state.

Past work on this field leans on value-based methods. Policy-based ways are far less explored, for a clear reason. The crowd state drives both moves and rewards as time runs. That loop blocks the classic gradient tricks from single-agent learning. The team builds a policy gradient that works without a model. The state space is finite and the action space compact. The result opens a new path for crowd-scale control.
arxiv-2601-11317:
Robbe Vermeiren builds orthogonal bases from rational functions in this preprint. His 2026 work gives two algorithms for the task. Rational functions are ratios of two polynomials. Vectors of them arise in control and signal work.

The bases are orthonormal under a discrete inner product. That means pairs are clean and each vector has unit size. The builds rest on a pencil-based form of a known problem. That problem is the inverse generalized eigenvalue problem. Work by Van Buggenhout and others set that stage. Vermeiren shows how the bases serve rational approximation. Approximation with rational forms can fit poles that polynomials miss.
arxiv-2601-11417:
Tyler Reinmund, Lars Kunze, and Marina Jirotka study machine learning in care work. Their 2026 preprint deals with health care and social welfare. Sociotechnical challenges are clashes between a tool and its setting. A learning tool may clash with how care is truly done.

Past accounts of such clashes tend to blame one side. Some blame designers who miss the social side of care. Others blame hard technical limits in the tools. Both views give weak help for comparing cases. The team seeks a shared way to describe these clashes. A common frame would let cases be set side by side. That could guide fixes that respect both code and care.
arxiv-2601-11517:
Koyena Pal, David Bau, and Chandan Singh ask if explanations travel between models. Their 2026 preprint deals with large reasoning models. Such models write a chain of thought as they solve tasks. That chain reads like a natural-language explanation of the work.

A readable chain could be a strong tool for insight. It surfaces the model's path in terms humans can check. But it is unclear if such explanations generalize. A chain from one model may not fit another's process. It may also fail to match the model's true steps. The team tests that portability across reasoning models. The answer matters for trust in chain-of-thought audits.
arxiv-2601-11617:
Xu Wang, Boyao Han, Xiaojun Chen, Ying Liu, and Ruihui Li present PointSLAM++. Their 2026 preprint builds a dense neural SLAM system. Real-time 3D reconstruction is crucial for robotics and AR. SLAM maps a space while tracking the sensor in it.

Depth noise often breaks structural consistency in such maps. Pose estimation also turns shaky when depth data err. PointSLAM++ uses a Gaussian point cloud representation. The Gaussians are hierarchically constrained to hold structure. Constraints keep walls and edges true as the map grows. Gaussian primitives then render the scene for the map. The system takes RGB-D input, color plus depth. Robust poses under noise are the stated design aim.
arxiv-2601-11817:
Yumou Wei, John Carney, John Stamper, and Nancy Belmont flip a common view of privacy tools. Most rules act as a shield that users must hold up by hand. Users face opt-in and opt-out picks whose effects are hard to foresee.

They use the Johari Window, a frame for what is known to self and to others. In that view, rules guard the open self and hide the rest. The team argue for tools that help users speak up, not just hide. Their aim is to let users use what AI infers, on their own terms.
arxiv-2601-12217:
Li Ye and Yisheng Song study interval B-tensors and interval double B-tensors in a systematic way. An interval tensor is a family of tensors bounded by low and high terms. B-tensor classes have set sign and sum traits that help in maths tests.

They give checkable conditions that are both needed and enough. The checks rest on the extreme point tensors of the family alone. That turns a check over a vast family into a finite task. Such shortcuts help in optimization and game theory with tensors.  Finite checks make the class tests of real use.
arxiv-2601-12317:
Yiming Huang automates insight finding in two-way tables with a workflow that joins explainable AI and language models. Auto data analysis is a long goal. Agent tools such as DeepAnalyze and DataSage use model-led tool calls for fine work.

Huang asks what a preset, AutoML-like workflow can do in place of free agents. His system, Explanova, hunts insights in N by M tables in that set way. A fixed workflow may be cheaper and more easy to audit. The work tests that trade.  The table case is a set test for the workflow claim.
arxiv-2601-12417:
Yi-Long Duan, Tuohuniyazi Tuniyazi, and Gang Guo study neutrinos from exploding stars. When a massive star dies, its thrown off matter slams into gas that rings the star. That crash can speed up protons and make high energy neutrinos. The team focus on two classes of these blasts, Type II and Type IIn.

They take density profiles for the ring gas from real observations. With those in hand, they compute the neutrino fluxes that should result. They then test how the flux shifts as key inputs change. The inputs are the density scale, the outer radius, and how well protons gain energy. They also vary the share of energy held in magnetic fields.
arxiv-2601-13117:
Mihail Stoian and co-authors tackle a weak spot in database tools. Cloud database firms spend a lot on query optimizers, the part that picks how to run a query. A core step is to guess how big each join will be. A bad guess can wreck the whole plan.

Staff and scholars alike call that guess step the weak heel of the tool. The team gives lower bounds for join size, caps that a true size cannot fall below. Their method is named xBound. Firm bounds give the tool a floor to plan from. That floor can also guide how much stock and time a query gets. For cloud teams, firmer bounds mean fewer slow plans.
arxiv-2601-13217:
Bingsen Chen and co-authors test if deep research agents can fix a report over many rounds. Such agents search and write long reports on call. Past tests treat that write as a one shot task. Real scholars, though, draft and then fix their work in rounds, by self thought or peer notes.

The team asks if agents can do that round work with care. A user note may ask for a fix in one part. A weak agent may break sound parts or miss the note. Their finds mark the agents as not yet safe at multi round fix work. For teams that sell such agents, the test sets a bar that one shot scores hide.
arxiv-2601-13317:
Samantha Sudhoff, Pranav Perumal, Zhaoqing Wu, and Tunazzina Islam set paid climate ads next to free social posts and read both with one lens. Talk on climate shapes what the public grasps and what laws get made. But that talk runs on two kinds of stage with split pay rules.

Paid ad stages reward aimed, planned pleas. Free feed stages host raw talk by users at large. The team builds a theme model that can be read by eye. It maps which themes rule each stage and where they meet or part. For climate talk staff, the split shows whose voice a theme is, not just that it trends.
arxiv-2601-13417:
Yujian Xiong and co-authors enhance eye fundus pics with a GAN led by a sliced Gromov-Wasserstein guide. Fundus pics are the base of eye screen and diagnosis. Their grade is oft marred by noise, flaws, and uneven light. GAN and diffusion tools can lift such pics by pull toward clean pic forms.

The team finds a flaw in that pull. Pics of kin ills can spread apart in the learnt space, and class bounds blur. Their guide keeps that inner shape while the pic is cleaned. It uses a sliced form of the Gromov-Wasserstein span, a way to match shapes. For eye teams, a clean pic that bends class shape is a risk, not a gain.
arxiv-2601-13517:
Nicholas J. Evans and co-authors show a new phase space paint method to tame space charge in strong hadron beams. Strong beams blow up from their own charge push. Multi turn charge swap injection is the stock way to build such beams in rings. Paint sets how the beam fills its phase space as it is built.

Their method is called eigenpainting. It loads bits into one mode of a coupled ring. That gives full four dim hold of the fill form. A form set by mode can spread charge so its push harms less. For ring teams that chase brighter beams, a new paint knob is a real gain.
arxiv-2601-13617:
Yi-Han Luo and a large team work on light sources for quantum links in space in 2026. Sending quantum states over vast gaps is key for world-wide quantum nets. Satellites have sent linked light over a thousand kilometers in past tests. Future fleets and deep-space probes need sources that are small, tough, and frugal with power.

The team built a photon-pair source that works in near-visible light. Pairs of linked photons let two far sites share a quantum link. A compact source that sips power suits small satellites well. The work is a step toward quantum nets that span the globe and beyond.
arxiv-2601-14017:
Pavel Pavlíček and co-authors shape quantum correlations by counting photons in twin beams in 2026. A twin beam is a pair of linked light beams. Spatially-resolved photon counting with an iCCD camera lets them tailor the beams. They divide the idler beam into three equally intense parts.

Post-selection then keeps only cases with a set photocount in the signal beam. The result is idler fields with high degrees of nonclassicality. They also carry tripartite quantum correlations, links shared by three parties. Tailored multi-party light states feed quantum networks and tests of quantum theory.
arxiv-2601-14117:
Oskar Riedler and Thomas Tony show a rigid class of maps must be simple products in 2026. Scalar-rigid maps are Riemannian submersions, by works of Llarull, Goette and Semmelmann, and Tony. A submersion projects a big space onto a smaller one in a smooth way. The team shows these maps are essentially Riemannian products.

The product splits into the base manifold and a Ricci-flat fiber. As an application, they obtain a Llarull-type theorem. It covers non-zero degree maps onto products of manifolds with set curvature traits. Such rigidity results limit how curved spaces can relate.
arxiv-2601-14217:
Axel Fünfhaus, Titus Neupert, Thilo Kopp, and Roser Valentí define a new topology marker for many-body systems in 2026. Integer and fractional Chern insulators show a quantized anomalous Hall conductivity. That trait comes from spontaneous breaking of time reversal symmetry. In time-reversal symmetric spectra, that marker cannot spot nontrivial topology.

The team introduces many-body Euler numbers as a counterpart to many-body Chern numbers. Euler numbers can flag topology while time reversal stays intact. New markers widen the hunt for topological phases of matter. Such phases may host robust quantum devices in the future. The new count works where the old one is blind. It opens a class of phases that past scans would have missed by rule.
arxiv-2601-14517:
Yilong Dai and six co-authors survey learning-based PDE solvers in this 2026 paper. Partial differential equations are central to scientific modeling. Modern workflows increasingly rely on learning-based parts to support model reuse, inference, and integration across large computational processes. Physics-aware data-driven approaches have grown fast in that role.

Yet the field lacks a unified perspective. Without one, the relationships, limitations, and proper roles of the methods stay unclear. The authors give that unifying view for two big families. They are physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Readers get a map that sorts what each family does, where each fails, and where each belongs in real workflows.
arxiv-2601-14617:
Yunfeng Lin, Li Xu, Yong Yu, Jiangmiao Pang, and Weinan Zhang present a robot software system in this 2026 paper. Deploying learning-based controllers across heterogeneous robots is challenging. Platform differences, inconsistent interfaces, and inefficient middleware all get in the way. A controller tuned on one robot rarely drops cleanly onto another.

Their system, UniCon, is a lightweight framework that standardizes states, control flow, and instrumentation across platforms. It decomposes workflows into execution graphs with reusable components. It also separates system states from control logic, which enables plug-and-play deployment across various robot morphologies. Readers get a path to move learned controllers between robots without rebuilding the stack each time.
arxiv-2601-14717: Planar univalent harmonic mappings are smooth maps of the complex plane that do not fold onto themselves. This 2026 math paper investigates how such mappings change the Lebesgue measure, the area, of measurable sets. The work is motivated by Problem 3.25 of Koh and Kovalev from HQM2010. The authors establish sharp quantitative area distortion inequalities. They cover disks and arbitrary measurable sets under sense-preserving harmonic self-maps of the unit disk. Sharp means the bounds cannot be improved. The evidence pack lists no authors for this entry.
arxiv-2601-15317:
Daisuke Hirota asks why groups that split apart also pull together. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a social paradox: division and cohesion often intensify at the same time. He gives a structural answer that does not depend on the details of any one group.

The theory is static and rests on relation maintenance. Social ties must meet minimum conditions, set over an abstract space of positions. From those minimal constraints alone, the paper derives its claim. Cohesion without fragmentation is impossible: holding some ties close forces other ties to break apart.
arxiv-2601-15817:
Nina A. Lange and five co-authors fight a limiting effect in optical waveguides in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is lithium niobate. It is widely used in nonlinear and quantum optical devices. Examples include frequency generation and photon pair sources. In waveguides, the photorefractive effect caps performance. It limits the input and output powers a device can handle. It also distorts the nonlinear spectral response.

The title contrasts two management routes: high-temperature and cryogenic solutions. Each regime changes how the effect behaves. Choosing between them is a practical design decision. Quantum photonics needs bright, clean sources. Photorefraction stands in the way of both traits. A clear comparison of fixes helps device builders pick the right thermal strategy.
arxiv-2601-16117:
Abdul Hannan and coauthors make speech nets that can shed layers to fit small gear. Their 2026 preprint deals with edge gear with tight and shifting means. A fixed net can be too big for weak gear. Layer drop turns a fixed net into one that can skip parts. Skips cut cost but can hurt speech scores if done with no care.

The team adds a teach step to the drop plan. A full net teaches the lean net as it learns to skip. That teach step aims to keep scores high at low cost. The net can then shift its size as gear means shift. The work targets live speech tools on phones and like gear.
arxiv-2601-16317:
Jian Li and four coauthors study noisy quantum heat acts with a plain noise stand in. Their 2026 preprint deals with heat acts that cool or drive quantum states. Noise and flaws touch all real acts of this kind. They touch acts built to cut noise in the first place. Cool acts can lose both speed and worth when noise hits.

The team uses a mixed state noise path as a stand in. That path, the depolarizing channel, is plain yet rich. It lets them trace how noise bends act scores. Clear bends guide design of cool acts that hold up. The work aids teams who run heat acts on real gear.
arxiv-2601-16417:
Umar Qureshi, Brendon Bullard and Ariel Schwartzman tag all jets in a crash at once. Their 2026 preprint, named PanopTag, deals with jets from particle hits. To tag a jet is to name the grain that made it. Deep tools have lifted tag scores much in past years. Yet past tools still tag each jet one by one.

One by one tags miss links that join jets in one crash. Tag all at once can use those links for each call. Links tell of shared birth paths in the crash. Use of links should lift tag truth for hard jets. The work shifts tag work from lone jets to whole events.
arxiv-2601-16817:
Antonin Boisneault, Marcella Bonazzoli, Xavier Claeys, and Pierre Marchand split hard sound tasks for fast solves. Sound waves in rooms and the open air obey one core rule. Big zones make that rule slow to solve whole. Their 2026 preprint cuts the zone in parts that don't overlap. Each part is solved, then the parts trade edge facts.

Their join pairs two solve styles at the seams. One style fills the zone's guts, the next its skin. A tuned trade rule speeds how the parts agree. Fast sound solves aid hall design and noise plans. They also help map how sound spreads from roads.
arxiv-2601-17117:
Hua-Peng Gu, Fangzhou Jiang, Xian Chen, and Ran Li push a dark halo fall past old bounds. Vast black holes show up too soon in the young cosmos. Plain seed tales strain to grow them in time. Dark halos that self-bump may fall in to seed them. Past work set that fall in calm, non-relativistic form.

Their 2026 preprint drops the calm tack. It adds full relativity to the fall math. Fall paths then cap how big a seed can grow. Those caps face the young holes scopes now see. The work tests if dark falls can truly seed them.
arxiv-2601-17617:
Jingjie Ning and co-authors analyze agentic search at large scale. LLM search agents now handle multi-step information tasks. The field lacks proof of how those sessions unfold. The team studies 14.44 million search requests. They span 3.97 million sessions from DeepResearchGym. Logs show intents and trajectory dynamics across real use.

Such scale turns anecdote into pattern. The study tracks how retrieved evidence is used, step by step. Designers can see where agents loop, stall, or succeed. That guides better agent planners and search tools. The work gives the IR community a shared fact base. Agent claims can now be checked against logs.
arxiv-2601-17717: Kaituo Zhang and eleven co-authors survey how to judge synthetic data made for large language models. The 2026 preprint takes a metric-based view of two questions. First, is the data good enough to train on? Second, can the data and its scores be trusted? The survey sorts the measures in use and compares what each one can and cannot show.
arxiv-2601-18017:
Runjie Song and Kengo Deguchi study waves that grow on swirling flow over a curved wall. Their 2026 preprint deals with Görtler vortices, rolls that form when flow follows a concave surface. These vortices support fast, wavelike disturbances through a second round of instability. Lab work hints that the growth of these waves, at full strength, sets up the shift to turbulence. Predicting that growth well and cheaply has stayed out of reach.

The authors push past the secondary instability view. They target the finite-amplitude stage, where the waves are no longer small. That stage is where transition is decided. Better models here serve aircraft, turbines, and any flow over curved skin.
arxiv-2601-18117:
Boxiao Chen and Jiashuo Jiang price the cost of letting each product team set its own prices. Their 2026 preprint studies decentralized pricing in multi-product firms. When managers ignore how one product's price shifts demand for others, the firm loses money. The authors measure that loss with the price of anarchy, a ratio between selfish and coordinated outcomes. Their pricing game has each manager set prices to lift their own product's revenue.

Diagonal dominance turns out to shape when a Nash equilibrium exists and how bad it can be. The results tell firms when decentralization is cheap and when it bleeds profit. Coordination has costs too, so a clear loss bound helps leaders choose a structure.
arxiv-2601-18217:
Zhihan Liu and co-authors measure the cost of training an agent in one world and using it in another. Their 2026 preprint studies reinforcement learning for language model agents. Generalist agents are often post-trained in a narrow set of environments. They are then deployed across far broader, unseen domains. The authors call the skill lost in that jump a generalization tax. They ask which traits of the training environments and which modeling choices drive the tax up or down.

Knowing the drivers lets builders pick training grounds that travel well. It also tells them when a low tax is a mirage. As agents move into open-ended work, this cross-domain question becomes central.
arxiv-2601-18417:
Ivan Batistić, Pablo Castrillo, and Philip Cardiff build a faster way to solve stress math for solid parts. Their base tool splits a part into small cells and tracks force in each cell. Plain forms of the tool stop at a low grade of truth. The team push the grade up, so bends and loads show in finer detail.

They pair the fine grid with a solver that skips a costly step. The solver, named in the title, guesses and checks its way to the answer with no need to build one huge table of slopes. Fresh slopes come from a fit to near cells, and sums at cell faces keep the count sharp. The mix aims for lab-grade truth on parts like beams and blocks, at a cost that firms can pay.
arxiv-2601-18817:
Nadim Rooholamin, Kabir Bakhshaei, and Giovanni Stabile build a lean model of rough flow that firms can run in far less time than a full sim. A full sim of rough flow in a pipe or past a wing takes a huge grid and days of chip time. A lean model keeps the big moves of the flow and drops the rest. The catch is to keep the lean form true to the full one's laws, such as the law that mass can't be made or lost.

Their plan builds the lean form straight from the full grid, then adds a learned fix for the dropped moves. The grid in view has all flow facts in the same cells, a form that makes law care hard. Their path keeps mass true with no extra props. Lean forms that keep the laws could speed design loops for cars, planes, and pumps.
arxiv-2601-18917:
Semih Cantürk and seven co-authors build a shared test frame for graph inverse problems. Many graph tasks run in reverse: instead of guessing from a known graph, they infer the graph itself from data. Such tasks span finding hidden links, tracing graphs over time, and hard search problems.

Work on each task grew up alone, with its own tools and no shared base. GraIP gives these tasks one bench and one frame so methods can be compared fairly. A shared bench can show which ideas travel across tasks and which only work on the one task they were built for.
arxiv-2601-19217:
Tim Menzies and seven co-authors look back, from an imagined future, at what software journals must become. In 2025, they write, publishing in the field faced a crisis of scale. Communities grew worldwide and fast methods like language models flooded the pipeline, straining the old journal system.

Writing as if from 2036, the team sketches the future the field needs to have built. The playful frame lets senior figures state hard truths about review load, speed, and quality control. Their piece is a call to fix scholarly publishing before scale breaks it for good.
arxiv-2601-19417:
J. Brieussel, R. Tessera, and T. Zheng study random walks on groups, a core topic in modern mathematics. A random walk moves step by step in random directions. The question here is how far the walk can stray from its start over a set number of steps. The groups involved grow in a controlled, polynomial way, which keeps the walk's spread orderly.

The authors prove concentration inequalities for the largest displacement of the walk. In plain terms, the chance of a very large escape falls off sharply, like a bell curve tail. The walk is centred and uses steps from a fixed, bounded set of moves. Such bounds matter wherever random walks model real processes, from diffusion to algorithms. The result gives a firm grip on how wild a walk can get.
arxiv-2601-19817: Bowman Hall reports a computing study of hard-to-catch fake primes. The samples are composite numbers of about three hundred fifty bits. They were built with the Arnault method, so they pass every Miller-Rabin primality test up to base eleven. Two hundred such numbers were generated and checked. Every one of them fails the strong Lucas probable prime test. The gap between the two tests matters for cryptography, where a composite mistaken for a prime can weaken keys.
arxiv-2601-20317:
Yipu Zhang and ten colleagues present VersaQ-3D, a reconfigurable accelerator chip for fast 3D reconstruction. New transformer models can rebuild a 3D scene directly from images, with no per-scene tuning. But a billion-parameter model demands too much memory and compute for instant on-device use.

VersaQ-3D uses versatile quantization, representing numbers at mixed precision, to slim the model for hardware. A reconfigurable design lets one chip serve both feed-forward reconstruction and related tasks. Fast on-device 3D would help augmented reality, robot perception, and digital twins respond in real time. That is the gap this chip is built to close.
arxiv-2601-20417:
SpeechMapper is a cheaper way to connect speech models to large language models. Current speech systems bridge the two with projection layers and train everything on speech instruction data. That strategy is computationally heavy and prone to overfitting the tasks and prompts it saw in training.

SpeechMapper trains a speech-to-text embedding projector instead. By keeping the heavy components fixed, it lowers cost and resists overfitting. The authors aim for models that generalize better to new speech tasks. Cheaper, sturdier speech interfaces would help voice assistants work across more settings and speakers.
arxiv-2601-20717:
Arie Bodek, Hyon-San Seo, and Un-Ki Yang sum up precision tests of a key number in particle physics. Their 2026 paper reviews the weak mixing angle near the Z pole. The Z pole is the energy where the Z boson is made most often. The mixing angle links the weak and electric forces in one value.

The summary centers on an improved extraction of the effective leptonic angle. It builds on a published CMS measurement at the Large Hadron Collider. That measurement used the forward-backward asymmetry in Drell-Yan events at thirteen TeV. In such events, a quark and antiquark make a lepton pair. The paper gathers what these precise numbers say about the standard model.
arxiv-2601-20917:
Masked Lagrange reconstruction is presented in this 2026 paper as a way to split digital signing power among many parties. The target is ML-DSA, the standard signature scheme fixed by FIPS 204. A threshold version lets any T of the parties sign together. The signatures stay at the standard size and verify with unmodified FIPS 204 tools. Rival methods impose limits, such as honest-majority rules or many rounds of interaction.

The paper's technique aims to lift those limits while keeping standard output. That matters for shared custody of keys in finance and infrastructure. No verifier should need special software to trust the result. The work is a focused advance in applied cryptography. It shows that post-quantum signatures can be shared without breaking the standard.
arxiv-2601-21117:
Daniel Köglmayr and three co-authors teach a machine to remember several chaotic patterns after just two glimpses. Their 2026 paper studies two-shot learning of multiple strange attractors. A strange attractor is the tangled shape a chaotic system traces over time. The brain combines short- and long-term memory to store many pieces of information. The authors take inspiration from that design. They extend a recent machine learning technique that does the same.

Their system pairs a next-generation reservoir computer with extremely randomized trees. The reservoir acts as short-term memory; the trees hold the long-term store. Together they process, store, and recall multiple attractors. Learning each from only two examples is the hard part. Success hints at machines that memorize dynamics like brains do. The work joins neuroscience ideas with chaotic time-series learning.
arxiv-2601-21717:
Shogo Nakakita bounds the sample cost of estimating a covariance matrix with a popular sampling algorithm. The unadjusted Langevin algorithm draws samples by following a noisy downhill rule. For strongly log-concave, smooth distributions, its samples can estimate the covariance.

The author compares one long chain against many parallel chains. The single chain wins by a logarithmic factor in dimension and target precision. The gain comes from the burn-in phase cutting bias more effectively. Clear sample bounds help practitioners choose chain layouts with math, not folklore, when sampling feeds a covariance estimate.
arxiv-2601-21817:
Mingyuan Xu, Xinzi Tan, Jiawei Wu, and Doudou Zhou tackle a growing problem. How to rank large language models when no correct answers exist to check against. A common fix is to let other models act as judges. The catch is that judge models differ a lot in reliability.

Treating all judges as equal can produce biased leaderboards and misleading confidence, the authors note. In fact, more data can make a ranking more confidently wrong when judges are pooled the wrong way. Their 2026 preprint proposes a judge-aware ranking framework that accounts for those differences. Fair ways to weigh judges matter, because public rankings steer which models people buy, fund, and build on.
arxiv-2601-21917:
Amir Ali Ahmadi and Georgina Hall prove a discouraging result about a basic computational task. Finding critical points of a function, the flat spots where optimization methods hope to land. Even for simple classes of nonconvex functions, they show that computing even rough approximations is intractable.

Concretely, if a fast algorithm existed that took a polynomial in many variables, of degree as low as three. And returned a point close to critical, that would contradict what complexity theory leads us to expect. Their 2026 preprint draws that line carefully. Negative results like this are valuable: they tell algorithm designers to stop hunting for guarantees that cannot exist. And to aim at structure or heuristics instead.
arxiv-2601-22117:
Francesco Di Braccio and Viresh Patel answer a question about covering colored graphs with tidy cycles. Color the edges of a graph with several colors, and give the graph a high minimum degree, so every vertex has many connections. A question from Letzter and Pokrovskiy asks how many vertex-disjoint cycles, each in a single color, are needed to cover every vertex.

The answer should depend on the number of colors and the minimum degree. Di Braccio and Patel resolve the problem up to a factor that grows only slowly with the number of colors. Their 2026 preprint settles most of a clean extremal question, the kind whose tidy statement hides years of work in graph theory.
arxiv-2601-22317:
Ege Demirci, Francesco Bullo, Ananthram Swami, and Ambuj Singh recover missing flows on a network while keeping the books exact. Flows here are loads that move on edges, in grids, roads, or pipes. Their 2026 preprint presents FlowSymm, a model that never breaks the local rule that flow in equals flow out.

The model acts on flows that already obey the rule, so each step stays legal. A graph heed step learns weights for those acts from edge traits. A light polish step then sharpens the fit. The design suits power, traffic, and travel data.
arxiv-2601-22417:
Yumiao Wang and a large team boost the yield of a rare nuclear state that could power a new kind of clock. The state, in thorium-229, links the nucleus and the atom in a rare way. Their 2026 preprint notes that making it well, on demand, is still a hard lab problem.

Their route uses a cascade decay, fed inside storage rings and electron beam ion traps. A richer yield would speed work on nuclear clocks, which promise time marks sharper than today's best. It would also aid fine tests of physics. The work is a recipe for supply.
arxiv-2601-22617:
Hongxi Yan, Qingjie Liu, and Yunhong Wang cut the cost of long chain-of-thought reasoning by stopping weak chains early. Large reasoning models think in long steps, which costs much compute. Their 2026 preprint, EntroCut, finds that the spread of the model's early output odds tells good chains from bad ones.

Cutting a doomed chain early saves time with little loss. The signal comes free, from odds the model already gives. The trick suits small reasoning models most, where each run counts. It offers speed without retraining. The work is a sharp, cheap gate.
arxiv-2601-22917:
Tom Raynes and eight co-authors work toward counting chimpanzees from camera trap videos, automatically. Estimating how many apes live in an area rests on measuring how far each animal is from the camera. Today, people read those distances by hand from huge piles of video, a slow and costly task.

Automating the distance step could speed up population counts across whole forests. Reliable counts guide protection work for great apes, whose numbers are under pressure. The study links computer vision with field ecology in a direct, useful way. Camera traps gather the video corpora around the clock, so automation promises counts across seasons rather than single expeditions.
arxiv-2603-01617:
Gianmarco Del Sarto, Franco Flandoli, and Marta Lenzi ask why Arctic temperatures swing more as the climate warms. Their 2026 work uses a simple energy-balance model of the Sellers type, with random sunlight input. Carbon-driven forcing may raise not just mean heat, but also how much heat varies.

They start with fast sunlight noise and slow temperature change, then reduce the pair to one equation. In that form, noise multiplies the state, which can amplify swings near ice-sensitive settings. A clear formula for steady variance shows it grows as the forcing parameter rises. A spatial version shows the same growth in linked swings between places. The result names a clean mechanism for wider, more synced Arctic swings under forcing.
arxiv-2603-02317:
Hanpu Liu, Yan-Fei Jiang, Eliot Quataert, and colleagues build a synthetic spectral library for puzzling red objects in this 2026 paper. Little Red Dots are compact distant objects that defy standard black hole models. Their light looks like a blackbody with star-like features at red wavelengths. That hints at a thick atmosphere at a few thousand degrees.

Their library varies surface temperature and gravity across thick atmosphere models. Gravity here acts most directly as a stand-in for surface density. Pure blackbodies prove crude next to these detailed spectra. Several features track surface density well, including a kink from hydrogen opacity and a calcium absorption line. One local object matches a very low density on all three checks, which disfavors a static, held-up atmosphere.
arxiv-2603-02817:
Ryan Griffiths, Timothy Butterley, Richard Wilson, and James Osborn improve a sky-watching instrument that measures air shimmer for telescopes. Their 2026 paper advances the SHIMM, a fast infrared sensor that profiles optical turbulence day and night. Knowing where turbulence sits helps observatories and laser ground stations plan around it.

They derive new weighting functions, correct for the blur from nonzero exposure times, and estimate how fast turbulence evolves by pairing the profile with a defocus method. End-to-end simulations matched the recovered values closely, with tiny errors and strong correlations. A simple four-layer air model also held up, even in rough daytime conditions. They report the instrument's sensitivity limit and flag a mixing effect between the ground layer and the next layer up.
arxiv-2603-02917:
Lucas Hanouz, Marc Kaplan, Jean-Sébastien Kersaint Tournebize, and colleagues run two quantum tasks on hardware built for one. Most quantum networks today only distribute encryption keys. Their 2026 paper implements quantum oblivious transfer and quantum tokens on the same key-distribution hardware, a step toward multi-purpose networks.

The contribution is largely method: a full-stack framework that runs the same user applications on simulated or real back ends. Because the simulator copies the real device's losses and errors, code can be validated before touching hardware. All software sources are open for reproduction. The team reviews security against known bounds and explains the engineering choices that made real-hardware runs feasible. Their process lowers the expertise barrier for testing new quantum protocols.
arxiv-2603-03217:
Hashir Kuniyil, Asad Ali, Syed Arslan, and colleagues turn a photon detector's recovery lag into a quantum hacking tool. Quantum key distribution promises secrecy, but its single-photon detectors need dead time to recover after each click. Security proofs usually treat that recovery as a fixed constant.

Experiments show the effective recovery stretches substantially when the incoming count rate climbs into the high regime. An attacker who floods the detector can therefore suppress detections unevenly across measurement bases, turning mismatch errors into plain loss. In one common protocol family, that stealth keeps the error rate below the abort threshold while erasures climb. Countermeasures built for timing attacks do not cover this recovery effect, so security models must include detector dynamics explicitly.
arxiv-2603-03317:
David Kogan and Sam Nguyen of Google introduce Retcon, a prompting method for steering chatbots turn by turn. Support agents, teaching assistants, and game characters all need behavior that can change mid-conversation: a new tone, a harder question, a reaction to events. Their 2026 paper notes that ordinary prompting loses that control as conversations lengthen or drift from earlier turns.

Retcon uses a few well-chosen examples to give precise control at each turn, without retraining the model. In their tests it performs far better than both zero-shot prompting, which gives no examples, and traditional few-shot prompting. The result is a light, practical tool for builders who need a conversational agent whose behavior stays adjustable throughout a long exchange.
arxiv-2603-03417:
Yegon Kim and four colleagues improve how language models pick their best answer. A popular trick generates many candidate solutions in parallel and lets a verifier choose. Two bottlenecks follow: picking correctly is hard, and generating many full solutions is slow. Their 2026 paper argues both trace back to one cause, how well the verifier is calibrated.

Existing verifiers score each candidate alone, ignoring the context of the rival answers. The Multi-Sequence Verifier instead reads all candidates jointly and models their interactions, which sharpens calibration and improves best-answer selection. A streaming variant watches candidates as they form and stops generation early once the winner is clear. In tests it reached the same target accuracy at roughly half the latency of isolated scoring.

austen-northanger-abbey-1817:
Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey came out in 1817, after her death, a Gothic parody. Catherine Morland, a keen reader of Gothic novels, lets her fancy run wild. Austen wrote the book young, and its bounce shows her early comic gift at work.

Catherine visits Bath, makes friends, and falls for the witty Henry Tilney there. At his abbey home she hunts for horrid secrets that do not exist at all. A locked cabinet and a laundry list deflate her wildest dark dreams in Bath. She learns that real life has its own quiet wrongs to face bravely. Austen teases Gothic craze while she defends novels and their young readers.
austen-persuasion-1817:
Jane Austen's Persuasion came out in 1817, after her death, her final full novel. Anne Elliot gets a quiet, autumnal second chance at love in its pages. At nineteen she broke her engagement to Wentworth on a friend's advice and pressure.

Eight years later, Wentworth returns, now a rich naval captain with fame. Anne watches him court others while her own bloom and spirits slowly revive. A fall at Lyme and a famed letter at Bath resolve the long strain. Austen writes with a mellow depth unique in her six great novels here. Many readers rank this tender book as her most moving work.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-17:
Volume seventeen of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud joins three tractates: Maccoth, Shebuoth, and Eduyoth. Maccoth treats false witnesses and the cities of refuge. Shebuoth is the tractate of oaths, and Eduyoth gathers testimonies that fix points of law.

Maccoth rules that lying witnesses suffer the fate they planned for their victim, and maps the refuge cities for a man who kills by accident. Shebuoth then sorts oaths: rash vows, oaths in court, and oaths that bind the future. Eduyoth closes the volume as a record of agreed rulings, kept so later courts could lean on them. The trio shows law guarding truth itself.
balfour-declaration-1917:
Arthur James Balfour, the foreign secretary of Britain, sent this short letter on November 2, 1917. He sent it to Lord Rothschild, head of the great bank house. Balfour asked him to pass its words on to the Zionist Federation.

In one brief passage, Britain backs the plan for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. The letter adds that the rights of the folk now in that land must not be harmed by the plan. Few short letters have shaped the fate of a land as this one has since.
barrett-threshold-of-the-unseen-1917:
William Barrett sums up forty years of hunts in On the Threshold of the Unseen, his book of 1917. Barrett was a man of science who helped found the chief band for such study. He had sat in dark rooms, weighed frauds, and met claims of all kinds. Here he tells what he holds stands firm past all fair doubt.

Ghosts, thought leaps, and life past death get a calm, grave weigh. He backs faith, yet keeps a tester's care. The book is a life's work in one tome. It is the field's best short sum from a founder.
bogoras-koryak-texts-1917:
Waldemar Bogoras gathered these Koryak texts in the field in northeast Siberia, and the set came out in 1917. The Koryak are near kin to the Chukchi of the same coast. His work formed part of the Jesup work in the North Pacific.

Each text stands in the Koryak tongue with an English version set beside it. Bogoras took care to keep names, songs, and odd turns of speech just as he heard them. The tales and rite texts include shaman songs, myths, and speech used in rites. For those who study lost tongues and oral lore, the book keeps the Koryak voice on record.
bukharin-imperialism-world-economy-1917:
Nikolai Bukharin wrote Imperialism and World Economy in 1917, with an introduction by Lenin; this entry uses the International Publishers edition of 1929. Bukharin, a young Bolshevik theorist, built a companion work to Lenin's own study of imperialism. His focus was the economics beneath the politics.

Bukharin described how trusts and banks fuse into finance capital, and how state capitalist trusts then compete on a world scale. War, in his account, grows from that competition as surely as price wars grow among firms. Lenin prized the book and borrowed from its scheme. It remains a clear statement of the Marxist theory of imperialism's economics, written before its author rose and fell in Soviet politics.
byron-manfred-1817:
Lord Byron wrote Manfred in Switzerland during the stormy summer of 1816, the same season that produced Frankenstein. He called it a dramatic poem rather than a stage play. It was published in 1817 and quickly became one of his most famous works.

Manfred is a nobleman and magician living alone in the Alps, crushed by guilt over a lost beloved. He summons spirits and demands forgetfulness, but refuses to bow to any power, good or evil. Even at death he defies the demons who come for him. The poem is Byron's answer to Faust and the purest portrait of his defiant hero.
chekhov-lady-with-dog-1917:
Constance Garnett's 1917 volume of Anton Chekhov's stories takes its name from The Lady with the Dog. In that tale a bored Moscow banker meets a young married woman at the seaside town of Yalta. Their casual flirtation deepens, against all plans, into the one real love of their lives.

The other stories in the volume show Chekhov's mature range in Garnett's smooth English. Clerks, landowners, doctors, and wives pass through brief scenes that reveal whole lives. Nothing is forced and little is resolved, yet every detail tells. The title story alone is often called the finest love story in Russian writing. The volume is a fine door into Chekhov.
chekhov-party-1917:
The Party and Other Stories reached English readers in 1917 in Constance Garnett's translation. The title story follows Olga Mihalovna through a name-day party at her country house. Smiling for guests all day, she hides a failing marriage and her own despair until the strain breaks through.

A Doctor's Visit, another strong piece in the volume, sends a young doctor to a factory owner's sick daughter. He finds the illness rooted in wealth, idleness, and a useless life. Chekhov builds such stories from talk, glances, and small acts rather than big events. These middle-period tales show his art at its calmest and most exact. Garnett's set made them standard reading in English.

Method papers mattered because photo judgments carried real weight for missing men's files. A loose standard could raise false hope or bury a true match. Here the analysts set out careful rules for their own craft. Historians of the POW effort value such texts for showing the science behind the casework. The file turns the lens on the identification process itself.

The estimate counts sites and keepers the way other papers count battalions. That cold method served warm ends: finding men and keeping bombs from them. It also produced the fullest single picture of Laotian captivity available in 1969. Historians can measure the secret war's hidden prison network from lists like this one.

clarke-leibniz-collection-papers-1717:
Samuel Clarke edited A Collection of Papers in 1717, printing his exchange of letters with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, the great German philosopher. The two men wrote through 1715 and 1716, with Princess Caroline as their go-between, until Leibniz's death ended the contest. An appendix and letters on liberty travel with the main papers.

Space and time stand at the center: are they things in themselves, as Newton and Clarke held, or relations among things, as Leibniz argued? Vacuum, miracles, and God's rule over the world all enter the fight. The Leibniz-Clarke correspondence became the defining debate of early modern metaphysics. It still teaches students how two first-rate minds argue a question to its roots.

coleridge-biographia-literaria-1817:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge meant to write a short preface about his life and opinions. Instead the preface grew into Biographia Literaria, his sprawling book of autobiography and literary theory, published in 1817. All twenty-four chapters are included here.

Coleridge explains his famous split between imagination, which creates and unifies, and fancy, which only rearranges. He also gives a long, respectful argument with Wordsworth's views on poetic language. Mixed in are memories of his schooldays, his friendship with Wordsworth, and his opium struggles. The book founded much of modern literary criticism in English, flaws and all.
conrad-shadow-line-1917:

The ship is becalmed in the Gulf of Siam, the crew falls sick with fever, and the previous captain's madness seems to haunt the vessel. The narrator must hold his ship and himself together at the border, the shadow line, between youth and maturity. Conrad dedicated it to his son and the young men at war. It is among his most perfect short works.
