cooper-mystery-of-witch-craft-english-16:
Thomas Cooper, a Puritan preacher, published The Mystery of Witch-craft in 1617. His title promises an uncovering of witchcraft's truth, nature, occasions, and growth. Cooper writes for Jacobean readers who feared witches and wanted a system they could trust, and he gives them one, orderly from the first page.

He defines the crime, lists its signs, and explains how the devil recruits his servants. Scripture and recent English cases support each claim. The book is methodical rather than sensational. It shows the Puritan mind building demonology into a tidy doctrine. For historians it is a clear window on the beliefs that sent English witches to trial.
coover-experiments-in-psychical-research:
John E Coover published Experiments in Psychical Research in 1917, reporting work done at Stanford University. Coover held a research post set up to test claims of telepathy and other psychic powers. His book was an early American attempt to test such claims inside a university lab.

Tests used cards, drawings, and word lists, with sender and receiver kept apart and results scored against chance. Coover found that his long runs of trials gave no clear proof of telepathy beyond what chance would predict. That sober result made the book a landmark: it set a high bar for later lab work on claimed psychic gifts.
croce-logic-1917:
Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, published in English in 1917, is the third volume of Croce's Philosophy of Spirit. It treats thinking proper. This is the theoretical form of spirit that stands beside intuition, its partner and opposite.

Croce argues that the concept is pure when it is universal and concrete at once. He also holds that philosophy and history are the same act of thought seen from two sides. His famous claim for that identity is stated here. The book completes, with the Aesthetic, his account of how the mind knows. It is the most technical of his major works.
dannunzio-tales-native-town-1917:
Tales of My Native Town gathers D'Annunzio's early stories in a 1917 English edition. The native town lies in the Abruzzo of his boyhood. Peasants, fishermen, priests, and shepherds crowd the brief tales.

These folk live close to the earth and to old folk beliefs. Sights, sounds, and smells of the region soak every page. The great decadent of later fame is not yet on show here. A young writer drunk on his home ground writes instead, fresh and direct. For new readers, these tales rank among his easiest and most winning works, a clean start before the fevered novels.
david-beuthers-gewesenen-churfurstl-sach: David Beuthers Probation-Meister, 1717. The Dresden assay master. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
de-palingenesia-sive-resuscitatione-arti: De palingenesia, 1717. The artificial resurrection. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
dhaturatnamala-1917: Dhaturatnamala, 1917. The Sanskrit alchemical garland. This book preserves that text. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Its place in history is secure. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
die-auffrichtig-entdeckte-probier-und-sc: Die auffrichtig entdeckte Probier- und Scheide-Kunst derer Venetianer, 1717. The Venetian assaying. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
eliot-prufrock-1917:
T. S. Eliot published Prufrock and Other Observations in 1917, his first book of poems. The opening poem gives the love song of J. Alfred Prufrock, a timid man at a social gathering. Prufrock longs to speak and act but fears how others will judge him. Other poems sketch lonely rooms, streets, and women in London and Boston.

Eliot's lines mix high and low speech in a new, ironic music. Images of fog, evenings, and empty talk build a mood of drift. The book was small but its impact was large. It announced a break with the poetry of the past. Many see it as the moment modern poetry truly began.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-17: The seventeenth volume offers more fruits of Montaigne's tower. He reflects on travel, change, and the self that endures through all. The voice is intimate, unhurried, and wise. Four hundred years have not dimmed its charm.
europmc-pmc10017517:
Zecchini and a large team report that a cell chemical called fumarate can trigger the release of mitochondrial DNA and switch on immune defenses, in a 2023 study. Mutations that block the breakdown of fumarate cause a rare inherited condition with kidney cancer. Fumarate then builds up inside cells to high levels.

The team traced how that buildup pushes DNA out of the cell's powerhouses in tiny packages. The loose DNA acts as an alarm signal to the immune system. The finding links cell fuel use to immune activity in a new way.
europmc-pmc10034917:
Sharma and co-authors review current and emerging ideas about the tumor microenvironment in glioblastoma, in a 2023 paper. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive common brain tumor in adults. Its surroundings mix cancer cells with brain cells, immune cells, and blood vessels in a dense, shifting web.

The review describes how that web feeds the tumor and shields it from drugs and immune attack. It surveys new treatment ideas that target the surroundings rather than the tumor alone. Readers get a clear picture of why this cancer resists care and where hope lies.
europmc-pmc10465717:
The GBD 2021 Anaemia Collaborators charted anaemia across the world from 1990 to 2021. Anaemia means the blood carries too little haemoglobin, the part that moves oxygen. The study spans 204 nations and areas, split by age and sex. It also weighs 37 root causes of the condition.

In 2021, 24.3% of all people had anaemia, a total of 1.92 billion cases. That share had fallen from 28.2% in 1990, yet case counts rose with population growth. Young children, women, and people in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia bore the worst load. The condition cost 52.0 million years of healthy life that year. Lack of iron in food was the top cause.
europmc-pmc10544417:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed cancer-linked fibroblasts in 2023 and fresh ways to use them in immune therapy. Fibroblasts build the support web around a tumour. They can speed blood vessel growth, spread, and drug resistance. They also reshape the zone to shield the tumour from immune attack.

Yet the group is far from uniform, Zhang stresses. Some subtypes slow tumour growth rather than aid it. That split means drugs must strike with care, aimed at the harmful kinds alone. The review sums up where these cells arise and how subtypes differ. It tracks trials that target them across many cancers. Early immune therapy pairs that include them get a close look.
europmc-pmc10904817:
Qian and colleagues review a family of helper proteins that run cell energy systems in this 2024 paper. The PGC-1 family has three members that switch on genes for mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy. They also help control cell stress, swelling, and the folding of new proteins. Faults in them are tied to many diseases.

The review maps what turns these helpers up or down and which partners they work with. It then traces their roles in cancers, heart disease, brain disorders, kidney disease, and metabolic ills, meaning diseases of how the body handles fuel. The review weighs their value as markers for diagnosis and for judging a patient's outlook. It also surveys early lab studies of therapies that target these proteins.
europmc-pmc11059217:
Kim and colleagues review natural cell sacs as delivery vehicles for therapy in this 2024 paper. Exosomes are nano-sized sacs cells secrete, and they carry proteins, fats, and nucleic acids between cells. They mix well with body tissue, load varied cargo, and reach deep into tissue. Those traits make them attractive as drug carriers.

The review covers their use in chemotherapy, gene therapy, and heat-based cancer therapy. Because sacs from a patient's own cells are recognised as self, they open a path to personalised treatment. Three hurdles are named plainly: weak cargo loading, fragile structure, and unclear origins of mixed sac batches. The authors call for large-scale production with tight quality control and for more animal and human trials. They still rate sacs as efficient, stable, and safe carriers in prospect.
europmc-pmc11149917:
Jiang and a large team evaluate a broad RAS-blocking drug in lab models and patients in this 2024 study. RAS proteins act as growth switches, and faulty versions drive many cancers. Earlier drugs blocked only one faulty form. Their compound, RMC-6236, targets the active, GTP-loaded state of RAS across many forms. GTP is the small molecule that switches RAS on.

Broad blockade with RMC-6236 was active at doses that were tolerated, the team reports. At those doses it drove profound tumour regressions in animal and cell models of cancers driven by RAS. The same exposures were associated with objective responses in patients, meaning measurable tumour shrinkage. The paper presents both the lab evaluation and the early patient evidence. It frames the drug as a candidate for the wide set of cancers that RAS mutations drive.
europmc-pmc11165417:
Zhang and colleagues pool global data on excess weight in children and teens in this 2024 systematic review. Overweight and obesity in youth raise the risk of lifelong disease. Rates vary by country and have climbed in many places. The team set out to measure the global prevalence and to sort the risk factors behind it.

Across the pooled studies, overweight and obesity proved highly prevalent in children and adolescents, the authors found. Risk factors fell into three groups: inherent factors, dietary factors, and environmental factors. Inherent covers traits a child is born with, while the other two cover food and surroundings. The authors conclude that excess weight is common in this age group worldwide. They call for control measures that act on behaviour, environment, and culture together, not on diet alone.
europmc-pmc1180517:
Holmes and colleagues reported a 2005 genome study of human influenza A virus. They compared 156 complete genomes of the H3N2 type. All samples came from New York State between 1999 and 2004. Tracking how flu changes helps experts pick vaccine strains each year.

Several virus lines were found living side by side in the same seasons. Gene segments had swapped between lines in repeated mixing events. One swap gave later viruses a key surface gene. Holmes links that swap to the Fujian-like outbreak of 2003 to 2004. The work appeared in PLoS Biology.
europmc-pmc1187917:
Brach and colleagues studied walking width and falls in 2005. Older adults often fall, and unsteady gait raises that risk. Speed and stride timing had known links to falls. Step width shifts, how much side-to-side spacing varies, were less clear.

Gait was recorded for 503 adults with an average age of 79. All could walk on their own in daily life. Both very steady and very uneven step widths tied to fall history. The link held for people walking at near normal speed. Brach suggests width balance, not just steadiness, signals fall risk.
europmc-pmc1236917:
Kahn proposed a new body measure for heart risk in 2005. Body mass index, or BMI, may not capture fat risk well. His lipid accumulation product uses waist size and blood fat level. Both values reflect excess fat stored around organs.

Data came from a national survey of about 9,180 adults. The new measure was compared with BMI across 11 risk factors. Many adults ranked high on one measure but not the other. Kahn found the lipid product flagged risk better overall. A tape measure plus a blood test may beat height and weight alone.
europmc-pmc1241417:
Birnbaum and Fenton reviewed cancer risk from early-life chemical exposure in 2003. Developing bodies grow and change fast, which raises their sensitivity. Human data link prenatal radiation clearly to later cancer. Parental chemical exposure hints at brain tumors and leukemia in children.

Animal studies show early exposure to many chemicals raises tumor rates. Prenatal estrogens, natural and synthetic, raise breast and vaginal tumors in people. Halogenated chemicals raise liver tumors after early exposure. Dioxin also delays breast tissue development in rodents. Birnbaum argues hormone disruptors deserve cancer scrutiny from the earliest ages. The pair wrote for Environmental Health Perspectives. Young mice and rats were the test stock in most of this work. Birth and the first days of life are the key time frame here.
europmc-pmc1314917:
Lewis and the Kenya Aflatoxicosis Investigation Group surveyed market maize during a deadly outbreak in 2005. In April 2004, aflatoxin poisoning struck rural Kenya. It caused 317 cases and 125 deaths. Homegrown maize was the known source, but market maize was unchecked.

Surveys covered 65 markets and 243 vendors in affected districts. Of 350 products tested, 55 percent topped the Kenyan limit of 20 parts per billion. Seven percent exceeded 1,000 parts per billion. The worst district averaged 52.91 versus 7.52 in the least affected. Lewis ties market contamination to outbreak geography. 35 percent of products also topped 100 parts per billion. Local farm maize most often crossed the limit.
europmc-pmc1468417:
Tuberculosis germs carry a DNA stretch that varies by strain, letting labs type them fast. Brudey and co-authors mined the fourth world database of those types in 2006. The method, spoligotyping, reads the pattern of gaps in that stretch. The database held 39,295 strains from 122 countries.

The team sorted them into 1,939 shared types and 62 broad lineages. The update added 26 new families tied to place. A blind computer check backed most of the groupings. Brudey shows the resource maps how TB strains spread and relate across the globe. It aids labs, outbreak work, and studies of the germ's past.
europmc-pmc1501017:
Programmed cell death may help destroy lung tissue in COPD. Demedts and co-authors reviewed that idea in 2006. COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, involves airway swelling and loss of lung tissue, mostly from cigarette smoke. Apoptosis is the body's tidy way of killing off cells.

Lungs of COPD patients hold more dying wall and vessel cells than healthy lungs. New cell growth does not keep pace, so tissue thins into emphysema. Animal work points to a growth factor, VEGF, whose loss triggers such death. Demedts suggests blockers of death enzymes, like caspase-3, could one day slow the loss of lung tissue.
europmc-pmc2040517:
Zak, Stanton and Ahmadi tested in 2007 whether the hormone oxytocin makes people more generous. Oxytocin is linked to social bonding and empathy, the ability to share another person's feelings. Participants received 40 units of oxytocin or a placebo, without knowing which. They then played a one-shot money-splitting game with a stranger, who could reject the offer.

People given oxytocin were 80 percent more generous than the placebo group. Oxytocin had no effect on a separate one-way transfer task, which separates generosity from pure altruism. Together, oxytocin and altruism predicted almost half the variation in generosity between people. Oxytocin's effect on generosity was twice its effect on altruism. The authors link generosity to emotional identification with another person, not just selfless giving.
europmc-pmc2125117: A medical paper with morphological studies in experimental cretinism. The thyroid dwarfs. This article preserves that endocrinology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125417: A medical paper on the influence of typhoid bacilli on the antibodies of normal and immune rabbits. The typhoid antibodies. This article preserves that immunology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2131217: A medical paper on the influence of thyroidectomy, splenectomy, gonadectomy, and suprarenalectomy. The removed glands. This article preserves that endocrinology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131617: A medical paper with studies of tissue maintenance, changes with diminished blood bulk. The bloodless tissue. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2141017: A biology paper on the respiration of luminous bacteria and the effect of oxygen tension. The glowing breath again. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2214817:
Illingworth and co-workers built a new catalogue in 2008 of CpG islands, dense clusters of the DNA letters C and G found near gene starts. Most islands lack methylation, a chemical mark that silences genes. The team fished out unmethylated islands using affinity chromatography, a separation based on binding. Sequencing the library defined a human blood island set including many missed by computer prediction methods.

About half the islands sat at known gene start sites; the rest lay inside or between genes. On an array covering over 17,000 islands, six to eight percent were methylated in blood, brain, muscle and spleen DNA. Islands inside or between genes were more prone to methylation. Tissue-specific methylation clustered at development genes, including HOX and PAX family members.
europmc-pmc2253517:
Ellinghaus, Kurtz and Willhoeft released LTRharvest in 2008, software for finding LTR retrotransposons in genome sequences. These are jumping genetic elements bordered by long terminal repeats, which makes them suited to computer detection. High-quality annotations of such elements lag behind genome sequencing. Their tool searches de novo, from scratch, using known element features such as repeat length, spacing and sequence motifs, without needing a reference library.

Against gold-standard annotations for yeast and fruit fly, the software reached sensitivity up to 90 and 97 percent respectively. Specificity was 100 percent for yeast and 72 percent for fly, matching or beating earlier tools. Its main advantages are speed on very large data sets and flexibility in using known features. It processed the largest human chromosome in about eight minutes on a standard Linux computer. The software is open source.
europmc-pmc2267817:
Shivaswamy and co-workers mapped single nucleosome movements across the yeast genome in 2008 after a physiological shock. Nucleosomes are DNA spools that package the genome and gate access to genes. Their exact positions and reshuffling were not fully defined for any genome. Using ultra-high-throughput sequencing, the team mapped nucleosome positions before and after a perturbation causing genome-wide transcription changes, then related movement patterns to gene activity.

Nearly 80 percent of the genome carries positioned nucleosomes in a limited set of stereotyped patterns. Remodelling after the shock usually meant evicting, adding or shifting just one or two nucleosomes at a gene's promoter, not broad regional change. Such moves tended to expose binding sites for the transcription factors driving the response. Some promoters remodelled with no transcription change, so no simple global rule links the two.
europmc-pmc2447617:
Xiao and colleagues trialled the hormone progesterone for severe head injury in 2008. Progesterone is best known as a pregnancy hormone, but animal studies showed it protects injured brains. The team enrolled 159 patients who reached their neurotrauma centre within eight hours of injury with deep coma scores of 8 or less.

Patients were randomised to progesterone or a dummy treatment. At three and six months, the progesterone group scored more favourable outcomes on the Glasgow Outcome Scale, with significance values of 0.034 and 0.048 at the two checks. Their independence scores, covering daily living tasks, were also higher at both follow-ups. By six months, deaths were significantly fewer in the progesterone group. Brain pressure readings ran lower with the drug but not significantly so. No complications were tied to the treatment. The authors called for a larger multi-centre trial.
europmc-pmc2507717:
Godin and colleagues reviewed research in 2008 on why health professionals do or do not follow clinical evidence. Their focus was social cognitive theories, which explain behaviour through a person's thoughts, beliefs, and intentions. The team searched seven databases for studies that used such a theory to predict what clinicians intend to do and what they actually do.

Seventy-eight studies qualified, and 72 of them measured intention. The Theory of Planned Behaviour was the framework used most often. Across studies, the theories explained on average 59 percent of the differences in intention. For actual behaviour the figure was only 31 percent. Results also varied widely with study design. The authors judge the theory a fair tool for predicting behaviour, while urging more care in defining the setting studied.
europmc-pmc2605917:
David and colleagues validated in 2008 a way to find which brain region drives activity in a network, using a rat model of absence epilepsy. Functional MRI can map connected regions but struggles to say who leads, because blood flow timing distorts the neural sequence. The rats' seizures begin in a patch of somatosensory cortex, giving the team a known answer to check against.

They recorded brainwaves and MRI together, then confirmed with electrodes inside the brain. Analysing raw MRI signals failed to find the driver, since blood responses varied between regions. But when they first estimated the hidden neural states behind the signals, using Granger causality and dynamic causal modelling with blood effects explicitly removed, MRI correctly identified the cortical driver. The authors call it the first experimental proof of the approach.
europmc-pmc2640117:
Azad and Beard reviewed in 1998 the germs called rickettsiae and the ticks, fleas, and lice that carry them to people. These germs cause typhus and spotted fever, illnesses that still kill people around the world. They can live only inside the cells of a host, whether that host is a person or a biting insect.

The authors stress that the insect, not the patient, keeps these germs going in nature. The germs copy themselves well inside their insect hosts and can persist there for life. They pass from one insect life stage to the next, and even into the insect's eggs. This long shared history shapes how the diseases appear: quiet in wild animal cycles, then sudden outbreaks when people cross paths with infected insects.
europmc-pmc2652117:
Rockman and Kruglyak mapped in 2009 how genes shuffle in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, a lab animal used worldwide. When eggs and sperm form, chromosomes swap pieces, and the swap rate shapes how traits pass down. The pair bred a large panel of mixed worm lines and read their DNA at fine detail.

They found each chromosome splits into zones with steady swap rates, a pattern that held for the sex chromosome too. The end zones, covering about 7 percent of the genome, barely swap at all. Among 125 wild worms they found only 41 distinct gene patterns, and some supposed wild strains looked like lab escapees. One Hawaiian strain stood apart from the rest. Wild worms, the data show, rarely mate outside their own line, so their gene patterns stay linked over long stretches.
europmc-pmc2693517:
May and a large team described in 2009 how they built Normalization Process Theory, an account of how new practices become routine in health care. Good ideas often die in the clinic: a proven tool or way of working fails to settle into daily habit. The theory explains what social work makes a practice stick, from first trial to invisible routine.

The paper is unusual: it shows the theory being made, step by step, over ten years. The team first drew general patterns from many qualitative studies of health work. They shaped those into an applied model, then extended it by logic into a formal theory meant for testing. At each stage they checked the parts did not clash, still explained the evidence, and held up under criticism from outsiders. The exercise, they argue, is a template for honest theory building.
europmc-pmc2698117:
Deb and colleagues built in 2009 a lab model that pushes tuberculosis bacteria into true dormancy, the sleeping state that makes the disease so hard to cure. Dormant bacteria shrug off drugs aimed at growing cells, so patients need months of treatment. Older models used one stress at a time and never produced fully dormant bacteria.

The new model stacks four stresses the germ meets inside the body: low oxygen, high carbon dioxide, thin food, and acidity. Under the pile-up, the bacteria stopped dividing, lost their waxy staining trait, and loaded up on fat stores. They also became broadly drug tolerant. A mutant unable to make its main storage fat stayed easier to kill, and restoring the gene restored tolerance. Dormancy genes for fat making, the authors argue, are prime targets for drugs against latent infection.
europmc-pmc270017:
Stark and colleagues built in 2003 one of the first computer methods to predict the targets of microRNAs in the fruit fly. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules that dial genes down by gripping their messages. Only a handful of targets were known, because the grip is short and imperfect, defeating simple sequence matching.

Their screen searched the conserved tail regions of fly genes for grip sites, then graded each candidate by the shape and energy of the predicted pairing. It recovered all five targets already proven in the lab. Its top predictions clustered tellingly: one microRNA's list was rich in Notch pathway genes, another's in cell-death genes. The team tested six fresh predictions in the lab and confirmed all, doubling the world's count of proven animal microRNA targets at a stroke. They caution that single predictions hover near the edge of statistical belief until tested.
europmc-pmc2713417:
Jansson and co-authors profiled in 2009 the chemicals in stool from twins to find markers of Crohn's disease, a long-term gut swelling illness of unknown cause. Both genes and environment play a role, and gut microbes are required for the disease to start. Current blood markers cannot stand alone, so a non-invasive stool test would help.

Using a high-precision mass method that weighs thousands of chemicals at once, they studied seventeen identical twin pairs with healthy and ill twins. Distinct chemicals clustered in pathways for amino acids, fatty acids, bile acids, and arachidonic acid, a fat linked to swelling. Several chemicals also tracked with specific gut microbes, which suggests stool markers for diagnosis and tracking.
europmc-pmc2717117:
Neergaard and co-authors argued in 2009 for qualitative description, a plain form of qualitative health research that stays close to what people say about their own experience. Researchers often feel pushed to label simple work as phenomenology or grounded theory, grander methods it does not truly use. That pressure, the authors say, leads to posturing and hides a useful option.

They set out the strengths and limits of the method and give examples of its use in health studies. It fits mixed-method projects, survey building, and studies that need firsthand accounts from patients, relatives, or staff. It also suits projects with little time or money, as long as its limits stay in mind.
europmc-pmc2718517:
Silby and co-authors sequenced in 2009 two more strains of Pseudomonas fluorescens, a soil and plant-surface bacterium, and compared them with a third known genome. Some strains help plants by feeding them, fighting fungi, or waking plant defenses. Knowing only one genome hid how diverse the group truly is, and what drives its plant effects.

The three genomes differed so widely that the group looks more like a species complex, a cluster of close species, than one single species. Strains shared a core set of genes but carried very different extra genes for nutrient use and plant contact. That split helps explain why strains vary so much in how they live on roots and leaves.
europmc-pmc2831917:
Nelson, Hatch, and Webster checked in 2010 whether stain-proofing chemicals in blood track with cholesterol, weight, and insulin resistance in the general United States population. The chemicals, called PFCs, coat packaging and fabrics and persist in the body for years. Data came from the national NHANES survey of 2003 to 2004, covering ages twelve to eighty.

Three of the four chemicals studied rose alongside total cholesterol. People in the top quarter for one chemical, PFOS, carried total cholesterol about thirteen points higher than those in the bottom quarter, a gap measured in milligrams per deciliter. The fourth chemical ran the other way. Links with body size and insulin resistance were weak and patchy, so the authors call the work exploratory.
europmc-pmc2846417:
Shea and colleagues traced adult muscle stem cells in 2010 to answer whether they can renew themselves inside the body during repair. Satellite cells, marked by the protein Pax7, sit quietly beside muscle fibers until injury wakes them. Using genetic tags switched on at set times in mice, the team followed these cells through injury and healing.

After damage, quiet cells divided; some built new fiber while others slipped back into quiet rest, fully restocking the stem pool. A signaling brake called Sprouty1 proved essential for that return trip: cells lacking it could not settle back into rest and instead died. Without Sprouty1 the self-renewing pool shrank, marking reversible rest as an actively guarded state.
europmc-pmc2869317:
Gibbs and a large team hunted in 2010 for DNA variants that tune gene activity and chemical tagging inside the human brain. They read DNA, gene activity, and methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, in four brain regions from each of one hundred fifty donors. Six hundred samples let them link each person's variants to molecular traits, called quantitative trait loci.

Such loci proved abundant for both traits across the genome, not rare exceptions. Gene activity loci clustered tens of thousands of DNA letters from gene starts, while tagging loci sat almost exactly at the tagged site itself. The strongest effects often appeared in several brain regions at once. Tagged sites outside island regions, the tag-dense stretches near genes, were the most likely to be under genetic control.
europmc-pmc2893117:
Galanello and Origa reviewed in 2010 beta-thalassemia, the inherited failure to make enough of hemoglobin's beta chain. Symptomatic cases arise in roughly one in one hundred thousand births worldwide, and ten times more often in the European Union. Three forms span the severity range: minor, usually silent; intermedia, moderate; and major, which declares itself in the first two years of life.

Children with the major form need regular red cell transfusions to survive. Lifesaving transfusions slowly overload the body with iron, damaging the heart muscle, liver, and hormone glands, so iron-removing therapy must accompany them. Patients with the intermedia form present later and can often avoid regular transfusions. The review covers genetics, diagnosis, and the management balancing act.
europmc-pmc2893517:
Garin and the MHADIE group tested in 2010 the World Health Organization disability survey, WHODAS-2, in people with chronic disease across Europe. The survey gives one score for disability and scores for seven areas of life. Over eleven hundred patients with one of thirteen chronic states took it at seven centers. They also took a standard health survey, at the start and again weeks later.

The survey's structure held up under factor tests, a check that items group as planned. Scores were stable when stable patients took the test twice. They also lined up well with the standard survey and split patients by how ill they were and by work status. Scores moved when health changed over three months. One shared ruler can thus compare disability across very different diseases.
europmc-pmc2914717:
D'Ippoliti and the EuroHEAT team measured in 2010 how much heat waves raise deaths across nine European cities, using one shared definition of a heat wave. Definitions that mix daytime highs, nighttime lows, intensity, and duration let them compare cities fairly over summers from 1990 to 2004, with the extreme 2003 summer analyzed separately. Effects were counted in residents over sixty-five, the most heat-vulnerable group.

Excluding 2003, mortality on heat wave days rose from under eight percent in Munich to about a third higher in Milan. Long, intense episodes tripled the effect of milder ones. Mediterranean cities pooled near a twenty-two percent rise against about twelve percent for northern continental cities, and breathing-related deaths climbed most of all. Cities cannot import each other's heat plans uncritically.
europmc-pmc2954317:
Tang and colleagues followed single cells as inner mass cells from mouse embryos turned into embryonic stem cells in culture, in a 2010 study. That switch trades a normal growth programme for endless self-renewal plus the power to form any tissue.

Reading RNA cell by cell, they caught major molecular transitions, shifts in message variants, and broad changes in metabolism genes. Repressive regulators rose while activating ones fell, a balance that may protect stem cell flexibility. Small RNAs also split into two camps, one targeting early development genes and another targeting stemness genes, guarding the new state.
europmc-pmc2972217:
Lee, Park, Takahashi, and Wang reported in 2010 that the cell's energy sensor AMPK partners with ULK1, a starter protein for autophagy, the process that digests worn cell parts. A growth signal complex called mTOR normally holds ULK1 back, by an unclear route.

The sensor binds a specific stretch of ULK1, and that grip is required for autophagy to proceed. Switching the sensor on drew in a third partner and led to chemical marking of a mTOR component, shutting mTOR down. Cells carrying a version of that component immune to marking failed to start autophagy, confirming the chain.
europmc-pmc3009617:
Germain reviewed Fabry disease, a progressive inherited disorder of fat processing, in a 2010 article. A missing or faulty lysosomal enzyme lets a fatty substance build up inside cells across the body, in people of all ancestries.

Males with no enzyme activity can show the full picture: burning limb pain, skin spots, kidney failure, heart thickening, hearing trouble, and strokes. Females range from near silent to severe because one X chromosome switches off at random. Enzyme testing settles diagnosis in males, while women need genetic testing. Childhood pain is often mistaken for growing pains or joint disease.
europmc-pmc3071317:
Moldofsky and Patcai studied in 2011 the long shadow of SARS in Toronto patients who still could not return to work well over a year after infection. Most were health care workers. The team recorded their sleep in the lab and compared their symptoms with healthy volunteers and with patients who have fibromyalgia, a chronic pain and fatigue condition.

Survivors showed lasting fatigue, widespread muscle pain, weakness, low mood, and sleep that did not refresh. Their brain waves during sleep were unusually unstable, with breathing pauses tied to dream sleep. The pattern closely resembled fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, with a few differences in pain and brain wave measures. The authors present chronic post SARS illness as its own syndrome overlapping both conditions. Their warning proved timely for later pandemics: surviving a severe virus can mean years of disability.
europmc-pmc3091517:
Steelman and a very large team reviewed in 2011 two growth signaling highways that cancers hijack, and that also shape aging. When these pathways, which relay growth signals through chains of switch proteins, are damaged by mutation, cells multiply without restraint and refuse to die on cue. That combination sits behind many tumors and behind resistance to treatment.

The review explains what each pathway does in healthy tissue, where they talk to each other, and which mutations most often lock them on. It then turns to newer territory: the same pathways help maintain cancer stem cells, the seeds of relapse, and they influence cell aging and whole body aging. Adjusting their activity could therefore serve two goals at once, the authors argue. Better control might both treat cancer and slow aspects of aging, a prospect they survey with care.
europmc-pmc3104217:
Jennifer Madans, Mitchell Loeb, and Barbara Altman reported in BMC Public Health in 2011 on an international effort to measure disability in a shared way. A voluntary group linking statistical offices from more than a hundred nations had worked since 2001 under United Nations support. Their task grew urgent once a UN rights treaty required tracking equal chances for disabled people.

The group built its work on a World Health Organization framework for health and daily function. Its main product was a short set of six questions for national censuses, now adopted for UN guidance, with longer sets still being tested in many languages. The paper explains how shared questions let countries compare results fairly.
europmc-pmc3108117:
Christos Damalas and Ilias Eleftherohorinos wrote a 2011 review in an environmental health journal on the risks that farm chemicals pose to people and nature. Such products protect crops from pests and weeds, but concern has grown over exposure at work and traces left in food and water. Their paper surveys how harm is judged.

Risk, they note, depends on the product used, the dose, the weather, and how long the chemical lasts in soil and water. Farm workers, spray crews, and families near treated homes face the highest contact. The authors call for better tools to predict harm, safer product designs, careful spraying practice, and farming methods that need fewer chemicals overall.
europmc-pmc3140517:
Wanyang Liu and colleagues identified a gene behind a rare brain vessel disease in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The disease narrows arteries at the base of the brain, mostly in East Asian families, and a suspect region on one chromosome was known but not the gene. The team combined family linkage mapping with full protein-coding scans.

One variant in a large gene stood out, shared by affected families on a common inherited background stretch. In a case-control study the variant carried a very large rise in disease risk, and further rare variants in the same gene appeared in Asian and European patients. The gene's normal roles include protein tagging, and silencing it in zebrafish distorted blood vessel growth. The work names a clear genetic suspect for the disease.
europmc-pmc3197617:
Hokyoung Son and colleagues systematically broke the control genes of a cereal head blight fungus in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The fungus attacks wheat, barley, and rice and poisons grain with toxins harmful to people and livestock. Control genes, called transcription factors, orchestrate the traits behind that damage, so the team built mutants across the whole family.

Mutants in more than six hundred control genes were scored on seventeen traits. The result was a database of over eleven thousand measurements covering growth, development, stress survival, attack ability, and toxin output. Factors governing sexual development proved unusually interconnected with other traits and deeply conserved across fungi. The mutant library and its trait database now serve as a reference for gene-control networks in this and related fungi.
europmc-pmc3203117:
Sabrina Cipriani and colleagues studied a bile acid receptor called GP-BAR1, also known as TGR5, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The receptor is abundant in the ileum and colon, and earlier work suggested it calms immune cells. The team asked how it affects the gut barrier and inflammation in mouse models of colitis.

Mice without the receptor had abnormal mucus-producing cells and disorganized tight-junction proteins, making the gut leakier and colitis more severe. A computer screening search identified the antibiotic ciprofloxacin as a molecule that activates the receptor, and it quieted inflammatory signaling in immune cells. Treating colitic mice with ciprofloxacin or another receptor activator eased the disease, and receptor levels rose in inflamed gut tissue, including Crohn's disease samples.
europmc-pmc3247717:
George Fine and colleagues reviewed metal oxide semiconductor gas sensors for environmental monitoring in this 2010 paper in Sensors. These sensors are cheap, tough, light, and long-lived, with fast, sensitive responses, and they are widely used to watch trace levels of gases such as carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide. The review explains how their response arises from the sensor's surface.

The authors connect the sensing behavior to surface structure, then describe how the materials are synthesized and how the route chosen reshapes that structure. They survey progress on detecting gases such as carbon monoxide. Nitrogen oxides and ammonia get their own treatment, plus the harder problem of carbon dioxide. Recent advances from their own community include selective zeolite coatings, new perovskite materials, and a chemical vapor deposition method for laying down the sensing films.
europmc-pmc3303817:
Jami and Mizrahi asked how similar the gut microbe communities of cows really are, in a 2012 study. The first stomach of a cow, the rumen, hosts microbes that turn tough plant matter into food the animal can use. The team read bacterial DNA from sixteen lactating cows and compared the communities animal by animal.

Counting exact species gave only about half the community shared between cows. When the analysis also credited close family ties between bacteria, similarity climbed much higher. Thirty two bacterial genera appeared in every single cow, though their amounts swung widely. The authors conclude that cows share a core rumen community, and that the rumen environment favors bacteria from related families with similar skills.
europmc-pmc3315017:
Lambert and colleagues mapped hidden zones inside a small deep brain structure using standard hospital scans, reporting in 2012. The structure, the subthalamic nucleus, helps control movement and is a favorite target for implanted stimulators that ease Parkinson disease. Animal work had long suggested it holds three zones handling movement, thinking, and emotion, but proof in living humans was missing.

Using diffusion imaging, which traces the brain's wiring, the team sorted points inside the nucleus by their connection patterns. Three clusters emerged in the expected arrangement, with the movement zone at the back and the emotion related zone at the front. The sorting worked within normal scan times, a first for living patients. The authors say such maps could help surgeons place stimulator leads more precisely.
europmc-pmc3343417:
Trzaskowski and co-authors reviewed the tiny internal switches that turn the largest family of drug target receptors on and off, in a 2012 article. These receptors, called GPCRs, snake through cell membranes seven times and relay signals from hormones, light, and smells into the cell. Most medicines on the market act on them.

Deep inside each receptor sit several switch like arrangements of building blocks. A binding drug flips some switches, while a blocking drug flips others, steering the receptor toward different signaling routes. The review weighs four known switches, from an ionic lock to a transmission switch, against the newest crystal structures and computer simulations. It also covers how receptors pair up and how signals pass through pairs, knowledge the authors say can guide the design of more selective drugs with fewer side effects.
europmc-pmc3420917:
Barkan and colleagues cracked a recognition code in 2012 used by a huge family of plant proteins to read RNA. These pentatricopeptide repeat proteins, working in mitochondria and chloroplasts, grip single RNA strands at exact spots, but how they chose their letters was unknown. Each protein strings together a few to thirty repeating units.

Computer analysis pinned the choice on two amino acids within each repeat. The team then proved the code by reprogramming one protein to bind brand-new RNA sequences in the test tube. The modular system differs from every RNA-reading scheme known before. It should let scientists predict the natural targets of countless such proteins and redesign them for fresh tasks.
europmc-pmc3436717:
Aarons and colleagues described a study protocol in 2012 for a planned way to adapt proven child-protection programs without gutting them. Programs that work in trials get tweaked in the field, usually ad hoc, and nobody knows how much change is safe. Their Dynamic Adaptation Process names a program's core elements and its bendable parts in advance.

Six California regions were assigned to the new process or to business as usual while rolling out a program to prevent child neglect. The process adds training on allowed adaptations, fidelity checks with support, and planned fixes for system-level obstacles. The study also tests automated phone and web tools for rating fidelity and client satisfaction. Mixed methods will trace how adaptation and fidelity move together.
europmc-pmc3437017:
Obata and Fernie reviewed in 2012 how metabolomics, the full chemical census of a plant, dissects responses to abiotic stress. Drought, heat, light, and poor soil all scramble plant metabolism, which must rebalance to survive while making protective compounds. New measurement tools now capture that scrambling in detail.

The review surveys the analytical methods, then walks through responses to water shortage, temperature extremes, light shifts, nutrient limits, salt, and oxidative stress. Some answers are shared across stresses, others are specific to one. Classic stress compounds such as proline get their due, and branched-chain amino acid handling emerges as widely important under stress. Where the data allow, the authors sketch the control circuits doing the reconfiguring.
europmc-pmc3439417:
Leffler and co-authors revisited a forty-year-old riddle in 2012: why do species with wildly different population sizes carry such similar levels of genetic diversity? The puzzle, first spotted in protein data, helped launch modern population genetics and the neutral theory of evolution. With cheap sequencing now flooding in, the authors argue the question deserves fresh attention.

If diversity simply tracked headcounts, big populations should be far more varied than small ones, yet the observed range is mysteriously narrow. The review lays out candidate forces, from selection sweeping away variation at linked sites to populations fluctuating over time. The gap matters practically, since low diversity may limit how species adapt to new pressures. Conservation work hangs on the answer too.
europmc-pmc3440417:
Bhat and colleagues reported in 2012 that aged, worn-out astrocytes accumulate in the aging brain and pile up further in Alzheimer's disease. Astrocytes are the brain's support cells, and in dishes they slip into this retired state, called senescence, under stress. Aging is Alzheimer's biggest risk factor, yet which part of aging opens the door was unclear.

Using a marker protein of senescence, the team tracked such astrocytes in brain tissue. They rose steadily from youth through old age, and ran significantly higher in Alzheimer's frontal cortex than in matched controls. Alzheimer's signature protein, amyloid, pushed cultured astrocytes into senescence directly. The retired cells also pump out inflammatory signals. Their buildup, the authors propose, links getting old to getting Alzheimer's.
europmc-pmc3470917:
Mihaylova and co-authors reviewed statistical methods for studying health care costs in Health Economics, surveying work up to 2011. Cost data are awkward: many patients cost nothing, a few cost a great deal, and the spread is rarely even. Yet policy turns on mean costs, so the method chosen matters, above all in randomized trials.

The review sorts methods into twelve broad families, from simple normal models to mixture and Markov chain approaches. For large samples, the authors favor simple methods, since sample means settle toward normality. Smaller samples may need methods that handle one or two quirks of the data, with checks on assumptions. Mihaylova's group warns that the most complex methods remain little tested and need expert hands.

fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-1-macrocosmi-1:
English physician Robert Fludd began his history of both worlds in 1617. This first tract treats the macrocosm, the great world outside man. Fludd defended Rosicrucian ideas in print against sharp critics.

He maps creation from God through stars, elements, and living kinds. Music, number, and light order his cosmos at every level. Engravings by famed artists made the set a visual landmark. The Latin text is dense and wholly confident. The volume opens a grand system in which heaven and earth mirror each other at every step. Few systems of the age reach so far.
frus-1861-d117:
John Lothrop Motley, bound for Vienna as minister to Austria, received a letter from William H. Seward on 27 August 1861. Motley was the new American minister to Austria, bound for Vienna. The letter is document 117 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Motley was a famed historian of the Dutch republic before he was an envoy. Seward sent him to a court that prized rank and form. The August letter belongs to the start of Motley's term, as he learned the trade of diplomacy at Vienna. Motley's histories of the Dutch wars against Spain still sat on scholars' shelves in 1861.
frus-1861-d17:
Norman Judd wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 August 1861. The dispatch is document 17 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd's post in Berlin gave him a view of German opinion as the war dragged on. He reported what he saw and heard for a Secretary who read every such line with care. The letter forms one link in a chain of reports that ran from Berlin to Washington all through 1861. The Berlin file is modest in size, yet it runs the full span of the year's record.
frus-1861-d217:
A State Department letter of 23 July 1861 told Mr. Marsh what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 217 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d117:
A dispatch dated 1 August 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 117 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.

frus-1862-d217:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, opened a new run of letters on 20 June 1862, writing to Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington. The letter is Document 217 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William Stuart was acting head of the legation while Lord Lyons was away.

With Lyons absent, Stuart handled Britain's American business through a hard summer. Seward dealt with him as he had with Lyons, by frequent short letters. The Stuart file that follows covers months when Union arms faltered in Virginia and European talk of stepping into the war grew louder. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d317:
Document 317 completes the four Seward dispatches to Paris dated 24 September 1862 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The set went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Four letters in a day also hint at the steamer schedule: when a ship sailed, the bag had to be ready. The set sailed into an Atlantic of changed politics, since emancipation was now Union policy. Read together, Documents 314 through 317 give the fullest single-day picture of Washington's Paris brief in the whole 1862 file. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d417:
Writing from Madrid on 30 March 1862, Horace J. Perry sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 417 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

End of March 1862 found Spain pulling back from the joint Mexican venture as French aims there grew plain, a split Washington welcomed. Perry's post let him report that shift from inside the Spanish capital. His letters home formed one strand of the record by which the Union tracked Europe's mood. It did so port by port and court by court, while its armies fought to restore the nation.
frus-1862-d517:
On 6 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. The instruction is Document 517 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward wrote with Lee's army on Union soil and the government bracing for the Maryland campaign. His September orders to Europe's posts struck one note: confidence, and no welcome for foreign interference whatever came. At The Hague that note fell on friendly ears. Pike's long file with Seward shows two plain-spoken men keeping a minor post in exact step with a major policy. The dispatch belongs to the tense fortnight in which the Union's fate, at home and abroad, hung on one campaign.
frus-1862-d617:
On 22 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to Bradford R. Wood. It is Document 617 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Late April 1862 was the spring's most hopeful moment in Washington, with New Orleans about to fall. Orders to friendly minor courts in those weeks spread the improving story and kept routine business current. Wood's Denmark file shows how the Department maintained its whole network at once. No post was too small for a monthly letter. No minister was left to guess at the government's line. The instruction is a modest piece of that maintenance, valuable to the reader chiefly as part of the complete pattern.
frus-1862-d717:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1862. He was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The letter is document 717 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, late in the two men's fall exchange.

By October the Molina file had grown into one of the busier small files in the volume. His letters kept Costa Rica's questions in front of the State Department, and Seward's answers kept the tie in good repair. This letter is a late piece of that work. It shows a small land's envoy doing his job with care in a capital gripped by war.
frus-1863p1-d117:
On 13 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 117 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of a pair often bore the fuller tale: a talk writ large, a set of facts laid out. Adams wrote so through the spring of 1863. This letter is the mate to document 116. In the run of the file, the pair shows a post sorting a mass of news into clean parts. They were bound for a reader ten days away by sea.
frus-1863p1-d17:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 20 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London, and the letter is document 17 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote in the last days of a hard year.

The year 1862 had brought the Union near ruin more than once, and Britain's stance still hung in the scale. Seward's letters to London pressed the same claims with fresh force as news changed. This one belongs to the year-end run, when Washington took stock and told its envoy how to open the new year. It is desk work of the highest stakes.
frus-1863p1-d217:
An instruction dated 18 June 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 217 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d317:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 November 1862. His note is document 317 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Small cases fill this part of the volume: a vessel, a cargo, a British subject under arrest. Together they show how a war at sea kept landing on diplomats' desks. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d417:
A note dated 17 March 1863 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 417 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d517:
Among the day's business on 18 May 1863 was a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d617:
Document 617 in the volume is a letter of 12 September 1863 from William H. Seward to William Stuart. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d117: Ambassador Harriman wrote to Roosevelt on November 12, 1943, the day the president sailed from Virginia. His dispatch is Document 117 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Harriman stayed at his Moscow post, gathering the last readings of Soviet intent before Tehran. The record names the date and the two men and no subject. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the voyage papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d17: W. Averell Harriman, then serving as the President's personal representative, wrote to Roosevelt on July 5, 1943, and the report is Document 17 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A date the catalog's title omits is supplied by its own older note, a small warning to read records with care. Harriman would soon become ambassador to Moscow. The record names the men and the day; his report's contents rest in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d217:
Prime Minister Churchill sent President Roosevelt telegram number 504 from London on 13 November 1943, a personal and most-secret protest about French actions in Syria and Lebanon. French forces had seized the Lebanese president and ministers, and Churchill calls the acts lamentable outrages.

He argues the arrests mock the Atlantic Charter and show what de Gaulle's leadership of France means, warning of grave fallout across the Arab world. His proposed course is joint and hard: demand the prisoners be freed and the assembly restored. If de Gaulle refuses, the Allies should withdraw recognition from the French National Committee. They should also halt the arming of French troops in North Africa. He adds a warning that de Gaulle, with armed forces at hand, might do anything.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d317: President Roosevelt received a brief telegram from Secretary of State Cordell Hull, sent from Washington on 25 November 1943. It relays Lisbon's cable 2835 of 23 November, which announces that the group of American army and navy technicians had left Horta the day before for Terceira Island in the Azores. Hull adds that the early departure of these American technicians was thanks to British cooperation at Horta. The short message marks the American build-up on the Portuguese islands moving from negotiation to men on the ground.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d417:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent Secretary of State Hull an urgent telegram from Moscow on 6 December 1943. Numbered 2131, it explains what he knew of the Soviet announcement that had scooped the Tehran communiqué. Harriman had returned to Moscow only the night before.

The newspaper announcement of 4 December, he writes, was a complete surprise to him. The conference agreement was plain. The two declarations were to be released not before eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. Release was to be simultaneous in London, Moscow, and Washington. For security, no mention of the conference was to be made before that hour. He was present when that was understood. Molotov, newly back himself, has not yet been seen, so Harriman can offer no explanation yet, though he guesses the Reuters reports and Senator Connally's broadcast pushed Moscow to speak.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d517:
Lincoln MacVeagh, the American ambassador to the Greek government-in-exile in Egypt, wrote to Secretary of State Hull on December 12, 1943. The exiled Greek government worked from Cairo while German forces held Greece itself. The State Department printed MacVeagh's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

MacVeagh reported on a government without a country, split by politics and shadowed by armed resistance movements at home. His messages helped Washington judge what Greece would need when liberation came. For readers, this report opens the Greek side of the Cairo story, where the questions were not invasions and fleets but legitimacy, relief, and who would rule after the Germans left.
frus-1944-quebec-d117:
Charles Bohlen, chief of the State Department's Division of Eastern European Affairs, wrote this secret memorandum for Secretary Hull on September 4, 1944. The Polish ambassador had just visited him with an urgent appeal from Premier Mikołajczyk and Foreign Minister Romer. Attached is the Polish memorandum itself, dated September 4.

The appeal begged for food, arms, and medical supplies for the Home Army fighting in Warsaw. It reported the Old Town lost, munitions nearly gone, and food rationed only to September 7. A large British air operation had just been judged impossible. Bohlen noted Admiral Leahy had promised to raise the matter with the president and the Joint Chiefs.
frus-1944-quebec-d17:
Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, wrote to President Roosevelt on July 26, 1944. Hopkins lived at the White House and saw Roosevelt daily, so a written message from him usually marked a considered judgment. It appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Hopkins advised Roosevelt on everything from Russian relations to the management of allies, and his written words carried into the planning for the Quebec Conference that September. A Hopkins memorandum in the pre-conference file shows the President's inner circle preparing the ground. For readers, it is a glimpse of the advice Roosevelt trusted most, given by the man who knew his mind best.
frus-1944-quebec-d217:
Roosevelt reported success to Hull from Quebec on September 15, 1944. After many long conversations with Churchill and Lord Cherwell, he wrote, the general matter of postwar plans regarding industries had been worked out. He enclosed the memorandum on Germany that he and Churchill had initialed that day, and he expected Hull to approve.

The general idea, Roosevelt said, was not rehabilitating the Ruhr, the Saar, and similar districts, and he called the result eminently satisfactory. He had also worked out the locations of the occupying forces. His travel plans close the note: he would leave Saturday evening for Hyde Park, where the prime minister and his wife would join him Monday for a couple of days.
frus-1945-50-intel-d117:
Acting Secretary Acheson sent a memorandum to the members of the National Intelligence Authority on 5 August 1946. The authority was the board of secretaries that owned the Central Intelligence Group. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A memorandum to the whole authority put a question before every member at once, in identical words. By August the FBI and CIG fight over Latin America needed the board's ruling, and Acheson's paper belongs to that endgame. Readers should watch how the system handled its first great internal dispute. Not by a president's order, but by the board the January directive had built for the purpose. The machinery, tested here, either worked or showed its cracks.
frus-1945-50-intel-d17:
Attorney General Tom Clark wrote to President Truman on 19 September 1945, the day before the OSS was dissolved. Clark's department housed the FBI, whose director reported to him. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The attorney general's voice mattered in the intelligence fight because the FBI's foreign work hung in the balance. Clark wrote as the president's choice neared, putting the Justice Department's case at the top level. Readers can set his letter beside Hoover's papers to Clark from the same weeks. Together they show a department aligning its front. The bureau chief pressed his chief, and the chief pressed the president, in the last hours before the order fell.
frus-1945-50-intel-d217:
The Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) addressed a letter to the Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee (Gurney) on 3 June 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 217 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. That season, the talk in Washington was of one big law to join up defense, foreign policy, and intelligence.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. The letter went to the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee while Congress debated the law that created the CIA.
frus-1945-50-intel-d317:
Dated 13 May 1947, "Central Intelligence Group Paper No. 24/1" comes from the top level of the government. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 317 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Papers of this kind were the working stock of the system. They were drafted, read, marked up, and filed so the next office could pick up the thread. Read with its neighbors, it helps fill the gaps that grand accounts skip over. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d417:
A memo dated 23 February 1950 was prepared for James Lay, executive secretary of the National Security Council. It is document 417 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Lay's office set the Council's agenda and moved its papers to the President. A memo addressed to him was aimed at the center of the policy machine. Readers meet the staff layer that turned the views of departments into choices laid before Harry Truman. A memo for Lay was, in effect, a memo for the President's desk by a longer road.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d117:
Turf, as much as policy, divides this 23 September 1944 report by James Riddleberger. He headed the Division of Central European Affairs. His note tells the Secretary of State what happened at a War Department meeting on the interim directive for Germany. The note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Treasury men Pehle, Luxford, and Taylor made plain that their department expected a say on every phase of German problems, political as well as economic. They claimed the Treasury plan had the Cabinet Committee's approval and the President's blessing. They also said earlier economic papers, cleared by a foreign policy committee, had been repudiated by both Morgenthau and Hull and should get no further attention.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d17: On 2 November 1944, the eve of his re-election campaign's end, Roosevelt still found time to write Churchill. The message is document 17 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Even domestic politics did not pause the correspondence, because British and American staffs were already preparing the ground for the Malta stop and the Yalta meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d217:
Secretary Morgenthau offered the President a grand bargain with Russia on New Year's Day, 1945. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, proposes a Treasury plan for large-scale aid to the Soviet Union in her rebuilding years. It is not more Lend-Lease, and not relief.

The plan aims at lasting gains for the United States as well as for Russia. Morgenthau has talked it over with Harriman for a year, and the ambassador wants it advanced. The Russians, he understands, will not take the first step but would welcome a constructive American program. Churchill's great worry at Quebec was the stretch right after victory in Europe. A concrete plan offered now, Morgenthau argues, would iron out many of the troubles clouding Soviet relations. He asks for an early talk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d317:
Washington kept feeding the Malta talks from home, as this February 1, 1945 cable from Acting Secretary Joseph Grew shows. Sent in the name of William Clayton, it reports a hitch in the shipping pact signed the past August. Eight Allied states had agreed to keep joint control of merchant shipping until after the war with Japan ended.

Sweden, a major sea carrier, was being courted to join the pact. But word had come that Russia was hinting Stockholm should stay out. Grew doubted the hint would stop Sweden signing, yet Stockholm worried about the Soviet mood. The cable flags an early crack in Allied unity over postwar seas.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d417:
No agreement yet: that is the honest top line of the foreign ministers' draft report to the sixth plenary, dated February 9, 1945. On Poland, the ministers had debated at length on the basis of an American paper. Following Molotov's proposal, the presidential committee idea was dropped.

On the formula for a Polish government, Molotov asked for time. He wished to lay the new American points before Stalin before making a final statement. Discussion would continue later. The report tells the leaders plainly that their ministers had failed to close the Polish question. Reparations and other items follow in the same draft, in the same unfinished state.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d117:
General Deane sent Eisenhower the Moscow mission's party list for Berlin on July 3, 1945. The telegram is document 117 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, with instructions to pass the names to Colonel Lowry, the Joint Chiefs' representative already in Berlin.

The civilian side is led by Ambassador Harriman and reparations chief Edwin Pauley, with embassy secretary Edward Page, minister Isador Lubin, and the reparations commission's counsel and chief of staff. The military side lists Deane himself, Rear Admiral Maples, and Brigadier General Ritchie, plus a handful of junior officers. Deane singles out Lieutenant Chase as an excellent Russian interpreter. The message ties the Moscow-based experts into the delegation that would serve Truman at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d17:
Truman answered on Venezia Giulia and the meeting in this extract of May 21, 1945. Within the next two weeks, he told Churchill, he might have more information. It would bear on a date and location for the proposed tripartite meeting, if Stalin agreed to participate. He hoped Stalin would agree to come west into Germany, or further west.

But he added a caution from his advice: Stalin was not likely to go beyond Soviet-controlled territory. The unprinted portion of the message dealt with Venezia Giulia itself, the Adriatic flashpoint then arming. The extract shows the meeting's geography narrowing toward the Soviet zone weeks before Potsdam was chosen.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d217:
Edwin Pauley removed one word of doubt in a letter to Ivan Maisky dated July 14, 1945. The letter is document 217 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Maisky, chairman of the reparations commission, had noted at a steering committee meeting that Pauley used the word may in his notice about reparations at the summit.

Pauley confirms in writing the verbal assurance he had already given. The subject of reparations will definitely be brought up by the President at the meeting of the Big Three, he writes. More particularly, he will bring up the questions raised in his letter of July 3. The firm wording ended the skirmish over whether Germany's bill would reach the leaders, a point Moscow had probed through several channels.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d317:
Complaints against the Soviet section of Rumania's Control Commission fill General Schuyler's top secret message of July 14, 1945, to the War Department. Relations with General Susaikov and his staff, Schuyler wrote, stayed entirely unsatisfactory. Since the fighting with Germany ended, the American delegation had taken even less part in commission business than before.

His specific charges begin with unanswered letters. Susaikov, he said, left many official letters unanswered despite repeated reminders. The message reached the American delegation at the Berlin conference on July 15, as a relay from the War Department. It gave the Potsdam negotiators a commander's bill of grievances against Soviet practice in Rumania.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d417:
Germany as one economic unit is the theme of extracts from the briefing book paper on policy toward Germany. The United States, they argue, should make clear that dividing Germany into occupation zones does not imply barriers to goods moving between zones. No zone, the paper shows, can live as a closed economy.

The American zone lacks food and is almost wholly without coal and other major industrial materials. The British zone has an even larger food deficit, but holds the coal. The Russian zone has a food surplus and suffered far less bomb damage. The extracts end with agreed principles: uniform ration scales across Germany, and joint programs for coal production and allocation.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d517:
Poland's case for its western frontiers is delivered in a letter from Deputy Foreign Minister Modzelewski to Ambassador Harriman, written at Moscow on July 10, 1945. On his government's commission, he sends a memorandum with enclosures concerning the Polish postulates as regards the western frontiers of the Polish Republic. He asks Harriman to convey the material to Washington.

The enclosure, he hopes, might be used when those questions are possibly examined at the forthcoming Big Three conference. It opens on first principles: what the world wants is peace, a durable peace safeguarding at least the next few generations. That durability, the memorandum argues, must be sought in territorial solutions that ensure every nation room to exist and develop.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d617:
The United States Chiefs of Staff set a policy on French and Dutch forces in the Japan war, July 10, 1945. Their top secret memo is document 617 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It answers a British proposal that the Combined Chiefs state a joint line.

The U.S. chiefs agree in principle to a joint statement. French and Dutch forces, they say, cannot play a major part in Far Eastern operations now. Still, their wish to join should be weighed, and help that fits plans already laid should be welcomed. One condition is firm. No French or Dutch force will be taken unless full control rests with the Allied commander in charge. Its use must turn on military grounds alone, settled by him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1017:
Soviet delegates submitted this second paper on trying the important war criminals at the foreign ministers' meeting of July 30, 1945. Like its twin, it calls for an international tribunal in the very near future. The court would try leaders whose crimes had no fixed place, under the Moscow Declaration of 1943.
