The name list here is longer, and Secretary Byrnes remarked on the difference at the meeting. Papen, Hans Frank, and Schacht join the ten names in the earlier paper, and Doenitz was added by hand. The paper repeats the pledge to press neutral countries to surrender war criminals in hiding.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1117:
On the day Potsdam opened, 17 July 1945, the Acting Secretary of State wrote to Senator Arthur Vandenberg. Vandenberg was the Senate's leading Republican voice on foreign affairs. A Republican in a Democratic cabinet's trust was a rare and prized thing in 1945.

Keeping him informed was how the White House built support in both parties for the peace to come. The message brought a key lawmaker inside the tent while the bargaining was still secret. It marks the home politics that stood behind the talks abroad. A peace that the Senate would not back could fail, and this cable worked to prevent that.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1217:
Vincent, chief of the Division of Chinese Affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn on 23 July 1945. Vincent's desk owned the China file inside the State Department. His note moved expert judgment up to a senior chief while the summit sat.

China questions at Potsdam touched Soviet pledges in Asia and America's hopes for a stable ally. The desk chief's view fed the stands the team took. A note of this kind is the expert layer speaking in its own channel. It shows the department's China knowledge being put at the service of men deciding far larger questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1317:
Pauley, the American member of the Allied Commission on Reparations, wrote to the President on 19 July 1945. Edwin Pauley's mission had toured beaten Germany to judge what the nation could pay and what could be taken in goods, plants, and labor.

Reparations were among the sharpest fights at Potsdam. The Soviet side claimed vast sums; the Americans feared a repeat of the debts that poisoned the last peace. Pauley's reports gave the president the facts from the ground. This message is his word to the top, feeding the summit's hardest money bargain with first-hand evidence.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1417:
The communiqué issued at the end of the Yalta Conference in February 1945 is reprinted in the Potsdam volume. It was the public statement of what Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin had agreed in the Crimea. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A communiqué speaks to the world, so its tone is proud and its edges smooth. Read beside the Yalta protocol, also reprinted here, it shows the gap between what the leaders announced and what they had in fact signed. The Potsdam editors placed both Yalta texts at the back of their volume as a bench mark. Readers can measure the distance traveled between February and August 1945 in these pages.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-117:
Cavendish Cannon, first secretary at the American embassy in Lisbon, sent this report to H. Freeman Matthews, the State Department's director of European affairs, on July 26, 1945. Portugal was a neutral state whose ports and politics drew close Allied watch. Cannon's post gave him a clear view of Lisbon's mood during the war's last summer.

Reports from neutral capitals fed the wider picture behind the Potsdam talks. Leaders deciding Europe's future needed to know how states outside the room would react. Cannon wrote for a Washington reader, in a working officer's plain style. The piece shows diplomacy's quiet outer ring at work during the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-17:
Charles Bohlen's longhand notes of a July 18, 1945 meeting capture Stalin sharing Japan's peace feeler with Truman. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers, transcribed from pencil notes. Stalin handed the President a note from Ambassador Sato and a message from the Emperor.

In Bohlen's fragments, the two leaders weigh how to answer Tokyo. Stalin judges that a reply with no specifics would amount to a refusal. The character of Prince Konoye's mission, he notes, is not known. Truman calls that course satisfactory. Bohlen links the feeler to fear of what the Allies will do, and Stalin adds that Japan can see Allied forces and tanks massing. An editors' note explains the record's odd fate. Bohlen surely made a formal memo of the meeting, as was his habit, but no such memo has been found.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d717:
On July 30, 1945, Byrnes wrote again to Hurley in China, in document 717 of the Potsdam volume. The Secretary kept the channel warm through the conference's last days. Hurley's mission dealt with a China divided by civil strife and invasion. News between Potsdam and Chungking moved by cable, under wartime rules.

Repeated letters in a few days signal active business. The Secretary needed his ambassador aligned as decisions neared. Readers can watch a working tie in motion, message by message. The document adds an Asian strand to a volume mostly set in Europe. It shows the war's two halves joined in one office's in-tray.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d817:
Barnes reported from Bulgaria on July 25, 1945, in document 817. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters thread the volume's whole span. This one dates from Potsdam's midpoint, as the Balkan questions hardened. It joined the second Potsdam volume.

A midpoint report from Sofia shows a post measuring its shrinking room. Barnes reported what the commission allowed him to see. Readers sense the care in his phrasing: facts stated, protests logged. The document adds to the proof that the eastern missions kept faith with the record. Their words remain the West's best witness there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d917:
Sir David Waley signed this British paper of July 23, 1945, offering tentative changes to the American reparations proposals. It amends the draft program document by document. The British want removals kept inside a general program approved by the Control Council.

Removals must not clash with the needs of occupying forces or with approved living standards in Germany. They must also fit the rule that Germany be treated as one economic unit. Other edits put paying for approved imports first, and add monetary gold and securities to the restitution list. Waley also floats swapping set lists of goods between the western and Russian zones.
gao-gaoreports-b-296317: Antmarin, Tzanakos, and Domar tripled the July 2005 fight — three firms, one protest — and GAO's ruling settles all. The firms challenged the award, and the call weighs each claim. Triple-firm filings get one careful answer. Three firms, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299317: L-3 Communications Titan tripled its March 2007 protest — three case numbers, one defense-tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three claims. The firm challenged the awards; the call weighs each claim with care. Triple filings get one triple-checked answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-299517: Sumaria Systems doubled its June 2007 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim to a close. Paired filings get a paired answer from the referee.
gao-gaoreports-b-299817: S4, Inc. doubled down on its 2007 protest — two case numbers, one fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm said the agency's award was flawed; the call tests each claim to the finish. Persistence in the protest game gets one consolidated answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-307317: The State Justice Institute's newsletter ads got a fiscal ruling in this September 2006 GAO call, which tests the advertising charges. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the ad dollars were legal. The newsletters had to follow the law.
gao-gaoreports-b-307917: The Education Department's newspaper ad got a fiscal ruling in this 2006 GAO call, which tests the No Child Left Behind article spending. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the publicity dollars were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310617: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Superior Landscaping Company, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-417: Wrong-payment rules tripped the agencies in 2005, and GAO's report says the law's demands were hard to meet. The review lists the stumbles. The taxpayers' dollars deserved the accurate count. The count had to be right. The stumbles were listed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-617: PUHCA administration needed strengthening in 2005, and GAO's report says opportunities existed to improve SEC oversight. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the utility giants deserved watching. The administration had to be stronger. The utility giants deserved watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-817: Missile defense sustainment funding needed ensuring in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required for operation and support dollars. The findings demand the money. The report warns that the shield deserved keeping. The funding had to be adequate. The shield deserved keeping.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1117: Homeland Security's credit cards were a fraud magnet in 2006, and GAO's report says weak controls left the department highly exposed to abuse. The findings target the plastic. The report warns that the purchase cards needed locks, not just limits. The cards had to be controlled.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-117: Nursing home quality needed more than oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says challenges remained in ensuring high-quality care. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the frail elderly deserved safe homes. The challenges had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-517: Two Sioux tribes' compensation claims got a GAO analysis in 2006, and the report examines the Crow Creek and Lower Brule claims. The findings do the math. The report shows the historic debts deserved honest reckoning. The claims had to be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-617: Wall Street's diversity was slowly shifting in 2006, and GAO's report tracks management-level diversity trends from 1993 to 2004. The findings do the counting. The report shows the corner offices were changing color, slowly. The trends had to be faced. The counting had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-917: Transportation research needed better oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says opportunities existed to improve the research programs and user satisfaction. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the lab work should serve the road users. The research had to deliver.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1117: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report on end-stage renal disease: who receives kidney transplants, how often transplants fail, and what the program costs Medicare. Kidney failure treatment is one of Medicare's most expensive commitments. GAO's analysis gives Congress data on outcomes and spending for a program where the government is effectively the insurer of last resort.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-17: The GSA's broker experiment needed work in 2007, and GAO's report says the early rollout of the national broker contracts showed gaps. The findings flag the flaws. The report warns that the government's landlord should not lease blind. The deals needed daylight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-717: The mail's big reshuffle needed explaining in 2007 — GAO's report says the Postal Service's processing realignment wanted better integration and plainer talk. The findings press for a coherent story. The report's demand: tell the public what the new mail map means.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-817: Other nations were doing better by women and low-skill workers in 2007 — GAO's report shops the globe for policies that helped them land and keep jobs. The findings import ideas worth stealing. The report's pitch: the best labor policy may already exist somewhere else.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-917: New rail lines were queuing up in 2007 — GAO's report says demand for transit-building grants would grow, but the grant machinery needed fixing. The findings pair a transit boom forecast with a bureaucratic tune-up list. The report bets on trains while demanding better tracks for the money.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-17: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report found that thousands of health care providers enrolled in Medicaid were abusing the federal tax system — collecting government health payments while owing large unpaid tax debts. Investigators matched provider records against tax data to expose the pattern. The report raises an uncomfortable question: should programs that pay with taxpayer money do business with tax cheats?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-317: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at state and Local Governments: Growing Fiscal Challenges Will Emerge during the Next 10 Years. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-517: The Government Accountability Office dug into nursing Homes: Federal Monitoring Surveys Demonstrate Continued Understatement of Serious Care Problems and CMS Oversight Weaknesses in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-617: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on tax Compliance: Businesses Owe Billions in Federal Payroll Taxes. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
garland-son-middle-border-1917:
Garland tells his own story in A Son of the Middle Border, printed from work begun in 1898. In a letter up front he says he first dictated the tale in third person. He calls it his story and the story of his people, the Garlands and the McClintocks.

Boyhood in Wisconsin, Iowa, and Dakota Territory unfolds as his family chased the farming frontier west. Log cabin and prairie claim frame a vivid, novel-like memoir. Garland meant the family record to stand for the whole era of settlement from 1840 to 1914. Issued in 1917, the book is both a personal history and a chronicle of the pioneer generation.
gawain-green-knight-webster-neilson-1917:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is the finest Arthurian poem in Middle English, written by an unknown poet. K. G. T. Webster translated it into English verse, and his version appeared in 1917. Unlike Weston's prose retelling, it keeps the beat and music of the original lines.

The Green Knight's challenge at Camelot sets the tale in motion. Gawain strikes off the giant's head, then must seek him out a year later to receive the same blow. On the way he faces winter weather, a tempting hostess, and a test of his word. The poem joins dread and comedy in one bright knot.
gerrard-the-church-and-eugenics-1917: The Church and Eugenics, Gerrard's 1917 work. The Catholic view. This book preserves that book. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
hamsun-growth-of-soil-1917:
Knut Hamsun published Growth of the Soil in 1917, a novel about a man who builds a farm from wild land. Isak walks into the Norwegian wilderness and clears fields stone by stone. His wife Inger joins him, and a home, children, and livestock follow. Neighbors settle nearby, and a small community grows.

The story moves at the pace of seasons and hard labor. Against Isak's steady work, Hamsun sets greed, crime, and town values that pull others astray. The novel won wide fame and helped earn Hamsun the Nobel Prize. It remains a powerful praise of the land and of patient, simple work.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume seventeen: old Fritz, the lonely last years, the king outliving his age. Carlyle's hero in winter, still working, still defiant. The most moving section of the vast work, as the thunder quiets. The old king's loneliness is the most human part of Carlyle's epic.
index-librorum-prohibitorum-1917: Index Librorum Prohibitorum, 1917 edition. The Church's banned-books list. This book preserves that index. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-17:
Westward push and fresh danger shape Volume 17, issued in 1898. Thwaites covers the Hurons and Three Rivers across 1639 and 1640. At peak trust, the mission reaches toward new nations in the west.

Black robes carry the cross deeper into the continent each season. Their letters weigh new tongues, new trails, and new allies with care. Far off, the Iroquois wars begin to close around them. Growth and threat fill the same pages in tense balance. The volume catches the mission at full stretch, just before the noose tightens around it. Ambition and peril grow side by side here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makshan-samuel-:
Samuel ben Phinehas ha-Kohen Makshan, a Bohemian Talmudist, gets a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Prague, he worked in the sixteenth century. His writing survives as commentaries on the most-read parts of Scripture. All three of his named works treat the scrolls read in synagogue.

The article lists his books with their tangled dates. Tehillaat Dibre Shemuel comments on the Aramaic version of Esther, printed at Prague in 1594 or 1601. Bibliographers disagree on the year, and the entry says so plainly. Bet Din shel Shemuel covers Rashi on Esther and Ruth, printed at Lublin in 1606. A third work comments on Lamentations, issued at Cracow without a date. The notice rests on the standard bibliographies of Furst and Steinschneider. It preserves a Prague scholar through the small trail of his printed pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marik-solomon-1: Solomon Marik, a Spanish surgeon, is the subject of one of the thinnest entries in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The article states plainly that no details of his life are known. What survives is his book, written in Spanish in Hebrew characters. It is titled Libro de la Cirogia, a book of surgery. A fragment sits inside a miscellany volume in Munich's royal library. The entry adds two men of similar name. David and Abraham Marich were Spanish exiles allowed to settle at Ferrara in 1493.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-samuel-10:
Samuel Mayer of Hechingen held two professions at once. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906 and call the feat unique in Germany. He was born on January 3, 1807, and studied Talmud at Mannheim and Würzburg, taking a university degree at Tübingen. In 1830 he became rabbi of his native Hechingen, a pulpit he kept until his death on August 1, 1875. Meanwhile he read law, was admitted to the bar in 1849, and became the only German rabbi who was also a practicing lawyer.

That double training produced his great work, twelve years in the making. It is “The Rights of the Israelites, Athenians, and Romans.” Three volumes compare the public, private, and criminal law of the three peoples against modern legislation. The entry also lists the Jewish periodicals he edited. It also lists his history of the Jews of Hohenzollern-Hechingen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memphis-10617:
Memphis, Tennessee, was the largest city of its state. Cyrus Adler gives it a Jewish communal history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city's own rabbi, Max Samfield, wrote it with him. A few Jews lived there for a time before 1845. One early settler was Joseph J. Andrews. In 1847 he gave land for a burial ground. From that gift grew a Hebrew Benevolent Society in 1850. The congregation B'nai Israel grew from it in 1853. It worshipped first in a leased hall. From 1858 it used a converted bank building.

The article then follows the split that came. Rabbi Simon Tuska, chosen in 1860, leaned to moderate Reform. An organ, a mixed choir, and family pews came in. Then the traditionalists seceded in 1862 as Beth-El Emess. Tuska died suddenly in 1870. Samfield, installed in 1871, was still in the pulpit in 1904. That makes the entry partly a memoir of its co-author's own congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-m:
Meshullam ben Machir, also called Don Bonet Crescas de Lunel, was a French scholar who settled at Perpignan and died there in 1306. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Most of what the article records comes from the grief of his relative Abba Mari.

Abba Mari mourned Meshullam in a letter of condolence sent to the Perpignan community and again in one of his liturgical pieces. The entry also reports Heinrich Gross's view that Meshullam is the same man as Sen Bonet de Lunel, author of a commentary on Ibn Ezra's Bible commentary. Its short bibliography points to Gross's Gallia Judaica and to Renan and Neubauer on the French rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mielziner-moses:
Moses Mielziner, born at Schubin in Posen on August 12, 1828, was a rabbi and author who carried German Jewish learning to America. Cyrus Adler and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. His father, the town rabbi, started his Talmud study, while a gifted school principal gave him his secular education.

After yeshivah study at Exin, Mielziner went to Berlin for both Talmud and university, entering the university in 1848. Samuel Holdheim steered him to a post as teacher and preacher at Waren in Mecklenburg, but an Orthodox reaction forced him out in 1853, to his congregation's regret. The entry follows him across the Atlantic; he died at Cincinnati in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mogulesko-sigmu:
Sigmund Selig Mogulesko, born in Bessarabia on December 16, 1858, was the Yiddish stage's best comedian, as Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik declare in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A synagogue choirboy with a fine voice, favorite meshorer to famous cantors, he went young to Bucharest and studied at its Conservatory of Music.

He joined Abraham Goldfaden soon after the Yiddish theater itself was founded, and toured Russia, Austria, Rumania, and England with its companies. America took him about 1886, and New York kept him, three years of illness aside. He composed for the stage as well as clowning on it — the entry, written in 1904, catches him mid-reign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morgulis-michae:
Michael Grigoryevich Morgulis was a Russian jurist and author born at Berdychev on March 25, 1837. He fought his way from the ḥeder to the law faculty, as the Jewish Encyclopedia recounts in 1906. He was a brilliant boy in the government rabbinical school at Jitomir. There he defended its modern policy against Orthodox attack. His paper reached the Ministry of Education.

He graduated in 1861. His government schooling forced him into a government rabbinate. Only the patronage of Pirogov freed him, after three years, to enter the University of Kiev for law. He published as he studied. His topics ran from wonder-working righteous men to the old and new Cabala, and to Frank and the Frankists. He also wrote on criminal procedure among the ancient Jews. He presented his thesis in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-kohen-:
Moses ha-Kohen of Corfu was a Greek Talmudist and liturgical poet of the late sixteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He seems to have been rabbi, or head of the yeshiva, at Corfu. The editor of his book had been his pupil.

His Yashir Mosheh, printed at Mantua in 1612, versifies the Book of Esther with its midrashic legends. The Jews of Corfu recited it on Shabbat Zakor. The same volume holds his Mi-Kamokah, recited on Yom Kippur. He composed many other liturgical poems and a commentary on the Targum, keeping Hebrew verse alive on his island.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munius-moses-11:
Moses Munius was a French rabbi born at Mutzig in 1760, said to descend from Löwe ben Bezaleel of Prague. Isidore Singer and Isaac Lévy wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained at the great yeshiva of Prague, he headed a Talmud school at Strasburg for twenty years. He ended his life as rabbi of Rixheim, dying in 1842.

One act of his is remembered. During the Revolution, the rabbi Simon Cohen was arrested by Schneider, the feared accuser of Strasburg's tribunal. Munius went to Schneider himself and pleaded for Cohen, at real risk to his own life. Schneider promised release but was arrested and executed before he could act. Munius left manuscripts that witness his deep Talmudic learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nibhaz-11517: Nibhaz was a god worshiped by the Avites. Wilhelm Bacher and Ira Maurice Price wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Second Kings names him beside the god Tartak. The Avites were settled near Samaria after its fall. Sargon II took that city in 722 B.C. Both gods are unknown in eastern and western pantheons. Some Hebrew copies read the name as Nibhan. Greek copies vary too, giving no clue to his identity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-numbers-book-of:
Numbers is the fourth book of the Pentateuch. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, the Editorial Board's Executive Committee, and George A. Barton wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Greek and Latin titles come from its census. Hebrew calls it Be-Midbar, in the wilderness. The Talmud names it the book of numberings.

Its matter falls into three great groups. Sinai laws and doings fill the first ten chapters. The wanderings' story runs through most of the rest. Laws for Moab's plains close the book. The census counts 603,550 men fit for war. Levites are set apart for the Tabernacle's service. The camp marches by tribes around the shrine. Spies, Korah's revolt, and Miriam's death mark the road. Thirty-eight years and more the narrative covers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-opferpfennig-go:
The Goldener Opferpfennig was a tax laid on German Jews. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was a tax on each man and woman in person. The funds went straight to the emperor of Germany. Ludwig the Bavarian set the tax in 1342.

Jews in Germany were held to be crown goods, in law. So all their taxes went to the emperor by right. In time, local lords claimed a share of that right. Ludwig was oft short of funds in his reign. He pledged the right to tax Jews for his loans. To keep a firm stream of funds, he set this new tax. Each Jew past twenty with goods paid one florin a year. The goods had to be worth twenty florins at least.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-lazz: Lazzaro Ottolenghi was an Italian rabbi and preacher of note. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Acqui in the year 1820. He died in Rome in the year 1890. He held posts at Turin, at Moncalvo, and at Acqui. He spent the last years of his life in Rome. He wrote Hebrew poems, talks on faith and right, and a comedy on mixed wedlock.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perahyah-b-niss:
Peraḥyah ben Nissim was a Tosafist of the thirteenth century. He worked in the second half of that century. The Executive Committee and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Tosafists wrote notes that gloss the Talmud. Little else about his life has come down.

He wrote novellae on several Talmud treatises. Some of them were reprinted at Venice in 1752. His notes on Shabbat survive only in manuscript. He used Arabic words in his Hebrew prose. He quoted Abraham, the son of Maimonides, with clear honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phinehas-12117:
Phinehas was a priest, the grandson of Aaron. Four writers shared his article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, the Executive Committee, and Schulim Ochser. His father Eleazar led Israel's priesthood after Aaron. His name stands for zeal in later books.

At Shittim Israel fell to worshiping Baal-peor. Phinehas killed Zimri and the Midianite princess Cozbi. His zeal stopped the plague that punished the camp. God then promised his line the priesthood forever. Later he marched as priest against Midian. He also led the embassy about the Jordan altar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-potocki-pototzk:
Count Valentine Potocki was a Polish noble who took up Judaism. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was burned at the stake at Wilna on May 24, 1749. Jews of Russia honor his memory to this day. They call him the Ger Zedek, the righteous proselyte.

More than one form of his story has come down. One form comes from a Polish book by Kraszewski. He claims to have used a Hebrew source. It tells of young Potocki and his friend Zaremba at study in Paris. There they met an old Jew bent over a large book. That meeting turned the young count toward Judaism. The article weighs the tale and its sources with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitz-jose:
Joseph Rabinowitz was a Russian missionary who preached to the Jews. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Orgeyev in Bessarabia in 1837. He died at Kishinef in 1899. He was raised as a Hasid in a strict home. In time he gained worldly learning and the Russian tongue.

For a while Rabinowitz worked in the lower courts of his town. He then settled at Kishinef for his later years. In 1878 he wrote a long piece in Hebrew. It treated the reform of the rabbinate in Russia. That piece ran in a Hebrew journal of the time. It stands at the root of his later mission work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-recife-pernambu:
Recife is a Brazilian seaport, capital of Pernambuco state. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It began as fishermen's huts before the French came in 1561. The Dutch captured it and Olinda in 1631.

The article says Dutch rule drew many Jews to Recife. Liberal policy let them worship and keep the Sabbath. Portuguese writers said Jews held much of the city's trade. By 1639 they reportedly outnumbered Christians two to one. One Recife Jew ranked among Brazil's richest men. Dutch rulers sought craftsmen to build the city up. Many Portuguese Jews sailed from Holland to join it. The entry shows a brief golden age under Dutch rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romi-daniel-b-j:
Daniel b. Jehiel Romi was a scholar and poet of the tenth and eleventh centuries. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was probably brother of Nathan, author of the Aruk. His work survives in manuscript form.

The article says he wrote a commentary on the treatise Zera'im. He also wrote a yozer hymn in twenty two verses. That hymn serves the Sabbath of Hanukkah. It recounts the story of Antiochus in verse. His forms follow those of the old payyetanim, or hymn writers. A De Rossi manuscript, number 959, holds the hymn. Five sources support the short entry. They include Zunz, Rapoport, and Landshuth. Readers meet an early Italian voice in synagogue poetry. His link to the Aruk's author adds interest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salamon-nahum-1:
Nahum Salamon was an English inventor born in London in 1828. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He may be regarded as founder of Britain's sewing-machine trade, the entry says.

Salamon early saw the promise of the sewing machine in industry. He brought the Howe, the pioneer machine, from America into England. He also set up Britain's first plant for making bicycles, at Coventry. Under his Coventry Machinists, that city took first place in the trade. Late in life he helped popularize saccharin, the sugar substitute, in England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-juda: Samuel ben Judah was a scholar and head of the Jewish community at Lemberg. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his brief entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Outside the city, on the eighth of Iyyar in 1667, a Sabbath day, he suffered martyrdom in a terrible form. The entry records nothing more of his life, his work, or the manner of his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sasslower-jacob: Schulim Ochser wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Jacob Koppel ben Aaron Sasslower, a Russian Masorite of the seventeenth century. He lived at Zaslav, in the government of Volhynia. His Naḥalat Ya'aḳob appeared at Sulzbach in 1686. It treats the chanting accents of the Ten Commandments in Exodus. One set of accents serves Sabbaths, another serves Pentecost. A supplement on the Masorah is added.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semon-charles-1:
Charles Semon was a Danzig-born giver who became a leading citizen of Bradford, England. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Born in 1814, he settled in the Yorkshire mill town and rose in trade. Bradford elected him mayor in 1874.

Semon built a convalescent home at Ilkley and gave it to the town. He helped start a local branch of the Anglo-Jewish Association. He also pressed the British government, through the chamber of commerce, over a Romanian trade treaty. At his death in 1877 he left a large sum for Bradford schools. The entry honors a migrant who served two communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shulman-naphtal: Naphtali Herz Shulman was a Russian Hebrew author born at Stary Bychow. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He died at Amsterdam about 1830. He edited Mussafia's Zeker Rab, printed at Shklov in 1797. His edition added an index of biblical words with Judeo-German translations and grammar notes. He also made Shir we-Hallel, a hymn in Hebrew, Russian, and German. Wilna's Jews sang it for a grand duchess's birthday in 1806.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-shet:
Simeon ben Shetah taught the Law and presided over the Sanhedrin under Queen Alexandra. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was the queen's own brother, tradition reports. That tie bound him closely to the royal court.

Under Alexander Jannaeus the Sanhedrin was almost wholly Sadducean. Simeon stood as its only Pharisee at first. Yet he succeeded in ousting the Sadducean members there. He replaced them with Pharisees on the great court. Then he recalled Pharisee exiles hiding at Alexandria in Egypt. Joshua ben Perahyah returned among those fugitive scholars. Joshua became president again, with Simeon as his deputy. On Joshua's death Simeon took the presidency himself. The entry shows a Pharisee turning a hostile court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soave-moses-138:
Moses Soave was an Italian Hebraist born in Venice on March 28, 1820. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He earned his living as a private tutor. He taught in Venetian Jewish families for many years. He also built a library of rare and valuable works.

Two years before his death he gave up teaching for study. He wrote lives of Sara Copia Sullam and Amatus Lusitanus. He also wrote on Abraham de Balmes and Leon de Modena. He edited a Hebrew medical guide from an old manuscript. His book on the Soncino printers appeared in 1878. He died in Venice in 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinitz-clara-:
Clara Steinitz was a German novelist born at Kobylin on April 16, 1852. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about her in 1906. She was born Clara Klausner and wrote as Hans Burdach. She was educated at Halle and married in 1873. Her husband was Siegfried Heinrich Steinitz.

Steinitz published her first novel in 1878. More novels followed over the next two decades. Their German titles include works from 1884, 1886, and 1890. She also translated novels from foreign languages into German. Her translations include books by Bayard Taylor and Octave Feuillet. She rendered works by Boyesen and Bellamy as well. The entry records a productive woman writer of the period.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmud-torah-14:
A Talmud Torah is a free public school for poor boys. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Orphaned boys form its core pupils. It teaches Hebrew, scripture, and basic Talmud law. Graduates move on ready for the yeshiva.

In earliest times the father alone taught his children. Ezra and his Great Assembly may have started public schooling. Their Jerusalem school served fatherless boys of sixteen. Joshua ben Gamla later spread schools to every town. His rule covered all children past age six or seven. Discipline ran strict in those classrooms. Rab still urged teachers to spare the rod. A slow pupil became monitor until learning clicked. The entry traces Jewish schooling from home to system.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tobia-ben-moses:
Tobia ben Moses was a Karaite scholar, poet, and translator at Constantinople. M. Seligsohn wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He worked in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. His surnames praise his worship, learning, and teaching skill. He also traveled to Jerusalem for study.

Tobia was born into a Rabbinite family. Reading Karaite works converted him to Karaism. His family and opponents persecuted him for that choice. He held that truth outweighs family and even life. At Jerusalem he studied under Jeshua ben Judah. He translated many Arabic Karaite works into Hebrew. His Yehi Me'orot treats the commandments at length. Its authorship was long disputed among scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-treves-ancient-:
Treves, the Roman Augusta Treverorum and German Trier, held Jews from early times. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The city linked Gaul and Rome on trade roads. No record names its Jews before 1066. That year Archbishop Eberhard threatened expulsion or baptism.

The archbishop was murdered before Easter that year. In 1096 Emiko's pillaging bands reached Treves. Some Jews killed themselves rather than convert. Others sheltered in Archbishop Egilbert's palace. Henry IV later let converts return to Judaism. Expulsion came anyway in 1262 under another archbishop. Lombards replaced the Jews and proved worse usurers. Elector Baldwin later employed Jewish finance agents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trieste-gabriel: Gabriel Trieste was an Italian merchant and philanthropist born in 1784. Isidore Singer wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He served as president of the Jewish community in Padua. He died at Padua in 1860. Two of his gifts earn special mention in the entry. One fund of 24,000 Austrian lire promoted art among young Jewish artists. The other was a prize of 1,000 gulden, offered in 1850. It rewarded publication of a history of the Jews. Trieste also translated Troki's Hizzuk Emunah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-utrecht-14617:
Utrecht, a Dutch province and city, expelled and readmitted Jews across centuries. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews lived there before Spain's expulsion era. In 1424 they were banished from the city. Their synagogue became a church of the Virgin Mary.

They plainly returned, for a 1444 ordinance threatened torture. That ordinance was quickly repealed by the council itself. Jews then settled at nearby Maarsen village instead. By 1664 German and Portuguese communities stood distinct. Portuguese Jews were wealthy merchants, and Germans poorer peddlers. A 1736 ordinance gave Portuguese Jews official residence rights. German Jews gained the same rights in 1789. France granted full citizenship in the 1790s.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vitebsk-14717:
Vitebsk is a Russian city on the Düna River. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Russian chronicles name the city as early as 1021. It passed between Lithuania, Poland, and Russia over centuries. Wars repeatedly pillaged it, and Peter the Great burned it in 1708.

Jewish traders likely came by the fourteen hundreds. Records show a Jew leasing the city's inns in 1522. Jews there won tax exemptions by 1551. The entry follows their trade and communal growth. It became part of Russia in 1772. In 1802 it was made capital of its province.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wehu-rahum-but-:
Wehu Rahum is a prayer of plea for mercy. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It begins with a verse from Psalm seventy eight. It is recited on Mondays and Thursdays before Tahanun. The prayer is built mostly of Bible verses. It falls into seven named parts.

Old prayer books give the prayer in varied forms. Amram's Siddur holds three versions of it. Maimonides gives a quite different one for daily use. A legend ties its origin to the Temple's fall. Jews cast adrift by Vespasian reached Bordeaux by miracle. Three cousins among them were linked to its making. The entry joins textual history with the tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilczynski-erne:
Ernest Julius Wilczynski was an American mathematician. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Hamburg on November 13, 1876. His family moved to America in 1885. He attended high school in Chicago. In 1893 he returned to Germany for study.

At Berlin, Wilczynski studied astronomy and mathematics. He took his doctorate in 1897. His thesis treated fluid motion and the sun's rotation. He then computed for the Nautical Almanac Office. He taught at Columbian University and at California. California made him assistant professor in 1902. His book on projective geometry appeared in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-emile-150:
Emile Worms (born 1838) was a French lawyer who wrote on trade and money. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Luxembourg, he took a law degree at Paris in 1864. The year before, a prize went to his essay on Hanseatic trade.

In 1867 he won a second prize for his work. That year he began to teach law at Paris. He soon took a chair of law at Rennes. He held that chair for more than thirty years. France sent him to world meets on counts and trade. His books treat joint stock firms and stock deals. They also treat the flow of cash and paper notes. One book gives the trade past of Germany in full.
journal-of-discourses-vol-17:
Young's seventieth year lends Volume Seventeen, from 1875, a backward gaze. The prophet surveys the kingdom he built across the Great Basin. Desert made to blossom stands as his life's plain, visible proof.

Discourses recall the exodus, the first camps, and the gathered Saints. An old leader counts his works as the succession draws near. Pride and warning mix in his late, summing voice from the stand. The flock hears a founder bless and brace them in one breath. Few volumes in the set feel so much like a testament before the end comes. Age lends his counsel a weight no younger voice could match.
larochefoucauld-maxims-heard-1917:
François de La Rochefoucauld, a French duke who had fought and schemed at court, published his Maxims in 1665. John Heard Jr. translated the full set of 504 maxims into English in 1917. Each maxim is a sentence or two, honed until it cuts.

Again and again La Rochefoucauld finds self-love hiding behind fine motives. Friendship, pity, courage, and even virtue itself come under his cold gaze. Yet the tone is polished, not bitter, and many lines ring with rueful truth. Readers have mined the maxims for three centuries as a guide to human nature. They founded the French tradition of the moralist, the cool judge of manners and hearts.
lawrence-look-we-have-come-through-1917:
Lawrence shaped this 1917 book as a verse sequence: a chain of poems telling one story. It tells of his elopement with Frieda Weekley and their marriage through the war years. Its blunt title announces a survivor's pride.

The poems move from the scandal of their flight to Germany, through poverty and suspicion in wartime England, toward a hard-won sense of arrival. Lawrence called it the essential story of his war years, though no battles appear in it. The fighting here is domestic: love tested by exile, gossip, and want. It remains his most sustained poem sequence, and one of his most personal books.
lenin-imperialism-1917:
Vladimir Lenin wrote Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism in 1916, and it appeared in 1917; this entry uses the Vanguard Press edition of 1926. Lenin wrote in exile in Zurich during the First World War. He sought the economic roots of that war in the growth of giant firms and banks.

Lenin argued that free competition had given way to monopoly, and that finance capital now ruled and divided the world among great powers. Colonies and spheres of influence, in his account, must be fought over again and again. The theory of imperialism as capitalism's highest stage shaped communist thought and anti-colonial movements across the twentieth century.
lenin-state-and-revolution-1917:
Vladimir Lenin wrote The State and Revolution in 1917, while in hiding in Finland. It appeared that year, and this entry uses the Vanguard Press edition of 1926. Lenin set out, from Marx and Engels, what should happen to the state after a workers' revolution.

The old state machine, he argued, must be smashed, not merely taken over, and replaced by a commune-like order of armed workers. That order, the dictatorship of the proletariat, would then wither away as class rule ended. Lenin left the book unfinished as the October Revolution began. It became the core text of his theory of the state and a lasting point of argument among Marxists.
linnaean-society-gloucester-sea-serpent-:
Learned men of New England took sworn proof on a sea serpent in the summer of 1817. The Linnaean Society's report tells of a great marine animal seen near Cape Ann, off Gloucester, by scores of witnesses. A committee of the society was charged to take the facts down in form.

Witnesses swore to the beast's size, its humps, and its swift, smooth run through the bay. The committee prints their words and weighs them like a court of law. No earlier sea serpent case got so strict a hearing from men of science. The report set the bar for how such claims should be tried.
lowie-culture-and-ethnology-1917:
Lowie published this slim 1917 volume early in his career, collecting essays that state the Boasian program in miniature. It is a book about how anthropology should be done, written against the loose evolution schemes of the older generation.

The essays take up diffusion, the spread of customs between peoples, and convergence, the separate invention of similar traits. Lowie argues that culture is a patchwork of borrowings, not a ladder of stages. He also defends the culture concept itself as the field's core tool. Short as it is, the book captures the moment American anthropology changed direction.
machado-poesias-completas-1917:
Antonio Machado gathered his Poesías completas in 1917, and the text here is the Spanish original. No English translation of the complete poems is in the public domain. The volume holds Soledades, his early book of inward, garden-haunted verse, and Campos de Castilla, the sterner poems of his Soria years.

In the Castilian poems, bare hills, rivers, and old towns carry thoughts on Spain and loss. His wife Leonor's early death shadows the finest of them. Machado's language is plain, his music quiet, his feeling deep rather than showy. Spain counts him its greatest lyric poet of the twentieth century. This collected edition was the form in which his own age read him whole.
machen-terror-1917:
Nature itself turns on man in Machen's wartime mystery of 1917. The Terror tells of deaths on farms and roads that no human hand can own. Beasts band, strike, and vanish, and a hush of fear falls on the country.

Machen wrote with the Great War at full roar, and the dread of the hour fills his fields. His guess at the cause ties the revolt of the beasts to man's own fall from grace. The book is the weird tale of the war years at its most strong. It channels a whole age's fear into the hedgerows.
maier-silentium-post-clamores-1617:
Michael Maier answers the Rosicrucian uproar in Silentium Post Clamores, in Latin from 1617: silence after the outcry. The emperor's physician defends the unknown brotherhood with deep learning. Alchemy, music, and the hidden arts fill his eloquent plea for the Rosy Cross and its promised reform of all human knowledge.

Maier asks why the brethren keep silent amid such clamor. His answer weaves wisdom literature with courtly tact and hope. The book opens a window on the dreams of 1617 in Europe. It stands as the most eloquent defense the Rosicrucians ever received, from a man whose own alchemical works remain classics of their kind.
maier-symbola-aureae-mensae-1617:
Michael Maier, physician and alchemist at the court of Rudolf II, published his Symbola Aureae Mensae at Frankfurt in 1617. The Latin title names a golden table of twelve nations. Maier surveys the alchemical heroes of twelve peoples, each with an emblem, judging their claims to the true art.

The book is the most lavishly illustrated Rosicrucian work of its age. Copperplate emblems give each nation's champion a visual argument. Maier defends alchemy's lineage as a council of nations seated at one table. His survey doubles as a history of the art before chemistry had a name. The visual canon of the movement's program stands here, plate by splendid plate.
mickiewicz-pan-tadeusz-noyes-1917:
George Rapall Noyes published his translation of Adam Mickiewicz's Pan Tadeusz in 1917, the first complete English version of Poland's national epic. Mickiewicz wrote the long poem in exile in Paris in 1834. It opens with a hymn to Lithuania, then part of the Russian Empire, as his lost homeland.

The poem follows a gentry feud, a love story, and secret hopes as Napoleon's army nears in 1812. Hunting feasts, mushroom gatherings, and court cases fill its verses with old Polish life. Noyes rendered the poem in English prose with full notes. For English readers, his version opened a classic that Poles learn by heart.
millay-renascence-1917:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published Renascence and Other Poems in 1917, her debut collection, crowned by the title poem. The voice of the Jazz Age's new woman first speaks here, in lyrics of candor. Millay had written Renascence at nineteen, and its prize scandal of 1912 first carried her name to editors.

Renascence, a long lyric, rises from a grave's imagined depths to a soul's rebirth in rain and light. The other poems, sonnets and songs of love, death, and the sea, show her formal gift and her frankness. Thursday, The Dream, and Sorrow display the wit and ache that would make her a popular poet laureate of youth. Camden, Maine, and Vassar stand behind verse that New York bohemia would soon claim as its own. The book is a debut of rare completeness, its best poems still anthology fixtures.
millikan-electron-1917:
Robert A. Millikan spent years isolating and measuring the electron, and his 1917 book reports that work. The oil drop experiment sits at its center. By watching tiny charged oil drops hang in an electric field, Millikan fixed the charge of one electron. That number, written as e, became a basic constant of physics.

The book also reports his photoelectric tests of Einstein's equation for light. Those tests backed the idea that light itself comes in quanta. Millikan lays out methods, data, and doubts with unusual care. Readers can follow each step of the measurements. The volume turned hard lab work into settled fact.
nasa-tm-19690028890-a-new-interpretation:
James O. Ballance, of Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, offers a new reading of satellite gauge data. His report, number 53898, is dated September 1969. Explorer 17 and Explorer 32 carried modified Redhead magnetron density gauges. Densities from such gauges persistently disagreed with densities derived from satellite drag, and each research camp blamed the other's method.

Ballance analyzes the gauge response through its geometry and gas-surface interactions. The data's flow-like behavior demands a new interpretation, he finds, with total loss of atomic oxygen at first wall collisions. A wall process, most likely recombination, likely adds its own signal. For his worked example, the new density differs from the old one by a factor of two.
openalex-w1974615017:
R. Aaij and the LHCb Collaboration reported this decay measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in November 2013. The team studied a B meson decay to a K-star and two muons. Such rare decays test the standard model sharply. Form factors are theory inputs that can blur such tests.

The team built observables that avoid form-factor fog. Data came from one year of LHC proton collisions. Four observables were measured across six energy bins. Clean measures let theory and data meet directly. Any mismatch could point to new particles or forces. The method set a standard for later rare-decay work.
openalex-w2032332317:
Kirsten Jung, Jesus Molinari and Elisabeth Kalko studied how bat echolocation calls evolved. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Free-tailed bats hunt insects in open spaces. Their calls help them find prey and steer. Call design may reflect family history, habitat or body size.

The team built a large dataset of bat calls. It covered eight genera and eighteen species. Most species showed the typical open-space call design. Calls were more alike within a genus than between genera. Close relatives kept near-identical calls despite different body sizes. The authors conclude that ancestry shapes call design strongly. Habitat and hunting needs still play a role. Prey sensing added smaller effects on top.
openalex-w2092348317:
Raquel Cordeiro Theodoro, Marcus Teixeira, Maria Sueli Felipe and colleagues worked out how to tell apart species of a fungal genus. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Paracoccidioides fungi cause a whole-body infection in Latin America. Several hidden species hide under old names. Full gene sequencing for typing is costly.

The team tested small gene differences between isolates. Three gene regions separated four species cleanly. Under the microscope, most species looked identical. One species grew distinctively long spores, though. The authors also traced the group's geographic history. Its spread began in northwest South America long ago. Simple tests can now name the species involved.
openalex-w2113558017:
Georges Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration spotted lopsided jet pairs in lead collisions. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in 2010. Jets are sprays of particles from hard collisions. In proton collisions, jet pairs balance each other. Hot, dense matter may drain energy from one jet.

The team used the ATLAS detector at the LHC. They studied jet pairs flying in opposite directions. In head-on collisions, pairs grew strongly unbalanced. Many events held one strong and one weak jet. The effect grew with collision centrality. It was absent in proton collisions. Strong energy loss in hot matter may explain it. The observation was a first of its kind.
openalex-w2143709617:
Ashley Cooper, Anna Goodman, Angie Page, and colleagues published this study in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2015. They describe how much children and teens actually move and sit, using body-worn motion sensors. Earlier reports often relied on self-report and covered narrow ages or few places.

The database pooled twenty studies from ten countries, with over twenty-seven thousand young people. Boys were less sedentary and more active than girls at every age. After age five, total activity fell with each year, mainly as light activity shrank and sitting grew. From age seven, heavier children were less active, and activity levels differed clearly between countries.
openalex-w2466635817:
Stéphanie D'agata, David Mouillot, Laurent Wantiez, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2016. Marine reserves are conservation's flagship tool, yet nobody knew whether the best reserves match truly remote wilderness reefs. The team compared reef fish across a gradient of human reach in New Caledonia.

Reefs over twenty hours' travel from the main market held far more functional diversity and top-predator bulk. They beat even New Caledonia's oldest, largest, strictest reserve, protected for nearly four decades. Wilderness reefs carried ecological roles found nowhere closer to people. The authors argue wilderness should serve as the benchmark for judging reserves, and as the last refuge for the most vulnerable fish roles.
openalex-w2565297817:
Hannah N. Gruner, Mariela Cortés-López, and Daphne A. Cooper, with colleagues, wrote this 2016 study in Scientific Reports. It looks at circular RNAs in the aging mouse brain. Circular RNAs are stable RNA rings formed when gene segments splice backwards. They are especially common in nerve tissue, hinting at brain-related roles.

The team profiled RNA in cortex, hippocampus, and heart from young and old mice. They detected nearly seven thousand distinct circular RNAs, including hundreds never reported before. Analysis uncovered a strong bias for these RNAs to increase during aging in neural tissue. Their stability, with no free ends for enzymes to attack, may help them build up over time. The findings raise the question of what these accumulating rings do in the old brain.
openalex-w2766639217:
Klaus Hermann Maier-Hein, Peter Neher, and Jean-Christophe Houde lead a large team stress-testing brain tractography in Nature Communications in 2017. Tractography uses diffusion MRI scans to trace white matter pathways and map the human connectome. The method is central to brain connectivity research, yet it had never been systematically validated against known truth.

The team ran an international competition using a simulated brain-like dataset where true connections were known. Twenty research groups submitted ninety-six distinct analysis pipelines. Most pipelines recovered ninety percent of the real bundles, but only about a third of their volume. They also generated large numbers of false-positive bundles that do not exist. Better scan quality did not fix these errors. The authors conclude that new ideas, not just better data, are needed before connectome maps can be trusted.
openalex-w2809058317:
Alexandra Moreno-García, Alejandra Kun, and Olga Calero lead this 2018 review in Frontiers in Neuroscience, on lipofuscin in the aging brain. Lipofuscin is a pigment that builds up inside cells across a lifetime. Aging is the biggest risk factor for neurodegenerative disease, yet its molecular machinery is poorly understood. The review examines what lipofuscin does in age-related brain degeneration.

Lipofuscin accumulates because cells cannot fully break it down. Its glow under the microscope interferes with standard tissue analysis techniques. Researchers use treatments like Sudan Black to block that autofluorescence. The catch: those treatments block studying lipofuscin alongside disease markers at the same time. Newer methods quantify the pigment in brain tissue from its high fat content. Because lipofuscin clearly marks cell aging, interest in its possible causal role keeps growing. The review consolidates what is known and where measurement must improve.
openalex-w2954222817:
Samuel Demok, Nancy Endersby-Harshman, Rebecca Vinit, and colleagues published this study in Parasites and Vectors in 2019. It reports the first checks of insecticide resistance in two mosquito species in Papua New Guinea. Both species spread dengue, chikungunya, and Zika, and resistance to pyrethroid sprays is widespread elsewhere.

Little was known about these mosquitoes in the southwest Pacific, though resistance had been found in nearby Indonesia and not in Australia. The team collected mosquitoes with egg traps in Madang and Port Moresby, on the north and south coasts. Adults were raised in an insectary and exposed to treated papers in standard World Health Organization tests. The study maps where susceptible and resistant populations occur.
openalex-w2956829917:
Karina Mendes, Renata Silveira, and Cristina Galvão wrote this reflection piece in Texto and Contexto Enfermagem in 2019. It shows how a reference manager program, EndNote, can support the building of integrative reviews in nursing and health research. Such reviews sum up what is known on a health topic.

Good integrative reviews can guide clinical practice with research-based advice and can expose gaps for future studies. Choosing the primary studies is a key step, and software makes it more orderly. The authors explain how the tool finds duplicate references, sorts studies by language and period, and builds citations. They argue this makes reviews more transparent and easier to repeat.
openalex-w3020814017:
Jason Corburn, David Vlahov, Blessing Mberu, and colleagues published this article in the Journal of Urban Health in 2020. It addresses health in the informal settlements, or slums, of the Global South during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors argue these neighborhoods were the least prepared places on Earth for the virus.

Basic needs such as clean water, toilets, sewers, drainage, waste collection, and sound housing are unreliable or missing in such settlements. Crowded rooms also make distancing nearly impossible. The authors set out steps to arrest COVID-19 in these communities, joining urgent outbreak control with longer work on wellbeing. Their case is that pandemic policy fails if it ignores the places where the urban poor actually live.
openalex-w3082833917:
Juan Kú-Vera, Rafael Jiménez-Ocampo, Sara Valencia-Salazar, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Veterinary Science in 2020. It examines secondary plant metabolites, the extra chemicals plants make, as tools to cut methane from farm animals. Cattle and other ruminants burp out large amounts of this greenhouse gas.

Methane output depends on the microbes in the rumen, the animal's first stomach. Feed makeup shapes that microbe mix more than breed or age do. Plant compounds such as tannins, saponins, essential oils, and flavonoids can shift the mix away from methane makers. The review weighs the evidence for each class of compound and the doses used, as livestock science hunts for feeds that warm the planet less.
openalex-w4395675017:
Jiang Yong Hu, Zhuo Wang, Zongyi Sun, and colleagues present NextDenovo, a software tool for genome assembly. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology in 2024. Long DNA reads from nanopore machines carry many errors. The team built a tool that corrects those errors and then assembles the reads.

The authors used NextDenovo to assemble thirty-five human genomes from around the world. Those genomes let them map segmental duplications and gene copy number differences across populations. The tool reaches high accuracy while staying efficient. Work like this could make population-scale genome assembly with nanopore data routine, giving researchers fuller pictures of human genetic variation.
openalex-w7212422017:
Ana Maria Furtado de Oliveira leads a team that ran job-skill meets for men held at an APAC unit in Maranhao, Brazil. The APAC model is a faith-based jail path built on trust and work. Men who leave jail in Brazil face a hard wall: few doors to a fair job, and a deep stain from their past. That wall feeds the risk of fresh crime. The meets aimed to arm them for work.

Group tasks built the soft skills firms ask for: calm, trust, and work with peers. The men also got a clear view of what the job mart wants now. The talks, the team says, drew sharp thought on the blocks in their path, and showed real paths back in. A job here is more than pay. It is a new tale a man can tell of his life.
openalex-w7213327317:
Suéllen Danúbia da Silva leads a team that looks back at the games children played before screens took over. Their 2026 article, published in Brazil, asks how old games shape the cultural formation of children today. It draws on published research on childhood, play, and culture.

Games such as hopscotch, hide and seek, tag, singing games, and jump rope are presented as more than fun. The authors argue that they build identity, social skills, creativity, and shared values across generations. Keeping such games alive at home and at school, they conclude, helps children stay connected to their cultural roots.
openalex-w7213415717:
Giovanna de Andrade Moreira and co-workers examine off-label use of human antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia in dogs and cats. Their 2026 review works from SciELO, PubMed, and Brazilian health law, mostly covering 2011 to 2025. The focus is the legal frame and the veterinarian's duty.

Brazilian rules from 2004 and 2011 allow extra-label prescribing, the review finds. Yet they set no clear limits for the decision. Drug actions principles and international consensus guidance partly fill that gap. Commonly used drugs include amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, doxycycline, and ciprofloxacin. The authors stress careful, documented judgement when human medicines are used in animals.
openalex-w7214056617:
Gilsonia Portela dos Santos and co-authors argue for philosophy classes in basic education. Their 2026 bibliographic study consults SciELO, a philosophy journal portal, Google Scholar, and classic books, in Portuguese with no time limit. Aims include defining education and philosophy and relating the two.

Philosophy helps pupils think critically and take positions amid complex daily life, they find. It supplies a framework that widens how a student understands everyday questions. Abstracts were screened to select the work closest to the study aims. The authors treat school philosophy not as an ornament but as formation: a subject whose relevance shows in how pupils reason about the world they already inhabit.
plain-words-from-america-a-letter-to-a-g:
Douglas Wilson Johnson, a professor at Columbia University in New York, wrote Plain Words from America as an open letter to a German correspondent. That man had pleaded Germany's cause to him. The letter first appeared in the Revue de Paris in September 1916. The pamphlet followed in 1917, while the First World War was still being fought.

Johnson begins by explaining his long silence. He had read the German letters and clippings with care. He could not agree about Germany's blame for the war or her methods of fighting it. He also doubted a reply would do good. He grants his correspondent's intense emotion, with sons fighting and Germany condemned by the neutral world. Then he sets out the American case in the plain words of his title.
plaw-114-329-2017:
American Innovation and Competitiveness Act is Public Law 114-329, passed by the 114th Congress and signed in 2017. The act puts funds into new ideas through study and growth work. Its aim is to improve how well the United States competes in the world.

Title I, on making basic study count for more, lists many parts. It backs merit-based peer review, clear and open grant work, and an update of a program that spreads study funds to more states. It also covers cyber study, web and data tech study, lab program fixes, and watch over large shared study sites of the National Science Foundation. Later parts cover staff watch, the United States Antarctic Program, and campus safety for a standards lab.
plaw-115-1-2017:
Tested Ability to Leverage Exceptional National Talent Act of 2017, or TALENT Act of 2017, is Public Law 115-1. Passed by the 115th Congress, the act amends title 5 law to write the Presidential Innovation Fellows Program into law. The program brings skilled guests into government for set terms.

The act states the policy first. It is in the national good for the government to draw the brightest minds, skilled in tech or new ways of work, to serve on the nation's biggest tests. The program urges proven founders, chiefs, and creators to join agencies and work with agency heads. Goals named are to save lives and taxpayer cash, fuel job growth, and improve how the government serves the people. The head of General Services must keep the program and supply its staff and funds.
plaw-115-10-2017:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration Transition Authorization Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-10, passed by the 115th Congress. The act grants power for the programs of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the space agency known as NASA.

The contents list the plan. Title I grants funds for fiscal year 2017. Title II covers the keeping of national space pledges. Title III covers the best use of the space station and low-Earth orbit, with parts on station running, travel to the station, a station handover plan, and space talk systems. Title IV then turns to deep space flight by humans, where the sample ends.
plaw-115-11-2017: The 115th Congress passed Public Law 115-11 in 2017, and it is a joint resolution that voids a federal rule. Congress states that it disapproves the rule sent in by the Department of Defense, the General Services Administration, and the space agency. The rule dealt with the Federal Acquisition Regulation, the main rule book for federal buys, and was printed in August 2016. The resolution states that the rule shall have no force or effect.
plaw-115-12-2017: Passed in 2017, Public Law 115-12 is a joint resolution that voids a land rule. Congress states that it disapproves the rule sent in by the Bureau of Land Management of the Department of the Interior. The rule, called Resource Management Planning and printed in December 2016, set the steps used to make, revise, or change land use plans. Those plans sit under the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976. The resolution states that the rule shall have no force or effect.
plaw-115-13-2017: The 115th Congress passed Public Law 115-13 in 2017, and it is a joint resolution that voids a school rule. Congress states that it disapproves the rule sent in by the Department of Education. The rule dealt with answerability and state plans under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965. It was printed in November 2016. The resolution states that the rule shall have no force or effect.
plaw-115-14-2017: The 115th Congress passed Public Law 115-14 in 2017, and it is a joint resolution that voids a school rule. Congress states that it disapproves the rule sent in by the Department of Education. The rule dealt with teacher preparation, how new teachers are trained, and was printed in October 2016. The resolution states that the rule shall have no force or effect.
plaw-115-15-2017: Public Law 115-15 is the Vietnam War Veterans Recognition Act of 2017, passed by the 115th Congress and approved on March 28, 2017. The law changes one line of the flag code in title 4 of the United States Code. It adds National Vietnam War Veterans Day, March 29, to the list of days when people are urged to display the United States flag.
plaw-115-16-2017: Pago Pago, in American Samoa, is where Public Law 115-16 puts a new name on a health clinic. Approved on March 31, 2017, the law names the Department of Veterans Affairs clinic there the Faleomavaega Eni Fa'aua'a Hunkin VA Clinic. Any mention of that clinic in a federal law, rule, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-17-2017: Public Law 115-17 is a joint resolution passed by the 115th Congress and approved on March 31, 2017. A joint resolution of this kind cancels a federal rule. Here Congress rejects a rule sent in by the Department of Labor. The rule had named the jobs for which states could drug test people who apply for unemployment pay. Under the resolution, that rule has no force or effect.
plaw-115-18-2017: Public Law 115-18 is a joint resolution approved on March 31, 2017, about a war memorial in Washington, D.C. The resolution approves a site in Area I for a memorial to members of the Armed Forces. Those honored served on active duty in support of Operation Desert Storm or Operation Desert Shield. The Secretary of the Interior had urged that site, and federal law required Congress to approve it.
plaw-115-19-2017: Public Law 115-19, approved on April 3, 2017, deals with the board of the Office of Compliance. That office handles workplace rules for Congress under the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995. The law sets the terms for new board members who replace members whose terms end in 2017. Three seats ending in March get terms of three or four years, and two seats ending in May get five-year terms.
plaw-115-2-2017: Public Law 115-2, approved on January 20, 2017, makes a one-time exception to a rule in title 10 of the United States Code. The rule bars a person from serving as Secretary of Defense within seven years of leaving active duty as a regular officer. The law lets the first person named to the post after its passage serve if at least three years have passed since that duty ended. It applies to no one else.
plaw-115-20-2017: Alaska wildlife refuges are the subject of Public Law 115-20, a joint resolution approved on April 3, 2017. In it, Congress cancels a rule from the Department of the Interior. The rule dealt with hunting and trapping on those refuges, under the heading of non-subsistence take of wildlife. It also covered public input and closure steps. Under the resolution, that rule has no force or effect.
plaw-115-21-2017: Public Law 115-21 is a joint resolution approved on April 3, 2017, in which Congress cancels a federal rule. The rule came from the Department of Labor and dealt with job safety records. It spelled out a boss's ongoing duty to keep a correct record of each injury and illness that must be logged. Under the resolution, that rule has no force or effect.
plos-pbio-0020217:
Anke Steppuhn, Klaus Gase, Bernd Krock, and their team tested nicotine's role in wild tobacco plants for PLOS Biology in 2004. Nicotine is a poison the plant makes in its leaves. The team lowered nicotine in plants growing in nature and watched what insects did.

With less nicotine, more leaf-eating insects fed on the plants, and damage rose. That is direct field proof that nicotine defends the plant, not just a lab guess. The study also weighed costs, since making poison takes energy the plant could spend on growth or seeds. Field tests like this one ground chemical ecology in real conditions, where weather, rivals, and many insect species all play a part.
plos-pone-0000017:
Eshwar Mahenthiralingam, Adam Baldwin, Pavel Drevinek, and co-authors put an old typing tool to a new use in 2006. Multilocus sequence typing identifies microbes by reading a set of their housekeeping genes. A metagenome, by contrast, is all the DNA scooped from an environment at once, a mix from many species, most never grown in a lab.

The authors showed that sequence typing could pull order out of that mix, naming the strains hiding in the metagenome. Their title says the method breathes life into the data: raw sequences become known organisms with known traits. That matters wherever microbes matter, from soil and water to the bacteria that infect vulnerable patients.
plos-pone-0000117:
Pertti Happonen, Sari Voutilainen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It asks whether a common gene variant changes how coffee drinking affects the risk of a sudden coronary event, such as a heart attack. The gene makes an enzyme called COMT, which breaks down stress hormones.

Coffee has been blamed and praised for heart risk for decades, with mixed study results. The authors test whether a person's version of this gene tips the balance of coffee's effect. If genes change who is harmed or helped by coffee, broad advice to all drinkers may need to become more personal.
plos-pone-0000217:
Olivier Tenaillon, Olin K. Silander, Jean-Philippe Uzan, and colleagues published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks how to put a number on complexity, how complex a living thing is, using the tools of population genetics. Instead of counting body parts, the authors ground complexity in the genetics of populations.

Complexity is easy to sense and hard to measure. Their definition ties it to mutation, selection, and drift, things that can be counted and measured. The paper offers a yardstick for comparing organisms from bacteria to mammals, and for testing claims about whether evolution tends toward greater complexity.
plos-pone-0000317:
Hiroaki Murakami, Derek B. Goto, Takashi Toda, and colleagues published this cell division paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dis3 is a ribonuclease, an enzyme that chews up RNA. The authors show its activity is required for mitotic progression, the orderly march through cell division. It also links heterochromatin, densely packed DNA, to the kinetochore, the handle by which chromosomes are pulled apart.

A defective Dis3 stalls division and disturbs chromosome handling. Connecting an RNA-chewing enzyme to chromosome segregation was unexpected, and it is the kind of link few had looked for. The finding helps explain how cells keep their silent DNA regions and their division machinery working together.
plos-pone-0000417:
Yoshiyasu Arai and colleagues located where each beat of spinal rhythm begins in the chick embryo, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Even before birth, the spinal cord can generate rhythmic activity, the patterning behind stepping and swimming. The team asked which side region of the cord starts each cycle.

Their title gives the answer they found: each cycle arises from the ventrolateral region of the cord. Knowing where a rhythm starts helps map the circuits that produce it. Chick embryos are a classic system for this work. Their spinal circuits can be studied while still developing. That helps explain how locomotion circuits are built.
plos-pone-0000517:
Ewan P. Plant and colleagues studied how the ribosome reads near-miss instructions, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The ribosome builds proteins by reading codons, three-letter words in the genetic message. Near-cognate codons differ by one letter from the correct word. They should be rejected. Working in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the team studied how the cell tells near- from non-cognate codons.

Reading errors produce faulty proteins, so the ribosome proofreads, but not perfectly. Understanding the discrimination steps explains the accuracy of all protein production and how antibiotics that jam the ribosome exploit its weak points. Yeast is the standard test bed for this universal machinery.
plos-pone-0000617:
Alex S. Nord, Karen Vranizan, Whittemore Tingley and colleagues built a model of gene trapping for PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene trapping inserts new DNA into mouse embryonic stem cells to disrupt genes and reveal what they do. It is the most widely used form of insertional mutagenesis in mammals. Yet the rules that govern how well it works were not fully known.

Their model uses two features of each gene: its length and how strongly it is expressed. A good model would let labs predict which genes a trap will hit and which it will miss. That matters for large projects that map gene function across the whole mammalian genome.
