plos-pone-0000717:
Hervé Philippe, Henner Brinkmann, Pedro Martinez and colleagues argued that acoel flatworms do not belong where textbooks put them. Acoels are small marine worms traditionally classed in the phylum Platyhelminthes, the flatworms. Molecular phylogenetic analyses suggest instead that acoels are surviving members of the earliest diverging Bilateria, the great animal group with left-right symmetry.

Their evidence comes from phylogenomics, family trees built from many genes at once. Moving acoels to the base of the bilaterian tree changes what scientists infer about the first bilaterians. Traits acoels lack might be later inventions rather than losses. Few classification fights carry stakes that deep in animal history.
plos-pone-0000817:
Dorit Ben-Shachar and Rachel Karry linked a general gene switch to energy genes behaving oddly in schizophrenia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The prevailing hypothesis treats schizophrenia as a polygenic disease, where many genes combine with each other and with environmental stimuli to produce its varied symptoms. The authors investigated whether the ubiquitous transcription factor Sp1 is abnormally expressed in the disease.

Their title states the chain they propose: Sp1 expression is disrupted in schizophrenia. That disruption offers a possible mechanism for the abnormal expression of mitochondrial complex I genes NDUFV1 and NDUFV2. One faulty master switch could explain several downstream faults at once, an appealing pattern in a complex disease.
plos-pone-0000917:
Ziming Weng, Roger Barthelson, Siddarame Gowda and colleagues showed how mixed virus infections inside one host breed diversity, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When viral genomes recombine or swap segments, new viruses can emerge. Long lasting infections raise the odds, because several genotypes can copy themselves side by side in a single host.

The team followed an RNA virus held in persistent infection. With multiple genotypes present, recombination ran freely and produced wide variety. That variety is raw material for new viral forms. The study explains one route by which plant and animal viruses keep changing under our feet.
plos-pone-0001017:
William Laurance, Henrique Nascimento, Susan Laurance and colleagues measured how uneven forest edge effects can be, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When forest is cut into fragments, the edges change: light, wind and invading species press in. Those edge effects drive much of what happens next, yet they vary greatly in space and time.

The team assessed that variability across Amazon forest dynamics, plant makeup, invading species and carbon storage. Their landscape divergence idea holds that fragments do not all follow one path. Management based on a single average edge could mislead badly. The study argues for reading each fragment's own trajectory.
plos-pone-0001117:
Shai Shaham's 2007 PLOS ONE article deals with a practical question in genetics: how many altered genomes has a screen actually checked? Genetic screens in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans can mean examining thousands or tens of thousands of animals, each carrying scrambled DNA.

Shaham lays out how to count the mutagenized gametes a screen has covered. That count shapes how researchers judge a screen's progress. It also helps them guess how many genes can produce a given trait, and weigh the cost of going further. The paper gives worm geneticists a clearer way to plan screens and to know when one has run long enough.
plos-pone-0001217:
TOR is a protein kinase, a master switch for cell growth found in nearly all complex life. Kathrin Thedieck and colleagues identified new partners of the mammalian version, mTOR, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. mTOR sits in two distinct complexes, TORC1 and TORC2, with different jobs.

The authors report that two proteins, PRAS40 and a PRR5-like protein, are new mTOR interactors that regulate apoptosis, programmed cell death. Adding members to the mTOR complexes refines the wiring diagram of growth control. Because mTOR is a major cancer drug target, its full cast of partners matters.
plos-pone-0001317:
Serotonin receptors of the 5-HT4 type are drug targets for gut and brain disorders. Wei Chun Chang and colleagues studied how this receptor signals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. G protein-coupled receptors like 5-HT4 signal through a limited number of pathways. They play crucial roles in many processes, but their diversity makes in vivo study hard.

The authors address modifying ligand-induced and constitutive signaling of the human 5-HT4 receptor. Constitutive signaling means the receptor is partly active even with no serotonin present. Tools that tune each mode separately would help both research and drug design.
plos-pone-0001417:
Petr Ilyinskii and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a flu protein that harms the cells that make it. Shots built on this protein, called M2, had shown mixed success in past tests. The team had found that M2 kills host cells grown in the lab. They asked whether curbing that harm could make shots work better.

The authors report that blocking M2 driven cell death lifts its drag on shot strength. In other words, the protein was hurting its own use as a vaccine base. Fixing that flaw could revive a shot idea with broad appeal. A flu shot that works across strains stays a top goal.
plos-pone-0001517:
Alexander Chesler and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on switching genes in smell nerve cells. New smell neurons are born through life, but how they wire in was a mystery. The team built a way to add genes to young smell neurons in live mice. The method uses a mild electric pulse after birth.

With genes added to chosen cells, labs can test what each gene does as the cell matures. The cells grow in their real place, not in a dish. That realism is the method's strength. It should speed work on how smell circuits form and renew.
plos-pone-0001617:
Kentaro Ohkuni and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell division in yeast. A checkpoint holds division until all chromosomes are gripped right by the split frame. Faults in grip parts plus checkpoint faults can kill the cell. The team hunted for new grip partners by that clue and found a protein called Ybp2.

They show Ybp2 binds the core grip point of yeast chromosomes. Without it, division goes off course. Each new grip part refines the model of how cells part their genes with such care. Yeast grip parts oft mirror our own, so the work feeds human cell science too.
plos-pone-0001717:
Daniel C. Jupiter and Vincent VanBuren built a visual data mining tool for gene network studies in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Microarrays, which measure the activity of thousands of genes at once, had grown fast, but making sense of their output still challenged many labs. A plain list of genes that changed does not say how they connect or what to test next.

Their tool helps users rebuild transcription regulatory networks, the webs of gene switches, by exploring microarray results visually. The full text gives the tool's design, example analyses, and how it guides new experiment plans. Putting network structure on screen, instead of leaving it in tables, helps biologists turn gene lists into testable stories about cell control.
plos-pone-0001817:
Patricia L. Ryan and John A. T. Young tested a disputed claim about anthrax toxin entry in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The cellular protein LRP6 had been reported as important for efficient intoxication of a human prostate carcinoma cell line, M2182. Other studies, using cells from gene-knockout mice, found no role for LRP6 at all. The contradiction mattered for understanding how anthrax toxin enters cells.

Ryan and Young present evidence against a human cell-specific role for LRP6 in anthrax toxin entry. The full text gives their cell tests and toxin assays. Settling which host proteins the toxin truly needs focuses biodefense research on entry routes that are real.
plos-pone-0001917:
Shijun Wang and co-authors showed that how players learn can keep cooperation alive on sparse networks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cooperation is key to many complex systems, yet in game models it rises or falls sharply with the shape of the network of players. On some layouts, cheats win and the group falls apart.

The team added rules that let players learn from success and try new tactics, rather than copy in a fixed way. With those learning and novel elements in the rules, cooperative layouts held up far better. The result hints that real groups stay kind not just by layout, but by how members adapt.
plos-pone-0002017:
Nora Volkow and co-authors scanned brains to see how a stimulant drug eases mental work, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Methylphenidate and kin are used by more and more people as cognitive enhancers, a trend that is much debated. How they help, and why they aid some people but harm others, was not clear.

The team tested the idea that the drug cuts the fuel the brain needs for a task. As the title states, methylphenidate decreased the glucose the brain needed to perform a cognitive task. A brain that works on less fuel may feel sharper, at least on the tested task.
plos-pone-0002117:
Miyuki Suzawa and Holly Ingraham studied how a farm herbicide switches on hormone genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Atrazine remains a widely used broadleaf herbicide in the United States. It has been linked to reproductive abnormalities in fish and amphibians, which raised fears about hormone disruption by farm chemicals.

Using zebrafish, the team report that environmentally relevant levels of atrazine elevate activity in endocrine gene networks. As the title states, the effect runs via NR5A nuclear receptors, which are not steroid receptors, in fish and mammalian cells. A non-steroid path widens the list of hormone systems this chemical can touch.
plos-pone-0002217:
Akira Takashima and Masakazu Takahata studied how one identified nerve cell adds up its inputs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A neuron's dendrites, its branching input arms, are studded with channels that open with voltage or chemical signals. How those active channels are spread over the branches shapes how the cell combines incoming signals.

The authors worked on a nonspiking interneuron, a nerve cell that signals with graded voltages rather than spikes. They tested how different patterns of active conductance over its dendrites change synaptic integration. The fine detail matters, because a cell's wiring diagram alone cannot predict what it will compute.
plos-pone-0002317:
Adélaïde de Heering and Bruno Rossion tested how long experience with children's faces reshapes adult face perception, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. People who work with young children see those faces daily for years. The team used the composite illusion as a marker of holistic face perception. In that illusion, two face halves are fused into a whole. Holistic perception means seeing a face as one unit.

They report that prolonged visual experience with faces of 4- to 6-year-old children modulates the adult face system. Perception is tuned by the faces a person meets most. The result shows the face system stays plastic well into adult life.
plos-pone-0002417:
Burke and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Tarryne Burke, Bruce Page, Gus Van Dyk, among others. Its subject is risk and Ethical Concerns of Hunting Male Elephant: Behavioural and Physiological Assays of the Remaining Elephants. Hunting of male African elephants may pose ethical and risk concerns, particularly given their status as a charismatic species of high touristic value.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002517:
Laddy, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dominick J. Laddy, Jian Yan, Michele Kutzler, among others. Its subject is heterosubtypic Protection against Pathogenic Human and Avian Influenza Viruses via In Vivo Electroporation of Synthetic Consensus DNA Antigens. The persistent evolution of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) highlights the need for novel vaccination techniques that can quickly.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002617:
Ishikawa and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Yuki Ishikawa, Hitoshi Aonuma, Toru Miura, among others. Its subject is soldier-Specific Modification of the Mandibular Motor Neurons in Termites. Social insects exhibit a variety of caste-specific behavioral tendencies that constitute the basis of division of labor within the colony.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002717:
In 2008, David Sevillano and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was high protein binding and cidal activity against Penicillin-Resistant S. pneumoniae: a cefditoren in vitro pharmacodynamic simulation. Authorship is credited in the record to David Sevillano and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Although protein binding is a reversible phenomenon, it is assumed that antibacterial activity is exclusively exerted by the free (unbound) fraction of antibiotics. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002817:
Brian Null and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of High-Resolution, in vivo magnetic resonance imaging of drosophila at 18.8 tesla. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Brian Null, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. High resolution MRI of live Drosophila was performed at 18.8 Tesla, with a field of view less than 5 mm. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002917:
Anna Kanerva, Sergio Lavilla-Alonso, Mari Raki and co-authors tested controllable cancer-killing viruses for cervical cancer in 2008. Trials had shown that oncolytic adenoviruses, viruses bred to attack tumors, are safe in advanced cancer. Stronger viruses could bring more toxicity, so an off switch would be valuable.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team analyzed viruses whose copying could in principle be regulated, or shut down if needed. That is systemic therapy, treatment through the whole body, with a safety brake. The work speaks to a central design problem in virus-based cancer care: power balanced with control.
plos-pone-0003017:
Emmanuel Comoy, Cristina Casalone, Nathalie Lescoutra-Etchegaray and co-authors transmitted atypical BSE to a primate in 2008. Human variant CJD comes from eating prions from cattle with classic BSE. Atypical BSE forms, mostly silent in ageing cattle, had lately been found at slaughter, raising a new safety question.

The atypical form called BASE passed from asymptomatic ageing cattle to a primate in this study, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, that transmission shows atypical prions are not harmless by default. Food safety surveillance needs to treat them as a real, if unquantified, risk. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003117:
Issam Zineh, Amber Beitelshees, Gregory Welder and co-authors studied the chemokine ENA-78, heart prognosis, and statins in 2008. Endothelial inflammation with chemokine involvement contributes to acute coronary syndromes, sudden heart artery events. ENA-78 is encoded by the gene CXCL5 and attracts neutrophils, a white blood cell type.

The team tested whether variation in CXCL5 is associated with prognosis after acute coronary syndromes. They also investigated the modulatory effect of statins, widely used cholesterol drugs, on that link. Published in PLOS ONE, gene plus drug data speak to personalized heart care. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003217:
Yipeng Wang, Jing Hong, Xiuhong Liu and colleagues report a snake antimicrobial peptide in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cathelicidins are a family of antimicrobial peptides that act as multi-purpose effectors of innate immunity, first found in mammals. Several had also lately been found in chickens and fishes. No cathelicidins from other non-mammalian vertebrates had been reported at that point.

The team characterize a cathelicidin from the banded krait, Bungarus fasciatus, and call it a potent peptide antibiotic in the title. Readers get a new natural defence molecule from an unexpected source. Snake peptides may inspire antibiotics that work in new ways.
plos-pone-0003317:
Hege Langli Ersdal, Douwe A. A. Verkuyl, Kenneth Björklund and colleagues report on a childbirth operation in Zimbabwe in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Obstructed labour remains one of the leading causes of maternal and foetal death and morbidity in poorly resourced areas. In such areas, round-the-clock caesarean section cannot be guaranteed. Death rates linked to caesarean section are still high. Symphysiotomy is an alternative in such settings.

The study covers postoperative outcome, width of the symphysis joint, and knowledge, attitudes and practice among doctors and midwives. Readers get outcome data plus a picture of how staff view the procedure. Both are needed to judge its place in emergency obstetric care.
plos-pone-0003417:
Delia Goletti and colleagues tested tuberculosis blood tests across Europe in this 2008 study. Newer tests read interferon-gamma released by immune cells, and they improved detection of hidden TB. The open question was how well they find active disease in daily practice. Many clinics in the TBNET network took part.

The team compared single tests with paired test results. Combining tests changed accuracy in ways clinics need to know. The study measured those trade-offs on real patients, not ideal samples. Its findings guide which test mixes doctors should trust for active TB.
plos-pone-0003517:
Emma R. Andersson and co-authors studied a growth signal in the mouse midbrain in this 2008 paper. Wnt5a is a morphogen, a signal that shapes growing tissue. It works through a pathway that orients cells within a sheet. The ventral midbrain grows the dopamine cells lost in Parkinson's disease.

Wnt5a regulated both the shape of that region and its dopamine cells. Groups known as A9 and A10 developed under its guidance. Knowing how those cells form may aid future cell therapies. Their construction rules come from studies like this one. Parkinson's kills these very cells, so their birth rules draw intense study.
plos-pone-0003617:
Federica Rizzi and co-authors proposed a gene test for prostate cancer in this 2008 paper. Prostate cancer is a major cause of cancer death in Western countries. Catching it early, while curable, is highly desirable. Current screening methods carry real limitations.

Their novel gene signature is read by a method called RT-qPCR. Expression analysis of several genes forms the fingerprint. A molecular test could beat older screening on accuracy. The signature aims to guide diagnosis for men at risk. Early prostate tumors can often be cured by surgery or radiation alone.
plos-pone-0003717:
Rachel L. Erlich, Rebecca C. Fry, Thomas J. Begley, and colleagues published this yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Anc1 is a yeast protein that travels with several complexes that read genes. Yeast lacking Anc1 are sensitive to agents that damage DNA. Its human relatives turn up in some leukemias.

The authors show Anc1 takes part in the postreplication repair pathway in baker's yeast. That pathway lets cells cope with damage left behind after DNA copying. The repair role shows a gene-reading helper also guarding the genome once replication has passed.
plos-pone-0003817:
Abigail Clements, Fabien Gaboriaud, Jérôme F. L. Duval, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. To understand how Klebsiella pneumoniae causes disease, its cell surface must be understood first. That surface is the first barrier against immune defenses and the handle by which the bacterium attaches to host cells.

The team analyzed the major saccharides, or sugars, associated with the bacterial surface. They show these sugars contribute to how the bacterium associates with host cells. The sugar coat is thus both shield and handshake in infection, and a possible target for blocking it.
plos-pone-0003917:
Sung-Min Ahn, Kyunghee Byun, Deokhoon Kim, and co-authors studied how a gene switch guides stem cells in 2008. Knowing how stem cells choose a fate matters for future cell therapies. It also matters for research on cancer stem cells. The team worked with immortalized neural stem cells.

Their PLOS ONE article follows genome-wide changes as the switch Olig2 drives cell change. They found the Wnt signal path quiets as cells mature. A gene called Dickkopf-1 rises at the same time. Those shifts mark steps that push stem cells toward nerve cell fates. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004017:
Annika M. Sääf, Maria Tengvall-Linder, Howard Y. Chang, and co-authors profiled gene activity in eczema skin in 2008. Atopic eczema is a common chronic inflammatory skin disorder. Genetic studies had found linked regions but few clear genes. Gene activity in diseased skin itself was little known.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a reciprocal pattern in eczema samples. Inflammatory genes rose while lipid genes fell in the skin. Skin lipids form the barrier that keeps water in and germs out. The paired pattern ties barrier failure to immune flare in one picture. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004117:
Jeffrey M. Ellenbogen, Justin C. Hulbert, Ying Jiang, and co-authors tested sleep's effect on verbal memory in 2009. After learning, the brain processes memories during consolidation. Sleep is one known driver of that post-learning change. Behavioral studies link sleep to stronger episodic recall.

Their PLOS ONE article reports sleep boosts resistance to interference. Words learned before sleep survived later distracting material better. Protection from interference is a distinct benefit from simple strengthening. The finding refines advice on timing study and sleep. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004217:
Julian Finn, Tom Tregenza, and Mark Norman published this field study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dolphins are famous for complex social and foraging behaviour, but direct underwater observations of wild dolphins feeding are rare. At mass spawning gatherings of giant cuttlefish in Australia's Upper Spencer Gulf, the authors watched a wild female dolphin hunt.

They describe the complex prey handling she used to prepare her cuttlefish meal, step by step. Preparing a toxic, ink-filled prey animal safely takes skill. The account is a rare close look at how a dolphin turns a difficult animal into food.
plos-pone-0004317:
Valerie White and colleagues published this malaria pathology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The causes of coma and death in cerebral malaria remain unknown. Malarial retinopathy, damage visible in the retina, has been identified as an important clinical sign for diagnosis and prognosis in this disease.

As part of a larger autopsy study of children in Malawi who died in coma, the team examined the retinal pathology of pediatric cerebral malaria. The eye offers a window on the brain's small vessels. What the retina shows at death can test ideas about what kills these children.
plos-pone-0004417:
Tiny specks once hailed as a new form of life, called nanobacteria, are put on trial in a 2009 PLOS ONE study by John D Young, Jan Martel, Lena Young, and colleagues. These specks are very small, change shape, and gather a hard mineral called hydroxyapatite. They had been blamed for many diseases in which calcium builds up outside the skeleton.

By adding mineral-forming ions to cell cultures, the team tested whether the specks were truly alive. Their verdict, stated in the title, is that the specks are not living things at all. They are leftovers of normal calcium balance in the body and by-products of growing cells in the lab. The result helped close a long scientific dispute.
plos-pone-0004517:
Powerful HIV drugs may carry a long-term cost for the liver, a question examined by Erica Moodie, Nitika Pant Pai, and Marina Klein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Highly active antiretroviral therapy, called HAART, transformed HIV care. Yet deaths from liver disease rose in the years after HAART arrived, and its effect on liver scarring in people also infected with hepatitis C was not well understood.

The team compared two groups: people infected with HIV alone, and people infected with both HIV and hepatitis C. Some earlier snapshot studies had hinted HAART might protect the liver, which made the question harder. A careful comparison of the two groups can separate drug effects from virus effects. The answer guides how doctors watch livers during lifelong HIV treatment.
plos-pone-0004617:
Computer screening finds small molecules that pry apart a cancer-spreading partnership, report Pratima Chaurasia, Mihaly Mezei, Ming-Ming Zhou, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sleeping cancer cells can wake years later and form metastases. The molecular mechanism of that change remains obscure. The team had established that a surface interaction between the urokinase receptor, uPAR, and an integrin, alpha5beta1, plays a key role.

When that interaction breaks, dormant cells stay asleep. The authors used computer-aided identification to find small molecules that disrupt the uPAR and integrin contact. They present the approach as a new paradigm for metastasis prevention: not killing cancer cells, but keeping strays permanently dormant. Prevention of that kind could change how cancer survivors are treated.
plos-pone-0004717:
Michele Zampieri and colleagues showed how a repair protein guards a gene switch from unwanted methylation, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cells often show two odd traits at once. Some gene switches gain thick chemical caps while the rest of the genome loses them, and the cause was not well known.

The team studied a protein that sits on the switch of a gene that keeps caps in check. Its active work keeps that switch free of caps. The result offers a clear guard role in healthy cells. Loss of that guard may help start the odd cap patterns of cancer.
plos-pone-0004817:
Jean-Marie Pages and colleagues described efflux pumps as the masked side of beta lactam resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Beta lactamase production and porin decrease are well recognized steps of acquired resistance in this species. However, such steps proved absent in isolates non susceptible to cefoxitin yet susceptible to other agents tested, prompting search for alternative explanations of the phenotype.

Efflux pumps expel drugs before they can act. Their role is often overlooked in routine testing. Recognizing pump mediated resistance changes treatment choices. It also matters for infection control. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004917:
Martine Bruley Rosset and colleagues showed dendritic cell immunization with xenogenic PrP breaks tolerance and prolongs survival in scrapie, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In prion diseases, normal PrP transforms into pathogenic infectious PrP Scrapie form. Antibodies against normal PrP can block that change in the lab and protect animals in tests. The team used dendritic cells loaded with foreign prion protein as a vaccine. Mice were then challenged with experimental scrapie to test protection.

Breaking self tolerance enables protective immunity. Survival prolongation proves principle in vivo. Prion vaccines remain challenging but plausible. Dendritic delivery overcomes tolerance barriers. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005017:
The blood carries a balance between cysteine and its twin, cystine. That pair forms the main thiol redox control system outside cells. Smita Iyer and colleagues linked it to inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. They measured the pair's redox potential in healthy adults. Then they asked what sets levels of the inflammatory signal IL-1 beta.

When the balance tips toward oxidation, IL-1 beta levels climb. The redox state directly tunes inflammation. The finding links blood chemistry to immune fire. It suggests a measurable dial for inflammatory risk. Doctors might one day read that dial in patients. It also gives researchers a new handle on chronic inflammation.
plos-pone-0005117:
The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans wears a tough outer cuticle. The cuticle is built from cross-linked collagens and cuticulins. It is required for movement and protection. Julie-Anne Fritz and Carolyn Behm identified a new protein in its making. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The protein is CUTI-1, a novel tetraspan membrane protein.

CUTI-1 is involved in cuticle formation. It also maintains epithelial integrity beneath the cuticle. Without it, the worm's armor fails. Little was known about how the complex cuticle assembles. This finding names a new player in that assembly. The worm is a classic model for development. Its skin offers a simple window on how animals build protective layers.
plos-pone-0005217:
Puberty changes family life in obvious ways, including a shift toward later sleep in teenagers. Frey and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether the timing of puberty itself shapes that sleep shift. They focused on menarche, the first menstrual period, in girls.

The study linked when menarche occurs to a girl's preferred sleep phase during adolescence. Earlier or later puberty went with a different tilt of the body clock. Knowing that puberty timing steers sleep helps parents and schools judge whether a teen's late nights are defiance or biology.
plos-pone-0005317:
Baker's yeast has lived alongside humans for millennia in brewing and baking. Lately it has also emerged as an opportunistic pathogen in vulnerable patients. Diezmann and Dietrich compared yeast isolates from clinics, homes, and the wild in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team studied how the populations diverged and how they resist oxidative stress, a key defense challenge inside the body. Clinical strains differ from tame and wild ones in telling ways. Tracing where clinic isolates come from helps hospitals understand a familiar microbe turned invader. A germ that lives in bread and beer can still turn on a weak host. So labs that treat yeast as tame in all cases may miss a risk that this work brings to light.
plos-pone-0005417:
For four decades, the Baltic Sea has suffered nutrient over-enrichment, with stronger algal blooms and falling water clarity. Bryhn used a well-tested dynamic mass-balance model in PLOS ONE in 2009 to find phosphorus loadings the sea can sustain.

The model also seeks phosphorus management that is both effective and cost-effective for the countries around the sea. Cutting phosphorus everywhere equally wastes money where cuts do little. A shared model lets nine coastal nations aim spending where the sea benefits most. The sea spans nine lands with one shore, so no one land can save it alone. And a shared cost map gives each of them a fair share of the work and a clear gain for the price.
plos-pone-0005517:
Oliver Maddocks and co-authors linked a gut bacterium to bowel cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Certain E. coli bacteria that stick to the bowel wall are found more often in people with bowel tumours than in healthy people. Long-term infection with them has been tied to tumour growth.

The team showed that these bacteria lower a protein that fixes errors in DNA. With repairs weakened, mutations can build up in bowel cells. That offers a concrete way in which a common gut germ could help start cancer. The finding also raises questions about how long such infections must last before repair loss becomes dangerous.
plos-pone-0005617:
Qosay Al-Balas and co-authors reported candidate compounds against tuberculosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Tuberculosis kills millions of people each year and infects a huge share of the world's population. Treatment is long, and drug resistance plus HIV co-infection make it harder.

The team tested a family of small compounds against the standard tuberculosis strain. They also targeted an enzyme the germ needs to build its wall fats. Compounds that hit a vital enzyme and kill the germ in the lab are starting points for new drugs. New tuberculosis drugs are badly needed, since the standard cure takes months and many patients stop early.
plos-pone-0005717:
Bijay Jaiswal and colleagues reported in 2009 that tumors with a mutated NRAS gene need a two-pronged drug attack. RAS genes are proven cancer drivers, yet no drug has blocked RAS itself well in patients. So researchers target the helper paths that carry RAS signals instead.

The team found that blocking BRAF alone is not enough in NRAS-mutant tumors. Adding a block on CRAF, or on the PI3K path, made treatment work. That pairing rule can guide drug trials for a stubborn tumor class. It also shows why single drugs so often fail against RAS cancers.
plos-pone-0005817:
Miranda Kramer and co-authors examined clots pulled from heart arteries during emergency treatment in 2009. A heart attack usually starts when a plaque in a coronary artery ruptures and a clot forms on it. Oddly, rupture and full blockage are often separated in time.

The team studied the pathology of aspirated clots from patients with major heart attacks. The clots' features hint at how old they are and how they formed. That knowledge can shape how doctors time and choose treatments in the first hours. Clot material, usually discarded, becomes evidence here.
plos-pone-0005917:
Martin Löwer and Gisbert Schneider built a predictor in 2009 for the shipping labels bacteria use to inject proteins into host cells. Gram-negative pathogens use a type III secretion system, a molecular syringe, to deliver virulence factors. The signal that marks a protein for that syringe is subtle and varied.

Their program learns the signal from genome data and flags likely cargo proteins in new genomes. Spotting the arsenal early helps researchers judge a strain's danger. It also nominates targets for drugs that would disarm rather than kill bacteria. The predictor turns raw genomes into threat assessments.
plos-pone-0006017:
Proteins work in teams, and the map of their partnerships hides fine order. Kakajan Komurov, Mehmet Gunes and Michael White set out to read that order in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses statistical network analysis to dissect how a functional protein network is organized, neighborhood by neighborhood, around each protein in the web.

Looking at local neighborhoods reveals design rules that a whole-network view can miss. Such rules help explain how cells keep order among thousands of working parts. The fine-scale map also serves drug research, since a protein's neighbors often decide whether blocking it will help, harm, or barely register at all.
plos-pone-0006117:
Fitness bred into an animal over generations may carry hidden costs. Nathan Palpant, Michael Szatkowski, Wang Wang and colleagues tested rats bred for low aerobic capacity in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper starts from the fact that oxygen metabolism predicts general health, and asks whether low intrinsic fitness travels with a weak heart under oxygen shortage.

The two did co-segregate: the low-capacity line also showed hypoxia-induced cardiac pump failure. Shared inheritance ties everyday fitness to crisis survival of the heart. The work gives heart research a model where the risk is built in by selection, much as low fitness runs in human families, rather than imposed by a single gene knockout.
plos-pone-0006217:
Coronaviruses copy themselves on bubble-like sacs that sprout inside infected cells. Xiaoling Xu and colleagues solved the crystal structure of part of a viral anchor protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, nsp4, comes from mouse hepatitis virus, a coronavirus studied as a model.

Three viral proteins anchor the copying machinery to those sacs, and nsp4 is one of them. The solved piece is the tail end that sits in the cell fluid. Knowing its shape clarifies how the copying factory is assembled. Structural details like this can later guide drugs that block coronavirus replication.
plos-pone-0006317:
Herpes-family viruses hide in the body for life, switching between quiet and active phases. Heiko Adler and colleagues removed an inhibitory receptor, CEACAM1, and watched gammaherpesvirus infection in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Control of these infections needs co-signals that both excite and restrain immune cells.

Without the inhibitory receptor, both lytic and latent infection were perturbed. The brake thus shapes the infection's whole course, not just its peaks. Co-inhibitory receptors had been little studied in this setting. The work shows quiet immune brakes deserve attention alongside accelerators.
plos-pone-0006417:
Growing insulin-making beta cells in the lab could supply transplants for diabetes, but the cells drift as they grow. Holger Russ and colleagues used genetic lineage tracing on beta cells from adult human islets in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Expanding functional beta cells in vitro is attractive for beta-cell replacement therapy.

The traced cells underwent epithelial-mesenchymal transition as they expanded in culture. That identity change explains why expanded cells lose function. Knowing the drift's nature points to ways to prevent or reverse it. Lineage tracing proves the new cells came from real beta cells.
plos-pone-0006517:
Yoshihisa Yamano and co-authors reported abnormal immune cells in a virus-linked nerve disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 is a retrovirus associated with HAM/TSP. That condition, HTLV-1-associated myelopathy, is a chronic neuroinflammatory disease of the spinal cord. Infected people carry virus in their T cells for life.

The team found abnormally high levels of virus-infected T cells with a specific marker pattern. These cells produce interferon gamma and carry the CCR4 and CD25 markers. Their abundance may drive the spinal cord inflammation. Tracking them could help monitor disease and test treatments.
plos-pone-0006617:
Diego Mastroeni and co-authors compared brain chemistry marks in identical twins in PLOS ONE in 2009. The twins were discordant for Alzheimer's disease: one twin had it, the other did not. The team focused on DNA methylation, a chemical mark that can turn large sets of genes up or down at once. Such marks may help drive Alzheimer's, they reasoned.

They looked at cortical nerve cells from both twins and compared the marks. Twins share the same DNA, so gaps in outcome point to marks or life events. Any methylation gaps they found are leads on what pushes one brain toward disease. Twin pairs give human research its best match of genes.
plos-pone-0006717:
Noriatsu Shigemura and colleagues studied why people differ in tasting umami in PLOS ONE in 2009. Umami is the savory taste triggered by glutamate, as in MSG. It is one of the five basic taste qualities. It helps guide intake of amino acids in food. Umami also grows stronger when certain flavor compounds combine.

The team examined the genetic and molecular basis of individual differences. People vary in how strongly they perceive umami. Receptor gene differences are a natural place to look for the cause. Explaining taste differences can inform nutrition and food design. It also adds a concrete case to the genetics of the senses.
plos-pone-0006817:
Helen L. Lutgers and colleagues measured life expectancy in a large Dutch diabetes cohort in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most earlier studies showed higher death rates in type 2 diabetes. Treatment had changed greatly in recent years. Goals for metabolic control grew stricter. Cardiovascular risk management also improved.

The cohort, called ZODIAC-10, was treated in primary care. The authors calculated life expectancy for these patients. Updated numbers test whether better care closed the survival gap. Primary care numbers reflect typical patients, not just hospital cases. The results help doctors give patients honest, current prognoses.
plos-pone-0006917:
Cloé Paul-Victor and Lindsay A. Turnbull varied growing conditions to test a classic plant trade-off in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plants divide a fixed reproductive budget between seed size and number. Bigger seeds should mean fewer seeds. Plotted on log scales, the trade-off should follow a fixed slope. That neat prediction assumes resources stay fixed.

Growth conditions changed the resources plants actually had. The authors tested how the size-number balance responded. Real plants bend the textbook trade-off with their environment. Understanding the bend matters for crop breeding and ecology alike. Seed size affects both yield and survival in the wild.
plos-pone-0007017:
Françoise Lazarini, Marc-André Mouthon, Gilles Gheusi, and colleagues studied radiation and new brain cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adult mammals keep adding neurons to the olfactory bulb throughout life. Most are born in the subventricular zone beside the brain's ventricles. They then migrate forward into the bulb. Cranial irradiation can disturb that supply line.

The team irradiated that zone in adult mice. They tracked effects on the cells and on behavior. The results matter for cancer care, where brain radiation is common. Protecting this stem cell niche may preserve smell and related brain functions after treatment.
plos-pone-0007117:
Nicolas Dard, Tran Le, and Bernard Maro removed a polarity protein from mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early mammalian embryos divide their cells into lineages. Asymmetric division and cell position both guide that sorting. By the sixteen-cell stage, two distinct cell populations appear. A polarity kinase called aPKC lambda helps set them apart.

Switching that kinase off changed how lineages were allocated. The effect depended on context, not one fixed rule. The study shows early fate choices are flexible and negotiated. That flexibility may help embryos recover from early disturbances.
plos-pone-0007217:
Senthil Kumar A. Natesan, Lori Peacock, Ka Fai Leung, and colleagues studied unusual transport proteins in a parasite in 2009. The parasite is Trypanosoma brucei, which causes sleeping sickness. Rab proteins normally guide vesicles, small packages that move material inside cells, to their targets.

Two divergent Rab-related proteins, RabX1 and RabX2, had barely been characterized. The authors test what they do in the parasite. They report no role in intracellular trafficking, but a possible role in infecting flies. Their result redirects attention from cell transport toward the parasite life cycle.
plos-pone-0007317:
Pan-Jun Kim, Dong-Yup Lee, and Hawoong Jeong analyzed sugar-tagging pathways in mammalian cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Glycosylation attaches diverse sugar structures to proteins and lipids. Those glycans guide protein folding and clearance, cell growth and death, development, and many other fundamental processes in living cells.

The process is highly complex, with many branching routes. The authors study N-linked glycosylation pathways, one major class. They report a centralized modularity in how those pathways are organized. A central, modular layout may let cells produce wide glycan variety from a manageable core system.
plos-pone-0007417:
Chenxi Zhou, Mario Tiberi, Binhui Liang, and colleagues studied ion exchange in mouse eggs during meiosis in 2009. Early mouse oocytes show highly active bicarbonate and chloride exchange. Such exchange is a class of transport involved nearly everywhere in regulating cell pH and volume, keeping internal conditions stable for development.

During meiosis, that exchange becomes inactivated and later reactivates. The authors link the timing to signaling by the MEK and MAPK pathway. They also track localization of the Ae2 exchanger in the egg membrane. Their PLOS ONE work explains a quiet period in egg chemistry.
plos-pone-0007517:
Kerstin Wunderlich and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 searching for a new way to block influenza. Vaccines protect incompletely, and resistance to current antiviral drugs keeps emerging. The virus's copying machine, its polymerase, is a promising target. One of its three parts is called PA. The team hunted for a short peptide that could bind PA and jam the machine.

They identified a peptide that does exactly that. It blocked replication of both influenza A and influenza B viruses. A peptide that grips the polymerase could seed a fresh class of flu drugs. Having one compound cover both virus types is a practical bonus. The study is an early step, but it proves the PA target can be hit. From such hits, drug development can begin.
plos-pone-0007617:
Ingvild Odsbu, Morigen, and Kirsten Skarstad published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how bacteria keep copying DNA when supplies run short. Chromosome replication runs from a moving fork that needs a steady flow of building blocks. An enzyme, ribonucleotide reductase, makes those blocks. It had been proposed that the supply enzymes cluster in a structure that organizes new DNA. The team reduced the enzyme's activity in E. coli and observed the fork.

With less supply, the replication fork slowed down. Its localization, however, did not change. The machinery stayed in place even as its fuel ran low. That robustness says something about how the replisome is anchored. It also tests the compartment idea under stress rather than in comfort. The study separates two questions that are easy to confuse: how fast the fork runs, and where it sits.
plos-pone-0007717:
Marjorie Mauduit and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a malaria vaccine approach based on weakened parasites. Shots of irradiated sporozoites, the parasite stage injected by mosquitoes, can give full protection. That protection works even across malaria species.

Protection was long credited to one surface protein, called CS. The authors show that immune responses to other parasite parts matter too. Those extra responses help explain the cross-species effect. The finding broadens the list of targets vaccine designers should consider. It may lead to malaria vaccines that protect against more than one species.
plos-pone-0007817:
Paul Grini and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It identifies a gene a flowering plant needs to make seeds and pollen. The plant is Arabidopsis, the standard lab plant. The gene, ASHH2, makes an enzyme that tags histones, the spools DNA winds around.

Those tags help set which genes are active or silent. The authors show ASHH2 is required for ovule and anther development. Without it, the flower's male and female parts fail. The work shows how gene-control tags shape plant reproduction. That knowledge feeds into crop science and seed production.
plos-pone-0007917:
Yazi Ke and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows that diabetes makes Alzheimer's-related damage worse in mice. Diabetes is marked by high blood sugar from too little insulin or resistance to it. Insulin also plays a role in the brain.

Insulin helps handle the two proteins that define Alzheimer's disease, amyloid and tau. The team induced diabetes in a transgenic mouse model of the disease. Tau pathology grew worse under the diabetic state. The result strengthens the case that metabolic health shapes brain aging. It may guide prevention aimed at both diseases.
plos-pone-0008017:
Ramachandran Saraswathi and colleagues described a DNA-guarding protein in mycobacteria for PLOS ONE in 2009. When food runs out, these bacteria pack their DNA into a tight bundle for safety. The protein in view, MsDps2, does the packing in one species of the family.

Two master gene switches, sigma A and sigma B, govern when the protein is made. Knowing its controls shows how the germ readies itself for hard times. Kin of this germ cause tuberculosis, so each detail of their survival kit is a possible target for new drugs.
plos-pone-0008117:
Dolores Perez-Sala and colleagues showed that a protein's tail can be its death warrant in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells must shred worn proteins to stay healthy, and they tag most doomed proteins for the shredder. The protein in view is RhoB, a small switch tied to cell growth.

Its tail end routed it to a different disposal path, through the cell's digesting sacs rather than the shredder. The tail is thus an address label the waste system reads. Address labels like this may be copied in drug design, to send harmful proteins to their end.
plos-pone-0008217:
Shelley N. Facente and colleagues examined rapid HIV test accuracy in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. A cluster of false positive results in San Francisco raised concern. The tests involved were oral fluid kits close to their expiration date. The team decided to test whether time to expiration affects the false positive rate. They used the OraQuick rapid antibody test in their analysis.

A rising false positive rate near expiry would have direct practical costs. False results cause stress and trigger needless follow-up testing. The findings help clinics decide how to stock and rotate kits. They also protect trust in rapid testing programs.
plos-pone-0008317:
Loknath Gidijala and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a new way to make penicillin. For years, this famed drug has been made only by one mold, Penicillium chrysogenum. No other host could make it. The team set out to build a fresh host for the job. They chose a yeast named Hansenula polymorpha, a known maker of proteins for labs and firms.

Their changed yeast made penicillin and sent it out of the cell well. Yeast grows fast and is easy to change in the lab. A yeast line could make drug work and drug research much more simple. The study proves a yeast can do a job long held by a mold alone.
plos-pone-0008417:
Neil D. Clarke and Guillaume Bourque reported a competition win in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The DREAM3 challenge asked teams to predict signaling responses in systems biology. Their group produced the best predictions overall. They were tops by a substantial margin in the cytokine sub-challenge. They nearly tied for best in the phosphoprotein sub-challenge as well.

Their winning method was simple weighted-average imputation, a basic interpolation strategy. A simple approach beating complex models carries a lesson. Community-wide experiments should respect strong baselines before adding complexity. The paper shares that lesson for systems biology.
plos-pone-0008517:
Richard van Zyl-Smit and co-authors review TB blood tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The tests are interferon-gamma release assays, or IGRAs. They detect tuberculosis infection from a blood sample. Variability in results matters for tests near the cut point. A small shift can flip a result from negative to positive. Little was known about variability within the same person. The team systematically review studies on that variability.

They also examine if a skin test boosts later blood test results. Tuberculin skin testing may prime the immune response it measures. Their review defines how much variation is normal noise. That helps clinicians judge conversion and reversion in repeat testing.
plos-pone-0008617:
Sandhya Vasan and co-authors report a phase 1 HIV vaccine trial in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their candidate is ADVAX, a multigenic DNA-based vaccine. It expresses HIV-1 genes from clade C and B prime strains. Genes include env, gag, pol, nef, and tat. Sequences came from a recombinant form prevalent in Yunnan, China, an area of high HIV incidence. The team conduct a dose escalation trial in volunteers. Phase 1 tests safety and immunogenicity, not efficacy.

ADVAX proves safe at the doses tested in this trial. It also elicits immune responses to HIV antigens in recipients. Such a multigenic DNA vaccine can advance to larger efficacy studies. The trial is a step for vaccines matched to Asian HIV strains.
plos-pone-0008717:
Zhenggen Huang, Junjie Yang, Gaoxing Luo, and colleagues tested young pig skin as a graft source. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bad burns heal poorly because skin loses its glands and fine ridges. Stem cells and engineered skin still struggle to restore those features. Embryonic skin precursors might build more complete skin.

The team transplanted pig embryo skin precursors into nude mice. The grafts grew into integrated skin on the mice. Crucially, no teratoma tumors formed after transplanting. A safe graft that forms true skin layers could change burn care if the approach scales.
plos-pone-0008817:
Robert Kleemann, Marjan van Erk, Lars Verschuren, and colleagues mapped insulin resistance as it builds over time. Their systems study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin resistance drives type-2 diabetes and heart disease. Its chain of causes, tissue by tissue, stayed poorly mapped. Single-gene studies had failed to capture the whole process. A time-resolved, multi-tissue approach was needed instead.

The team followed changes across tissues as resistance developed. Early and late events separated into a clear sequence. Some tissues changed first and may trigger the rest. That order suggests when and where treatment could work best.
plos-pone-0008917:
Huaiyu Yang, Martin Bogner, York-Dieter Stierhof, and colleagues built a glowing sensor for a key plant food in root tips. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glutamine is a main carrier of nitrogen inside plants. It is often the most abundant amino acid in roots. Watching it move in living tissue was not possible before. A genetically encoded fluorescent reporter changed that. The sensor glows differently as glutamine levels shift.

With the reporter in Arabidopsis roots, transport could be watched live. Uptake at root tips proceeded without the proton help many expected. A new window on nitrogen feeding opens for plant science. Better nitrogen use means less fertilizer waste.
plos-pone-0009017:
David Altmann and co-authors checked whether a heart damage marker in sepsis really means clots, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Patients with severe sepsis or septic shock often show raised troponin I. Troponin I usually signals heart muscle death, as in a heart attack. One suspicion was that small clots in heart vessels cause the release.

The team looked for evidence of clot-linked heart muscle death in these patients. They found none tying the raised troponin to thrombus-driven damage. The marker rises in sepsis, but apparently by another route. Doctors should not read high troponin in sepsis as proof of a heart attack.
plos-pone-0009117:
Ryan Martin and David Pfennig tested how a mother's investment shapes her offspring's feeding type, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some amphibian young develop quite different body forms for different foods. That variety within one species is called resource polymorphism. A mother's own state can pass down and shape her young, too.

The amount a mother invested influenced which form her young expressed. Eggs provisioned in different ways produced different feeding types. A mother's condition can thus switch on what looks like a new body plan. Effects like these may help explain how novel traits first appear in evolution.
plos-pone-0009217:
Martin Barth and co-authors published this fly vision study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In the fruit fly Drosophila, the wiring of the first visual relay changes with experience early in life. Those changes follow a critical period just after the fly emerges. The authors looked for other ways this circuit reshapes itself.

They found two further mechanisms that work in parallel. The synapses of light-sensing cells change over the day-night cycle, a form of circadian plasticity. Those daily shifts in the photoreceptor terminals control how efficiently the eye codes what it sees. The work shows that even a fly's vision is tuned by the time of day.
plos-pone-0009317:
Brian Tuch and co-authors published this cancer sequencing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors differ from normal tissue in both gene use and gene copy numbers. Reading all of a tumor's RNA, called RNA-Seq, was becoming cheap and fast. It promised to replace older microarray methods for studying tumors.

The team used transcriptome sequencing on primary tumors. They found cases where one copy of a gene spoke louder than the other. Those allelic imbalances lined up with places where copy numbers had changed. The study shows a single sequencing run can reveal both what genes a tumor uses and how its DNA has been rearranged.
plos-pone-0009417:
Michael Hubert and co-authors published this placenta study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The placenta's working surface is built by fusion. Single trophoblast cells merge into a shared layer that exchanges nutrients with the mother's blood. A switch protein called NR2F2 rises sharply as that change begins.

In lab-grown human trophoblast cells, NR2F2 messages peak on the first day of differentiation. That rise is nearly ninefold. The team examined the factor's role in driving the change of cell type. Knowing the switches of placental development matters because failures here underlie dangerous pregnancy conditions.
plos-pone-0009517:
Anjali Goswami and David Polly compared skull variety in two mammal groups in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carnivores and primates both show a huge range of skull shapes. Why some groups vary more than others is an open question. One idea points to modularity. A modular skull is built from parts that can change somewhat on their own.

The team measured skull shape and modularity across both groups. They tested whether more modular skulls allow greater variety of form. Their results bear on how development shapes evolution. If parts can vary freely, selection has more raw material to work with, and new forms arise more easily.
plos-pone-0009617:
Daniel Sol and co-authors compared brain size in migrating and resident birds in PLOS ONE in 2010. Why brains vary so much in size across species is a long debate. Migration makes heavy demands: long flights, new places, shifting food. One might expect migrants to carry larger brains. The team compared songbird species that migrate with close kin that stay in one place all year.

Migratory species tended to have smaller brains than residents. That result runs against the simple guess. It may reflect the cost of growing brain tissue on a tight energy budget. The study adds a sharp data point to the science of how brains evolve.
plos-pone-0009717:
Seasonal flu changes a little every year, and tracking those changes guides vaccine choice. Kamol Suwannakarn and colleagues traced flu viruses circulating in Thailand from 2006 to 2009. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The team followed two influenza A types, H1N1 and H3N2, at the molecular level. Gene changes showed how each strain evolved season by season. The four-year span let the team compare successive seasons directly. Regional records like this fill gaps in the global flu picture. They help health officials spot new variants early. Each season's vaccine must match the strains in circulation.
plos-pone-0009817:
Malaria parasites vary from place to place, and that variety can affect how sick people get. Ndeye Sakha Bob and colleagues studied parasite types in Dakar, Senegal. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The work focused on patients in the capital city.

Polymorphism means the parasites carry many genetic forms at once. The team linked those forms with cases of severe malaria in the city. Dakar is a West African urban area, where malaria patterns differ from the countryside. Knowing local parasite variety helps doctors and planners fight severe disease.
plos-pone-0009917:
A lab-made gene inserted into tobacco plants unexpectedly shut flower color off. Jeff Velten, Cahid Cakir, and Christopher Cazzonelli reported the accident and what it teaches. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tobacco is a workhorse plant for genetic engineering tests.

The transgene carried AtMYB90, a gene meant to boost pigment production. Instead, a spontaneous dominant-negative mutation arose within the transgene. That broken copy overpowered the normal pigment machinery and inhibited flower pigment production. The case warns genetic engineers that inserted genes can mutate into blockers. Flower color made the failure easy to see at a glance.
plos-pone-0010017:
Sarah Auburn, Andrew Fry, Taane Clark, and co-workers added genetic evidence in PLOS ONE in 2010 on why some malaria becomes severe. Their focus was a signaling route in cells tied to a protein called Gs. That route had already been linked to how malaria parasites enter red blood cells.

The authors weighed that prior work alongside conditions common in people of African origin and a large body of drug knowledge. They argued the evidence still supports a role for Gs signaling in severe malaria. If true, a well-studied drug target may sit close to the heart of the worst cases.
plos-pone-0010117:
Joris M Koene is first author on a 2010 PLOS ONE study of seminal fluid in a pond snail that is both sexes at once. Seminal fluid can carry substances that shift a mate's body to favor the donor's sperm. Such substances were known only from separate-sex animals.

The team identified eight new peptides and proteins, small chain molecules, from the snail's prostate gland and tested their effects. One protein, named Ovipostatin, cut egg mass production in receiving snails. Its gene was fully read, a first for a simultaneous hermaphrodite, meaning an animal with both sex roles. Sexual selection, the authors show, acts even when sexes combine.
plos-pone-0010217:
The authors were Derek Arnold, Morgan Tear, Ryan Schindel, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested how sight and sound combine in speech perception. Different senses interact, often changing what we think we saw or heard. Combining cues can make perceptual decisions more precise than either sense alone, a benefit seen in lip-read speech during noise.

The team studied how listeners combine audio and visual speech cues. They weighed the possible computational rules behind that combination. The rules matter for hearing aids and speech technology that use a speaker's face as well as voice.
plos-pone-0010317:
Ravi Marreddy and co-workers reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a milk bacterium used to make proteins in the lab. Lactococcus lactis is a workhorse for producing added proteins, including hard membrane proteins. Getting cells to build large amounts of such proteins often fails, though. The team asked what inside the cell sets that limit.

Their answer points to a build-up of amino acids, the small units that link into proteins. As added protein output rises, these units pile up and growth suffers. The finding matters for structural studies, which need pure protein in quantity. It also suggests a clear target: ease that inner pile-up, and yields may climb. The work treats the cell as a factory with a findable bottleneck.
plos-pone-0010417:
Manfred Hartbauer studied how two aphid species defend their colonies together in PLOS ONE in 2010. Aphids are soft, slow insects eaten by many enemies. Some species rely on ants for protection; others grow a soldier caste. The two species here lack both of those common defenses. Yet they live in groups, which should attract predators. Hartbauer asked what defense they use instead.

Group living without guards or soldiers seems reckless for such prey. The answer appears to be collective action by ordinary colony members. Coordinated responses can startle or repel attackers even without weapons. That expands the known menu of insect defenses. It also shows evolution can solve the same problem in a new way. Weak insects, together, may not be so weak.
plos-pone-0010517:
Reginaldo Kuroshu, Junichi Watanabe and Sumio Sugano presented a cheaper way to sequence full-length gene copies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Full-length cDNA clones show a gene's true structure, including its alternate forms. They are prized resources for studying what proteins do. Older sequencing approaches for them were slow and costly. The team combined fresh assembly with reference-guided assembly into a hybrid method.

The hybrid kept accuracy while cutting cost per clone. Cheaper full-length sequencing means more genes can be covered completely. That helps labs in smaller institutions, not just genome centers. Gene structure errors can mislead years of follow-up work. A reliable, affordable pipeline prevents many such errors.
plos-pone-0010617:
Tiziana Funaioli and colleagues studied how paired plant compounds twist light, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compounds, called bicolchicides, belong to a new pseudoaromatic class. When two light-absorbing parts sit in one molecule, they affect each other's signals.

The team measured circular dichroism, which records how a sample absorbs twisted light. The signals revealed how the paired parts are arranged in space. Reading those signals correctly is hard without careful comparison and reference compounds. The work gives chemists a firmer basis for using this method on complex natural compounds.
plos-pone-0010717:
Janet Raboud and colleagues reviewed how SARS spread to health workers in Toronto in 2003, in PLOS ONE in 2010. During that outbreak, the virus passed to staff inside hospitals despite standard precautions. Patients on breathing machines seemed especially risky to treat, but which steps carried the risk was disputed.

The multi-center study compared infected and uninfected staff who treated intubated patients. Certain airway procedures and lapses in protective gear stood out. Routine care at a distance carried far less risk. Clear facts of this kind let hospitals write rules that protect staff without shutting down vital care during the next outbreak.
plos-pone-0010817:
Mary Fletcher and colleagues evaluated blood markers for chronic fatigue syndrome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The syndrome brings crushing fatigue without a clear lab test. Two immune signs had recurred in earlier work: weak natural killer cell killing, and raised levels of a surface marker called CD26 on lymphocytes. Neither had been validated as a biomarker.

Measured afresh in patients and controls, both signs differed as earlier work suggested. The team weighed them against strict biomarker standards. Having any objective measure would change life for patients whose illness is often doubted. The study moves the pair from hints toward tests, while noting the validation still to come.
plos-pone-0010917:
Merlijn Meens, Matthijs Compeer, Tilman Hackeng and co-authors published this blood vessel study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Endothelin-1 is a powerful, long-lasting vessel-tightening signal tied to cardiovascular disease, yet drugs blocking its receptor have disappointed in some trials. The authors suspected the signal grips its receptor almost irreversibly, so blockers arrive too late.

In isolated rat arteries, standard blockers and relaxing factors only briefly eased the tightening, which kept returning. Stimulating the sensory-motor nerves around the vessel, however, ended the contraction outright. That effect ran through a nerve-released peptide called CGRP and physically pried the signal off its receptor. Meens and colleagues uncover the body's own release valve for a stubborn constrictor, a mechanism drug designers could imitate.
plos-pone-0011017:
Blaine Zern, Hunghao Chu and Yadong Wang published this drug delivery study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growth factors could heal many tissues, but injected freely they vanish from the blood within minutes. In the body, many are sheltered by heparin, a natural sugar chain that binds and protects them, and the authors copied that trick for a wound-healing factor called FGF-2.

They used a body-friendly positively charged polymer to pull the heparin and growth factor complex out of solution into a solid release matrix. Changing the polymer's size tuned how fast the factor leaked out, and the released factor kept its biological activity. Zern and colleagues offer a simple, adjustable depot for fragile healing proteins. Controlled release could finally make growth factor therapy practical in chronic wounds and tissue engineering.
plos-pone-0011117:
Minozzi, Buggiotti, Stella and colleagues searched cattle genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some cattle fight off a chronic gut infection better than others. That infection, a form of Johne disease, is caused by a germ related to the TB germ, and response varies by animal.

The team hunted for gene regions tied to how strongly cattle make antibodies against the germ. Such regions mark inherited differences in defense. Breeders could use them to select animals that resist the disease. Cutting losses in herds would also reduce germ spread on farms and lower costs for farmers.
plos-pone-0011217:
Aruscavage, Hellwig and Bass examined dying worm cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. When cells die in a controlled way, their DNA is cut into pieces in a ladder like pattern. In the roundworm, the team asked whether the smallest DNA pieces are a step in that cutting process.

They showed the small pieces are indeed intermediates of the fragmentation that marks this form of cell death. Confirming the hallmark validates worms as a model for studying how cells dismantle themselves. That process goes wrong in cancer and in wasting diseases, so a tractable model has broad use.
plos-pone-0011317:
Chan, Hsiao, Lee and colleagues evaluated flu policy in Taiwan for PLOS ONE in 2010. Older people die from flu at high rates, and vaccine benefit depends on how well the year's vaccine matches circulating strains. After the SARS outbreak, Taiwan also strengthened public health efforts, and the team measured both effects on elderly flu deaths.

Matching vaccine strains and the post SARS efforts together reduced influenza linked mortality among the elderly. That offers a public health model other countries can copy. It shows vaccine strain selection, a yearly global decision, has life and death weight. It also credits lasting system reforms, not only emergency responses.
plos-pone-0011417:
Joon Seol Bae and colleagues profiled large-scale DNA variation in Korean volunteers in 2010. Most gene studies chase single-letter changes, but whole segments of DNA can also be missing, duplicated, or rearranged between people. Those structural changes affect many genes at once, yet reference data came mostly from European samples, leaving Korean genetics under-mapped.

Using samples from the Korean HapMap group, the team charted structural variants across the genome and built a population reference. Disease studies in Korea can now check whether a structural change is a harmless common variant or a rare suspect. The catalog also serves wider East Asian research. It is a reminder that a genome reference drawn from one population can mislead studies in another, and that local data repair that bias.
plos-pone-0011517:
Marguerite Hunt and co-authors reported in 2010 very bright green fluorescent proteins from a tiny marine animal. Biologists tag cells and proteins with glowing markers to watch life under the microscope, and brighter markers give clearer pictures at lower light, which is kinder to living samples. The new proteins come from Pontella mimocerami, a small copepod, a drifting crustacean of the open sea.

The copepod's green fluorescent proteins proved exceptionally bright compared with standard laboratory markers. New glow tools from nature have a strong track record, since the most famous marker also came from a sea animal. Microscopists gain sharper beacons for following single molecules and faint structures. The find also rewards basic curiosity about plankton: an obscure copepod held a tool that laboratories everywhere may soon use daily.
plos-pone-0011617:
Tobias Haase and co-authors mapped the inner layout of an important enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, soluble guanylyl cyclase, senses nitric oxide in cells and then produces a messenger called cGMP. Knowing how its parts sit together is key to understanding how the sensing step switches on production.

The team attached glowing protein tags to the enzyme's ends and measured energy transfer between them. The signals showed the nitric oxide sensing part lies close to the producing part. That closeness shapes how the enzyme works and may guide drugs that target it in heart and blood vessel disease.
plos-pone-0011717:
Jan-Philip Schülke and co-authors compared helper proteins that tune hormone receptors, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Steroid hormone receptors are clients of the folding machine Hsp90, assisted by co-chaperones bearing a repeat motif called TPR. These helpers are thought to govern the activity and specificity of the whole platform.

The authors tested how different TPR proteins each affect the steroid receptors. Their side-by-side comparison shows the helpers do not act alike: each tunes hormone signalling in its own way. That variety helps explain how the same folding platform can serve many different hormone pathways precisely.
plos-pone-0011817:
Rame Taha and co-authors studied stress damage in a human gut cell line, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faulty mitochondria and oxidative stress sit at the heart of many diseases, yet they had seen little study in the gut. That gap is odd, since the gut lining meets oxidants from food day in and day out.

With Caco-2/15 cells as a gut stand-in, the team checked how oxidative strain hits the cells' power output. Their dish-based view shows how gut cells stand up to chemical siege over time. The results inform work on gut diseases where oxidants swamp the lining's defences.
plos-pone-0011917:
Wenli Zhang and co-workers tested in 2010 whether retinoic acids could strengthen a bone-forming signal. BMP9 is among the strongest bone-building members of its protein family, though one of the least studied. Retinoic acid signaling, related to vitamin A, is known to shape development, cell specialization, and bone balance.

The team found that retinoic acids potentiate, or boost, the bone-forming differentiation that BMP9 drives in mesenchymal progenitor cells, the flexible cells that can become bone. Two signals working together more strongly than either alone is useful knowledge for bone repair. It suggests combination treatments could coax stubborn fractures or bone defects to heal with lower doses of each agent.
plos-pone-0012017:
Petra Neumann-Staubitz and co-workers characterized in 2010 a clathrin mutant designed as a switchable tool for studying cell uptake. Clathrin coats the pits where cells pull material inside, and its work is deeply conserved, though yeast and vertebrates may need it differently. Because clathrin protein lasts a long time, simply removing its gene shows only slow, long-term effects.

Their temperature-sensitive heavy chain mutant lets researchers disable clathrin quickly in a living vertebrate system and watch immediate consequences. A fast off-switch separates clathrin's direct jobs from the cell's later workarounds. Tools like this turn a housekeeping protein into an experimental subject.
plos-pone-0012117:
Bénédicte Menn, Stéphane Bach, Teri Blevins, and colleagues tested a drug treatment for stroke in animals for PLOS ONE in 2010. Protecting brain tissue after a stroke is notoriously hard, and most attempts have failed. One target is a family of enzymes that become overactive in injured brain cells. The drug they tested calms one member of that family.

Given after the stroke-like injury, the treatment still protected nerve cells in their models. It also lowered the harmful enzyme activity measured in the living brain. A treatment that works even when delayed matters, because real stroke patients rarely reach care in the first minutes. Results like these keep a difficult drug strategy alive.
plos-pone-0012217:
Annett Hessel, Michael Schwendinger, Daniela Fritz, and co-authors built a flu vaccine on a harmless virus backbone, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their target was the pandemic H1N1 flu that swept the world in 2009. The carrier, a weakened poxvirus, was loaded with flu parts so one shot could raise both antibody and killer-cell defenses, broader protection than standard flu shots give.

In mice the vaccine raised strong immune responses and protected animals from flu challenge. Protection even transferred with immune material from vaccinated animals to unvaccinated ones. A platform that can be reloaded for each new flu strain is exactly what pandemic planners want on the shelf.
plos-pone-0012317:
Martial Ndeffo Mbah and Christopher Gilligan modeled the fight against sudden oak death in PLOS ONE in 2010. This pathogen kills oaks and other trees across mixed forests, and the standard defense is culling infected trees before they spread it onward. Culling, though, first requires finding infections that hide inside outwardly healthy-looking stands, and money spent searching cannot be spent cutting.

Their model balances spending between detection and eradication for the best overall control. That balance shifts with how hidden the infections are and how fast the disease moves. Forest agencies facing this epidemic, and others like it, can use the logic to stretch limited budgets across the whole job instead of excelling at half of it.
plos-pone-0012417:
Yen-An Tang, Wei-Ling Wen, Jer-Wei Chang and colleagues tested a new drug that blocks gene-reading enzymes in lung cancer cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and treatment for advanced cases works poorly. The drug targets histone deacetylases, enzymes that tighten DNA packing and silence genes, a strategy already used in some blood cancers.

The new blocker killed lung cancer cells by triggering programmed cell death, wrecking their inner skeleton, and reopening silenced genes. Attacking on three fronts at once may make it harder for tumors to resist. Cell results are only a first step, but they justify animal tests of this compound.
plos-pone-0012517:
Elizabeth Punnoose, Siminder Atwal, Jill Spoerke and colleagues read cancer markers from tumor cells caught in blood, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Circulating tumor cells break off from cancers and drift in the bloodstream, offering tumor material without a biopsy. Testing markers on them could let doctors track a cancer's traits and drug sensitivity over time.

The team showed biomarker analyses can be run on these rare captured cells reliably. Reliable blood-based testing would spare patients repeat tissue biopsies and let oncologists watch resistance emerge in near real time. The work supports the liquid biopsy approach now spreading through cancer care.
plos-pone-0012617:
