Aaron, Kempf, Criniti and co-authors tracked side effects in women treated for HIV with nevirapine. The drug is widely used, yet reports link it to severe rash and liver injury in some women. Their 2010 study compared pregnant and non-pregnant women on nevirapine with women on other HIV drugs.

Data came from a multi-site group of more than six hundred women starting treatment. Looking for who suffered harm, and when, helps clinics use the drug more safely. The findings guide care for pregnant women, who must balance their own health with the baby's.
plos-pone-0012717:
Moisenovich, Ol'shevskaya, Rokitskaya and co-authors tested new light-activated compounds that kill cancer cells fast. Tumours often have broken self-destruct programs, so treatments that kill by another route are valuable. Their 2010 compounds are photosensitizers, which turn toxic when light hits them inside cells.

The compounds damaged cell fats and punched holes in cell membranes, killing human cancer cells and shrinking rodent tumour grafts. Membrane attack sidesteps the broken death programs entirely. Such direct killers could serve where standard chemo fails.  Light dosing gives doctors a way to aim the kill at the tumour site.
plos-pone-0012817:
Bader, Ruhe, Wang and co-authors traced a beagle disease to a single founding mutation. Musladin-Lueke Syndrome leaves beagles with stiff, fibrotic skin and joints locked by contractures. It mirrors a human condition called stiff skin syndrome, making the dog a natural model.

Their 2010 study found the cause in the ADAMTSL2 gene, carried down from a founder dog through the breed. A known cause lets breeders test and reduce the disease in beagles. It also gives human researchers a living model of the matching disorder.  Gene tests can now identify carriers before breeding.
plos-pone-0326717:
Liying Liu and colleagues wrote a step-by-step plan for giving drip drugs to mental health patients who act out with force. A drip is hard to start and hard to keep safe when a patient may pull the line or strike out, which puts both sides at risk. The team built the plan from past studies and talks with experts, and shaped it with a well-known quality model.

Experts then went through two rounds of review and reached firm, shared views on the draft. The final plan has three main parts, seventeen mid-level items, and forty-one fine points, from prep work to care after the drip ends. A shared plan like this gives ward staff one safe routine to follow in tense moments, not ad hoc choices.
plos-pone-0329717:
Benoit Paquette led a team of eight authors studying an unwanted side effect of radiotherapy, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Radiation treats triple-negative breast cancer, but plasma taken from patients during treatment can spur cancer cells to invade more. The team traced that effect to a protein called Rab4A.

Paquette's group showed that Rab4A helps drive the rise in invasion caused by treatment-time plasma. Blocking it could stop therapy from backfiring on the patients it aims to save. The finding is early, from cell work, but it names a precise point of intervention. It also warns clinicians that blood-borne signals during radiotherapy deserve study, not only the tumor under the beam.
plos-pone-0337817:
Cuc T T Nguyen and a large team tested whether a community programme could lift quality of life for rural Vietnamese adults whose blood pressure stays uncontrolled. Sixteen communities were assigned by chance to usual support or to an enhanced package adding personal storytelling sessions, home blood pressure monitoring, and expanded community health worker help. Just over six hundred and seventy patients were followed for a year with a standard health survey.

The enhanced group gained clearly on the physical side of quality of life at twelve months, by a margin the authors judge meaningful. Both groups received solid basic education about the condition. The authors present the package, built from neighbours' stories and home measurement rather than new drugs, as a workable model for rural chronic disease care in similar settings.
plos-pone-0341617:
Christy Bills led a team of six authors on this 2026 community science study hunting flashing fireflies in the western United States. Western firefly populations were largely undocumented. Through outreach and a reporting website, volunteers across Utah sent in sightings over nearly a decade, and the team verified records with field visits and collected specimens.

More than a hundred and thirty new localities were documented, greatly widening the known range. Bills describes the hurdles, from stray reports to protecting private land, and plans expansion into neighboring states as a model for public-powered biodiversity research.
plos-pone-0343917:
Sae-Lim and colleagues adapted a grief questionnaire for Thai caregivers in a 2026 study. The tool screens for grief that stays severe and long lasting after a loved one dies. Caregivers of patients with final-stage cancer often face that risk, but the original questions were written in English for other cultures.

The team translated the questions, had experts review them, and tested them with caregivers at a Bangkok hospital. Scores held steady over two weeks and lined up well with measures of worry, low mood, and caregiver strain. One weak question was dropped, leaving a short tool that Thai care teams can trust for screening.
plos-pone-0345817:
Md Minhajul, Md Rahman, and Md Tareque examine how moving house changes pregnancy care in Bangladesh. Their 2026 study uses the 2022 Demographic and Health Survey. Over forty-three hundred married women who had given birth in three years were analysed. Migration status sorted them into rural-to-urban movers, urban-to-rural movers, and stayers. The outcomes were receiving professional antenatal care and quality care, a stricter standard.

Rural-to-urban migrants did best of all. About sixty-nine percent received professional care, beating settled urban residents. Their adjusted odds were roughly half again higher. Urban-to-rural movers fared worst, falling below urban stayers. Quality care followed the same pattern, though levels were lower everywhere. Moving toward the city seems to carry women toward services, while moving away strands them. Maternal health programmes should track new arrivals in both directions, not just the cities swelling with newcomers.
plos-pone-0346817:
Douwe van Hinsbergen and colleagues announce a big upgrade to a free web tool. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tool, Paleolatitude.org, tells where a rock or fossil site sat on Earth long ago. That setting is key for reading ancient climates and life. The first version came out a decade ago.

Version three rests on a new global map of moving plates. It is the first such map to span the whole era of complex life. It also reports how unsure each answer is. Both the map's doubt and the sample's age feed that score. The shared tool lets climate and life scientists work from one moving Earth.
plos-pone-0347517:
Ozgenur Cetinbag-Kuzu, Zehra Aydoğan, and Mustafa Gökcan adapted a music reward questionnaire into Turkish and proved the translation works. The questionnaire measures how much pleasure a person takes from music, split into facets. No checked Turkish version existed before. Two hundred sixty-six adults completed it, from non-musicians to professionals. A smaller group took it again three weeks later.

The Turkish form kept the original structure. Its scores were steady across the three-week gap, and its parts hung together well. The team also charted how scores vary with musicianship, gender, and age. Musical pleasure ranges from flat indifference to chills. It matters in brain and mental health research. Turkish researchers now hold a checked ruler instead of a rough translation.
plos-pone-0348017:
Xiaokun Zhang, Sunnan Li, and Chunzhou Zhao put eye-track specs on top women hoop stars. They asked how sweat level and shot spot change the eyes and the score. Twenty-two stars from a champ team shot from three spots. Each shot came at low, mid, or high work rates. The specs logged each glance at hoop, board, and net.

Mid work gave the lean gaze: few glances, short looks, best score. High work split the gaze and stretched the looks. More glances meant worse shots at all rates. Straight shots drew eyes to the hoop. Side shots drew eyes to the board. The team backs eye drills at game pace.
plos-pone-0348117:
Cengizhan Kurt and colleagues asked whether a simple nutrition score can forecast death within a year after hip fracture surgery in older adults. Hip breaks kill up to four in ten older patients within a year, and poor nutrition worsens odds. Records covered more than six hundred patients aged sixty five and older at two large hospitals.

Just over one fifth of patients died within a year. Age, illness burden class, and the nutrition score each predicted death on their own when other factors were counted. The score sorted risk sharply: patients below a cut near ninety one died at vastly higher rates than those above it. A score from blood protein and body weight, the team argues, belongs in routine risk checks.
plos-pone-0348517:
Nouh Mounadi and co-authors screen plant compounds in simulation as possible blockers of two respiratory viruses at once: influenza A and a lesser-known cousin that also causes severe chest illness. Approved drugs exist for flu but options stay thin overall. The team docked known antiviral plant compounds against one key protein from each virus, then checked the best fits for drug-like behavior, stability in motion, and binding strength.

Dozens of compounds docked well against both targets, scoring better than the reference drugs used for comparison. A handful also passed safety and absorption screens, and motion tests supported their grip. Mounadi and colleagues present the shortlist as candidates for lab testing toward broad respiratory antivirals, not as ready medicines.
plos-pone-0348617:
Steve Joko, Christophe Antonio-Nkondjio, and co-authors combined a knowledge survey with blood testing in a village near Cameroon's capital to find out why malaria persists where awareness is high. Their 2026 study screened two hundred forty-nine residents for parasites and quizzed a subgroup in depth about what they know, believe, and actually do about the disease.

Knowledge and attitudes scored well and evenly across the village, yet daily practices lagged, though women practiced prevention better than men. A quarter of those screened carried malaria parasites, with school-age children hit hardest, evidence of quiet transmission without symptoms. Education showed mixed patterns depending on how groups were drawn. The authors call the core problem a knowledge-to-practice gap and urge interventions aimed at behavior and at the silently infected age group.
plos-pone-0348717:
Gilbert Mua Akwa and co-workers run the first injury surveillance of professional men's football in Cameroon, covering playoff tournaments in the top two leagues during one season. Africa has lacked such counts, though Europe tracks injuries closely. Their 2026 study has match-day medical officers log every injury needing attention across one hundred thirty-nine matches using standard forms.

One hundred seventy-one injuries were recorded, a high rate per hour of play. The second-tier league's rate ran more than double the top tier's. Legs took most knocks, cramps and bruises led the list, and a fifth of injuries were severe. Nearly half struck in the last half hour, pointing at fatigue. Better conditioning and medical readiness top the authors' advice.
plos-pone-0349017:
Marco Antonio Morales-Osorio and colleagues present the plan for a clinical trial testing remote rehabilitation for fibromyalgia, a long-term condition marked by widespread pain and foggy thinking. The protocol describes a twelve-week program that pairs exercise guided by artificial intelligence with lessons that teach patients how pain works in the nervous system. Fifty adults will take part across several centers.

Half the patients will use an app that watches their movements and gives live feedback during three exercise sessions a week, plus a weekly pain lesson. The other half will receive enhanced usual care. Pain change is the main outcome the team will compare. No results are reported yet; the value lies in a careful test of care that could reach underserved regions.
plos-pone-0349117:
Yuri Kosaka and colleagues examined how high pressure inside the eye distorts cataract surgery planning. Surgeons calculate the artificial lens power from the eye's length, but pressure stretches the eye slightly, and when pressure drops the eye shrinks back, throwing off the calculation. The team reviewed nineteen eyes operated on for high pressure and compared measurements before and after.

Eye length and pressure moved together moderately, and each unit of pressure drop shortened the eye by a tiny, consistent amount. After surgery the average pressure fall was large and the eye shortened measurably. Predicted vision errors differed between the two standard formulas tested. Applying a length correction for pressure cases should sharpen the match between planned and actual vision after surgery.
plos-pone-0349217:
Chung-Yuan Huang and Sheng-Wen Wang simulated a familiar frustration: a game everyone agrees is excellent that almost nobody played. They combined two models of social behavior, one for how opinions spread and shift through conversation, and one for how people adopt a product once enough of their circle has. Virtual consumers were placed on four kinds of social network, from regular grids to hub-dominated webs.

Agents could talk themselves into or out of liking the product, then act on the result. The simulations show how praise can circulate widely while purchases stall, when thresholds for trying something new are never crossed in the right clusters. For marketers and designers, the model separates two problems that are usually confused: winning minds and triggering first tries are different battles.
plos-pone-0349317:
Zhe Zhu, Shan Huang, and Wanqiang Xu studied what makes Chinese charitable foundations good at raising money in 2026. Fundraising keeps such groups alive, and single cause answers rarely capture how nonprofit success is built.

Fifty-four foundations were compared with a method that looks for recipes of conditions rather than lone factors. Open digital reporting and active programs were near essential. Two winning recipes emerged, pairing those strengths with either political ties or strong professional management. The recipe view helps foundation leaders invest in bundles that work together, instead of chasing one fix at a time.
plos-pone-0349417:
Marta Diaz-Guardamino and colleagues compare boat carvings on rocks in northwest Iberia and southern Scandinavia from late prehistory. High detail three dimensional records and map analysis were used on the Iberian carvings to read their forms and settings. Form by form comparison with Nordic boat art then tested how close the traditions really are.

Close matches in boat shapes support a late Bronze Age date for the Iberian carvings, roughly three thousand years ago. Nearly every Iberian site, even inland ones, kept a sight or travel link to navigable water. Shared boat art fits wide sea trade in metals like copper and tin across Atlantic Europe, mixed with ritual meaning for seafaring groups.
plos-pone-0349617:
Inside cells, chemicals transform in webs of reactions, and knowing which way influence flows along each link is hard when only steady snapshots exist. Nava Leibovich and Miroslava Cuperlovic-Culf surveyed and tested methods for guessing that direction, in this 2026 PLOS One review of biochemical networks.

They benchmarked statistical scores and neural network approaches on artificial networks built to behave like real metabolism. A few methods succeeded when the underlying reaction rules were known; many others guessed poorly. The authors are candid about limits: direction in such webs may often be unrecoverable from still observations alone, a warning for anyone modeling cell chemistry from routine data.
plos-pone-0350017:
Froucke van Gosliga and colleagues tested a pop up decision aid in hospital records to improve blood thinning shots that prevent clots in non surgical patients. Such shots are often missed despite clear guidance. Four hundred high risk patients were compared before and after the aid went live, with time trend methods used to strip out drift already under way.

Adequate prescribing rose from seventy eight to ninety one percent after launch. Once prior trend and timing patterns were counted, the clear gain shrank and could reflect chance. Baseline care was already strong at this site. Decision aids may still polish good practice, the authors conclude, but proof needs larger, multi site tests.
plos-pone-0350117:
Old and leftover medicines pile up in homes, and most people bin them, sending chemicals toward soil and water. Maryam Farooqui and colleagues surveyed about eight hundred eighty adults in Qassim, Saudi Arabia, about what they keep and how they throw medicines away, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Seven in ten had unused medicines at home, often stored in the fridge. Nearly nine in ten tossed them in household trash, and almost none had ever been taught safe disposal. Most agreed pharmacies or authorities should offer take-back routes. The authors call for rules and collection programs to close the gap.
plos-pone-0350617:
Jingyi Dong and colleagues surveyed eleven hundred ten Chinese college students to learn how believing study matters turns into actually engaging with it. Values alone do not guarantee effort, so the team tested a chain: values may build confidence, confidence may feed motivation, and motivation may drive engagement. They separated self-driven motivation from pressure-driven motivation, since the two pull differently.

Confidence and both kinds of motivation each carried part of the effect from values to engagement, and the chain held in sequence. One wrinkle stood out: paths running through pressure-driven motivation weakened engagement instead of helping it. Students who study because they feel forced gain less from valuing education. For universities, the finding favors building confidence and genuine interest over piling on pressure.
plos-pone-0350817:
Patrick Schmidt and Klaus G Nickel measured the stones used for tools at Sibhudu Cave in South Africa in 2026 work. Stone Age foragers there switched materials and tool shapes over a long span, and the team asked whether stone quality guided those choices.

Lab tests showed the local stones differ sharply: some flake easily but dull fast, others resist knapping yet stay strong in use. Stones needing less force were retouched more often, and long blades came mostly from stones that break predictably. Resistance to wear seemed to matter less. The pattern suggests skilled makers matched each stone to the job at hand.
plos-pone-0350917:
Sicheng Huang and colleagues at public health departments in China set out in 2026 to design a shared information system for sudden health emergencies. Their case was Zhuhai, a coastal city, and the goal was a framework that could serve city, county, and local street or township offices alike.

Working from published research and expert discussion, the team drafted a set of measures, then asked a panel of experts to judge them through two rounds of voting. The finished city and county version has five main modules, while a simpler version serves the lowest level. Early use pointed to readiness and response as the parts that matter most, giving other Chinese cities a tested model to copy.
plos-pone-0351117:
Heart rehabilitation programs coach patients toward lasting exercise habits, and Clare T M Doherty and colleagues asked participants what the coaching felt like from inside. Their 2026 PLOS One paper reports interviews and group talks nested inside a randomized trial for people with coronary heart disease.

Both coached and uncoached patients named surroundings and social support as key to staying active. The coached group described how sessions were delivered and which parts kept them engaged. Attendance records and personal diaries checked whether the program ran as planned. The findings are meant to help future programs keep patients moving after formal rehab ends.
plos-pone-0351217:
Yongjia Deng and colleagues interviewed twenty patients in a university weight management clinic in West Virginia, a state with very high obesity rates. Guideline based clinics treat obesity as a medical condition, yet joining and staying takes trust. Talks covered why patients came, what helped, and what got in the way of care.

Patients prized kind, non judging staff and wanted more contact between visits. Support held firm even when policy shifts threatened coverage for their treatment, which patients noticed and valued. Personal inner drive brought many through the door. Cost and coverage gaps and social shame still burdened care. More touch points and steady respect, the study suggests, keep patients engaged.
plos-pone-0351417:
Viruses being groomed as cancer killers and vaccine carriers must survive making, shipping, and storage. Sven Göbel and colleagues tested two such viruses, a Newcastle disease strain used against tumors and a chimeric yellow fever and Zika vaccine candidate, in this 2026 PLOS One stability study.

Both viruses shrugged off repeated freezing and thawing with little loss of infectious strength. Warmth was the enemy: above room temperature, infectious counts dropped substantially. Adding sugar as a stabilizer gave limited help. The authors map which steps of production and storage need cold control, practical knowledge for turning lab viruses into medicines that reach patients still potent.
plos-pone-0352017:
Arta Grosmane-Bataraga and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study testing whether two blood proteins can serve as markers for myasthenia gravis, a disease in which the immune system weakens muscles. The proteins are useful in several brain and nerve diseases, so the team measured them in ninety patients and forty healthy volunteers, and compared levels with standard severity scores.

Neither protein differed between patients and controls, and neither tracked with disease severity, past crises, or treatments. The authors conclude plainly that these markers should not be adopted for monitoring this disease, despite their value elsewhere. As one of the larger controlled analyses of its kind, the study helps steer the search for myasthenia-specific blood markers in other directions.
plos-pone-0352117:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors have withdrawn a study that claimed a protein called ISL1 can push human stem cells to become heart muscle cells. Concerns were raised after the work came out. Several figures looked wrong in ways that are hard to explain as honest error.

In one chart, the error bars looked far too even across all time points. In gel images, sharp breaks showed between lanes. Bands in different rows also looked too much alike. The first author answered some points, but trust in the data was gone. Readers should not rely on the study's claims.
plos-pone-0352317:
Sibel Balik and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on growing basil microgreens under LED lights in an indoor vertical farm. Light color recipes shape how these young greens grow and how nutritious they become. The team grew basil under three spectra: red-heavy mixes, a full spectrum, and one adding white and far-red light, then measured growth, color, and a long list of nutrients and flavor compounds.

The recipe with far-red produced the tallest plants, best yield, and brightest color, along with the most phenolic compounds. The full spectrum led on vitamin C, flavonoids, and oil content, while the red-blue mix gave the most dry matter and minerals. The authors recommend the far-red recipe for commercial growers, while noting results may differ by crop variety.
plos-pone-0352417:
Vedran Premuzic and seven colleagues ask whether timing matters for a blood-filtering therapy in severe muscle injury. Their 2026 study covers intensive care patients in Croatia. Crushed or starved muscle releases toxins that can shut down the kidneys. Hemoadsorption scrubs some of those toxins from the blood. Thirty patients received it alongside standard dialysis-style support. Twenty-five comparable patients received the standard support alone.

Within the treated group, starting early made the difference. Patients whose filtering began within twelve hours of kidney injury recovered kidney function better. Blood levels of the muscle toxins myoglobin and creatine kinase were tracked for three days. Follow-up ran to sixty days. Because the study was small and retrospective, it cannot prove cause. Its title-stated association still gives intensive care teams a practical prompt: when this therapy is used, do not delay it.
plos-pone-0353017:
Dane Wattle and co-authors documented the sea-floor life of key reefs in Australia's Groote Archipelago after back-to-back disasters. Mass coral bleaching and a tropical cyclone struck in quick succession, yet no formal benthic baseline existed for these waters. The archipelago's Traditional Owners, the Anindilyakwa people, hold deep sea knowledge but had not recorded reef change in survey form.

The 2026 study filmed reef sites and analysed frame composition to describe what covers the bottom now: coral, algae, rubble, and other benthic classes. Site health assessments accompany the inventory. Wattle and colleagues offer the baseline as shared ground for collaborative management, so future change can be measured against a documented starting point.
plos-pone-0353117:
Bewuketu Terefe, Nebiyu Mekonnen Derseh, and Tadesse Awoke Ayele map where young women across sub-Saharan Africa do and do not test for HIV, in this 2026 PLOS ONE spatial analysis. They pooled recent national survey data covering about one hundred and forty thousand women. Overall, fewer than four in ten had been tested — far short of global targets — and the map was strikingly uneven.

Testing clustered high in eastern and southern Africa and low in the west. Education, employment, media exposure, marriage, pregnancy, and wealth all nudged testing upward, while distance to a clinic dragged it down. The authors argue that blanket campaigns waste resources: the cold spots on the map need targeted outreach first.
plos-pone-0353217:
Ali Aligholizadeh and three colleagues published this 2026 agriculture study of two friendly fungi that live inside plants. Isolated from native plants, the fungi Aspergillus micronesiensis and Penicillium momoi were pitted against three Fusarium strains that rot tomato and grain crops. The team also tested them under salty conditions and built a powder product.

One fungus fought by crowding the pathogens out, the other by chemical attack, and together they curbed growth strongly. Both tolerated salt, and their powder stayed viable for over two years. Aligholizadeh sees dual-purpose helpers for stressed fields.
plos-pone-0353417:
Da Zhang and seven colleagues read the map of Hebei Province in China through its place names, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They catalogued more than eighteen hundred township names and tracked how names drawn from nature and from culture shifted over centuries. The study focuses on the transition belt where the Taihang Mountains meet the Great Wall corridor.

Nature-based names retreated toward the northeast mountains and coast, while culture-based names moved north. During the Ming and Qing dynasties the border belt shifted from military to civilian names. Slope, vegetation, migration, and ethnic mixing emerged as the main drivers — evidence that place names preserve a landscape's history long after events fade.
plos-pone-0354517:
Rebekah Sullivan, Andrew Gardiner, and Glen Cousquer study health care for homeless people in the United Kingdom who live with companion dogs. About one in ten people seeking shelter own an animal, most often a dog, and that bond can block access to housing and clinics. Their 2026 paper uses deep interviews with homeless dog owners and with health, vet, and housing staff.

Both sides described human and animal health as tangled together, not separate problems. Joint clinics at one site drew interest but also raised worries about space and safety. Sullivan and colleagues favor a looser goal: coordinated care across services that respects the pair as a unit. They argue that ignoring the dog often means losing the person too.
plos-pone-0354617:
Souleymane Abdou and Abdoul Moumouni Iro Sodo published this 2026 field study of quick-maturing cowpea in southeastern Niger. Cowpea feeds people and livestock across the Sahel, but drought, poor soils, weeds, and parasites cap yields. Twenty-one varieties were grown in six environments, and several stability methods judged which gave steady grain and fodder harvests wherever planted.

Environment shaped yields most, yet a set of named lines combined earliness with high, steady output of both grain and fodder. Abdou recommends wider testing across farming zones before release as climate-ready varieties for farmers.
plos-pone-0354717:
Saxton and colleagues, in a 2026 national survey study, estimate how a fairer blood donation rule would change who can give blood in New Zealand. Many countries long barred men from donating for a set period after sex with another man. New Zealand has moved to judging each donor's own behavior instead, and the team asked how many men that change would newly include.

More than three thousand men from this community answered an online survey. Most had donated before or wanted to, and most favored the individual approach. Under the old rule, only about one man in eight was eligible. Under the new individual assessment, that share rose to roughly four in ten. Newly eligible men tended to be in their thirties, more educated, and more connected to gay community life. The authors say the policy widens the donor pool safely.
plos-pone-0354817:
Kelly Holloway, Umair Majid, and Quinn Grundy interview Canadian doctors about prescribing immunoglobulin, a costly blood-plasma treatment whose demand keeps rising, in this 2026 qualitative study. Supply is limited worldwide, so doctors sit at the choke point between patients who need the treatment and a system trying to use it wisely. Twelve prescribing clinicians described how they actually make these decisions.

Three broad orientations emerged. Some doctors felt concern and uncertainty about prescribing at all. Others saw themselves as careful stewards of a scarce resource. A third group acted as advocates, pushing for their patients' access. The authors argue that policies built only on applying evidence mechanically miss these human stances, and that understanding them is essential for managing shortages fairly.
plos-pone-0354917:
Vladislav Soukhovolsky and colleagues modelled the flight and numbers of the conifer silk moth, a major forest pest across northern Eurasia. Foresters use light traps to track the moth, but catches are small when populations are low. Their 2026 paper draws on twenty-one years of trap records to build three linked models.

One model predicts when flight starts each season, using accumulated warmth after vegetation greens up in spring. That warmth total stayed stable year to year. A second model shows this year's catch depends mainly on the two previous years, matching known larval patterns. A third handles within-season catch shape. Together the models support forecasting pest numbers from trap data alone.
plos-pone-0355117:
Keji Shan and colleagues test in 2026 whether giving vitamin B12 together with a blue dye drug can ease septic shock in rats. Both agents alone have shown some promise when blood vessels lose tone badly. Rats were pretreated before a bacterial toxin triggered shock, and artery tissue was checked for gene changes alongside blood pressure, organ damage, and stress markers.

Combined treatment lowered several vessel relaxing signals, eased blood pressure problems in part, and reduced inflammation and tissue injury in lung, liver, and kidney. The authors link the benefit to a vessel wall pathway, while noting proof of cause still needs direct testing.
plos-pone-0355217:
Ivaan Pitua and six colleagues published this 2026 protocol, a detailed plan for a review of gout and high uric acid in people living with HIV. Modern HIV treatment has shifted attention toward long-term metabolic problems, and some widely used HIV drugs may raise uric acid. Nobody has yet totaled the worldwide burden.

Pitua's plan covers observational studies of adults, screened and scored by two reviewers working independently. The team will pool rates of high uric acid and gout, then compare results by drug era, region, and immune status. Registering the plan in advance keeps the later review honest and repeatable.
plos-pone-0355417:
Ameen Chaudry led a team of eight authors taking stock of diversity in orthopaedic surgery, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Orthopaedics remains one of the least diverse specialties in medicine. The team examined residency applications to ask where diversity currently stands in the pipeline that feeds the field.

Chaudry's numbers show how far the pipeline has come and how far it still has to go. Application data reveal whether diversity efforts fail at attracting applicants or at selecting among them, two very different problems. A specialty that treats patients of every background benefits when its surgeons reflect that range. Honest stocktaking is the precondition for programs that aim to widen the door.
plos-pone-0355717:
Ruiheng Wu, Houmin Xing, and Jeffrey P Townsend re-analyzed whole genomes from 494 Chinese liver tumors, asking not just which mutations recur but which ones actually give cancer cells an edge. Their 2026 study computed, for every recurrent mutation, a scaled measure of the selective advantage it confers, using each gene's background mutation rate as the neutral yardstick.

The usual giants, including CTNNB1, TP53, and a famous regulatory hotspot, showed intense positive selection. More interestingly, several rare candidates, including genes tied to collagen chemistry and immune signaling, carried outsized effects, while some previously nominated drivers looked no better than neutral passengers. The authors stress the rare finds are computational priorities for laboratory proof, not established drivers.
plos-pone-0356617:
Amina Mouhamed, Jim Al-Khalili, and Marco Sacchi published a 2026 theoretical study in PLOS ONE on a quantum puzzle at the heart of psychiatry's oldest drug. Lithium has steadied bipolar disorder for decades, yet nobody knows exactly how it works. Its two isotopes have different nuclear spins, and some studies hint they act differently in biology. They ask whether lithium's spin could steer a radical pair mechanism, a quantum effect where magnetism changes chemical outcomes, in a pairing of flavin with the vitamin C radical.

Using density functional calculations and spin simulations, they model how lithium's nuclear spin might shift the balance of reaction products from these fleeting radical pairs. The vitamin C radical is a plausible partner because it is plentiful in the brain and long-lived. Whether such spin effects matter in patients is unproven, the authors stress, but the calculations make the idea concrete enough to test.
plos-pone-0356717:
Naohiro Wakisaka and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies oropharyngeal cancer, cancer of the throat behind the mouth, associated with HPV, the human papillomavirus. The authors map where immune programs sit across the tissue compartments of these tumors.

Spatial organization means which immune activities happen in which parts of the tumor tissue. Where immune cells gather, and where they are shut out, shapes how a cancer behaves and responds to treatment. Head and neck cancer researchers and immunotherapy teams are the readers for a map of immune geography inside these tumors.
plos-pone-0356817:
Hui Zhang and Pengpeng Cai study silicon etching in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on predicting etched shapes. Wet etching carves silicon at rates that depend on crystal direction, a trait used to build tiny machines and through-silicon holes. Mask shape and conditions make the three-dimensional result hard to predict and control.

Using measured etch rates for a few crystal planes, the authors filled in rates for all planes and built a simulation based on the level set method, which tracks a moving surface. Tests under window, mesa, and double-sided masks matched real etched profiles well. The approach also adapts to other etch systems and to crystals such as quartz.
plos-pone-0356917:
Marika A. de Hoop-Sommen and coauthors published a 2026 modeling study in PLOS ONE supporting guidelines for a delicate switch in children's intensive care. A child is moved from continuous morphine or fentanyl to methadone, then tapered away to prevent withdrawal. Clinicians lack agreed conversion ratios and taper speeds. The team built physiology-based models of how children's bodies handle all three drugs, checked them against published data, and simulated many plans.

The simulations pointed to clear working ratios: a fentanyl-to-methadone ratio of one to ten and a morphine ratio of one to one kept methadone in the therapeutic range. Most published tapering schedules peaked at similar methadone levels, except the gentlest low-risk schedules of two protocols. An expert panel of pediatric intensivists and pharmacists turned the results into recommendations. The models support, rather than replace, bedside judgment.
plos-pone-0357017:
Jung Ah Lim and colleagues argue that the standard yardstick for low muscle mass in older adults quietly measures fat as well. They propose a fix using Korean national survey data. Their 2026 study analyzed body scans from more than three thousand adults over sixty-five. It compared muscle indexed to height squared against a ratio. The ratio sets muscle in the arms and legs against muscle in the trunk.

The height-based index rose with body fat. Paradoxically, people it flagged as low-muscle had less metabolic syndrome. The trunk-relative ratio behaved oppositely. It fell as fat rose, flagged genuinely higher metabolic risk, and tracked insulin resistance even after fat was accounted for. The authors suggest the ratio gives doctors a cleaner read on muscle depletion in aging patients.
plos-pone-0357117:
Philipp Naß and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for PRIMA, a German project turning ordinary GP practices into multiprofessional care centers. Germany's primary care is strained by aging patients, chronic disease, and workforce shortages. The model adds specially trained nurses to practice teams. It gives them extended duties and reorganizes who does what inside the practice. Triage software can be added, and chronically ill high-risk patients are the focus.

The evaluation compares patients in twenty intervention practices against matched controls from routine insurance claims, over twelve months. The main measure is how many emergencies occur that good ambulatory care should have prevented. Healthcare use, deaths, continuity, and costs are also tracked. A parallel study follows how the change actually unfolds in daily work. The aim is to show whether nurse-integrated practices deliver better, more productive care, evidence German health policy lacks.
plos-pone-0357917:
Hui G. Cheng and coauthors published a 2026 longitudinal study in PLOS ONE following Americans through a cancer diagnosis to map how health, habits, and finances change together. Using fifteen waves of a national retirement study spanning three decades, they identified several thousand newly diagnosed people, matched each to similar cancer-free controls, and aligned timelines to the diagnosis year.

Diagnosis hit like a step down: self-rated health dropped sharply and functional limits jumped, with only partial recovery afterward. Depressive symptoms spiked and stayed elevated for years, and physical activity stayed suppressed even longer. Some changes were welcome: smoking fell at diagnosis and stayed lower, while weight and drinking shifts faded. Work and money suffered too: employment dropped and out-of-pocket spending jumped by over two thousand dollars a year. Survivorship care, they say, should plan for this whole bundle, not just the tumor.
plos-pone-0359217: Diniz and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on field research at Fiocruz, Brazil's noted public health institute. They used the ideas of sociologist Pierre Bourdieu to weigh the challenges and chances in clinical field work. Field studies meet real life: transport, trust, and local politics shape results. Lessons from a century-old institute can guide research teams elsewhere.
plos-pone-0359317:
Yong-Han Cha, Jung-Taek Kim, Jin-Woo Kim, Hyun-Bin Kim, and Jun-Il Yoo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It uses artificial intelligence to profile thigh muscle volume on CT scans. The patients are elderly East Asian people who have suffered a hip fracture.

Muscle volume around the thigh matters because weak muscles slow recovery after hip surgery and raise the risk of further falls. Measuring that volume by hand on scans is slow, so an AI tool that profiles it automatically could enter routine care. Orthopedic teams treating hip fractures in aging populations are the natural readers.
plos-pone-0359417: Liu and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how well mumps vaccines protect children in Taizhou, China. The study covered children under fifteen and used real-world records, not a trial. Each sick child was matched with two similar healthy children for comparison. Real-world checks matter because protection in daily life can fall short of trial results, and gaps guide booster policy.
plos-pone-0359517: Sterling and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on an invasive fish in the Upper Mississippi River. Silver carp, brought from Asia, now crowd parts of the river system. The team described the population's makeup: ages, sizes, and growth. Such basic facts about numbers and age shape how managers try to slow the carp's spread and protect native fish.
plos-pone-0359717:
Ana Tsutsunava and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It associates genomic variants of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the TB bacterium, with minimum inhibitory concentrations for two newer TB drugs, delamanid and pretomanid. That concentration is the lowest drug level that stops the bacterium growing.

If gene patterns predict drug potency, laboratories could flag weak drug-bug matches from sequence alone, faster than growing cultures. Both drugs are vital for drug-resistant TB, where every effective medicine counts. TB reference labs and treatment programs are the readers for a genotype-to-potency link.
pmc-13122017:
Yasmin Ibrahim is first author on a 2026 perspective article asking why hepatitis B stays underprioritized in global health. Nearly two hundred and fifty-nine million people live with chronic hepatitis B, yet only a small fraction receive life-saving treatment, and the virus caused most viral hepatitis deaths in twenty twenty-two. Vaccines, tests, and treatments already exist.

Through personal stories of people living with the virus worldwide, the article traces roadblocks including stigma, discrimination, and weak funding. It draws lessons from HIV, COVID-19, and Ebola, where advocacy and sustained money drove progress. The authors call for greater investment, joined-up programs, and patient-reported outcomes in hepatitis B care.
pmc-13191817:
The European Food Safety Authority, EFSA, issued a 2026 scientific opinion on residue limits for the pesticide acequinocyl in berries. A company branch had applied through Germany to modify maximum residue levels, the legal caps on pesticide remains, for cane fruits and other small fruits and berries. EFSA assessed the supporting data under European rules.

The data sufficed to propose new limits, and lab methods can enforce them at a very low detection level. Trials also checked carry-over into honey and found no change needed to the current honey limit, though those trials used higher doses than intended practice, making the judgment conservative. Short- and long-term consumer intake from the proposed uses was judged unlikely to risk health.
pmc-13197317:
Malin Ramne and Eva Lendaro report a 2026 brain wave study of phantom limb pain. Phantom pain is pain felt in a limb that has been removed. Chronic pain often links to stronger slow brain waves at rest, so the team tested whether that pattern holds here.

They recorded dense scalp signals at rest in nineteen controls, six amputees without pain, and thirteen with pain. The study plan was logged before data work began. Across main and check analyses, no firm link tied pain to slow wave power or to peak rhythm speed. Some shifts tied to limb loss itself, not pain. Findings shifted with the measure used, so the authors urge caution.
pmc-13197617:
Döndü Ülker Üstebay and colleagues offer a 2026 case report on a rare inherited disorder with no diabetes so far. Faults in the TRMT10A gene can cause small head size, learning disability, seizures, and short stature. Blood sugar problems often join that list, but not in this patient.

Their patient was a fifteen-year-old boy with those core traits from early childhood. Brain scans were normal, yet brain wave tests showed seizure-like activity needing treatment. Gene sequencing found a harmful variant in both copies of the gene, matching recessive inheritance, where two faulty copies are needed. Early diagnosis lets doctors watch for diabetes and act fast if it starts. Long follow-up is vital.
pmc-13198717:
Omar Taher and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a child's bowel blockage with two causes. A Meckel diverticulum is a pouch on the small bowel left from before birth. In this boy it twisted the bowel, then a second blockage followed surgery.

The eight-year-old had a week of belly pain and vomiting. Scans showed a blocked small bowel with a swirl sign. Keyhole surgery found the dead pouch and twisted bowel, and surgeons removed that bowel segment. After brief recovery, swelling and bile vomiting returned. A second keyhole operation found a single tissue band near the join and freed it. The lesson: early focal blockage after surgery may need prompt re-check by scope.
pmc-13200417:
Chiara Robin Bojarzyn and colleagues studied flu virus growth when cell sugar use is blocked in a 2026 paper. Influenza A virus leans hard on host cell metabolism to copy itself. Blocking glycolysis, the cell's sugar-burning path, curbs the virus, but a TCA cycle fuel called oxaloacetate might rescue it.

Infected cells with blocked sugar burning made far fewer viruses. Adding oxaloacetate reversed that drop, restoring viral proteins, genomes, and titers. The sugar mannose rescued growth to a like degree. Chemical profiling showed pyruvate, a sugar-burning product, piled up with oxaloacetate added. Direct pyruvate rescued almost as well. The virus taps this backup fuel axis when its main path fails.
pmc-13217217:
Elbeltagi and colleagues systematically review whether ultrasound stiffness scans of the liver can flag insulin resistance in children. Insulin resistance sits at the root of fatty liver disease linked to metabolism. Liver elastography, which measures stiffness with sound waves, is painless and quick, and clinics use it more and more in children.

The open question is how well stiffness readings match standard blood-based signs of insulin resistance. The review gathers the scattered studies and weighs their agreement. A clear answer would matter. A scan that truly mirrors insulin resistance could spare children repeated blood draws. It could also catch metabolic trouble earlier. A weak link, instead, would warn doctors not to over-read stiffness numbers.
pmc-13237017:
Abdelmohsen, Wassif, and Ramadan build a shopping recommender that watches for fake reviews. Online shops lean on reviews to rank products, yet deceptive reviews warp what buyers see. Fake-spotting tools and recommenders have mostly been built apart, so a sly fake can still train the system that ranks for everyone.

Their system feeds a language model's estimate that a review is deceptive straight into the training of a neural recommender. Reviews judged likely fake then count for less as the model learns tastes. The goal is a ranking shoppers can trust more, tested on whether real users still get suggestions that fit them.
pmc-13241417:
Addario and colleagues at Maastricht printed a chip built to grow blood vessels into lab-made kidney organoids. Kidney organoids from human stem cells mature poorly without a blood supply. The chip was printed by extruding a sacrificial gel that later melted away. Two channels and three gel compartments resulted.

Endothelial cells lined the channels first, then organoids joined them in a tissue-derived gel. Five days of co-culture ran under gentle flow. Capillary-like sprouts grew toward and through the organoids, reaching their centers. The sprouts overlapped with early kidney markers, suggesting genuine integration.
pmc-13241517:
Yao's team at Zhejiang use deep learning to speed up the design of tiny hemispherical resonators. These devices serve in fine gyroscopes, and their quality factor is limited partly by thermoelastic losses. Modeling those losses the standard way is accurate but painfully slow. The team trained a hybrid network to predict the losses straight from shape.

Their model joins a pattern network with a transformer, fed extra training data fitted from sim results. Swapping part of the network for a second attention stage gave the best scores. Dropout checks showed the error bars were well set. Shape analysis favored squat shells with small anchor radius and thick walls for the highest quality factor.
pmc-13242517:
Theresa Waclawek and co-authors followed couples for ten days to test whether mindfulness shows up as compassion at home. Their preregistered diary study appeared in Communications Psychology in 2026. It enrolled 230 adults in long-term heterosexual relationships, including 114 couples where both partners took part. Each evening, participants reported their own mindfulness and rated their partner's compassion, giving the study an outside view of kindness.

On days when a person felt more accepting and mindful than usual, their partner rated them as more compassionate that same day. People with steadier mindful attention were also seen as kinder overall. Much of the link ran through self-absorption: mindfulness lowered it, and lower self-absorption freed up compassion. The authors say inner attention training can have visible social effects in daily life. Partner ratings, they note, keep the findings honest beyond self-report.
pmc-13243917:
E. Wohlfarth and colleagues updated a head-to-head lab comparison of five modern antibiotics against drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Their study appeared in JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance in 2026. The panel covered 401 clinical isolates collected in Germany in 2019 and 2020. Cefiderocol, a drug that smuggles itself into bacteria through their iron gates, faced four rival combination drugs, with resistance genes checked by sequencing.

Cefiderocol held up best. Against Pseudomonas, its resistance rate sat under two percent, while the rivals failed against a fifth to two-fifths of isolates. Against two other problem germs, the dose needed to stop growth was many times lower than for every rival. A commercial test kit for the drug was also checked against the reference method. The authors conclude that cefiderocol's activity against these problem pathogens exceeds the combinations tested. For hospitals facing the toughest resistant infections, that margin matters.
pmc-13244517:
Xueting Li and colleagues asked whether the amount of protein leaking into urine predicts how kidney patients respond to rituximab. Their study appeared in Annals of Medicine in 2026. All 123 participants had PLA2R-associated membranous nephropathy, an autoimmune kidney disease, confirmed by biopsy or antibody testing. The team split them by starting proteinuria, four to six grams a day versus above six, and followed remission for a year.

The lower-protein group responded faster and more completely at nearly every checkpoint. Partial remissions came earlier, and complete remissions were significantly more common by nine and twelve months. At the extreme, patients spilling more than twelve grams a day remitted least of all. The gradient suggests waiting until proteinuria soars may squander the drug's best window. The authors propose baseline proteinuria as a guide for when to start rituximab. Timing, in their data, is a treatment variable.
pmc-13246017:
Moon, Blumenschein, and Swetz measured broken ankles to guide screw placement, in this 2026 OTA International study. Some shinbone fractures come with a separate small break at the back of the ankle joint, often fixed with screws through the skin. Using CT scans from a trauma center, the team worked out the angle a screw should take to cross that back fragment squarely and hit its center.

They found the fragments in about half of the shaft fractures they reviewed. One standard angle and starting point would land the screw well in only about half of cases in one plane, though it did better in the other. Their conclusion is practical: surgeons should template each patient's screw path from the scan first.
pmc-13246817:
Merabtine, Sognigbe, Marcellaud, and co-authors interviewed digestive cancer patients in Benin about their routes through care, in this 2026 Supportive Care in Cancer study. At the national university hospital in Cotonou, the team conducted in-depth interviews with eleven patients who had used complementary or alternative medicine alongside, or instead of, conventional treatment.

Patients described long delays: symptoms first minimized, rounds of inconclusive consultations, and low awareness of digestive cancers, compounded by money problems and scarce medicines. Alternative medicine appealed for cost reasons, frustration with conventional care, relief of side effects, and a search for well-being. Patients asked for holistic care with nutrition and psychosocial support, and wanted doctors involved in supervising alternative treatments rather than ignoring them.
pmc-13247517:
Suenaga and co-authors report an immunologically puzzling diabetes case in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. A thirty-nine-year-old Japanese woman had lived fourteen years with stiff-person syndrome, an autoimmune nerve disorder often paired with type 1 diabetes. She arrived in diabetic ketoacidosis and was found to have autoimmune diabetes destroying her insulin-producing cells at speed. This happened despite long-term immune-suppressing treatment, and despite carrying a gene pattern thought to protect against the disease.

All three major islet autoantibodies were positive, and her remaining insulin output collapsed within thirteen months. Her HLA typing mixed a susceptibility pattern with a protective one and lacked the allele most tied to the syndrome in European patients. The authors say stiff-person autoimmunity can overwhelm genetic protection, with profiles differing across populations.
pmc-13249917:
Stich, Van Inghelandt, and Wu review computer simulation as a plant breeder's rehearsal room, in a 2026 Theoretical and Applied Genetics article. Breeding programs run for years and consume fields, seed, and labor, so every design choice is expensive to test live. Simulations let breeders compare crossing and selection schemes virtually, and check the statistical behavior of new methods before trusting them.

The authors survey every publicly available simulation tool they could find, spelling out what each assumes and where each falls short. Two uses get the deepest treatment: optimizing whole breeding programs, and validating new statistical procedures. They also touch on crop growth models and genotype-by-environment interplay as growing frontiers for the simulators.
pmc-13250217:
Broomand and colleagues grade infection prevention work across hospitals supported by Médecins Sans Frontières. Their 2026 BMJ Global Health study uses a stepwise assessment tool applied in one hundred seventy-three facilities between 2021 and 2023. Clean care is hard to guarantee in low-resource and humanitarian settings, where infections can spread fast.

Across nearly four hundred assessments, the median score sat at an upper-intermediate level of practice. Having a formal infection program and keeping bed occupancy below ninety percent best predicted strong scores. Repeat assessments brought the biggest gains to facilities that started weakest, while top performers barely improved. Weak tracking of surgical site infections stood out as a key gap for future work.
pmc-13253717:

The shift ran through retinoic acid signals, which grew stronger without DGAT1. The authors call DGAT1 a context-based regulator, meaning its effect depends on skin state.
pmc-13254017:
Hongye Li and colleagues review dandelion compounds that may protect the brain in a 2026 paper. The review covers their chemical structures, brain effects, and how structure shapes activity, plus uses in food and medicine.

These compounds seem to guard nerve cells by calming swelling, cutting oxidative stress, and blocking cell damage. The core skeleton of each compound sets its main activity, while small groups, like added oxygens or sugars, fine-tune it. The authors aim to support wider use of this non-toxic plant.
pmc-13254217:
Hao Luo and co-authors build a risk model for older heart failure patients in a 2026 study. The vulnerable phase after hospital care brings frequent readmission and death. The team trained 18 machine learning models with six algorithms and used SHAP, a method that shows how each factor shapes a prediction.

The top five factors were hemoglobin, a thyroid hormone measure, age, diabetes, and blood potassium. The authors stress the model's clear reasoning as a strength.
pmc-13254817:

pmc-13255017:
Mehmet Burak Mutlu and a large team test a genome mapping tool in autism in a 2026 study. Optical genome mapping can spot large structural changes that standard tests may miss. The team reviewed 34 people with autism, most also having developmental delay or added syndromic features.

All positive cases had complex autism with added features. The authors say the method adds value for selected patients in combined testing workflows.
pmc-13256117:

Searching four databases through August 2025, they found eleven cross-sectional studies, nine from South Korea, and graded their quality with a standard scale. Most studies were rated high quality.

The link followed a dose-response pattern, with high-risk users carrying the greatest odds, and attempts were also elevated in high-risk groups. pmc-13257117:
Neuhaus and colleagues reviewed two hundred eighty-seven oral cavity cancer patients treated at one center to map how tumors spread to neck lymph nodes. Treating six patients on the tumor side prevented one missed cancer, versus seventy-four on the opposite side. Staging scans missed often enough to matter, with modest predictive values. pmc-13258017:
Zushun Zhang and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of what limits audiences' experience of ancient Chinese poetry performed as music. Their test case was three creative concerts based on Wei's Music Score, a set of old music scores. Using ideas from leisure and tourism research on constraints, the team built a scale for the limits on poetry experience. They then surveyed concert audiences and analyzed the answers with a statistical modeling method.

The limits fell into three groups: personal constraints, constraints between people, and structural constraints, such as setting and access. The results supported a pathway in which personal constraints shape preference, preference shapes participation, and structural constraints also shape participation directly. The authors say the model can help spread traditional Chinese music at home and abroad.
pmc-13258117:
Nürettin Akçakale and co-authors review how tiny defects can make magnesium alloys both stronger and more workable. Magnesium is light, but its alloys usually force a trade-off between strength and ductility. Their 2026 critical review surveys defect engineering as a way around that compromise.

Four defect families anchor the discussion: nanograins, nanoprecipitates, nanotwins, and stacking faults. Each blocks or redirects the dislocations whose motion deforms metal, and together they can reinforce one another. Severe plastic deformation is one route to the fine grains involved. The authors argue that designing defect structures deliberately can yield tunable, next-generation alloys.
pmc-13259217:
Chengkun Liu and co-authors ask how many pressure sensors a giant water pipeline really needs. A trunk line in northeast China runs one hundred twenty-two kilometers with sensors placed by habit, many redundant. Using thousands of hourly snapshots, their 2026 study benchmarks four selection strategies against random picking.

Fifteen well-chosen sensors rebuilt nearly the whole pressure field, cutting the cleaned network by three-quarters. A hybrid method that also spreads sensors out guarded worst-case gaps far better for almost no accuracy cost. Reaching the strictest accuracy bar took more sensors under every strategy. The catch, they note, is covering all operating regimes during training.
pmc-13259617:
Sufen Cheng and co-authors review how one signaling axis teaches cancer cells to gorge on glucose. The PI3K/AKT pathway sits at the center of growth control and is often jammed on in tumors. Their 2026 review maps its grip on sugar metabolism step by step.

The pathway directs core enzymes of glycolysis, from hexokinase to lactate dehydrogenase, including some moonlighting jobs those enzymes secretly perform. It also negotiates with the cell's energy sensor and with fat-building and phosphate pathways. Blocking the axis to starve tumors is promising but tricky, the authors show. They close with combination therapy ideas and the hurdles ahead.
pmc-13260417:
Ashley C Parr leads a 2026 longitudinal study of brain development and substance use in young people. The team followed 802 participants aged twelve to thirty in a national cohort, across 6,078 visits. They measured tissue iron in the basal ganglia, deep brain structures tied to the reward chemical dopamine, alongside impulsivity and inhibitory control, meaning the ability to stop an impulse. Statistical modeling sorted participants into patterns of substance use over time.

Four trajectories emerged: no or low use at thirty percent, youth peak at twenty-six percent, adolescent increasing at seventeen percent, and adult increasing at twenty-six percent. Heavier use was associated with higher impulsivity, lower inhibitory control, and lower tissue iron, most clearly in early adolescence. The authors call adolescence a sensitive window for identifying risk and targeting prevention.
pmc-13260917:
Abdul-Rahman K Osman and co-authors present a 2026 study of how projectiles penetrate sandy soil at low impact speeds. Free-fall drop tests drove conical-headed projectiles of varied tip angles and masses into packed sand of differing density. Computer models, checked against the tests, extended the range to other friction angles, drop heights, widths, nose shapes, and impact angles. The team also examined crater shaping, acceleration, energy uptake, and stress in the soil.

Entry depth fell as sand density, friction angle, shot diameter, and tip angle rose. It increased with shot mass, drop height, and impact angle. Crater width grew mainly with drop height and shot diameter, and was fairly insensitive to friction angle. The authors built scale-free correlations and sensitivity checks to rank which factors govern entry and cratering under the tested conditions.
pmc-13261017:
Mohamed Barakat and co-authors present a 2026 engineering study of load frequency control in interconnected power systems. Keeping grid frequency stable after sudden load changes is a core challenge. The authors introduce a new controller design that replaces the proportional term of standard controllers with a second fractional integrator, giving twenty-seven possible configurations. A new optimization method, the cuckoo catfish optimizer, tunes its parameters, using strategies meant to avoid getting stuck at poor solutions.

The framework was validated on a two-area benchmark system and a three-area thermal and hydro system under one and two percent step load disturbances. Against five state-of-the-art controllers, the new design consistently gave faster settling times and reduced overshoot. Its error score, called ITAE, was 74.26, beating the best competitor's 82.67. The authors call it a simple yet powerful option for modern frequency control.
pmc-13261317:
Takafumi Kinoshita and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of motoric cognitive risk syndrome in community-dwelling older adults. The syndrome combines subjective cognitive decline, meaning self-reported worsening memory, with slow walking speed. It is studied as an early warning sign of dementia.

The analysis included 138 participants: 41 (29.7%) were healthy, 82 (59.4%) had subjective cognitive decline alone, and 15 (10.9%) had the full syndrome. In adjusted models, a standard health-check questionnaire score was significantly associated with both the syndrome and decline alone. The syndrome was strongly associated with physical frailty, with an odds ratio of 19.495. Neither condition was significantly associated with social frailty, and decline alone linked to neither frailty type. The authors suggest both measures could help detect early health deterioration in older adults.
pmc-13262317:
Mohammad Abbasi Teshnizi and colleagues present a five-patient case series, published in 2026, on a less invasive heart valve operation. All five had earlier repair for Tetralogy of Fallot, a birth defect of the heart, and later developed a leaking lung valve and a swollen right heart chamber. The new operation used a small cut at the front left of the chest.

All operations used a heart-lung machine through leg vessels, kept the heart beating, and fitted stented tissue valves. Bypass time averaged 37.8 minutes, and no patient needed conversion to a full chest opening. Breathing tubes came out after a mean 9.6 hours, and hospital stay averaged 6.8 days. At two months, valves worked well and right chambers had shrunk.
pmc-13263217:
Kader Can, Ayşem Üzer, and Reşat Apak develop a dual-readout test for two explosives in a 2026 journal article. Tetryl and NTO are energetic compounds that can appear alongside TNT in munitions, and telling them apart selectively is hard. Their method uses a copper oxide nanomaterial to drive a Fenton-like reaction, a chemical attack that frees nitrite from each explosive in a distinct way.

The freed nitrite then forms a pink dye through a classic color reaction, readable by a lab instrument or a smartphone app. Detection limits were lower by instrument than by phone for both compounds. The authors note their route is the first reported to selectively detect both tetryl and NTO, especially in TNT-containing munitions.
pmc-13264617:
Fabian A Boetzl led a 2026 field study asking how much crop fields add to wildlife in farm landscapes, next to permanent grasslands. Most plans treat grassland as the hero and crops as a loss. The team compared both habitats across five European countries for plants, butterflies, wild bees, and ground beetles.

They surveyed 86 paired grasslands and oilseed rape fields. Habitat type mattered more than the amount of grassland around a site. Plants and butterflies were richer in grasslands, while bees and ground beetles matched or beat grassland levels in the crop fields. Each habitat held its own set of species. The authors say saving farm wildlife needs friendly care of crop fields too, not just protection of grassland.
pmc-13264817:
Nita Perumal and colleagues published a 2026 cohort study from Germany on whether a seasonal mRNA COVID-19 vaccine dose guards against post COVID-19 condition, the long-lasting symptoms some people keep after infection. Older estimates came from the pandemic years, so post-pandemic data were needed. The study covered adults aged 60 and over.

Using nationwide outpatient claims, the team followed more than 19 million people in the 2023 to 2024 season. About 18 percent took one dose, and 0.2 percent overall met the long COVID case rule. The rate was 0.08 percent in vaccinated people against 0.22 percent in others. After adjustment, one dose linked to 63 percent lower risk over six months. The authors say the result supports vaccination choices for older adults.
pmc-13265017:
Zhongyuan Lin and colleagues published a 2026 gene study on belly pain in irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease, before and after a mind-body program based on the relaxation response. Pain is a hallmark of both conditions and ruins quality of life. Past work showed the program eased pain, so the team hunted blood gene changes tied to pain.

They reanalyzed public gene data from 14 bowel syndrome and 19 bowel disease patients across nine weeks of the program. After the program, hundreds of genes shifted in each group, and network analysis picked candidate pain genes, with one gene, FKBP5, appearing in both lists. At baseline, a separate gene set separated the two conditions. Pathways touched nerve growth, immune signaling, and calcium signaling. The authors stress the findings are exploratory and need proof in fresh groups.
pmc-13267017:
Arnarak Patricia Bloch and two colleagues report a 2026 pilot study on recovery after suicidal crisis in Greenland. Greenland has a very high suicide burden, yet little is known about what helps Inuit people heal. Six people who had attempted suicide as children, teens, or young adults gave interviews in their own language.

Recovery was described not as a private trait but as a shared, cultural process. Supportive relationships, ties to land and nature, and a sense of belonging helped people cope. Inuit ideas such as Sila and Inua, tied to weather, spirit, and inner life, supported meaning and hope. Services in people's own language also mattered. The authors urge prevention built on these strengths.
pmc-13267517:
Alina Marie Schmitz and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of a magnesium alloy for bones that fail to heal. Such nonunion breaks lack both bone growth and blood supply. The alloy, called WE43, slowly breaks down in the body and may spur bone and vessel growth. The team tested it in a standard thigh-bone nonunion model in mice.

The authors say the alloy needs graft support to work.
pmc-13267617:
Brandi N Reeves and a large team report 2026 results from the EXCEED-ET trial of an interferon drug in a blood disorder. Responses came fast, at a median of about eight weeks. Spleen and symptom measures improved for most patients. Gene-level responses appeared across all three driver mutations. Side effects were mostly mild, led by tiredness and brief liver enzyme rises.
pmc-13267817:

The combined score kept its predictive value across several statistical methods, including machine learning checks. It beat chance by a clear margin on accuracy measures. The authors say the cheap blood-based score could guide risk grouping, but it needs testing in new patient groups first.
pmc-13269317:
Zachary Cofran, Shawn Hurst, and John Hawks published a journal article in 2026 on the brain of Homo naledi, a small-brained extinct human relative. pmc-13269617:

pmc-13270217:

pmc-13270417:

pmc-13272217:

pmc-13272617:

pmc-13273217:

A preceding diagnosis of pyelonephritis, a kidney infection, linked to lower mortality, a finding highlighted by the authors. pmc-13273417:

pmc-13274817:
Huazhang Liu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on robot-assisted repair of complicated duplex kidneys in children. pmc-13276217:

pmc-13276317:

pmc-13276417:

pmc-13278017:

pmc-13278617:

pmc-13279017:

pmc-13280117:

pmc-13281317:
Harutoyo Hirano and colleagues built a math tool to predict blood strength at the start of heart bypass in a 2026 study. Its guesses were off by a hair on average, with a tighter spread of error. The authors say such tools could help surgical teams set the blood mix with more care. They note the tool was built on one hospital's records and needs wider tests.
pmc-13281617:

pmc-13281817:

The authors built it to sort true starvation cases from look-alikes. They tested it against standard reads to check both accuracy and clarity. They argue that shown reasoning is key to earning doctors' trust.
pmc-13282117:
Koichi Hashikawa and co-authors present a 2026 study on how mating behaviour develops in adolescent mice. The work centres on the medial preoptic area. pmc-13282217:

pmc-13282417:

pmc-13283017:
Joshua Nmezi authored a 2026 editorial on moral choices in end-of-life care. The piece views dying through both pain medicine and mental health lenses. It argues that deep distress near death is a distinct health problem called existential suffering.

Topics include stopping life support, do-not-resuscitate orders, food and fluids by tube, and deep sedation. Requests for assisted dying are also addressed in the piece. Four core values guide the analysis: choice, benefit, avoiding harm, and fairness. Roles for the pain doctor and the mental health expert are spelled out. Nigerian and African family-based decision styles get focused attention and sample scripts.
pmc-13283217:
A pressure-sensing channel guards myelin on thin optic nerve fibers, Julia Dyckow-Schubart's mouse work shows in 2026. The channel is Piezo2, best known for touch and pain in skin nerves. Its role in the brain and spinal cord was much less clear.

Gene tests found Piezo2 in mature myelin cells of the mouse optic nerve. Mice lacking Piezo2 in those cells grew clumsy with age in movement tests. Myelin packing broke down in thin optic nerve fibers in those mice. Gene shifts pointed to roles in myelin packing and white matter health. Human optic nerve lesions in multiple sclerosis also showed low PIEZO2 levels. Thin fibers may share this weak point.
pmc-13283617:
Drug switches after starting eye injections raise costs and delays, Sean T Berkowitz's registry team quantifies for 2026. Patients often start on bevacizumab, then switch to copy or branded drugs. Switches can delay care and raise costs for patients and clinics.

Records from the IRIS Registry covered treated eyes from 2015 to 2024. A total of 182,757 eyes met the study rules for inclusion here. Most eyes stayed on bevacizumab alone for their whole course. Smaller groups switched to a biosimilar, a branded drug, or both in sequence. Newer branded drugs added extra delay days versus the standard branded option. Double switches cost notably more than single switches.
pmc-13284017:
A health app for village health workers in India raised knowledge scores in a 2026 evaluation by Archana Patel and colleagues. The workers, called ASHAs, bridge rural families and public clinics. The M-SAKHI app supports live data capture and face-to-face counselling.

Tests before and after training covered 150 workers in the intervention arm. Poor knowledge scores fell by a large share after app training. Good scores rose from a small base to nearly a fifth of workers. Skill checks spanned meetings, server logs, phone skills, spot checks, and field visits. Only a fifth showed poor skills, and data misuse stayed uncommon.
pmc-13285417:
One year into the United States food and drug agency plan to cut animal testing, Yiting Lei, Rocky S. Tuan, and Zhong Alan Li weigh progress in a 2026 commentary. The 2025 roadmap bets on human-based tools such as organoids, organs on chips, computer models, and AI to judge drug safety. Animal tests draw fire for weak forecasts, high cost, and ethics.

The authors hail steps such as a standing new-methods program and shared validation rules, plus smoother paths for biologic drugs. Snags remain: uneven proof across harm types, patchy data sharing between countries, and habits that resist change. They propose clear steps to speed safe uptake in drug growth work.
pmc-13285817:
Ning Xu and co-authors present a 2026 computer method for outlining organs and lesions in medical scans. Transformer models read a whole image well but often blur fine edges and waste effort on empty background. Their hybrid design adds local detail modules and prunes away background tokens that carry no useful signal.

Tests ran on two public scan sets and one large private set of adrenal nodule images. Scores for overlap with expert outlines reached strong levels on both public sets, beating the balance the team sought between sharp borders and full context. The private set, a harder test, also gave solid results that held up well. The sparse design offers a practical path for tools that must trace complex targets in daily clinical work.
pmc-13285917:
Wen-Rui Tang and Ke Qian Chen offer a 2026 mini-review of allicin, the sharp compound in garlic, as a brain-protecting agent. Brain disorders from Alzheimer's disease to stroke share drivers such as cell stress, swelling, and cell death. The review gathers work on how allicin is made, measured, and delivered, and what it has done in lab models of those disorders.

Across animal studies, allicin curbed oxidative stress and inflammation, guarded cell power plants, and kept the blood-brain barrier tighter. Gains appeared in models of memory loss, Parkinson's disease, head injury, and several forms of stroke and bleeding. Two flaws hold the field back: the compound breaks down fast and reaches the body poorly in raw form. The authors press for proper human trials and new carriers that keep allicin stable and on target.
pmc-13286017:
Yuan Lin and colleagues report long-term results for a cornea transplant variant in a 2026 retrospective study with a learning model. The surgery swaps the cornea's failed inner layer while leaving the patient's own middle membrane in place, which suits eyes too fragile for the standard strip-first method. The team tracked sight, cell counts, and graft failure across years of follow-up.

The series held 114 eyes with worn-out corneal lining, followed for a median of about three and a half years. Vision improved by six months and then held steady through the later checks. Cell loss ran lower in Fuchs disease than in other causes, and grafts cut with a laser kept their cells better over time. A smart model sorted risk of graft failure well at one, two, and three years, though the authors want outside proof before clinics lean on it.
pmc-13286117:
Kaiki Oya, Jun Maki, and Midoriko Higashi report a seizure caught live during heart surgery in a 2026 case report. Tranexamic acid, a drug that slows bleeding, can trigger seizures after heart-lung bypass, but sedation and muscle relaxants usually hide the signs until hours later. A 44-year-old man received a second large dose right after bypass ended, and monitors told the story in real time.
