Thirteen minutes after bypass, open convulsions shook the patient for about a minute before calming drugs stopped them. Brain monitor readings had gone silent minutes earlier, and blood oxygen in his central vein dropped sharply during the fit, then both recovered. Later brain scans and tracings came back clean, and he woke and left the breathing tube without new problems. The team argues that pairing brain and oxygen monitors can catch such hidden seizures at once.
pmc-13286517:
Jian Wu and colleagues hunt for warning signs of slow wrist access in brain artery procedures in a 2026 retrospective study. Threading catheters from the wrist to the brain suits patients well, but building the route sometimes drags. Records of 277 successful cases at a Xiamen hospital were split by whether access took over fifteen minutes, then compared across body and vessel traits.

Seventy-eight cases landed in the difficult group. Hard needle entry at the wrist independently predicted trouble, as did failure to shape a standard catheter curve on the first routine try. Twisted neck and chest vessels, a sharp bend where the target artery branches off, and a winding neck artery segment each added their own risk. Common conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes, notably, did not separate the groups, pointing planners toward anatomy over diagnoses.
pmc-13287217:
Marius Pohl and co-authors reported in 2026 that African carpenter ants long treated as one kind, Camponotus maculatus, split into two groups that look alike yet differ sharply in body chemistry. The team combined scent profile testing, behaviour trials, and genetic barcoding to check whether the split is real.

Workers attacked ants carrying the other scent profile and behaved peacefully toward ants sharing their own, whatever colony they came from. Genetic clusters mostly matched the two chemical groups. The authors argue that chemical difference, rather than appearance, marks an early stage of separation in these social insects and should guide how such hidden groups are classified.
pmc-13287417:
Jiajun Xie, Huina Zhang, and Juan Ye report in 2026 a woman in her seventies whose drooping eyelid was first blamed on a stretched eyelid tendon. A brain scan also found an unrelated artery bulge. Surgery lifted the lid at once, which seemed to settle the matter.

Within a week the droop returned and varied across the day. Muscle electrical testing pointed to a junction problem between nerve and muscle. Blood tests found antibodies confirming eye-limited myasthenia gravis. A standard tablet treatment brought clear improvement. The authors warn that strong tendon damage can hide the tell-tale tiredness of myasthenia and delay the right tests.
pmc-13287617:
Yara Walid and co-authors tested oat compounds in 2026 in young female rats made to show a polycystic ovary pattern by a hormone-blocking drug given for 21 days. Oat extract rich in avenanthramides was given at two doses for two weeks, beside a grape compound used as a comparison.

Both oat doses and the comparison treatment brought hormone levels back toward normal. A fat-based inflammation signal in blood and ovaries fell sharply. Higher-dose oat extract restored normal ovary and womb structure under the microscope. No harm appeared in liver tissue. The authors read the effect as direct blocking of one inflammation enzyme pathway and propose oat compounds for further study.
pmc-13288717:
Vincent de Paul Djientcheu and co-authors report the first seventeen kidney transplants performed in Cameroon in a 2026 preliminary account from Yaounde General Hospital. The series, also a first for Central Africa, included nine women and eight men, and every donor was a family member.

Chronic glomerulonephritis led the causes of kidney failure, followed by high blood pressure damage, with some cases of unknown origin. Matching ranged from identical tissue types, including one pair of twin sisters, to partly matched relatives. Two operations brought complications from surgical placement and a leaking connection, yet every recipient was alive afterward with stable kidney function and good quality of life, on standard immune-suppressing regimens.
pmc-13289017:
Csanad Gered and colleagues frame a 2026 trial plan in Hungary. The TITRANT trial deals with lung settings in surgery. It covers keyhole womb operations. Bad air settings can harm lungs. The trial tests two ways to set one key pressure.

The trial will enroll 200 adults in all. Three centers will host the work. Half will get pressure set by chest scans. The scans use a method called EIT. Half will get pressure set by lung stretch. The goal is less lung harm after surgery. Power of the air flow is a key idea. Lower power may mean gentler care.
pmc-13289217:
Emile Twagirumukiza and colleagues published a 2026 survey analysis on contraceptive use among married women in Rwanda. They drew on the 2019/2020 Demographic and Health Survey. The focus was whether schooling, work, say in household choices, and views on wife-beating relate to current contraceptive use.

The group studied 7401 married women aged 15 to 49 who had given birth in the prior five years, using logistic regression models. Use stood at 64.1 percent in the sample overall. Primary schooling, paid work, and stronger say in decisions each linked to higher odds of use. Having two or three living children showed the strongest link, while older age linked to lower odds. The authors argue that schooling, jobs, and voice at home should sit at the center of family planning plans.
pmc-13289317:
Daeun Shim and colleagues present a 2026 mouse study on timing T-cell activation around radiopharmaceutical therapy. That therapy sends radiation through the body to reach spread cancer, and it can also stir the tumor immune setting. Since immune cells in tumors are sensitive to radiation, order may decide whether combined care helps or hurts.

Tumor-bearing mice got naive or pre-activated tumor-specific CD8 T cells before or after treatment with a radioactive agent called 90Y-NM600. Growth slowed most when active cells were already present before radiation began. A prostate tumor model with vaccination before radiation showed the same pattern, with more memory-type killer cells inside tumors. Blocking type I interferon signals was also tested to probe how the benefit works.
pmc-13289417:
Michelle Mendiola Pla and colleagues report a 2026 trauma registry review on survival after penetrating heart injury at an urban Level 1 center. Such wounds kill often, yet which injury and arrival traits best predict survival stayed partly unclear. Records spanned 2017 to 2025 and captured body signs, wound type, and chambers hit for each case.

Among 18 041 trauma activations, only 57 patients had penetrating heart injury, and overall survival was 25 percent in that group. Gunshots caused 67 percent of wounds and carried higher death risk than stab wounds in the models. Injury to several chambers, chest vessel injury, and belly injury each tied to death. Breathing on one's own and signs of life on arrival strongly favored survival.
pmc-13290117:
Surgery notes at a tertiary hospital fell short of national standards, an audit by Ajay Kamat and colleagues shows, and a simple fix lifted them. The 2026 clinical audit compared orthopaedic operative notes against standards from the Royal College of Surgeons of England and the British Orthopaedic Association.

One hundred notes from early 2023 were scored first: patient identification appeared in 72%, intraoperative findings in 65%, the postoperative plan in 58%, and surgeon details in 70%. The department then introduced a standard note template plus staff training and re-audited another hundred notes. Every domain rose sharply, and overall adherence climbed from 68% to 95%. Kamat and colleagues recommend building note training into induction for rotating staff to hold the gains.
pmc-13290517:
A seed-oil regulator gains a partner in oilseed rape, Zhuang Li and colleagues show in a 2026 study of erucic acid production in Brassica napus. The transcription factor ABI5, known for holding back germination, also switches on the marker gene FAE1 and raises erucic acid levels in seeds.

The team showed that the two genes' activity overlaps in developing seeds and that ABI5 sits in the nucleus and can drive gene expression. The mediator subunit MED25 binds ABI5 in living cells and in test-tube assays, and reporter and DNA-binding experiments place it inside the circuit that controls FAE1. Plants overexpressing ABI5 made more FAE1 transcript and more erucic acid. Li and colleagues present the pair as a mechanism steering long-chain fatty acid build-up, of interest for oil quality and industrial uses.
pmc-13290617:
A bodyweight HIIT module designed for Chinese college students earns strong expert backing in a 2026 development and validation study by Wendi Cui and colleagues. Student fitness has been slipping, and short, equipment-free interval training is a practical answer, but no validated module existed for this group.

Working from 20 published studies, the team collected 48 candidate movements. Ten physical education teachers screened them for feasibility in a first Delphi round, and nine experts then scored what remained with content validity methods. Twelve movements survived screening and eight made the final module, from high knees and burpees to mountain climbers and push-ups. Expert agreement was high, with a scale-level validity index of 0.976. Cui and colleagues offer the module as a ready framework and a base for trials of its fitness effects.
pmc-13290717:
Thirty-five years of research on cervical cancer in women living with HIV are mapped by Lin Sui and Rutie Yin in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. The two pulled 6,137 publications from 1990 to 2025 across several databases and charted who publishes, who collaborates, and where the topics are heading.

Output rose steadily, led by the United States, with China, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and India behind. The International Journal of Cancer and AIDS stood out as the field's core outlets. Attention is now gathering around screening, HPV vaccination across the life course, and deep learning. The authors also foresee precision therapy guided by the tumor immune environment, plus screening that low-resource settings can actually run. They offer the map to policymakers pushing toward cervical cancer elimination.
pmc-13291717:
Zhiqian Yang and co-authors report 2026 laboratory work testing whether the antibiotic tigecycline can slow somatotroph pituitary tumors. They used the rat GH3 cell line, which models growth-hormone-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors. Cells received tigecycline doses from 6.25 to 100 micromolar, and the team tracked viability, spheroid growth, cell death, and hormone output.

Tigecycline curbed cell growth in a dose- and time-dependent way and also held back three-dimensional spheroid growth. Treated cells stalled in the G0/G1 phase, showed weaker Akt/mTOR signaling, and died through the intrinsic apoptosis pathway. The drug also cut growth hormone production inside the cells and its release outside them. The authors offer these findings as early support for testing tigecycline against this tumor type.
pmc-13292017:
Faridokht Salahshoori and co-authors appraise a 2026 review of clinical guidelines for telerehabilitation, the remote delivery of rehabilitation care. Guideline quality varies widely, which can ripple into care quality and policy. Searching six databases plus grey sources turned up 2,575 records, and two reviewers scored the qualifying documents with the AGREE II tool.

Only seven guidelines made the cut. The American Physical Therapy Association's 2024 guideline alone scored high across all six quality domains. Three others landed in the middle and were recommended with changes, while three rated low for weak methods and thin stakeholder input. The authors call for rigorous, inclusive, evidence-based guidelines so remote rehabilitation stays safe and effective worldwide.
pmc-13292317:
Tomohiro Yasuda and Takashi Suemasu survey a 2026 spintronics topic: making the ferrimagnet Mn4N hit magnetic compensation at room temperature by doping it with impurities. Mn4N needs no rare-earth elements, carries small magnetization near 100 kA per meter, and shows strong perpendicular anisotropy. Near compensation points, magnetization can flip and domain walls can race far faster than usual.

The review compares films doped with copper, silver, gold, and palladium against earlier nickel and chromium work, all grown on strontium titanate substrates. Results cover how each impurity shifts magnetization and angular momentum balance. The authors also present ultrathin platinum films, about 4 nm thick, grown on magnesium oxide for injecting spin current through the spin Hall effect. They frame the package as groundwork for fast spin-torque devices.
pmc-13293417:
Kristina M. Kokorelias and colleagues set out, in a 2026 protocol, a planned review of coronary artery disease and heart failure in older adults who have faced homelessness. This group faces more heart risk and poorer care access, yet pooled data on their heart burden are lacking.

The review will follow standard reporting guides and count how common these conditions are, plus related deaths, in adults aged 50 and older with a history of homelessness. The lower age cutoff reflects faster aging in this group. By pulling scattered studies together, the team hopes to guide care and policy for a group often missed by services.
pmc-13293917:
Yanqiu Li and colleagues report a 2026 case described as the first pairing of smoldering multiple myeloma with activated PI3K delta syndrome, a rare inherited immune disorder. The young patient had repeated lung infections, swollen lymph tissue, genital herpes, autoimmunity, and raised IgM and IgG. Gene sequencing found a heterozygous PIK3CD change, also confirmed in the patient's son.

Bone marrow sampling and serum immunofixation showed monoclonal plasma cell growth, supporting the myeloma precursor diagnosis. No targeted therapy was given. The authors urge early genetic testing when the immune syndrome is suspected, since prompt recognition can improve outlook and family screening.
pmc-13294217:
Tshepo A. Ntho and coauthors survey health science students on HIV prevention pills in 2026, surveying students at one school in Limpopo Province, South Africa. Pre-exposure prophylaxis prevents infection but uptake lags across the region. A structured questionnaire reached 350 students at one institution, with analysis in SPSS and significance set at p below 0.05.

Good knowledge appeared in 88.6% of students, positive attitudes in 79.7%, and strong intention to use or support the pills in 80.3% in the reported shares. Social media was the top awareness source. Gaps persisted on who qualifies and how often to dose, and nearly half worried about risk compensation. Older and senior students scored stronger.
pmc-13295117:
Jiaxuan Li and a large team pair a protein degrader with an approved drug against stubborn prostate cancer in a 2026 study. The PARP blocker olaparib helps only patients with BRCA gene faults, leaving most castration-resistant cases without that option. Forcing a BRCA-like state could widen its reach.

Data from 921 patients across six public sets flagged the regulator CDK9 as raised in advanced disease. The degrader D45 lowered repair gene activity, piled up DNA damage, and made cancer cells behave as if BRCA-faulty. Giving D45 before olaparib killed more cells, shrank mouse tumours, and held up in human tissue pieces, with bearable side effects.
pmc-13295517:
Dave Osinachukwu Duru and colleagues review diabetes drugs and shoulder tendon disease in a 2026 scoping article. GLP-1 receptor drugs are widely used for weight and blood sugar control, yet their effect on rotator cuff tears and repairs was unknown. Four databases were searched up to late January 2026.

Six studies qualified, four in people and two in controlled animal work. Human data covering well over a million patients found no extra complications after cuff repair among drug users. Users did show more spontaneous cuff tears needing repair, while animal work found stronger, tidier healing with one drug, prompting calls for careful prospective studies.
pmc-13295717:
Miguel A Rodríguez-Domínguez and colleagues sum up decades of saving two Canarian giant lizards in a 2026 article. Gallotia simonyi of El Hierro and Gallotia bravoana of La Gomera are both critically endangered. Outdoor breeding centres have run since the 1990s and 2000s, feeding reintroduction attempts at natural sites.

Breeding records from 2006 to 2024 cover eggs laid, incubation practice, and hatchlings raised each year. Both measures differed between the species and across years, while health checks found most animals in good shape. Wild groups survive and releases show partial success, with one islet population of the El Hierro species holding steady.
pmc-13295817:
Xing Liu, Li Li, and Huilin Wang study mindfulness and distress in college athlete-students in a 2026 survey. Balancing study with heavy training loads strains mental health in this group. Two inner resources, reframing thoughts and feeling full of life, were tested as bridges in the link.

Four hundred thirty students from five universities in Hunan Province answered the survey. Mindfulness tied to stronger reframing habits and greater vitality, and both resources tied to lower distress. Statistical checks with repeated sampling supported indirect paths running through each resource. The authors frame the results as groundwork for later trials rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13296017:
Alexey P. Ershov and co-authors sequence, in 2026, the genome of a salt-tolerant bacterium taken from a Kazakh oil reservoir. Strain G3 eats oil components and survives salty formation water, traits that could help squeeze more oil from ageing fields.

Its genome carries genes for making protective solutes against salt stress and for breaking down both straight-chain and ring-shaped oil compounds. Other genes support nitrogen handling and production of alginate, plus signs of soap-like substances that could displace oil. The authors present G3 as a hardy candidate for microbe-assisted oil recovery in salty reservoirs.
pmc-13302917:
One hotter tempering pass beats two for die steel wear, Weiwei Song and colleagues find in a 2026 study of H13 hot-work steel. Bars were quenched at a thousand degrees, then either tempered once at 520 degrees or twice at 580 degrees. Hardness and wear were measured at room temperature and again at 580 degrees, alongside the microstructure each route produced.

The single lower temper left fine, scattered carbides and the peak hardness, about 591 Vickers, and it won the wear tests at both temperatures. The double temper coarsened carbides, eased stress, and gained toughness, yet hardness slipped slightly and wear worsened. Die makers get a clear default recipe.
pmc-13303017:
Telling a harmless adrenal lump from cancer spread gets easier when two AI methods vote together, Shengnan Yin and colleagues report in a 2026 study. Scans from 390 patients at two hospitals trained and tested a system that outlines each lump on its own. One branch read the scans with a deep learning network; another grouped tumor zones and mined their texture patterns.

The joint model scored best on every test set, clearly ahead of each branch alone. Lipid-poor gland lumps can mimic cancer spread on normal reads, which is why a noninvasive second opinion matters. The authors offer the tool as support for treatment choices, not a replacement for clinical judgment.
pmc-13303317:
Protected forests in China bank substantially more carbon in their soils than unprotected ones, Yuxian Zhang and colleagues estimate in a 2026 spatial modeling study. Field soil measurements trained random forest models that projected organic carbon density at two depths from 2000 to 2100 under several climate pathways. Reserve boundaries let the team contrast matched forests inside and outside protection.

Protected topsoil held 45.5 percent more carbon on average, and the full meter profile 33.4 percent more. Low-emission futures kept those stocks stable or growing; high-emission paths drained them, deepest layers worst. Extending protection, the authors calculate, could add stocks worth tens of billions of dollars under plausible carbon prices.
pmc-13303717:
Ying Zhou Soo and co-authors study drug resistance in Malassezia yeasts in a 2026 laboratory report. These fat-loving yeasts live on skin and can cause infection, and azole creams are the usual first treatment despite frequent relapse.

Long exposure to clotrimazole, ketoconazole, or fluconazole was tested for spillover resistance to other antifungals, along with activity of two pump genes. Clotrimazole exposure raised resistance across drugs, and ketoconazole raised the doses needed for every drug tested even after the drug was removed. Knowing which first drug drives wider resistance can help clinicians choose treatments that preserve future options.
pmc-13304517:
Alexsa J. Zurowski and Eugene Y. H. Yeung build age-split drug response charts for meningitis germs in a 2026 lab study. Charts made only from adult data can overstate drug resistance in children and push needlessly broad treatment.

Susceptibility data came from a community lab on Vancouver Island covering 2023 and 2024. Most pneumococcus samples stayed sensitive to a main treatment drug under the meningitis cut point, with a few in the middle range. Response rates differed across three age groups for one drug family in gut germs. Local age-aware charts support leaner, targeted meningitis treatment.
pmc-13305317:
Arman Mahmood, Allen Mao, and Ibrahim Sacit Tuna report a 2026 case of a brain swelling syndrome returning in a teenager with cyclic vomiting syndrome. Repeated vomiting spells with high blood pressure mark her long history.

The 16-year-old had a scan-proven episode years earlier that reversed on follow-up images. During a later hospital stay with lasting post-surgery high pressure, scans again showed fluid swelling at the back of the brain and in the cerebellum. Other pressure causes were ruled out one by one. Blood pressure treatment and seizure prevention brought clear improvement in symptoms and scans.
pmc-13305417:
Edit Posta and colleagues review gut microbes across kingdoms in autoimmune disease in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Bacteria, fungi, and viruses in the gut jointly coach the immune system, and imbalance may help break self-tolerance.

Evidence is strongest for bacteria, while fungal and viral findings remain patchier and disease-specific. Routes include leaky gut lining, altered microbe chemicals, and proteins that mimic body tissue. Patterns are traced across arthritis, lupus, Sjögren's syndrome, scleroderma, spine arthritis, vessel inflammation, and muscle disease. Diet choices plus microbe-based add-on treatments for restoring balance close the review.
pmc-13305917:
Dek Kahin Yosef surveyed households in Burao, Somaliland, in a 2026 study of diarrhoea and home conditions. Fieldwork from June to August 2025 visited 422 homes chosen through staged sampling across the city.

Questionnaires and direct checks covered water, toilets, handwashing and waste, alongside illness in the prior two weeks. Household prevalence was 7.1% in the reported figure, even though most homes used tap water, private flush toilets and handwashing stations. Missing soap at washing points emerged as the strongest linked factor, underlining a simple gap behind wider sanitation gains. The team says soap at washing points is a cheap first fix for homes.
pmc-13306117:
Sayuri Mori described a 2026 case of overactive thyroid caused by a newly found inherited receptor change. A 75-year-old woman with twenty years of goitre and mild overactivity arrived with full thyrotoxicosis, yet antibody tests for autoimmune disease were negative.

Potassium iodide alone failed, and radioactive iodine triggered severe gland breakdown with worsening hormone surge and heart failure in the reported course. Drug control and later full gland removal restored normal function, and tissue showed a benign overgrowth pattern. Blood gene testing then found a fresh change, written as D633N, in the TSH receptor gene.
pmc-13306417:
Antonio Rocca built a computer generator for fake earthquake shaking records in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Real strong-motion records stay scarce for very large and near-fault quakes, which weakens building checks and hazard estimates.

Signals are split into seven wavelet bands, each judged by its own critic inside a conditional adversarial network, with energy-based weights favouring low bands that carry most power. Earthquake magnitude guides generation toward chosen hazard cases. The authors argue the wavelet route captures physical and statistical traits of real records better than older frequency splits.
pmc-13308317:
Carina Brito and co-authors test in 2026 a nose given vaccine made of Toxoplasma gondii membrane proteins plus a CpG booster in mice, against acute infection. No vaccine yet guards people from this widespread parasite, which can harm unborn babies and people with weak defences most.

Dosed mice raised blood and gut antibodies and grew memory T cells that made a key defence signal in the lab. Gene tools named the proteins that drew the strongest response from the mix used here. After live challenge, dosed mice held far fewer parasites in belly fluid, spleen, and lungs than sham dosed mice. The mucosal route merits more work toward a human guard.
pmc-13308917:
Abdillahi Ahmed, Tara Hajarat, and Anil Sharma report in 2026 an incidental neuroendocrine tumour in the end of the small bowel, found on a check up colonoscopy. The patient, a woman aged 48 years with no symptoms, had a past large bowel growth cut out three years before this check.

The scope found a lone 6 millimetre bump whose skirt of folds fanned out like a sunflower on the screen. Biopsy showed a slow grade tumour that had pierced the gut lining, so endoscopic removal was set aside for that day. Robot aided surgery took out a 7 millimetre tumour with one spread lymph node in the specimen. Small bowel tumours of this kind spread to nodes often.
pmc-13309517:
Victorien De Meyer and colleagues test how well climate models copy intense low-pressure storms over North America in a 2026 study. Such storms drive much mid-latitude weather and many extremes. Checking model skill storm by storm is hard with older tracking methods.

A new grid-based method picks the strongest low at each place and sums its local life in three parts: depth, mean, and change. The team applied it to 27 global models plus one regional model for the years 1980 to 2014. Models shared set biases in the air around strong storms, and finer grids helped most near storm tracks and coasts. The authors offer the method as a sharper check on model storm skill.
pmc-13309617:
Vahidullah Tac and co-authors show a generative computer system designing new burgers in a 2026 study. Food choices shape both personal health and planet health, yet tasty, nourishing, and light-impact foods are hard to design at once. The system learned taste patterns from large sets of human-written recipes.

Without direct teaching, the system recreated the classic Big Mac, then made new burgers tuned for taste, low impact, or nutrition. In a blind tasting with 101 people at a restaurant, its tasty burgers matched or beat the classic on liking, flavor, and texture. A mushroom burger cut impact sharply, and a bean burger scored near double on nutrition. The authors frame the method as principled food design.
pmc-13311217:
Alessandra Sborgia and colleagues share 2026 two-year results for the MINI WELL lens, a non-diffractive lens placed in both eyes during cataract surgery. The lens aims to give clear sight at far, middle, and near range.

Twenty-three patients with 46 treated eyes were followed for 24 months at one center. Sight stayed steady at all ranges, and all patients reached 20/32 or better for far sight without glasses. Reading charts, contrast tests, and patient questionnaires were used to check daily function and safety. The results support the lens as a lasting option, though the group was small.
pmc-13311617:
Yoshino Kinjo and co-authors set out a 2026 registry protocol, OKINAWA-HF, on how heart failure drug therapy is used in real hospital care in Okinawa, Japan. Trial proof for these drugs is strong, but daily practice often falls short.

Seven teaching hospitals will pool records of patients admitted with new or worsening heart failure. The registry logs patient traits, lab results, and drugs at discharge to see who reaches guideline targets and what blocks the rest. Outcome tracking after discharge and AI measures from scans are secondary parts. The design aims to show where guideline care breaks down in practice.
pmc-13311817:
Hui Chen and co-authors present the 2026 analysis of tooth decay burden among women of childbearing age worldwide from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2040. Decay in this group affects both mothers and their children.

Global Burden of Disease 2021 data supplied case counts, prevalence, and disability years. In 2021 decay caused about 817.5 million new cases and 688,430 disability years in this group worldwide. South Asia held the highest counts. Incidence rates rose over the three decades while disability rates eased slightly. Forecasts see incidence climbing 2.83 percent by 2040, pressing hardest in lower-income regions. The authors frame the work as planning evidence for health systems.
pmc-13311917:
Nicholas Barron and co-authors describe their 2026 student-led pathology elective at an osteopathic medical school that lacked a pathology department. Few schools offer such early exposure, and specialty interest suffers for it.

The elective ran eight sessions in 2025: seven sign-out sessions at the microscope plus one grossing workshop, each mixing solo slide review with expert-led teaching, in person and by video. Twenty-three learners joined at least one session. Most starters had never handled a gross specimen nor sat in on a sign-out. Among paired replies, confidence rose by over a point on a five-point scale, and most said the course reshaped their view of pathology.
pmc-13312017:
Vladyslava Storozhuk and colleagues report a 2026 survey of blood parasites and bacteria in rodents living in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone in Ukraine. The zone, closed off after the 1986 reactor disaster, now serves as a long-term site for studying how radiation affects wildlife. The team examined 116 rodents from three species between 2019 and 2020.

Blood films and DNA tests found Trypanosoma and Hepatozoon parasites along with several kinds of bacteria. The team recorded Trypanosoma grosi in a striped field mouse for the first time in Ukraine, and found the zoonotic bacterium Bartonella grahamii among six Bartonella types. Some animals carried several infections at once. The authors call for wider testing, including for viruses, to judge how contamination shapes infections in the zone's wildlife.
pmc-13312217:
Erwin J.A.T. Mattijssen and Wim Kerkhoff compile a 2026 Interpol review of forensic firearm examination, surveying research published from 2022 through 2024. Firearm examiners compare bullets, cartridge cases, and weapons to link evidence with crimes, and these periodic reviews gather the field's recent progress for practitioners worldwide.

The authors searched the main forensic journals, including the AFTE Journal, Forensic Science International, the Journal of Forensic Sciences, and Science and Justice, among others. Their review organizes what those outlets published on firearm examination across the three-year window. It gives examiners and laboratory managers a single entry point to methods, validation work, and case experience reported in the period. Such stock-taking helps the discipline spot shared problems and decide where standards and training should move next.
pmc-13312917:
Nicola Graham and colleagues trace, in a 2026 study, how the heart-building factor GATA4 directs two of its target genes across species from frog to human. GATA4 is a master switch of heart development acting through downstream genes, only some of which were known, so the team hunted for targets that heart-forming signals also control.

Working first in frog embryo tissue primed to form heart, they identified TBX2 and PRDM1 as GATA4-dependent targets, one switched on and one held down. Disturbing either one disrupts heart formation in frog embryos. The same relationship held in human stem cell-derived heart muscle cells: without GATA4, TBX2 fell, PRDM1 rose, and cardiogenesis failed, with most cells drifting to other fates. Breaking TBX2 alone produced oversized, maladaptive-looking heart cells. The authors frame the trio as a conserved control circuit for making cardiomyocytes.
pmc-13313017:
Veronica Iuliano and colleagues survey, in a 2026 review, newly invented macrocycles, the ring-shaped host molecules at the heart of supramolecular chemistry. Their hollow, enzyme-like cavities grip guest molecules through many weak contacts at once, giving binding strength and selectivity chemists prize. Each generation of rings has widened what hosts can do.

The review recalls how calixarenes, resorcinarenes, and cucurbiturils dominated from 1980 to 2000. It then traces the 2008 arrival of pillararenes, rigid pillars rather than cones, which sparked a wave of deep-cavity cousins with names like biphenarenes, saucerarenes, pagodarenes, and prismarenes. The authors follow these hosts from synthesis into working functions, noting the field has moved far past model studies into environmental and other applications. Their survey maps how inventing a new ring geometry keeps opening fresh recognition chemistry.
pmc-13314617:
Jacintha Tieskens and co-workers set out a plan to add personal factors to global function guides for autism and ADHD, in a protocol published in 2026. Both states are common and shape daily life, yet diagnosis alone misses their variety and the strengths many people show.

The World Health Organization ICF frame reads function as a dance between a person and their setting. Tailored core sets exist for autism and ADHD, but one piece, personal factors such as coping style and life history, was left out. The protocol lays out how the team will extend those sets to cover that missing piece. A fuller frame could help services plan support around the whole person, not just a label, in clinics and schools alike.
pmc-13315117:
Tamer Abusido and co-workers report a rare lung development disease that showed late in a baby girl, in a case study published in 2026. Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misaligned lung veins blocks normal lung vessel growth and brings severe lung hypertension that shrugs off therapy.

Most babies sicken in the first days of life, but this girl arrived at 7 months with growing breath distress and severe lung hypertension of no clear cause. Heart imaging and lab tests found no answer, as the report relates. Support care and vessel-widening drugs failed to hold her, and she kept worsening. Late forms are often misread, which delays the true call until decline is fast. The case presses teams to weigh this rare disease when baby lung hypertension defies all standard care.
pmc-13316017:
S Raquel Ramos and a large team evaluated in 2026 a web-based virtual world program. It teaches heart and metabolic disease prevention to people living with HIV, who face higher risk than others. The LEARN trial used a waitlist-control design after interviews and beta testing with 25 people.

In the trial phase, 40 participants got the virtual program and 38 waited as controls, assigned by block randomization. Main outcomes were feasibility, judged by recruitment and retention, and acceptability, judged by engagement levels. Early effect sizes on knowledge and behavior were also examined. A game-like setting may reach learners that leaflets miss.
pmc-13316217:
Zenouska Ramchunder and a large team studied in 2026 fat-processing enzymes tied to sphingolipids in Friedreich's ataxia, hunting for new treatment targets. The inherited disease stems from a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene that lowers frataxin, harming mitochondria and driving cell death, with only one approved treatment available.

Sphingolipids increasingly link to nerve degeneration, and the team found their handling enzymes disturbed across several disease models. Adjusting those enzymes in cell and animal tests changed disease features, suggesting sphingolipid pathways can be targeted. Broader symptoms beyond nerve outcomes may also benefit.
pmc-13316417:
Kristen E Kahler and two colleagues ran a 2026 feeding trial at Kansas State University on whether a liquid mix of live microbes helps feedlot lambs grow and stay healthy. Seventy-two young crossbred lambs ate a rich grain diet for 63 days, half getting a daily oral dose.

Growth, feed intake, and feed efficiency did not differ between groups, and stool scores improved with time in both. Blood values shifted over the trial in both groups, with calcium tending lower in dosed lambs. Gut microbe groups in feces did shift with treatment for several types. The results suggest the product changed gut life more than body growth, a useful caution for producers weighing its cost.
pmc-13316517:
Sang-Hyeon Mun and Cheol-Sang Hwang share a 2026 protocol for finding a hormone parent protein, POMC, stuck in the wrong cell compartment. When its entry tag stays uncut, the protein piles up in the cell fluid instead of moving through the secretory path, a fault tied to stress and cell death.

The method first builds and checks an antibody that spots only the uncut tag form. Gentle digitonin treatment then frees the cell fluid while keeping organelles shut, and a stronger detergent opens the rest for comparison. Blotting and pull-down steps reveal the stuck protein, shown in human kidney-derived cells and adaptable to mouse brain cells. The recipe helps labs study protein traffic faults in disease.
pmc-13316617:
Ghada M Salum and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether the enzyme MMP-9 can help grade fatty liver disease and artery hardening without biopsies or scans. The enzyme reshapes tissue scaffolding in both conditions, which often travel together.

The study enrolled 88 people: 25 healthy controls and 63 patients with liver fat grades from mild to severe, plus four artery stages. MMP-9 levels rose with worse liver grades and with artery progression, and they tracked several standard scoring systems, most neatly the BAAT score. One striking scan result rested on just two patients with advanced plaque, which the authors flag as fragile. Paired with BAAT, MMP-9 may sharpen early risk checks.
pmc-13317317:
Woohyok Chang and colleagues report 2026 real-world results for faricimab eye injections in Asian patients starting treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of central sight loss in older adults. Their clinic sits in South Korea, and patients had never been treated before.

Eighty-eight eyes were tracked after four monthly starter doses, then spaced by disease activity. By week twenty, reading scores gained 7.1 letters on average and retinal swelling shrank sharply, with fluid nearly cleared in most eyes. By week sixty, over half the eyes stretched to sixteen-week gaps. Safety held up across a wider set of 168 eyes, with rare mild inflammation and no severe infection reported.
pmc-13317417:
Niroj Mali and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether calcium readings in waste fluid can stand in for blood readings. The setting is continuous kidney therapy with citrate, the standard way to stop the filter clotting. Blood draws after the filter are the gold standard but cost blood and time.

From June to November 2024 at West China Hospital, 36 critically ill patients gave 216 paired samples. Waste fluid and blood calcium tracked each other moderately, with a correlation of 0.551 in the paired set, and average values sat close. Agreement was fair in the first day yet faded by two to three days, and values swung mostly within patients over time. Waste readings may guide early care, not replace blood checks.
pmc-13319017:
Nicoletta Guaragnella and colleagues review, in 2026, mitochondria as the middle point of talk between cell compartments, from yeast to humans. Mitochondria sense and relay stress signals across the cell. One route, the retrograde pathway, runs from mitochondria through cytosol to the nucleus. It rewires metabolism when mitochondria falter.

Physical contact sites also carry the conversation. Membranes where mitochondria meet the endoplasmic reticulum control calcium flow. Calcium acts as both stress sensor and messenger there. In yeast, a tethering complex called ERMES shows the conserved design. Faulty mitochondria distort these contacts, and distorted contacts worsen stress responses. Links to nerve degeneration and cancer are discussed. The authors flag shared control points as possible drug targets.
pmc-13319917:
Liang Li and co-authors compare two jaw growths on three dimensional scans in a 2026 study to help tell them apart before surgery. One growth can act in a pushy way and return, while the other is a fluid filled cyst, yet they can look alike on scans. Shape traits from auto outlining software were set next to traits read by eye specialists.

Scans covered 151 cases of the first growth and 164 of the cyst type. The first growth ran larger in size and length and more often showed wavy edges, sideways bulge, shell break, root wear, and tooth shift. Size also linked to shell break in cysts but not in the first growth. The traits give surgeons firmer clues before they cut.
pmc-13320017:
Christopher Yu and co-authors measure heart and vessel illness in lymphoma survivors in a 2026 study from Ontario, Canada. Heart illness is a top cause of sickness after this blood cancer, yet fresh counts of its size next to peers without cancer were lacking. Records for adults treated from 2007 to 2018 were matched one to one with cancer free peers by age and sex.

Among 36334 survivors, the rate of hospital care for heart illness ran well above peers, at a level much like that tied to high blood pressure. Risk peaked in the first year after diagnosis and stayed high for at least ten years. The raw gap in risk at five years also grew wider across the study years, which backs early heart watch for survivors.
pmc-13320317:
Daniele Vitale and co-authors study gut made acids as messengers between liver and bone marrow in a 2026 mouse study. Liver strain reshapes immune replies, and past work showed that waking bone marrow seed cells boosts liver immune watch and trims tumors, but only when the waking lasts. Short waking alone fell short in the new tests, which pushed the team to hunt for the signal.

A diet rich in cholesterol and one bile acid jointly woke the seed cells and raised one bile acid sharply in blood. A drug that blocks bile acid uptake in the gut restored balance, lowered that acid, and calmed both seed cell waking and liver swelling. Bile acids thus carry a liver to marrow call with weight for fatty liver and cancer care.
pmc-13320417:
Peter Pütz and co-authors present a merged data set for tracking COVID waves in Germany from 2022 to 2024 in a 2026 data article. Sewage tests can flag virus spread even when clinic counts lag or shrink, but their worth shows best next to case based counts. Weekly sewage virus loads were lined up with four case gauges drawn from alert systems, self reports, and doctor visits.

The set spans 131 straight weeks from July 2022 to December 2024, with all gauges set to the same Monday start weeks. Sewage values sum samples from the prior Thursday to the current Wednesday and are weighted by people served. Notes on time joins and data shape help users weigh how sewage and case signals track, lead, or lag each other.
pmc-13320517:
Charlotte Hardy writes a 2026 letter about a Danish pilot study of the ReSPECT emergency care plan form. ReSPECT forms record what a patient wants if urgent care is suddenly needed, and Hardy leads a UK project on such planning in intensive care. Her letter welcomes the Danish work and draws lessons for British practice.

She praises testing across intensive care, palliative care, and general practice with doctors and patients, which mirrors real use. Six of 15 patients in the pilot, or 40 percent, had never before talked about their care wishes. Hardy also flags points that need fuller debate, including how the form compares with narrower do-not-resuscitate talks and other planning choices.
pmc-13320717:
Aleksandra Synowiec leads a 2026 study of how a common cold coronavirus infects the human gut. Human coronavirus 229E is usually viewed as an airway germ, yet gut illness during the COVID-19 pandemic raised wider questions. The team grew gut tissue from patients, called enteroids, and tested infection across ages and temperatures.

The virus grew well at cooler airway-like temperatures at every age. At core body temperature, growth was largely limited to fetal and child tissue, while adult gut tissue resisted it. The gut may thus act as a sheltered site for infection early in life. The model also gives drug teams a human tissue test bed for future treatments.
pmc-13321617:
Tobias Stumpf and colleagues link back muscle traits and bone texture to spine fractures in a 2026 scan study. Fracture prediction in osteoporosis is still weak, and muscle traits are left out of standard tools. Data came from the AGES-Reykjavik cohort, with CT scans of the first two lumbar vertebrae in 486 women and 340 men.

Fifty measures covered bone density, inner bone texture, and muscle size, density, and fat, beside age and body mass. Step by step models narrowed those measures to test how well each set separated people with existing fractures, 96 women and 78 men in the group. The work checks whether muscle and texture add signal beyond density alone.
pmc-13323017:
Nemanja Maletin and colleagues survey painkiller use in pregnancy among women in Serbia, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. An online questionnaire reached 538 women and covered habits before and during pregnancy plus a 19-item test of safety knowledge.

Just over half reported painkiller use during pregnancy, and half of those users took them in the first trimester. Paracetamol dominated, named by almost all users during pregnancy in the survey. A third of users took painkillers without asking a clinician first, and two thirds scored low on safety knowledge, with wide doubt about anti-inflammatory drugs. A health-professional background linked strongly to higher knowledge, pointing to a clear education gap.
pmc-13323317:
Tingting Hao, Yifan Li and Qingmei Zhang link sugar and fat measures to suspected early puberty in children with obesity, in a 2026 retrospective study. Their starting set held 100 hospitalised children at or above the 95th percentile for body mass index, treated between March 2022 and June 2025.

After exclusions, 95 children remained, with 27 classed as suspected early puberty by age-based rules and Tanner staging. That group showed higher glucose, insulin, insulin resistance, triglycerides, cholesterol measures, uric acid and bone age advance, with lower protective HDL cholesterol. Insulin resistance, triglycerides and uric acid stood as independent risk factors in adjusted models. The authors suggest metabolic checks in obesity clinics may flag early puberty risk.
pmc-13324317:
Jialin Liu and Siru Liu set out ethical rules for personal health language models, in a 2026 viewpoint. Consumer systems now answer symptom, medication and mental health questions. They also track self-management over time, usually with no clinician in the loop.

Six risk domains frame the analysis. These are privacy, accuracy, equity, transparency, human-AI interaction and regulation. Health literacy gaps and long data trails can amplify each risk. Persuasive chat design and split oversight add to the problem. Their governance plan turns four classic ethics principles into design controls. These include crisis safeguards, hallucination checks and role disclosure. Fine-grained consent, fairness audits and tiered certification complete the plan, plus post-launch safety reporting.
pmc-13325117:
Zhongyan Bao and colleagues study an egg yolk peptide that aids bone growth in zebrafish in a 2026 paper. The short peptide VPF, made of valine, proline, and phenylalanine, was screened for bone effects.

Doses from 0.2 to 10 micrograms per mL helped both normal fish and fish with a bone growth disorder. In the disorder model, 1 microgram per mL raised mineralization by 45.26 percent and swimming distance by 51.05 percent over controls. Computer docking placed VPF firmly on osteoprotegerin, a brake on bone-eating cells. Gene readouts confirmed more osteoprotegerin and less RANKL signaling. The peptide may suit functional foods aimed at bone health.
pmc-13325717: The Frontiers Editorial Office issued this 2026 item. It is only a retraction notice. It withdraws a commentary on the Sishen Pill and diarrhea tied to kidney Yang deficiency. The commentary dealt with gut microbes and the gut-kidney axis. The journal found an undisclosed conflict of interest. The editor who handled it was also an author of the article under discussion. That conflict undermined peer review. The chief executive editor approved the retraction under publication ethics guidance. The commentary authors did not answer the journal letters.
pmc-13326017:
Renjun Tu and colleagues uncover a backup adhesion circuit that guards fruit fly germline stem cells in a 2026 study. Stem cell niches must stay intact for years, yet the circuits that keep them sturdy are little known.

In the fly ovary, support cells use E-cadherin to hold N-cadherin down through Wnt signaling and the small RNA mir-994. Losing N-cadherin alone did nothing, but losing E-cadherin made it vital. When E-cadherin fell, N-cadherin rose and kept support cells alive with their long reaching arms. That rescue preserved the niche and stopped stem cell loss. A switch known for cell dispersal is here reused as a safety net.
pmc-13327717:
Dorthe Dalstrup Pauls and colleagues follow vulnerable children three years after a lifestyle camp in a 2026 study. Children aged 7 to 14 with overweight, obesity, or social difficulties attended a ten-week live-in program with many parts. Long-term results after such camps are rarely tracked.

The study enrolled 222 children, and 126 took part at three years, when most, 83 percent, still lived with overweight or obesity. Weight scores were lower than at the start, down from a BMI standard score of 2.48 to 2.00 on average, and quality of life stayed above starting levels. Girls regained some weight and body fat after treatment ended, while boys lost body fat, underlining the need for lasting support after camp.
pmc-13327917:
Maria M Della Rosa and colleagues test feed type against methane output in grazing dairy cows in a 2026 study. Seventy-two late-lactation cows on pasture received no concentrate or 5 kg a day of high-starch, high-fiber, or half-and-half concentrate at milking. Methane was tracked for 36 days with GreenFeed units, and collars logged eating behavior.

Daily methane output did not differ by diet, but milk output told another story. Corrected milk ran 16 percent higher in the mixed and starch groups than in unsupplemented cows, with fiber-fed cows in between. Methane per unit of milk therefore fell by 13 to 14 percent in those groups on their measures. Summer feeding can thus lift milk while trimming emission intensity.
pmc-13328117:
Andrew B Harvey and a large team chart a signaling protein in the developing heart in a 2026 study. CD109, a surface protein that tunes TGF-β signals, has surfaced in genome scans for coronary disease and in patients with congenital heart defects, yet its developmental role was unstudied. The team mapped its presence in mouse hearts and deleted it from vessel lining cells.

Cd109 showed strongly in coronary vessel lining and in valve tissue derived from the heart's inner lining, persisting across key stages. Silencing it in human lining cells disturbed vessel growth programs and tube building. Mice lacking it in those cells still formed hearts without overt flaws. Backup systems may cover its loss during development, the results suggest.
pmc-13328417:
Jie Yuan and co-authors grade cardiac rehabilitation videos on Chinese platforms in a 2026 content analysis. Short videos on Douyin and Bilibili now teach many heart patients, with uneven accuracy. Using heart recovery search terms, the team gathered 200 videos and scored them with three quality tools covering reliability and completeness.

Douyin clips ran shorter, newer, and drew more likes and comments, while Bilibili scored slightly higher on one benchmark. Hospital department uploads earned the top scores on all three tools, ahead of individual and other accounts. Patients should favor institutional sources, and platforms might label medical quality, the authors imply, since popularity clearly did not track trustworthiness.
pmc-13329517:
Youho Myong and colleagues gather views on brain-computer interfaces from people with high neck spinal cord injury in a 2026 study. Four people with chronic injury at level C4 or above joined a structured group talk led by rehab and engineering experts. Surveys before and after captured hopes, worries, and openness to the technology.

Five themes stood out: digital access, offline physical activity, social and mental health, ease of use, and acceptance. Participants wanted help with messaging, banking, web use, and home controls, plus less reliance on carers. Many accepted training and some accepted surgery, yet safety, upkeep, and reliability worried them. After discussion, openness to implants rose while outcome hopes grew more realistic. Lived experience should guide design, the authors argue.
pmc-13331117:
Bronwyn K Brew and colleagues link mother asthma in pregnancy to child asthma in Australia and Sweden in a 2026 study. Register cohorts held 35,194 mothers with asthma in New South Wales and 102,248 in Sweden. Monthly flare and inhaled steroid records ran from a year before pregnancy to a year after birth.

Steroid use held steady in pregnancy, then fell after birth while oral steroid use rose in the reported patterns. Child asthma risk ran higher after mother flares and after steroid use in adjusted models for both countries. Yet father exposure links and sibling checks pointed to hidden family traits as the true driver. Asthma control in pregnancy stays a priority, the authors stress.
pmc-13333317:
Wan Dalila Wan Chik and co-authors release a whole-genome resequencing dataset in 2026 for an advanced Malaysian rice line called NMR191 and the parent variety it came from. The mutant, bred by ion beam irradiation from Pongsu Seribu 2, combines resistance to blast disease with early maturity, traits tropical growers need as the climate shifts.

Sequencing on an Illumina NovaSeq X platform at roughly 30 times coverage produced 24.8 GB of clean data for the mutant and 28.6 GB for the parent. Reads were aligned to the Indica reference genome and mined for single-letter changes and small insertions and deletions across the genome. Raw reads sit openly in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive. The authors offer the paired genomes as a resource for variant hunting, comparative genomics, and future rice breeding and mutation research.
pmc-13333517:
Suleiman Abuhasanein maps living cancer medicines for bladder cancer in a 2026 review. The treatments are built from bacteria, viruses, and microbiome material rather than chemicals. Bladder cancer recurs, and options thin out fast once standard therapies fail. Living agents that can hunt, stimulate, and deliver inside the tumor attract interest.

The review sorts the field into five mechanisms. First, bacteria colonize tumors and destroy them, starving and bursting cancer cells. Second, the agents activate immunity, innate and adaptive. Third, engineered microbes deliver payloads inside tumors. Fourth, oncolytic viruses lyse cancer cells while priming immunity. Fifth, microbiome effects modulate how patients answer other treatments. Translation runs furthest for immune approaches, led by BCG and viral platforms in BCG-unresponsive disease, though studies stay small and follow-up short. Abuhasanein weighs delivery barriers, immune neutralization, and safety and regulation hurdles. He calls the bladder's access a real advantage.
pmc-13334317:
Atreyee Majumder and Lisa Dwyer Orr measured racial and ethnic gaps in bladder cancer care among Medicare patients in a cross-sectional study published in 2026. Bladder cancer survival differs by race, and the authors traced where care diverges from diagnosis onward.

Medicare fee-for-service claims from 2021 and 2022 identified 136,172 patients with newly diagnosed bladder cancer. Most were White, with Black, Hispanic, Asian or Pacific Islander, and American Indian or Alaska Native groups also represented. Rates of diagnosis and of receiving any treatment ran below 1.0 for every minority group relative to White patients. Hispanic and Black patients also reached specialists less often, with rate ratios of 0.891 and 0.930 respectively in the study. Timing from diagnosis to referral and treatment was compared as well.
pmc-13334817:
D. Ng and co-authors scoped the real-world data sources available for cancer research in Japan in a 2026 review. Cancer is Japan's leading cause of death, and demand for real-world evidence to guide care and policy keeps growing.

Searches of PubMed, Ichushi-Web, and Google Scholar covered studies from January 2020 to February 2025. Of 484 screened, 121 retrospective studies using ready-made databases qualified. Administrative claims supplied 52 percent, registries 44 percent, and electronic health record data just 6 percent. Each source showed trade-offs: claims lacked clinical depth, registries held rich genomic detail but much missing clinical data. The review maps what each source can and cannot support, helping researchers pick the right database before designing a study.
pmc-13334917:
A Thiebaut and co-authors measured the genetics of baboon facial shape in a 2026 quantitative study that challenges a classic trait used in fossil interpretation. The anteorbital drop, the profile of the nasal ridge, helps paleontologists sort baboons, macaques, and their relatives.

The team devised a way to quantify the trait, then modeled facial variation in a pedigreed, captive colony of 934 baboons at the Southwest National Primate Research Center. The colony included animals admixed from two Papio species. Their first hypothesis, that the trait varies little within a population, failed: the colony spanned variation seen across whole genera. The trait proved highly heritable, supporting part of the second hypothesis. The results warn fossil researchers that this convenient character is genetically lively and variable.
pmc-13335317:
Jian Zhao and co-authors tackled a production problem for heart cell therapy in a 2026 stem cell study. Cardiomyocytes grown from induced pluripotent stem cells promise heart failure treatment, but expanding them in bulk with a growth drug can push them into senescence and weaken grafts.

Cells were produced by a standard protocol or expanded with the GSK3β inhibitor CHIR99021, then transplanted into rats after heart attack to compare engraftment. A PAPD5 inhibitor, BCH001, was used to hold senescence back in expanded cells. Lab assays covered adhesion, protein markers, gene activity, and mitochondria alongside the animal grafts. The design asks whether high-yield manufacturing can keep cells young enough to repair heart muscle, a practical question for any future clinical supply chain.
pmc-13336817:
Bingzheng An and co-authors pinpoint a lysosome attack route against advanced prostate cancer in a 2026 study. The plant compound aloperine disables a helper protein, HSPA8, which normally feeds worn proteins into the lysosome for disposal. With that route blocked, a pump part called ATP6V1A piles up and over-acidifies the lysosome.

Swollen, leaking lysosomes then kill the cancer cells from inside. Cells try to survive by making more cholesterol to patch expanding membranes. Blocking that backup plan with the drug AY9944 made the pair far more deadly together. Hitting this axis could offer a new option where standard prostate cancer drugs have failed.
pmc-13337117:
Qiaoyu Gao and co-authors build a proton relay that makes reactive oxygen from plain air with no energy input in a 2026 study. Turning oxygen into singlet oxygen under neutral conditions suits green oxidation, but the proton-coupled steps crawl. Their interface joins molybdenum sulfide with copper chloride into a relay microenvironment.

Sulfur sites short on electrons store protons, which travel through copper-sulfur-molybdenum channels to activate oxygen sitting on electron-rich copper. The relay speeds the key step while keeping bonds intact, favoring singlet oxygen output. The system removed pollutants quantitatively and ran over 16 h in a pilot membrane filter in the reported trial. Self-driven catalysis could clean water without power-hungry inputs.
pmc-13337417:
Yu-Long Zhao and colleagues compare two feeding tubes for stroke patients who cannot swallow safely in a 2026 study at Taizhou People's Hospital. From 208 patients with moderate-to-severe swallowing trouble, 148 qualified for intermittent oro-esophageal feeding by a screening scale. Of those staying at least 28 days, 64 used a standard nasogastric tube and 60 used the intermittent tube.

The intermittent group improved swallowing more and gained more on daily feeding scores. By day 28 their blood albumin and total fluid intake ran higher, comfort was better, and tube slips and aspiration were less frequent in the reported comparisons. The screening scale helped choose who should start on which method, a practical aid for stroke wards.
pmc-13337717:
Suad M. Aladwani reports a 2026 campus survey in Kuwait on contact with environmental toxins. The cross-sectional study at Sabah Al-Salem University covered what people said they were exposed to, what they knew, and what steps they took to protect themselves.

Answers came from 1,110 participants across food and water, home and work, and daily habits. Perceived exposure ran highest for food and water, where 15.7 percent fell in the high group in the reported scoring. Other domains scored far lower on that measure. Tests compared groups by background factors and modeled who reported moderate to high exposure, giving campus health planners a map of awareness gaps.
pmc-13337817:
Yuyi Sun, Xiaodi Wang, and Xuefeng Wei test an explainable AI tutor for opera singing students in a 2026 study. Bel canto learners face heavy mental load when singing in several languages while shaping body expression. Their system was built to show its reasoning, not just give answers.

Sixty-four conservatory students studied Italian, German, and French works for 16 weeks in two groups. One used the explainable scaffold and one used standard AI help. Measures came from load questionnaires, expert scores, body tracking, and gaze recording. The scaffold group cut mental load by 38.9 percent in the reported results, well above the comparison group, and body expression scores rose sharply.
pmc-13338417:
Arthur H. Owora, Bowen Jiang, and Yash Shah test an asthma risk marker inside health records in a 2026 pilot trial. Preschool wheeze often fades, so spotting children headed for lasting asthma is hard. A machine learning marker using routine data promised better sorting.

Indiana pediatricians judged ten standard child cases drawn from records covering birth to age 3. Cases were children later diagnosed between ages 6 and 11. Half the design tested doctors with and without marker access in a four-group layout. Accuracy of forecasts was the main outcome, with ease of use and acceptance also rated. The pilot checks whether record-based risk scores change doctor judgment.
pmc-13341417:
Raised amylase after ERCP in children is explored in a 2026 pilot study by Xueqi Wang and colleagues. The single-center project covered 24 successful therapeutic ERCP procedures in patients under 18 with blocked bile or pancreatic ducts, between January 2024 and December 2025.

The enzyme rise without new pain occurred in 8 of 24 procedures, or 33.3%. Affected children started with higher inflammatory and liver markers and had longer, harder procedures with more accidental pancreatic duct entries and contrast injections. Their stool microbes showed lower diversity, more Enterococcus, and less Bifidobacterium. The authors treat these as candidate signals needing validation in larger groups.
pmc-13341517:
Specific self-harm acts connect to specific thinking skills in a 2026 network study by Yang He and colleagues. Surveys from 1,300 Chinese adolescents measured inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory alongside 12 self-injury behaviors, then mapped partial correlations between them.

Inhibitory control linked most strongly to punching walls or objects, working memory to biting oneself, and flexibility to pinching oneself. Scratching oneself sat at the network's center, while punching served as a key bridge between skill and behavior clusters. A fine-grained map like this could help clinicians match support to the exact behaviors an adolescent shows.
pmc-13345917:
Olivier Gemin and a large team present EasyGrid in 2026, a robot platform that automates cryo-electron microscopy sample making. Freezing biological samples into flawless thin ice remains the bottleneck of the field, and EasyGrid chains plasma cleaning, microfluidic dispensing, blot-free spreading, jet freezing, and light-based quality checks into one modular run.

Test runs prepared grids for several purified complexes. Their structures then resolved cleanly. Large mammalian cells froze more evenly than with hand plunging. Automation turns grid making from craft luck into a tunable, repeatable process, letting labs optimize systematically and push throughput for both loose-particle and in-cell imaging work.
pmc-13346117:
Caroline Hookway and a large team present a stem cell system, writing in 2026, for watching how epithelial cells change into a more mobile mesenchymal state. Human induced pluripotent stem cells were grown as flat two-dimensional colonies and as hollow three-dimensional forms called lumenoids, giving two views inside one setup.

Fixed and live imaging tracked cell movement, marker proteins, cell junctions, and contact with the basement membrane after the change was triggered. Movement began later in the three-dimensional cultures, and that delay was tied in a measurable way to how intact the membrane stayed. Shared data and tools are offered so other groups can compare results on the same basis.
pmc-13348017:
Mireille Gagnon-Roy and co-authors ask how people recovering from traumatic brain injury feel about receiving minimal cognitive assistance, help deliberately kept light so the person does as much as possible themselves. Their 2026 qualitative study follows five community-dwelling adults with moderate to severe injuries through a meal preparation task.

Participants took part in an evaluation, a guided cooking session using tailored minimal assistance, and an interview reviewing video of themselves. Overall they appreciated the help: it let them plan and carry out the task more efficiently, safely, and successfully. They valued being given time to think and try things alone, and the sense of independence that brought, while fuller help arrived when truly needed. At times, though, assistance felt intrusive or unhelpful. The authors conclude support must be tuned to each person's emotional response, and that personalisation should guide future assistive technologies.
pmc-13349917:
Yunyueng Jang and colleagues measured how two new bird flu viruses behave in chickens and ducks in a 2026 animal study in South Korea. The H5N6 virus arrived during the 2023-2024 winter, and a novel H5N3 type appeared in wild birds in late 2024.

Both viruses killed chickens fast, at about 2.6 and 2.2 days on average, at the same lethal dose. The H5N6 virus passed to every contact chicken, while H5N3 spread to none, likely because birds died too quickly. Ducks infected with H5N6 showed clear breathing signs. Knowing which new strains spread, and in which birds, shapes farm control measures.
pmc-13350017:
Jiawei Song and colleagues described a prenatal case in 2026 with two chromosome faults at once. One was the missing segment behind cri-du-chat syndrome. The other was a large extra stretch of chromosome 18. Single-fault cases dominate the literature. This pairing had not been well documented.

Ultrasound raised the alarm by finding several structural problems. Chromosome scanning plus family testing pinned down the molecular cause. Fetuses with an added duplication tend to show heavier malformations. They are also more wide-ranging than the classic syndrome alone. The authors discuss how such findings guide counselling. No shared care standard exists for these rare combined cases.
pmc-13350317:
Haoyi Zhang and colleagues reviewed suppressor immune cells in colorectal cancer in a 2026 article. These myeloid-derived suppressor cells blunt the killer cells that immunotherapy tries to unleash, one reason checkpoint drugs help few bowel cancer patients, especially the common stable subtype.

Tumour genetics, gut microbes, inflammation, metabolic stress, and treatment itself all expand these cells. Beyond blocking immunity, they feed blood vessel growth, break barriers, remodel tissue, and prepare sites for spread. Firming up how to define and count them in people is a key hurdle. The review argues they are a central target for making immunotherapy work in this cancer.
pmc-13351817:
Daniel O. Akanji, Krishnanand N. Kaipa, and Cong Wei present a 2026 control framework for tracking drifting patches on water with a self-driving marine vehicle. Patches move with shifting currents, and doubt about their edges grows over time. Each patch is drawn as a polygon whose corners move through estimated flow while carrying their own uncertainty values.

A flow-aware controller adjusts forward speed to ride helpful currents, and fresh sightings of a patch edge are merged to shrink doubt. Analysis shows doubt stays bounded if each patch is revisited within a set time limit. Tests replayed currents recorded by radar in the San Francisco Bay region and showed the expected sawtooth pattern of doubt rising, then falling at each visit.
pmc-13353217:
Samuel Pis-Vigil and co-authors present nVenn2, a faster tool for near-proportional Venn diagrams, in 2026. Proportional diagrams size each region by shared element counts, but region counts explode as sets grow, making large diagrams unreadable. The new version takes a more flexible route that trims diagram complexity.

Run time now grows mainly with the count of non-empty regions rather than the count of sets. When many combinations are empty, readable diagrams with many sets become practical. The tool is free as a standalone program, a web page, an R package called nVennR2, and a Python package called nVennPy. Every interface lets users restyle the finished diagram.
pmc-13354217: Timothy R Huerta leads a 2026 author correction notice for an article on building a research-oriented learning healthcare system across covered entities, first published online on 16 December 2025. The notice fixes a single name error: co-author Tyler Gorham had been misprinted as Tyler Gorman in the original article. The item itself is only an author correction notice, so its full content is that one corrected spelling and the citation of the article it amends.
pmc-13355717:
Andrea E Dillinger and co-authors tested gene therapy in 2026 in mice that lack norrin, a signal needed to grow blood vessels in the retina. Without it, mice and humans develop poor retinal vessels and blindness, as in Norrie disease. The team injected two virus types carrying the norrin gene into the eyes of young mice.

Both virus types fully restored capillary growth in the retina, kept its barrier sound, and rescued vision in the mutant mice. In a model of oxygen injury like that seen in premature babies, the therapy cut vessel loss and harmful new growth. The authors see promise for Norrie disease and related eye conditions.
pmc-13356617:
Christian L Bailey-Burke and co-authors ran a 2026 cost study on adding an immune drug before surgery for advanced skin cancer of the head and neck. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is common in older Americans, and advanced cases need combined care. Giving cemiplimab before wide removal surgery has shown better tumor response, but its value for money was unknown.

Their model, run over ten years, found the added drug cost about nineteen thousand dollars less per patient while giving slightly more quality-adjusted life years. Results hinged most on time frame and quality-of-life weights. The authors call the approach promising but say real long-term costs and outcomes need study.
pmc-13356917:
Rushikesh Wayal and co-authors surveyed 276 people in North Maharashtra in 2026 on what they know and think about dental implants. Implants have changed how missing teeth are replaced, improving looks, chewing, and stability, but use depends on public awareness. A twenty-question survey covered awareness, facts, attitudes, willingness, and barriers.

Awareness was moderate overall. Women scored slightly higher than men, and scores rose steeply with education and income: postgraduates scored more than double those with no formal schooling. Awareness linked strongly with knowledge and positive attitudes. The authors call for public education and better patient counseling to widen fair access to implant care.
pmc-13358517:
Ning Li and co-authors present a 2026 study on teaching computers to outline thyroid nodules on CT scans. Drawing these outlines by hand is slow and varies from doctor to doctor, yet clean outlines are the first step for scan-based diagnosis. The team built a deep-learning model that draws the outline on its own.

They trained and tested the model on CT scans from 500 patients with proven thyroid nodules, half harmless and half cancerous. The design pays close attention to ragged edges, where hand-drawn outlines often go wrong. A fast, steady tool like this could save doctors time and make later scan analysis more reliable.
pmc-13358617:
Chengfu Xian and co-authors test a bold step in lung transplant care in a 2026 study. After a transplant, patients usually stay on a breathing machine in intensive care. The team instead kept some patients awake on a heart-lung support machine, called ECMO, and removed the breathing tube while still in the operating room.

They compared 44 such patients with matched patients who followed the older paths, waking either with or without the support machine. Vital signs at the end of surgery were much the same across groups. Showing the awake path is workable could shorten machine time and intensive care stays for well-chosen patients.
pmc-13359817:
Riffat Munir and co-authors evaluate a COVID-19 testing system in a 2026 study. As the coronavirus kept evolving, tests had to stay sensitive while also flagging which variant a patient carried. The team paired an automated extraction kit with an assay that detects the virus and screens its mutations, and put the pair through laboratory checks in South Africa.

They tested 220 samples, including leftover nose swabs from several pandemic waves, from the wild type through Omicron, plus reference materials and lab-grown virus dilutions. Results were compared with the standard tests used for routine diagnosis. Solid performance across variants supports using the system for both patient care and variant tracking.
pmc-13360417:
Hruy Menghesha led a 2026 study of a robot-guided tool for checking lung spots deep in the chest. The tool steers a thin scope through the airways using shape sensing, aiming at small spots that are hard to reach. The team reviewed all cases at one center from August 2024 to March 2026. They left out cases done without cone-beam CT guidance or done only to place markers.

For each case the team recorded patient details and spot traits such as size and density. They then looked for which traits lined up with a firm diagnosis from the biopsy. Knowing the signs of success helps doctors pick which patients this costly tool will help most. It also guides how to plan each procedure for the best chance of an answer.
pmc-13360617:
Laura Johana González Zazueta led a 2026 scoping review of how clinical foundation models are tested. These large AI models read free-text medical notes to help with reasoning, writing documents, and pulling out facts. Yet the ways they are graded vary widely and lack shared standards. That gap is a risk when hospitals put the models to work on real records.

The review followed standard scoping methods and flow charts for study choice. From 448 records found, 16 met the bar for a close read. The authors mapped how each framework grades skill, clinical value, safety, and how well results carry to new settings. They also flag where the checks fall short. The map can guide safer, more uniform testing before these models spread in care.
pmc-13360917:
Stephanie Lim and Byron Martina wrote a 2026 review on how virus vaccines are built and tested. A good vaccine must teach the immune system to protect, and tests in animals must predict what happens in people. That prediction often fails, so the authors map the immune steps that matter. They cover first-response defenses, antibody making, and the memory cells that stand guard for years.

The review sorts lab test results into types: those with a direct human match, stand-in measures, and comparison tools. It also lists common reasons vaccines fail in human trials after passing animal tests. Flu and COVID-19 vaccines serve as worked examples. The authors aim to help designers choose animal models and measures that truly bridge to human results, cutting late and costly failures.
pmc-13362717:
Leon Smółka and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on the gut-kidney axis in kidney transplant care. A transplant gives the best life for people whose kidneys have failed, yet grafts still wear out early for many. The review weighs how gut microbes and the chemicals they make may sway immune tolerance, infection risk, drug handling, and heart risk after transplant.

Gut microbe balance shifts from kidney disease itself and from post-transplant drugs, infections, and diet. Microbe products such as short-chain fatty acids and uremic toxins link in studies to graft trouble, diarrhea, and uneven drug levels. The authors judge these signals promising as risk markers, but stress that most findings still need solid proof before they guide care.
pmc-13363117:
Elia Giacomo Galli and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a glioblastoma that spread through the coverings of the brain with rare speed. Glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumor, usually stays local, so spread along the dura, the tough outer lining, is uncommon.
