Their patient had the IDH-wildtype, grade 4 form with giant cells, and received maximal surgery plus the standard drug and radiation course.

Within three months, scans showed thick, wide dural growth far from the first site, with the dural tail sign often seen in slower tumors. Tissue checks confirmed direct tumor invasion, with a very high growth index. The authors review how such spread may occur and urge close watch of the whole neuraxis in similar high-risk cases.
pmc-13363617:
Lina Fan and colleagues present a 2026 review on blueberries as a food-based support for children's brain and emotional health. Rates of attention, mood, and learning disorders in childhood are climbing, and diet strategies that calm brain swelling and cell stress draw interest. The review gathers work from 2016 to 2025 on blueberry compounds, above all their purple anthocyanin pigments, and what they do in the gut and brain.

The compounds seem to tune gut microbes, ease brain swelling through a protective pathway, and support memory wiring. Small trials in healthy children report modest gains in mood, word memory, and focus. Trials in diagnosed children are still rare, and the pigments are fragile and poorly absorbed, so the authors call for solid trials and smarter food design.
pmc-13364617:
Jinwei Ma and co-workers build a 2026 light model to guess soil wetness for smart watering on low cost field gear. Big models need big data and strong chips. Their plan splits the wetness line into water cycles, pulls time traits, and feeds them to a lean filter that updates step by step.

A slide window lets the model drop old cycles and learn fresh ones as field states shift. Test scores match heavy models at a small share of the compute cost. The fit suits cheap edge boxes that must run all day in far fields on tight power.
pmc-13373217:
Chambers and colleagues discover a two-protein switch that turns on bacterial immune defenses when DNA is damaged, in 2026 microbiology research. Bacteria arm against invading viruses with immune operons, gene clusters that can kill the host cell to stop an infection spreading, so these weapons need off-switches. Upstream of many operons sit two proteins the team names CapK, a kinase, and CapS, a repressor that blocks the operon's transcription by binding DNA as a dimer.

Single-stranded DNA, a byproduct of DNA repair, directly activates CapK. The kinase phosphorylates CapS, breaking its dimer apart so it falls off the DNA and the immune genes switch on. The same protein pair appears inside an anti-phage toxin-antitoxin system, where DNA damage unleashes a nuclease toxin. Chambers argues the kinase-repressor module is a reusable plug-in for stress control, letting diverse bacterial defenses share one damage sensor.
pmc-13374017:
Aida Rebollar-Zepeda and co-authors dug into a math flaw in solution sums in a 2026 study. Lab sums often pair a bath model with gas-phase heat terms. For steps where molecule counts change, like two parts that join, the gas terms do not cancel out.

A plain test of one liquid's self-join showed the flaw in raw form. The join was a win on the core sums, yet the end sum still read as a loss, much like a gas. Checks on water and a wash fluid groups showed the same false fee. The team traces the root and gives a fix, so joined forms are not wrongly taxed.
pmc-13375017:
Kelvin Mupunga and co-authors pooled trials of a vein mineral for fast heart flutter in a 2026 review. The flutter is the most common heart pace ill in old age. The mineral is often added to pace drugs, but past pools split on if it truly helps.

Six trials with 480 patients set the mineral next to a sham drip. A fresh trial was new since the last pools, which spurred the redo. Pooled math weighed pace and rhythm gains in non-surgery adults. A firm read could end years of ward habit split, and guide when the cheap drip is worth its slot in fast care.
pmc-13377417:
Zhou and colleagues build a single-cell atlas of pig development, mapping gene use cell by cell across five tissues, before and after birth, in 2026 livestock research. The atlas profiles 252,033 cells and nuclei, resolving 83 cell types, using single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing. A view of tissue growth was missing for livestock, despite pigs' importance to farming and their closeness to humans as a biomedical model for growth and disease.

Tissues changed in coordinated waves, as stem and progenitor cells multiplied, committed to lineages, and matured into cell types. Immune cells followed a conserved two-branch pattern across the tissues. Combining the atlas with population data pinpointed a muscle enhancer of the MYOT gene that breeding selection targeted, driving divergence in meat quality between Asian and European pig breeds. A cross-species comparison with humans revealed cell types. Zhou offers the atlas as infrastructure for precision breeding.
pmc-13379317:
Lin Lin and a large team describe a 2026 biohybrid robot for delivering chemotherapy inside the bladder. Drugs washed into the bladder often fail to reach tumours well or pass through tissue. Their robot is built from algae fitted with magnetic material and loaded with a cancer drug.

Magnets steer the robots, and a computer system using live images guides them on its own. Swarms of robots can change shape, and flowing fluid helps push the drug deep into tissue. In mice with bladder tumours, the method delivered far more drug than a standard wash and shrank tumour burden greatly. The work points toward more precise bladder treatment.
pmc-13379717:
Muhammad A Zahid and colleagues present a 2026 review of cancers of the nose and sinuses that had grown into the eye socket. Such cancers are uncommon and often found late, because they grow deep in the face and cause vague early symptoms. Growth into the orbit changes how the disease is staged and treated.

The team reviewed records at a major hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, for patients treated from April 2022 to March 2026 whose scans showed spread into the eye socket. They recorded patient details, cancer type, patterns of invasion, and treatments given. The analysis looks for links between those features. The goal is to guide planning for a difficult group of patients.
pmc-13383017:
Arezoo Dehghan and colleagues search heart valve tissue for hard-to-grow microbes in patients with valve infection in Tehran in 2026 work. Standard blood tests miss some causes of infective endocarditis, a life-threatening heart infection. The team tested samples from 232 patients who had valve replacement surgery between 2021 and 2025.

DNA tests found Brucella species most often, followed by the Q fever microbe, Bartonella, and the Whipple disease microbe. Breathlessness linked to several of these infections, while fever and sweating linked to Brucella. The authors argue that tissue DNA testing should play a larger role when blood cultures stay negative.
pmc-13383217:
Azusa Yamazaki and co-authors show how high lipoprotein(a) levels distort a common cholesterol test in 2026 work. Standard LDL cholesterol assays rely on density separation, and a protein part of lipoprotein(a) can shift where particles settle. The team compared routine assay results with a chromatography method across 1,560 human samples.

Routine values ran higher than the reference method as lipoprotein(a) rose, and the gap grew clearly above a set level. A formula-based VLDL estimate moved the opposite way with rising levels. The authors conclude that density-based assays overstate LDL cholesterol when lipoprotein(a) is high, a caution for labs and clinicians reading results.
pmc-13384517:
Snehalakshmi Kavacheri Subramaniam and colleagues review links between sugar tagging of proteins and cell aging in lung disease in a 2026 article. Cell aging drives lasting inflammation and poor repair in chronic lung conditions. In parallel, faulty fucosylation, the adding of fucose sugar tags, alters airway surface and immune signals.

One enzyme, FUT8, adds core tags that can amplify pathways known to start and sustain cell aging. Those same pathways feed scarring in diseases like COPD, asthma, and pulmonary fibrosis. The authors propose the fucosylation-aging axis as a source of new markers and drug targets for these hard-to-treat diseases.
pmc-13386717:
Arda Toptaş, Onur Koç, and Semih Demirci link poor sleep before tooth extraction to harder recovery in a 2026 study. Records covered 111 adults aged 18 to 65 treated at Hacettepe University in Turkey. A standard sleep scale split patients into disturbed and sound sleep groups before surgery.

On the first day after extraction, the poor-sleep group reported stronger pain and greater emotional impact scores. Daily activity limits were also higher, and satisfaction with pain control ran lower in that group. Side effects like nausea and dizziness did not differ, which focuses attention on sleep as a recovery factor.
pmc-13389617:
Kristine Gvinepadze and Marika Toidze describe, in 2026, a 67-year-old woman whose systemic sclerosis appeared together with two rare problems. Systemic sclerosis, also called scleroderma, scars tissue and harms small blood vessels across the gut, skin, heart, eyes, kidneys, and lungs.

The woman tested negative for the usual specific antibodies yet developed autoimmune wasting of the stomach lining and a sudden blockage of the retinal artery. She showed large-cell anaemia even though her blood vitamin B12 level was normal, a pattern the authors link to early loss of stomach cells that make intrinsic factor. Clinicians gain a warning to watch stomach and eye complications in this disease, even when antibody tests come back negative.
pmc-13392517:
Zhao Ge and eight co-authors review coronary microvascular dysfunction, a fault in the heart's smallest vessels that can starve heart muscle of blood even when the large arteries stay open. The condition is common in people whose angiograms show no major blockage, yet it raises the risk of later heart events. Its causes remain only partly mapped.

Diagnosis mixes noninvasive scans with invasive tests done during catheter procedures, and no drug yet targets the faulty vessels directly. Much of the review follows one signalling route involving neuregulin-1 and its ErbB receptors, which touches vessel lining health, oxidative stress, scar-like remodelling, and new vessel growth. Studies of traditional Chinese medicine that may act on the same route are covered too, as a possible path toward combined, patient-matched care.
pmc-13392617:
Tosin T Fakiyesi leads a group reviewing how heart damage from anthracycline chemotherapy might be caught earlier, before it hardens into heart failure. These drugs remain central to treating many cancers, but injury can force dose cuts or early stops that weaken cancer control. Damage tends to grow quietly from cell injury to a weakening heart pump.

Older watch methods, above all the ejection fraction measure of pumping strength, often flag trouble only after it turns hard to reverse. The review weighs scans, magnetic resonance imaging, and blood markers of early injury, then turns to artificial intelligence tools and remote monitoring worn or used at home. The aim throughout is spotting risk sooner, while treatment changes can still protect both heart and cancer outcomes.
pmc-13392917:
EFSA's Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed weighed a licence renewal for zinc chelate of amino acids hydrate. The additive supplies zinc to all farm species in a form bound to amino acids. Maker Zinpro Animal Nutrition sought the renewal, and the panel checked company data showing the marketed product still matches its licence conditions. No new evidence emerged to disturb earlier safety findings.

The panel held that the additive remains safe for target animals and for consumers. For handlers it counts as an eye irritant and a skin and airway sensitiser, so contact by any route should be kept low. One question stayed open: the panel could not conclude on environmental safety, deferring to a forthcoming opinion on trace elements that will apply directly here. Efficacy required no fresh assessment for renewal.
pmc-13394017:
Hannah Jackson, Luke Grzeskowiak, Joanne Enticott, Sarah Wise, and Emily Callander examined who receives subsidised anti-nausea medicines in pregnancy under Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, and whether access tilts by wealth. Linked programme data covered nearly three hundred thousand pregnancies in Queensland from 2013 to 2018. Three antiemetics were tracked, including ondansetron, whose pregnancy use is off-label and unsubsidised, by area disadvantage level.

Off-label ondansetron swallowed the majority of public spending on these drugs in pregnancy, ahead of metoclopramide. Use of all three ran highest among women in the poorest areas and fell steadily toward the richest. Access showed a small pro-poor tilt. Spending showed a moderate one, since richer women's use costs the scheme less. The authors frame the pattern as an equity question for pharmaceutical policy on off-label prescribing.
pmc-13395417:
Yuan Wei and colleagues model, in 2026, how blue honeysuckle branches shake when a harvest machine vibrates them. Shaking must throw fruit off, yet trunks and roots soak up much of the energy. The team simplified a fruit branch to a Y shape and wrote its motion maths. Bench models and real branch tests followed.

When the shake runs near a branch's own pitch and angle, unstable parametric shaking can erupt. That wild motion boosts the force on fruit. Computer models and branch tests matched the maths on peak swing across pitches. The authors offer the model as a design base for honeysuckle harvesters. Right tuning could raise fruit drop and save effort.
pmc-13396217:
Fan and co-authors monitor, in 2026, an enzyme molecule at work by listening to its electrical conductance. Their subject is cytochrome P450 1A1, a liver enzyme that processes benzo[a]pyrene, a carcinogen in smoke and grilled food, through rival detox and activation routes. Trapping one enzyme in a scanning tunneling microscope junction, they recorded the signal in real time as the reaction reshaped the protein's helices and flipped the redox state of its heme center.

The signal fell as benzo[a]pyrene concentration rose, a negative correlation strong enough to build a kinetic model yielding a Michaelis constant between 24.2 and 43.2 micromolar. The recordings resolved four signal states, which the team matched to reaction intermediates by feeding metabolic intermediates as substrates. One signal peak rose about fivefold when the cofactor NADPH was added, then dropped by 60 percent when both NADPH and the carcinogen were present, illustrating the method's sensitivity.
pmc-13396317:
XiaoPeng Niu and co-authors review nano-biopesticides, crop sprays shrunk to the nanoscale, with a focus on one way of making them called nanosuspension. Their 2026 review starts from a familiar problem: heavy pesticide use breeds resistant pests, pollutes land and water, and harms health.

Nanosuspensions grind or build active ingredients into tiny particles held in liquid, which can make them dissolve better, last longer on the leaf, and release slowly. Some products instead use nanomaterials that kill pests on their own. The authors survey preparation methods and the tests used to check particle size and stability, and cover packaging designs that keep such products usable in the field.
pmc-13397517:
Published in 2026 with no byline shown, the study tracks lawsuits over body contouring surgery across 45 years in the United States. Operations such as tummy tucks and liposuction rank among the most done cosmetic procedures, with about 170,000 tummy tucks in 2024 alone. Infections, fluid build-up, poor scars and unhappy results often end up argued in court.

Cases were pulled from the Westlaw legal database for the years 1980 to 2025, keeping only suits where a doctor who did the procedure was the defendant. The review compares what sparked each claim, how cases ended and which problems arose. It also contrasts plastic surgeons with doctors from other fields who offer the same operations.
pmc-13397617:
Tracey Pérez Koehlmoos and colleagues report the fourth annual workshop on fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, held in Washington, DC on 17 September 2025. Published in 2026, the summary centres on conditions that occur alongside these disorders. Alcohol exposure before birth can shape development, behaviour and learning across a whole life, and ranks among the top preventable causes of disability in the United States.

Nearly 100 people from universities, clinics, federal agencies and advocacy groups shared findings from a four-year federally funded initiative. Talks covered prevention, screening, diagnosis, family support and care inside the military health system, which serves about 9.6 million people. Lessons from military families may also guide better civilian care.
pmc-13398517:
Hutchinson and co-authors revisit, in 2026, how the giant Late Triassic predator Postosuchus kirkpatricki actually moved, using three-dimensional musculoskeletal modeling of this crocodile-line archosaur from North America. Whether it walked on four legs or two, and whether it stood flat-footed or on its toes, has been disputed for decades. The team rebuilt its pelvic limb muscles digitally and compared joint ranges under competing anatomical arrangements.

Their reconstruction gives Postosuchus hindlimb musculature roughly three times as massive, relative to size, as a similar-sized Nile crocodile's. The main tail-driven thigh muscle was smaller than expected, though, because the animal's tail was gracile. An earlier collated dataset had estimated an 85 to 100 percent probability of bipedalism from body proportions and center-of-mass position, theirs sitting about 78 percent of femur length ahead of the hips. Weighing everything, the authors conclude the evidence genuinely conflicts, leaving posture unresolved.
pmc-13398617:
Yanqiu Zou and colleagues ask whether good sleep habits shield people with type 2 diabetes from vessel damage. Their 2026 UK Biobank study follows 12,456 participants with diabetes, scoring sleep on duration, body clock, insomnia, snoring and daytime sleepiness. Over 13.5 years of follow-up, 1,878 large-vessel and 3,066 small-vessel complications were recorded in the cohort.

Those scoring 4 to 5 healthy traits had lower large-vessel risk than those scoring 0 to 1, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.75 in the comparison given. Small-vessel risk also dipped, driven by nerve damage rates, while stroke showed no clear link. Blood markers partly carried the effect, and the authors probe whether diabetes severity changes the protection.
pmc-13400517:
Pushpa Narayanaswami leads a team measuring, in 2026, how generalized myasthenia gravis affects daily life in the United States beyond clinic scores. The disease weakens muscles and can disrupt work, money, sleep and family roles. Caregivers share much of that burden, so both groups were asked directly.

Interviews first produced 25 specific impacts grouped into eight life areas. A separate survey of 239 patients and 81 caregivers then rated each one. Work, planning and independence, finances, physical limits and sleep scored highest for patients. Caregivers ranked finances and sleep at the top too. The authors argue that judging a treatment value should count these lived effects, not only medical outcomes.
pmc-13400617:
Hesham Haffez and co-authors probe, in 2026, how diabetes and abnormal sperm measures combine to damage male fertility. Diabetes is rising worldwide and harms reproductive function, yet its added effect in men who already have poor semen quality was little studied. Cell death pathways in sperm were a focus.

Thirty-nine men were grouped by diabetes status and semen quality, then tested for hormones, sugar control, sperm movement and shape, plus death markers. Diabetic men had worse sugar control, higher pituitary hormones and lower testosterone. Men with both diabetes and abnormal semen fared worst, with the slowest sperm and the highest early cell death rates. Protein tests showed the internal death pathway switched on only in that combined group.
pmc-13400717:
Leah Leslie Dias and co-authors follow, in 2026, how memory, exploration and anxiety change across the rat lifespan. Aging alters sensory, emotional and social systems, but which behaviors shift and which hold steady needs careful testing. Two standard tasks were used: recognizing a new object, and exploring an open arena.

Rats aged six, twelve and twenty-four months, spanning early adulthood to old age, were tracked by automated video. Recognition memory dipped only slightly in middle age and stayed largely intact even in old animals. Anxiety-like behavior did not differ by age. Rearing and exploration, however, declined with age, which the authors read as a locomotor and curiosity change rather than a memory failure.
pmc-13401317:
Maria Fueth and colleagues present a 2026 case report of cutaneous angiosarcoma, a rare blood-vessel cancer of the skin, in a woman whose extreme obesity blocked standard cancer care. She weighed about 280 kilograms, with a body mass index above 100, and had stage IV lymphedema in both legs.

Ricardo argues that rent rises as farming is pushed onto poorer land, while wages and profit pull against each other. His best-known idea, comparative advantage, shows how two nations both gain when each makes what it makes best. The reasoning is dry and tight, and it still drives debate on trade.
robinson-merlin-1917:

russell-finished-mystery-vol7-1917:

russell-political-ideals-1917:

Russell argues that institutions should be judged by whether they free or stifle creative impulse. He sketches reforms in government, property, and education aimed at growth rather than obedience. sacconi-summa-de-catharis-1717:

Sacconi maps the Cathar churches of Italy and France, their bishops, their rite of consolamentum, and their split over how the evil world was made. He counts their numbers and names their houses with an ex-member's exactness. His aim was to arm preachers against them, yet his facts outlived his cause. Scholars still start with Sacconi for what the Cathars actually taught.
simmel-grundfragen-der-soziologie-1917:

His answer: sociology studies the forms of human association, the patterns by which people join, rule, compete, and cooperate. The same forms, the dyad, the triad, the stranger, recur in churches, armies, and markets alike. Content changes; the geometry of relations endures. The book is the Berlin master's late, brief statement of his life's theme. It remains the clearest short door into Simmel's work, the place where society's geometry is traced in a few bold lines.

He finds company towns run like feudal estates: scrip pay, cheated weights, and guards against organizers. A mine disaster turns his education into action, and he joins the strike he came to observe. Sinclair builds his case like a prosecutor. King Coal is his novel of the mine wars, still the fullest fictional record of them.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed names. It defines being associated with the networks to cover funding, planning, arming, and recruiting for them. States must file a written case when they propose a name. Lost passports must be voided fast and shared through Interpol. The expert Monitoring Team is extended for seventeen months.
un-sc-res-17: How far a UN probe's powers reach was tested in Security Council Resolution 17, passed on 10 February 1947. The team sent to study the Greek border fight had asked the Council a point of law. The team wished to ask the Greek state to hold back the death penalty for men judged for acts of state. Does its writ allow such a plea? The Council's answer is no. The team may plead a stay only where a man's words as a witness would aid its own work.
un-sc-res-1717: Resolution 1717 is a Security Council decision preserved in official-record form, transcribed for this collection by English Wikisource. The fifteen members act as one body in such texts, whatever their private disagreements. The entry preserves the public result of that process: a single document, numbered and complete, whose words carry the Council's authority.
un-sc-res-1817: Kept under the number 1817, a formal Security Council decision survives in this collection in official-record form. The transcription comes from English Wikisource. Inside, the members' findings come first, in the preamble's careful clauses; their decisions follow in numbered order. The entry's completeness lets any later reader test summaries against the source itself.
un-sc-res-1917:
Resolution 1917 recorded the Council's decision on Afghanistan, adopted on 22 March 2010. The London Conference that January had set fresh goals under Afghan leadership. A Kabul conference was planned for later in the year. Taliban and Al-Qaida attacks still threatened civilians, aid workers, and Afghan forces.

The Council extends the assistance mission, called UNAMA, until 23 March 2011. The mission leads the civilian aid effort and backs Afghan ownership of the recovery. It will help prepare the 2010 parliamentary polls and support Afghan-led peace talks. The text ties security, honest government, and growth together. It also presses for stronger regional cooperation and better protection of civilians.
un-sc-res-2017:
When the Council met on 31 October 2011, it adopted Resolution 2017 on Libya after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi, days after the civil war ended. Weapons from Libyan stockpiles were spreading across the region, and the Council feared they would reach armed groups.

The text calls on Libya's new leaders to secure all arms and guard them with care. It singles out shoulder-fired missiles that can bring down aircraft. It urges work with the global chemical weapons body to destroy Libya's chemical stocks. A sanctions panel must study the threat and propose ways to keep the weapons contained.
un-sc-res-217: Resolution 217 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1961. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-317: Catalogue data places Resolution 317, a United Nations Security Council text, in the year 1972. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-417:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 417 condemns South Africa's apartheid government for its violent crackdown on black citizens. The Council adopted the text on 31 October 1977. Reports told of torture of prisoners, deaths in detention, and bans on groups and newspapers.

The Council demands that the regime end its violence and free people jailed under security laws. It also demands an end to torture, to bans on the press, and to the Bantu education system. It asks governments to help victims, including students who fled the country. The Secretary-General had to report back by 17 February 1978.
un-sc-res-717:
Cambodia's settlement gained a United Nations advance team in October 1991. The Paris framework of August 1990 had been endorsed by resolution 668 (1990). Draft accords for a full settlement were now on the table. Prince Norodom Sihanouk had been elected chairman of the Supreme National Council. The Cambodian parties had declared a voluntary ceasefire and renounced foreign military aid.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 30 September 1991. It decided to set up, under its authority, a United Nations Advance Mission in Cambodia, UNAMIC. The mission would deploy as soon as the Paris accords were signed. Its first tasks were to help the parties keep the ceasefire and to start mine awareness work. The Supreme National Council and the Cambodian parties were called to cooperate with the mission in full. The Council welcomed the plan to reconvene the Paris Conference at ministerial level.
un-sc-res-817: Preserved as Resolution 817, this Security Council text carries a 1993 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The world court lost a senior judge in the summer of 1956. Judge Hsu Mo of China died on 28 June that year. His term on the bench still had years to run. Resolution 117, passed without a vote on 6 September 1956, set the way to fill his seat.

The Council chose the Assembly's next session for the vote. Judges there are picked by both big bodies at once. The eleventh session would host the ballot. Hsu Mo had served since the court's first days in 1946. He was a key figure in Chinese law. His death left one of the court's founding minds gone. The text is brief, a formal note of loss and a date for the cure.

Sierra Leone's peacekeeping mission gets only a few extra days in this brief text of 5 September 2000. UNAMSIL, the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, was backing a fragile peace process after years of civil war. In two short operative lines, the Council moved the mission's deadline to 20 September 2000. It also kept the country's situation under active review while it decided what should come next for the mission.

War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the setting for Resolution 1417, adopted on 14 June 2002. The UN Mission, MONUC, was still building toward its authorized strength. Killings and attacks in Kisangani in May had followed fighting there, and RCD-Goma held power in that city. The Inter-Congolese Dialogue at Sun City had made progress but produced no all-inclusive deal yet. Foreign forces were leaving, though slowly.

The Council extends MONUC until 30 June 2003 and calls on states to supply personnel up to the authorized 5,537. It holds RCD-Goma responsible for ending executions, rights abuses, and harassment in Kisangani and demands the city's demilitarization. It backs MONUC's work on disarming and sending home foreign fighters and its deployments to Kisangani and Kindu. It demands the total, speedy withdrawal of all foreign forces, with plans and timetables sent to MONUC. Reports are due at least every four months.

Cyprus's peacekeeping routine continued with Resolution 1517, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003. The Secretary-General reported on 12 November about the UN operation. He urged both sides to address the fate of missing persons urgently. Cyprus's government agreed the UN force should stay past December. Conditions on the island left little choice.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 June 2004. They demanded an end to all remaining restrictions on the force. Violations at Strovilia drew sharp concern. Turkish Cypriot forces had altered positions there since June 2000. The Council insisted the earlier military balance be restored. A report on implementation was due by 1 June 2004.

Resolution 1617 is a Security Council decision adopted on 29 July 2005. It renewed and tightened sanctions against Al-Qaida, the Taliban, and people and groups tied to them. It builds on the sanctions system first set up in resolution 1267 in 1999. That system was restated in several later resolutions.

Under its terms, all states must freeze the funds of listed persons. They must also bar their travel and block arms sales to them. The text spells out what counts as being associated with Al-Qaida or the Taliban. It asks states to give a statement of case when proposing names for the Consolidated List. It also extends the Monitoring Team that helps the sanctions committee, for seventeen more months.

A question from its own fact-finding commission in Greece is answered on 10 February 1947. The Commission of Investigation, created weeks earlier, had asked whether it could request Greece to postpone executions of people sentenced to death for political offences. The question reached the Council while the commission was working in the region.

The commission, the Council ruled, had no power to ask Greece, Albania, Bulgaria, or Yugoslavia to delay any execution. There was one narrow exception. If the commission had reason to believe that hearing a condemned person as a witness would help its inquiry, it could ask for a postponement on that ground alone. The Secretary-General was to pass this reading of the mandate to the commission.

Rwanda tribunal short-term judges are allowed to finish the cases they have begun, in this text of 13 October 2006. Eighteen ad litem judges had been elected in 2003 for four years ending in June 2007. Several were mid-trial in cases that would not end before their terms expired, and the Secretary-General had asked the Council to act.

The ad litem judges named in the text may keep serving past their terms until the cases they are assigned to are completed. One judge may also be assigned to a further case as needed. States are asked again to make sure their nationals serving as ad litem judges are released to sit for the tribunal, so its completion strategy is not held up by staffing gaps.

The chemical precursors that turn Afghan opium into heroin are targeted on 11 June 2008. Afghanistan's drug trade fed terrorism, organized crime, and money laundering. The key chemicals, above all acetic anhydride, are legal in normal trade but are smuggled into Afghanistan for drug making.

All states are called on to tighten cooperation against drug production and trafficking in Afghanistan, including stronger tracking of the world trade in precursor chemicals. Exporting states are urged to notify importing countries of every shipment of the relevant chemicals when asked, under the 1988 drug convention. The aim is to stop legal shipments being diverted into heroin production while keeping lawful trade moving.

Afghanistan's UN mission is renewed behind the London Conference agenda in Resolution 1917, adopted on 22 March 2010. The London Conference of 28 January 2010 had set priorities under Afghan ownership. A Kabul conference was planned for later in the year. Taliban and Al-Qaida violence, civilian casualties, and the narcotics trade remained severe.

The Council extends the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, until 23 March 2011. UNAMA and the Special Representative continue to lead the international civilian effort. They co-chair the Joint Coordination and Monitoring Board to align donor support with Afghan priorities. They improve civil-military coordination with ISAF. They give good offices for Afghan-led reconciliation and reintegration within the sanctions framework. They support preparations for the 2010 national legislative elections. UNAMA must also help the government prepare the Kabul conference and the transition toward Afghan leadership on security, governance, and development.

Weapons spilling out of Libya after its 2011 war are the worry in Resolution 2017, adopted on 31 October 2011. Arms of all kinds, above all shoulder-fired surface-to-air missiles, were spreading across the region. The Council feared they could fuel attacks by groups such as Al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb and unsettle the Sahel. Libya's chemical weapons stocks also still had to be destroyed.

The Council calls on Libya's authorities to stop the spread of arms, keep them in safe custody, and meet the country's arms control duties. It calls on Libya to keep working with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons to destroy its chemical stocks. States in the region are asked to weigh steps against this flow. The Libya sanctions committee, with its Panel of Experts, must judge the threats this spread poses and report with plans to counter it and guard stockpiles and borders.

Southern Rhodesia's white minority rulers declared independence from Britain on their own in November 1965. Britain, the ruling power, treated the move as an act of rebellion. The Council adopted Resolution 217 on 20 November 1965 to answer the declaration.

The Council condemned the seizure of power by a racist settler minority. It said the declaration of independence had no legal validity. Britain was called on to crush the rebellion and end the minority regime at once. All states were told not to recognize the illegal authority. They had to cut off arms and military supplies. Economic ties had to be broken as well, including an embargo on oil and petroleum products.

Israeli forces had seized Syrian and Lebanese soldiers and security staff on Lebanese territory on 21 June 1972. An earlier resolution, passed that June, had already pressed for their release, without result. The Council returned to the matter in Resolution 317, adopted on 21 July 1972.

The Council reaffirmed the June resolution. It deplored the fact that the captured men had still not been freed. Work by the Council's president and by the Secretary-General had not secured their release. Israel was called on to return the men without delay. The president and the Secretary-General were also asked to make fresh efforts. Their task was to see the resolution carried out at last.

South Africa's crackdown on apartheid's opponents is condemned in Resolution 417, adopted on 31 October 1977. The Council noted reports of torture of political prisoners, deaths of detainees, and a wave of bans on people, groups, and news outlets since 19 October 1977. It recalled its 1976 condemnation of killings of African protesters, including schoolchildren in Soweto.

The Council strongly condemns the regime's mass violence and states its solidarity with those fighting apartheid. It demands an end to violence and repression. It demands freedom for everyone jailed under security laws or for opposing apartheid. It also demands a halt to killings in detention and torture. It also demands that bans on anti-apartheid groups and media be lifted. It demands that the Bantu education system end. It demands that majority rule based on justice and equality replace apartheid and the bantustan policy.

Cambodia's peace settlement takes a step forward in Resolution 717, adopted in 1991. Draft agreements for a full settlement were ready, built on a framework the Council had backed in Resolution 668. The Supreme National Council of Cambodia had chosen Prince Norodom Sihanouk as its chairman, backed a voluntary ceasefire, and asked for UN staff to be sent quickly.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's plan and decides to set up a United Nations Advance Mission in Cambodia as soon as the settlement papers are signed. The mission's members are to head to Cambodia right after the signing. The Council calls on the Cambodian parties to work with the mission and welcomes the plan to reopen the Paris Conference so ministers can sign the agreements.

A new state from the former Yugoslavia sought a United Nations seat in 1993, but its name stood in the way. The applicant met the tests for membership set out in Article 4 of the Charter. A dispute had arisen over the state's name, and it had to be settled for the sake of calm in the region. Resolution 817 was adopted on 7 April 1993.

The Council recommended to the General Assembly that the state be admitted. Inside the United Nations, it would be referred to for the time being as "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia". That temporary name would hold for all United Nations purposes until the dispute was settled. The parties were urged to keep working with the co-chairmen of the peace conference on the former Yugoslavia. Their task was to reach a speedy settlement of the difference over the name.
wharton-summer-1917:
Edith Wharton published Summer in 1917, setting it in a poor Berkshire village she called North Dormer. Wharton usually wrote about rich New Yorkers. Here she turned to a young woman with almost nothing, and produced her boldest novel of female desire.

Charity Royall, adopted from a lawless mountain settlement, works in the village library and suffocates under her guardian's eye. A young architect, Lucius Harney, arrives to study old houses, and a summer love affair follows. Charity's awakening brings freedom and danger in equal parts, ending in pregnancy and hard choices. Wharton treats her heroine's longing without a hint of shame. The book shocked readers who expected safer fare from her.
whiston-astronomical-principles-religion:
William Whiston held Newton's chair at Cambridge and wrote on both science and faith. His Astronomical Principles of Religion came out in 1717. In it he read the Bible through the lens of the new astronomy of his day.

Whiston argued that a comet passing near Earth had caused the great Flood. He linked planets, comets, and scripture into one bold system of causes. The book mixes real skill in astronomy with deep trust in revealed truth. It shows an early clash, and an early truce, between Newton's cosmos and the Bible that shaped his age.
williams-al-que-quiere-1917:
William Carlos Williams was a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey, who wrote poems between house calls. Al Que Quiere, published in 1917, is the book where his own voice first comes through clearly. Its Spanish title means roughly 'to him who wants it,' and the full title carries an exclamation point. The poems turn away from fancy European models toward plain American speech.

Williams writes about local people, streets, flowers, and small daily scenes around him. He favors short lines, sharp images, and the rhythms of talk he heard every day. Some pieces are tender, others wry or blunt. The book laid the ground for his lifelong project: a poetry built from American things, seen up close.
woodward-piltdown-fourth-note-1917:
Arthur Smith Woodward, keeper at the British Museum, gave this fourth note on the Piltdown gravel in 1917. Grafton Elliot Smith adds a part on the brain cast of the find. Piltdown man was then held a true dawn man of England by its chief backers.

The note tells of a new find spot, with parts of a second skull of the same kind. That 'Piltdown II' skull seemed to prove the first was no freak or chance mix. In truth both were fraud, and the note shows the hoax at its most safe and sure hour.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol17:
Volume XVII of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1875, three years before Brigham Young's death. The stenographic record again holds his sermons beside those of his counsellors, the Twelve, and others. A church nearing thirty years in Utah speaks here with the weight of long habit.

Talks in this volume show leaders instructing a people many of whom were born into the faith. Doctrine is less argued than applied, fitted to farms, families, and towns. The year-by-year record gains value from such stretches, where the movement's settled voice can be heard plainly.
zimmermann-telegram-1917:
Arthur Zimmermann, Germany's foreign chief, sent his famed telegram in 1917. The secret offer invites Mexico to join a war on America. Texas and the Southwest are dangled as the prize for joining.

British codebreakers seize the message and pass it to Washington with care. American papers print it, and public fury sweeps the neutral nation. Within weeks, the United States declares war on Germany at last. One intercepted cable thus swings the whole Great War's balance. Few single messages in history have changed so much so fast for so many. Germany's bid for a second front collapsed the moment it leaked.
